The **Public Investment Fund** (**PIF**; Arabic: صندوق الاستثمارات العامة) is the [sovereign wealth fund](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sovereign_wealth_fund "Sovereign wealth fund") of [Saudi Arabia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saudi_Arabia "Saudi Arabia"). It is among the largest sovereign wealth funds in the world with total estimated assets of [US$](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_dollar "United States dollar")900 billion.[[2]](#cite_note-2) It was created in 1971 for the purpose of investing funds on behalf of the [government of Saudi Arabia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Government_of_Saudi_Arabia "Government of Saudi Arabia").[[3]](#cite_note-:0-3) The wealth fund has Crown Prince [Mohammed bin Salman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mohammed_bin_Salman "Mohammed bin Salman"), Saudi Arabia's *de facto* ruler since 2015, as its chairman.[[4]](#cite_note-:8-4)[[5]](#cite_note-5)

More than 60% of the fund's activities are within Saudi Arabia.[[6]](#cite_note-:11-6) Within Saudi Arabia, the fund's investments primarily go to private conglomerates owned by prominent Saudi business families who have close ties to the [Saudi ruling family](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/House_of_Saud "House of Saud").[[6]](#cite_note-:11-6) Outside of Saudi Arabia, the fund's investments into prominent foreign assets, such as [Premier League](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Premier_League "Premier League") football club [Newcastle United](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2021_takeover_of_Newcastle_United_F.C. "2021 takeover of Newcastle United F.C.") and video game company [Electronic Arts](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Leveraged_buyout_of_Electronic_Arts "Leveraged buyout of Electronic Arts"), have generated controversy due to the fund's lack of transparency and close control by the Saudi government, which has itself faced significant criticism around the [lack of human rights in the country](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Human_rights_in_Saudi_Arabia "Human rights in Saudi Arabia").[[7]](#cite_note-7)[[8]](#cite_note-8)[[9]](#cite_note-9)

## History

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Public_Investment_Fund&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: History")]

[![](//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/4/41/Yasir_Al-Rumayyan_at_FII_PRIORITY_Asia_Summit_2025_in_Tokyo_%28cropped_2%29.jpg/250px-Yasir_Al-Rumayyan_at_FII_PRIORITY_Asia_Summit_2025_in_Tokyo_%28cropped_2%29.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Yasir_Al-Rumayyan_at_FII_PRIORITY_Asia_Summit_2025_in_Tokyo_(cropped_2).jpg)

PIF governor [Yasir Al-Rumayyan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yasir_Al-Rumayyan "Yasir Al-Rumayyan") at the FII PRIORITY Asia Summit in Tokyo, 2025

The Saudi Arabian Public Investment Fund (PIF) was established by King [Faisal bin Abdulaziz Al Saud](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Faisal_of_Saudi_Arabia "Faisal of Saudi Arabia") in 1971[[10]](#cite_note-FT-scrambles-10) by Royal Decree M/24[[11]](#cite_note-11) with the stated intent to provide financing support for projects of strategic significance to the national economy.[[12]](#cite_note-12) For much of its history, the PIF was a passive entity that oversaw the Saudi state's equity in listed firms. When neighboring petrostates began using their sovereign wealth funds for influence, Saudi Arabia followed them. The PIF expanded its staff from 50 in 2015 to nearly 500 in 2018.[[10]](#cite_note-FT-scrambles-10)

In July 2014, the Council of Ministers granted the PIF authority to fund new companies inside and outside the Kingdom, independently or in cooperation with the public and private sectors, without the council's prior approval.[[13]](#cite_note-13) In March 2015, oversight of PIF was moved from the [Ministry of Finance](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ministry_of_Finance_(Saudi_Arabia) "Ministry of Finance (Saudi Arabia)") to the [Council of Economic and Development Affairs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Council_of_Economic_and_Development_Affairs_(Saudi_Arabia) "Council of Economic and Development Affairs (Saudi Arabia)") (CEDA). As part of this process, a new PIF was appointed, chaired by Crown Prince [Mohammed bin Salman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mohammed_bin_Salman "Mohammed bin Salman").[[14]](#cite_note-14) The board says PIF is aligned with the government's [Vision 2030](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saudi_Vision_2030 "Saudi Vision 2030")[[15]](#cite_note-15) with the aim to diversify the economy.[[16]](#cite_note-16) To bolster the resources of the PIF and help in the financing of investments into foreign companies such as Uber and Tesla, the PIF received cash from the [Saudi Central Bank](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saudi_Central_Bank "Saudi Central Bank"), issued debt, and benefitted from the proceeds of the privatisation of Saudi state assets.[[10]](#cite_note-FT-scrambles-10)

In 2022, a 4% stake in ownership of [Saudi Aramco](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saudi_Aramco "Saudi Aramco") was transferred to the PIF, which was repeated in 2023 as part of the fund's plan to increase [assets under management](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Assets_under_management "Assets under management") to over $1 trillion by 2025. The shares for the second 4% stake in 2023 were valued at around $78 billion. The move was intended to take advantage of higher hydrocarbon prices to fund the expansion of the PIF in its overarching goal to diversify investments.[[17]](#cite_note-17)

A 2021 report by Global SWF found that PIF's Governance, Sustainability, and Resilience (GSR) score had risen by 12% to an overall score of 40% (out of 100%) that year. This was partially attributed to the fact that PIF had started to build a dedicated ESG (Environmental, Social, and Sustainability) team.[[18]](#cite_note-Bloomberg-18) The fund achieved an annual return of around 8% between 2018 and 2022.[[19]](#cite_note-19)

## Investment projects

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Public_Investment_Fund&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Investment projects")]

The Public Investment Fund (PIF) holds a wide range of domestic and international investments. These include a 38% stake in POSCO Engineering & Construction, a 5% stake in Uber acquired for $3.5 billion, and combined 5% stakes in the video game companies Capcom and Nexon, purchased for approximately $1 billion.[[20]](#cite_note-:9-20)

In March 2016, the Saudi government announced that ownership of Saudi Aramco would be transferred to the PIF, and that the Kingdom planned to list 5% of Aramco's shares in an [initial public offering](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Initial_public_offering "Initial public offering") by 2017.[[21]](#cite_note-21)

Domestically, PIF owns and develops several large-scale projects. These include Qiddiya City,[[22]](#cite_note-22) leadership of the Red Sea Project,[[23]](#cite_note-23)[[24]](#cite_note-24) and ownership of the closed joint-stock company Neom.[[25]](#cite_note-25)[[26]](#cite_note-26)

PIF also holds a 5.7% stake, valued at about $500 million, in concert and ticketing company Live Nation.[[27]](#cite_note-27) In 2020, the fund purchased minority stakes in several major U.S. companies, including Boeing, Meta Platforms (then known as Facebook), and Citigroup.[[28]](#cite_note-28)

That same year, PIF disclosed investments of approximately $713.7 million in Boeing, $522 million in Citigroup, $522 million in Facebook, $495.8 million in The Walt Disney Company, and $487.6 million in [Bank of America](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bank_of_America "Bank of America"). It also reported a small stake in [Berkshire Hathaway](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Berkshire_Hathaway "Berkshire Hathaway")[[29]](#cite_note-29) and an $827.7 million stake in oil company BP.[[30]](#cite_note-30)

In addition, PIF acquired a 2.32% stake, valued at $1.5 billion, in India's Jio Platforms in 2020.[[31]](#cite_note-31)[[32]](#cite_note-32) Later that year, the fund reduced its total U.S. equity holdings from $10.1 billion to $7 billion in the third quarter, leaving its then $2.7 billion stake in Uber as its largest remaining U.S. investment.[[33]](#cite_note-33)

In 2016, [SoftBank Group](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SoftBank_Group "SoftBank Group") and the PIF announced that they would establish the [SoftBank Vision Fund](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SoftBank_Vision_Fund "SoftBank Vision Fund"), which aimed to invest up to $45 billion over five years in the tech sector.[[34]](#cite_note-34) The SoftBank Group confirmed that during the fiscal year 2019–2020, the Vision Fund incurred a loss calculated at $17.7 billion after the value of investments was written down. The losses were related to the investments in [WeWork](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/WeWork "WeWork") and [Uber](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Uber "Uber"). In the 39-year history of SoftBank, the Saudi Arabia-backed funds paid the group its worst-ever losses; the overall company losses were 1.36 trillion yen (more than $12.5 billion).[[35]](#cite_note-35)

During the 2017 Saudi–US CEO Forum, which was part of President [Donald Trump](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Donald_Trump "Donald Trump")'s official trip to Saudi Arabia, PIF announced plans to "invest $40 billion in infrastructure projects, mostly in the U.S." [Blackstone Inc.](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Blackstone_Inc. "Blackstone Inc."), whose CEO and founder, [Stephen A. Schwarzman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stephen_A._Schwarzman "Stephen A. Schwarzman"), is a top supporter of Trump, entered into a non-binding memorandum by which the PIF committed $20 billion to the project.[[36]](#cite_note-36) During the CEO Forum, US–Saudi arms deals were announced, including a pledge to "assemble 150 [Lockheed Martin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lockheed_Martin "Lockheed Martin") Black Hawk helicopters" in Saudi Arabia, representing 450 jobs in Saudi Arabia as part of the "$6 billion deal for Black Hawks."[[37]](#cite_note-37)

In October 2017, it was announced that PIF would aim to increase its assets under management to more than $400 billion and create more than 20,000 new jobs by 2020.[[38]](#cite_note-:1-38)[[39]](#cite_note-39) Al-Rumayyan presented a new [investment strategy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Investment_strategy "Investment strategy") for the fund, based on four objectives of maximizing assets, investing in new sectors, localizing technologies, and developing economic partnerships.[[38]](#cite_note-:1-38) He also said PIF would borrow conservatively to finance specific assets and would seek further partnerships such as those with Blackstone, Inc. and [SoftBank](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SoftBank "SoftBank").[[40]](#cite_note-40)[[41]](#cite_note-41)

In September 2018, Al-Rumayyan announced PIF's first step in incorporating loans and debt instruments into its long-term strategy, with an $11 billion loan facility.[[42]](#cite_note-42) The following month, he said the fund would aim to increase the percentage of international assets in its portfolio from 10% to 50% by 2030.[[43]](#cite_note-43)

At the [Milken Institute](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Milken_Institute "Milken Institute") in [Abu Dhabi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abu_Dhabi "Abu Dhabi") in February 2019, Al-Rumayyan announced that PIF would open new offices in London, New York City, and San Francisco and would increase its workforce from 450 to 700 by the end of 2019.[[44]](#cite_note-:3-44)[[45]](#cite_note-45) He also said the fund would invest in [renewable energy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Renewable_energy "Renewable energy") projects in Saudi Arabia, including local manufacturing of [solar panels](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Solar_panels "Solar panels").[[44]](#cite_note-:3-44)

In 2021, it purchased stakes in the [American video game](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Video_games_in_the_United_States "Video games in the United States") companies [Electronic Arts](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Electronic_Arts "Electronic Arts"), [Take-Two Interactive](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Take-Two_Interactive "Take-Two Interactive"), and [Activision Blizzard](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Activision_Blizzard "Activision Blizzard"). In May 2022, it purchased a 5% stake in the [Japanese video game](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Japanese_video_game "Japanese video game") company [Nintendo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nintendo "Nintendo"),[[46]](#cite_note-46) and the following month, an 8% stake in [Embracer Group](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Embracer_Group "Embracer Group") with a $1 billion investment.[[47]](#cite_note-47)

PIF held an indirect stake in [Twitter](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Twitter "Twitter") before its [acquisition](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Acquisition_of_Twitter_by_Elon_Musk "Acquisition of Twitter by Elon Musk") by [Elon Musk](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elon_Musk "Elon Musk").[[48]](#cite_note-48)

In November 2023, PIF acquired a 10% stake in [Heathrow Airport](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Heathrow_Airport "Heathrow Airport") after [Ferrovial](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ferrovial "Ferrovial") sold its 25% share.[[49]](#cite_note-:13-49) The remaining 15% was acquired by [Ardian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ardian_(company) "Ardian (company)").[[49]](#cite_note-:13-49) Subsequently, on 15 December 2024, it was reported that Ardian and PIF had successfully acquired 22.6% and 15%, respectively, of stakes in Heathrow Airport for a combined US$4.12 billion from Ferrovial and some shareholders in FGP TopCo.[[50]](#cite_note-50)

PIF acquired a 49% stake in [Rocco Forte Hotels](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rocco_Forte_Hotels "Rocco Forte Hotels") in December 2023, valuing the hotel group at £1.4 billion.[[51]](#cite_note-51)

In 2024, PIF acquired a 38% share of HOLON GmbH, Germany. HOLON is a subcompany of [Benteler International](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Benteler_International "Benteler International").[[52]](#cite_note-52) HOLON is launching the world's first electric autonomous shuttle with automotive standards in 2026.

### Former Donald Trump administration officials

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Public_Investment_Fund&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: Former Donald Trump administration officials")]

In 2021, PIF invested $2 billion into [Affinity Partners](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Affinity_Partners "Affinity Partners"), a private equity firm formed by [Jared Kushner](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jared_Kushner "Jared Kushner"), [Donald Trump](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Donald_Trump "Donald Trump")'s son-in-law, shortly after he left the White House, where he had worked during his father-in-law's first term as president. While considering making the $2bn pledge, PIF officials and advisers raised questions about the merits of the investment, but PIF management overruled the advisers.[[4]](#cite_note-:8-4) Even a year later, in April 2022, Affinity Partners primarily depended on Saudi money: it had some $2.5 billion under its management by that stage.[[4]](#cite_note-:8-4) Within the Trump administration, Kushner worked extensively on Arab–[Israeli](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Israel "Israel") diplomatic issues, and had been a staunch defender of Saudi ruler Mohammed bin Salman.[[4]](#cite_note-:8-4) According to ethics experts, the $2bn investment, which would boost the fund's yield and generate substantial management fees for Affinity and, consequently, for Kushner personally, created the appearance of potential payback for Kushner.[[4]](#cite_note-:8-4)

In 2021, PIF invested $1 billion in the investment fund established by former [Treasury Secretary](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Secretary_of_the_Treasury "United States Secretary of the Treasury") [Steven Mnuchin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Steven_Mnuchin "Steven Mnuchin") just after he left that position.[[4]](#cite_note-:8-4)[[53]](#cite_note-53)

In May 2022, it was reported that Affinity Partners was planning to direct its investments—and thus Saudi Arabia's PIF money—to Israel. Kushner conducted various pitch meetings with a range of Israeli startups before selecting two of them in which Affinity would invest. The Kingdom did not have formal diplomatic relations with Israel and was not a part of the public [Abraham Accords](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abraham_Accords "Abraham Accords") process at that stage. Kushner warned Saudi Arabian officials that it could lose opportunities in Israel to its neighbors who signed the Accords, including the [United Arab Emirates](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_Arab_Emirates "United Arab Emirates") and [Bahrain](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bahrain "Bahrain"). Saudi officials agreed to Affinity Partners' investment in Israeli startups, which was also believed to have been approved by Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman. Many saw it as groundwork for the potential normalization of [Israel–Saudi Arabia relations](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Israel–Saudi_Arabia_relations "Israel–Saudi Arabia relations").[[54]](#cite_note-:10-54) It was the first known occasion in which money from the Saudi PIF would go to Israel.[[54]](#cite_note-:10-54)

### Takeover of Newcastle United

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Public_Investment_Fund&action=edit&section=4 "Edit section: Takeover of Newcastle United")]

Main article: [2021 takeover of Newcastle United F.C.](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2021_takeover_of_Newcastle_United_F.C. "2021 takeover of Newcastle United F.C.")

On 14 April 2020, a £300 million agreement was reached for the sale of [Newcastle United F.C.](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Newcastle_United_F.C. "Newcastle United F.C.") from owner [Mike Ashley](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mike_Ashley_(businessman) "Mike Ashley (businessman)") to a consortium comprising the PIF, PCP Capital Partners, and the Reuben Brothers.[[55]](#cite_note-55) The [Premier League](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Premier_League "Premier League") did not approve the deal, leading Ashley to pursue legal action in an attempt to finalize the sale.[[56]](#cite_note-56)[[57]](#cite_note-57) On 7 October 2021, the consortium, led by the PIF, completed the acquisition after the Premier League received “legally binding assurances” that the Saudi government would not control the club.[[58]](#cite_note-58)[[59]](#cite_note-59)

The Premier League faced criticism from human rights organizations following the club's sale. [Amnesty International](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amnesty_International "Amnesty International") condemned the decision, citing Saudi Arabia's human rights record and calling for ownership rules that would prevent human rights violators from owning Premier League clubs.[[60]](#cite_note-60)[[61]](#cite_note-:5-61) The organization described the takeover as “an extremely bitter blow for human rights defenders.”[[62]](#cite_note-:6-62) Hatice Cengiz, fiancée of murdered journalist [Jamal Khashoggi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jamal_Khashoggi "Jamal Khashoggi"), also urged the Premier League to block the deal.[[61]](#cite_note-:5-61)

In April 2021, Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman reportedly urged UK Prime Minister Boris Johnson to influence the Premier League's decision on the proposed takeover, warning of potential economic consequences if it was blocked. This occurred amid a proposed Saudi investment of $30 billion in the UK over ten years.[[62]](#cite_note-:6-62) Amnesty International UK described the takeover as “a blatant example of Saudi sportswashing”.[[63]](#cite_note-63) The UK government declined to release details of its discussions with the Premier League, citing potential harm to diplomatic relations with Saudi Arabia.[[64]](#cite_note-64) The other 19 Premier League clubs criticized the takeover, arguing it harmed the league's reputation.[[65]](#cite_note-guardian-65)

### Establishment of LIV Golf

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Public_Investment_Fund&action=edit&section=5 "Edit section: Establishment of LIV Golf")]

See also: [LIV Golf](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/LIV_Golf "LIV Golf")

In October 2021, a division of the PIF, Golf Saudi, funded the establishment of LIV Golf Investments, with [Greg Norman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Greg_Norman "Greg Norman") declared its CEO. The private company introduced a professional tour, LIV Golf, known beforehand as the Super Golf League. It came as a new challenge against the [PGA Tour](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/PGA_Tour "PGA Tour"), along with the World Golf Tour and the Premier Golf League.[[66]](#cite_note-66)[[67]](#cite_note-67)[[68]](#cite_note-68)[[69]](#cite_note-69)

LIV Golf's strategy differed from other leagues as it offered the richest golf tournaments in history and was able to convince star players to take part.[[70]](#cite_note-70) In June 2022, the [LIV Golf Invitational Series](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2022_LIV_Golf_Invitational_Series "2022 LIV Golf Invitational Series") commenced its eight-event season, with total prize money of $255 million. The Saudi PIF backed the event with $2 billion in funds. LIV Golf offered the winner's prize of each regular event $4 million in prize money, in comparison to the [PGA Championship](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/PGA_Championship "PGA Championship")’s $2.7 million.[[71]](#cite_note-71) Some of the most prominent professional golf players participated in the event, including [Phil Mickelson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Phil_Mickelson "Phil Mickelson"), [Dustin Johnson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dustin_Johnson "Dustin Johnson"), [Graeme McDowell](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Graeme_McDowell "Graeme McDowell"), [Sergio García](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sergio_García "Sergio García"), [Martin Kaymer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Martin_Kaymer "Martin Kaymer"), [Louis Oosthuizen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Louis_Oosthuizen "Louis Oosthuizen"), [Charl Schwartzel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charl_Schwartzel "Charl Schwartzel"), and [Lee Westwood](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lee_Westwood "Lee Westwood").[[72]](#cite_note-72) Dustin Johnson was allegedly paid $150 million to join the Saudi-backed series.[[73]](#cite_note-73) Phil Mickelson also committed to the series after signing a $200 million contract.[[74]](#cite_note-74) However, some other renowned players also rejected the new league, with [Tiger Woods](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tiger_Woods "Tiger Woods") turning down an offer worth nearly $1 billion.[[75]](#cite_note-75) A vocal critic of the tournament, [Rory McIlroy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rory_McIlroy "Rory McIlroy"), also stood with PGA Tour and criticized players who joined LIV, stating they were "taking the easy way out".[[76]](#cite_note-76)

LIV Golf was also condemned as another [sportswashing](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sportswashing "Sportswashing") tool of Saudi Arabia, which is accused of several human rights violations, including the [assassination of Jamal Khashoggi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Assassination_of_Jamal_Khashoggi "Assassination of Jamal Khashoggi").[[77]](#cite_note-77) Norman and several participating players were questioned by reporters about their association with a Saudi-funded tour. Norman dismissed the questions, saying, "We've all made mistakes" and that Saudi wanted "to move forward".[[78]](#cite_note-78)

Phil Mickelson gave a controversial statement before the establishment of the circuit, saying that the Saudis were "scary motherf–kers to be involved with". He said, "We know they killed Khashoggi and have a horrible record on human rights". Despite that, Mickelson joined LIV Golf, calling it "a once-in-a-lifetime opportunity" to reshape the PGA Tour.[[79]](#cite_note-79) Graeme McDowell also gave similar answers and said, "We're not politicians, we're professional golfers. If Saudi Arabia wants to use the game of golf as a way for them to get to where they want to be, I think we're proud to help them on that journey."[[80]](#cite_note-80)

On June 6, 2023, it was announced that LIV Golf and the PGA Tour would merge their commercial businesses into a new for-profit company, with the Public Investment Fund reportedly investing billions into the new company.[[81]](#cite_note-81) Critics of the deal accused the PGA of hypocrisy and lamented what they saw as Saudi "[sportswashing](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sportswashing "Sportswashing")."[[82]](#cite_note-:12-82) Saudi exiles and human rights activists said that the PGA was accepting "Saudi blood money."[[82]](#cite_note-:12-82) The Associated Press wrote that the merger of the PGA Tour and LIV Golf marked a turnaround for the authoritarian regime in Saudi Arabia, as the Mohammed bin Salman regime had been isolated for years over human rights abuses and the murder of Jamal Khashoggi.[[83]](#cite_note-83)

In April 2026, PIF announced in its new five year strategy that it is reevaluating its priorities. This is against mounting pressures and financial commitments to host World Expo 2030 and the [football world cup](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2034_FIFA_World_Cup "2034 FIFA World Cup") in 2034.[[84]](#cite_note-84)

### Exposure to Credit Suisse crisis

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Public_Investment_Fund&action=edit&section=6 "Edit section: Exposure to Credit Suisse crisis")]

In 2022, PIF made a $1.5 billion investment in [Credit Suisse](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Credit_Suisse "Credit Suisse") as part of a broader goal of diversifying its portfolio into global banking. The PIF connected Credit Suisse to the [Saudi National Bank](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saudi_National_Bank "Saudi National Bank"), and made the Saudi National Bank the largest shareholder with less than 10% ownership (which, according to the Saudi National Bank, prevented them from having to deal with regulatory requirements for 10%+ shareholder ownership).[[85]](#cite_note-85) After the [March 2023 United States bank failures](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/March_2023_United_States_bank_failures "March 2023 United States bank failures") had gripped the global banking sector, Saudi National Bank chairman Ammar al-Khudair publicly stated on 15 March 2023 that they would "absolutely not" supply Credit Suisse with more capital (referencing the regulatory requirements for 10%+ shareholders as the reason why), which then promptly caused the share price of Credit Suisse to drop 25% more. On 19 March 2023, [UBS](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/UBS "UBS") confirmed their planned [acquisition of Credit Suisse](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Acquisition_of_Credit_Suisse_by_UBS "Acquisition of Credit Suisse by UBS").[[86]](#cite_note-86)

### ATP and WTA tour partnerships

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Public_Investment_Fund&action=edit&section=7 "Edit section: ATP and WTA tour partnerships")]

args.key_excerpts: The Public Investment Fund (PIF) is the sovereign wealth fund of Saudi Arabia... It is among the largest sovereign wealth funds in the world with total estimated assets of US$900 billion, created in 1971 for the purpose of investing funds on behalf of the government of Saudi Arabia. The wealth fund has Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman, Saudi Arabia's de facto ruler since 2015, as its chairman.
args.summary:
The Public Investment Fund (PIF) is the sovereign wealth fund of Saudi Arabia, headquartered in Riyadh at the Public Investment Fund Tower. It was established on August 17, 1971, by King Faisal bin Abdulaziz via Royal Decree M/24. As of May 2026, the fund holds approximately US$900 billion in assets under management, making it among the largest sovereign wealth funds globally. It is chaired by Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman (de facto ruler of Saudi Arabia since 2015), with Yasir Al-Rumayyan serving as Governor. Ownership rests with the Government of Saudi Arabia, and more than 60% of fund activities are domestic.

HISTORY: Originally a passive entity overseeing state equity in listed firms, the PIF expanded its staff from 50 in 2015 to nearly 500 in 2018. In July 2014, the Council of Ministers granted PIF authority to fund new companies independently. In March 2015, oversight moved from the Ministry of Finance to the Council of Economic and Development Affairs (CEDA). The fund is aligned with Saudi Vision 2030, aiming to diversify the economy. In 2022 and 2023, 4% stakes in Saudi Aramco were transferred to the fund (the 2023 transfer valued at ~$78 billion) as part of plans to exceed $1 trillion in assets by 2025. A 2021 Global SWF report scored PIF's Governance, Sustainability, and Resilience at 40%, with annual returns around 8% between 2018-2022.

MAJOR INVESTMENT PROJECTS: The fund holds stakes in numerous global companies including a 38% stake in POSCO Engineering & Construction, 5% of Uber (purchased for $3.5 billion), 5% stakes in Capcom and Nexon, a 5.7% stake in Live Nation, a 2.32% stake in Jio Platforms (worth $1.5 billion), and stakes in Boeing ($713.7M), Citigroup ($522M), Meta/Facebook ($522M), Disney ($495.8M), Bank of America ($487.6M), BP ($827.7M), and Berkshire Hathaway. In 2020, it disclosed investments of over $700 million in major US companies. Domestically, PIF owns Qiddiya City, the Red Sea Project, and Neom.

KEY PARTNERSHIPS: In 2016, PIF and SoftBank established the SoftBank Vision Fund (up to $45 billion over five years), which later suffered $17.7 billion in losses (fiscal 2019-2020) related to WeWork and Uber, resulting in SoftBank's worst-ever losses. In 2017, during the Saudi–US CEO Forum, PIF pledged $40 billion for infrastructure projects mostly in the US, with Blackstone committing $20 billion. PIF opened offices in London, New York, and San Francisco in 2019.

FORMER TRUMP ADMINISTRATION OFFICIALS: In 2021, PIF invested $2 billion in Affinity Partners, a private equity firm formed by Jared Kushner (Trump's son-in-law) shortly after he left the White House, despite internal concerns about the merits. The investment raised ethics concerns about potential payback for Kushner. PIF also invested $1 billion in the fund of former Treasury Secretary Steven Mnuchin. In May 2022, Affinity Partners directed Saudi money to Israeli startups—the first known Saudi PIF investment in Israel—viewed as groundwork for Israel–Saudi normalization.

NEWCASTLE UNITED: On April 14, 2020, a £300 million agreement sold Newcastle United F.C. from Mike Ashley to a consortium led by PIF. The Premier League initially blocked the deal, but on October 7, 2021, the acquisition was completed after "legally binding assurances" that Saudi Arabia wouldn't control the club. The sale drew criticism from Amnesty International ("an extremely bitter blow for human rights defenders") and other human rights advocates, who called it "a blatant example of Saudi sportswashing." In April 2021, Mohammed bin Salman reportedly urged UK PM Boris Johnson to influence the Premier League amid a proposed $30 billion Saudi investment in the UK.

LIV GOLF: In October 2021, PIF division Golf Saudi funded LIV Golf Investments with Greg Norman as CEO. The LIV Golf Invitational Series launched in June 2022 with $255 million in total prize money, backed by $2 billion in PIF funds. Notable players joining included Phil Mickelson ($200 million contract), Dustin Johnson (allegedly $150 million), and others, while Tiger Woods reportedly turned down a near-$1 billion offer. The league was condemned as a "sportswashing" tool. Mickelson controversially stated the Saudis "killed Khashoggi and have a horrible record on human rights" yet joined anyway. On June 6, 2023, LIV Golf and PGA Tour announced a merger of commercial businesses with PIF investing billions. In April 2026, PIF announced it was reevaluating priorities against mounting financial pressures from hosting World Expo 2030 and the 2034 FIFA World Cup.

CREDIT SUISSE: In 2022, PIF invested $1.5 billion in Credit Suisse and connected it to Saudi National Bank (making it largest shareholder under 10% to avoid regulatory requirements). In March 2023, Saudi National Bank's chairman publicly refused to supply more capital, causing Credit Suisse shares to drop 25%, contributing to the bank's acquisition by UBS on March 19, 2023.

TENNIS: In 2024, PIF announced partnerships with the ATP and WTA tours, including a $2 billion offer to buy and merge both professional tours into a single PIF-led tour (excluding grand slams); whether the offer was accepted remains unclear.

CURRENT PORTFOLIO (as of May 2025): Giga-projects include Neom, Red Sea Global, Qiddiya City, Roshn, and Diriyah Company. International investments include Electronic Arts (93.4%), LIV Golf, Newcastle United (85%), Lucid Motors (58%), Heathrow Airport Holdings (15%), Uber, Jio Platforms, Magic Leap, Accor, Reliance Retail, and Minerva Foods (34%). Additional entertainment holds include ATP Media, DAZN, Kings League, Professional Fighters League, and Professional Triathletes Organisation. Middle East and North Africa holdings span dozens of companies across sectors including Saudi Telecom Company (STC), Ma'aden, Riyad Bank, Alinma Bank, Saudi National Bank, ACWA Power, Riyadh Air, Saudi Arabian Military Industries, and many more covering real estate, financial services, utilities, automotive, construction, healthcare, and entertainment.

# China’s Big Fund 3.0: Xi’s Boldest Gamble Yet for Chip Supremacy

The third phase of Beijing’s semiconductor policy aims to learn from past mistakes. As stakes rise, can Xi Jinping secure China’s tech future and cement his political-economic legacy?

![Lizzi C. Lee](https://images.thediplomat.com/v1/td-list-xs-1/2021/08/thediplomat_2021-08-20-12.jpg "Lizzi C. Lee")
![China’s Big Fund 3.0: Xi’s Boldest Gamble Yet for Chip Supremacy](https://thediplomat.com/wp-content/uploads/2021/09/sizes/td-story-s-1/thediplomat_2021-09-07-7.jpg "China’s Big Fund 3.0: Xi’s Boldest Gamble Yet for Chip Supremacy")

China is stepping up its game in the global semiconductor race with the launch of the third phase of its National Integrated Circuit Industry Investment Fund, commonly known as the Big Fund. With a hefty investment of 340 billion yuan ($47.5 billion), this initiative is unfolding amid escalating technological tensions with the United States.

China’s ambitions in the semiconductor sector were first formalized in 2014 with the Big Fund’s initial phase. This phase saw an investment of 139 billion yuan, signaling a departure from mere state support to a more market-driven approach. By attracting funds from state-owned enterprises, financial institutions, and private investors, China aimed to build a robust semiconductor ecosystem. The first phase spread its investments across various sectors, nurturing significant players like Semiconductor Manufacturing International Corporation (SMIC).

The second phase, launched in 2019 with 204 billion yuan, focused on more specialized segments of the supply chain, such as etching machines and testing equipment. This phase was crucial in bolstering China’s self-sufficiency, especially in the face of increasing U.S. sanctions. However, it was not without its pitfalls. Corruption scandals and poor investment choices highlighted the need for stricter oversight, and geopolitical tensions further complicated progress.

**Big Fund 3.0: A New Strategy**

Enter Big Fund 3.0, designed to tackle past missteps and set a new course with revamped funding sources, investment targets, and strategic priorities. One notable change is the involvement of major banking institutions as key investors. With 19 founders, including the Ministry of Finance and heavy-hitters like the Industrial and Commercial Bank of China, this phase leans on centralized, state-controlled financial backing. This move underscores the high stakes but also ramps up the pressure to deliver results.

Moreover, the duration of Big Fund 3.0 has been extended to 15 years, from May 24, 2024, to May 23, 2039, reflecting the long-term nature and hefty capital requirements of the semiconductor industry.

Big Fund 3.0 embraces a dual approach, targeting both the entire semiconductor supply chain and specific critical areas. On one hand, it aims to foster growth across design, manufacturing, packaging, testing, equipment, and materials. This interconnected development ensures that advancements in one area spark progress in others, creating a robust and self-sufficient semiconductor ecosystem.

On the other hand, it zeroes in on critical bottlenecks that have historically stymied China’s progress. These include the development of large semiconductor manufacturing plants and essential components like high-bandwidth memory (HBM). Additionally, the fund prioritizes advanced chip technologies for artificial intelligence, reflecting AI’s rising importance in the global tech landscape. This targeted focus is crucial for overcoming technological challenges and cutting down dependencies on foreign technologies.

**Governance and Oversight: Tightening the Reins**

Big Fund 3.0’s governance structure reflects a strategic shift toward centralized oversight. The Central Science and Technology Commission (CSTC), a [new Communist Party coordinating body](https://thediplomat.com/2023/08/the-party-rules-chinas-new-central-science-and-technology-commission/), oversees the initiative, setting policy priorities and delegating execution to entities like the Ministry of Science and Technology. This centralization aims to ensure strategic coordination and effective management.

Responding to past corruption scandals, Big Fund 3.0 is implementing stricter governance measures. The appointment of Zhang Xin, a seasoned semiconductor technocrat, as president, signals a commitment to restoring confidence among investors and stakeholders. Ensuring wise investments and curbing corruption requires ongoing vigilance, robust oversight mechanisms, and a blend of technical expertise and professional fund management skills.

**Public-Private Synergy and Funding Reforms**

Enhanced public-private cooperation is another cornerstone of Big Fund 3.0. China plans to revamp its national laboratories and innovation centers by integrating scientific research with commercial applications. Collaborating with both private and state-owned companies, the aim is to create synergy between research and real-world applications.

Reforms in funding mechanisms are also on the horizon. Since the establishment of the National Integrated Circuit Fund in 2014, Beijing has promoted its own version of a venture capital model. The model has achieved some preliminary successes. Despite geopolitical challenges, China’s semiconductor industry has made significant strides, now accounting for nearly a quarter of global 300mm chip manufacturing capacity. SMIC, China’s leading chip foundry, has tripled its revenue and doubled its capacity, becoming the world’s third-largest foundry.

But experts generally agree that Big Funds 1.0 and 2.0 fell short of meeting the state’s ambitious technological goals. The new oversight system aims to address these shortcomings and achieve more ambitious objectives.

**Global Implications**

The significance of Big Fund 3.0 extends beyond technological self-reliance. By strengthening its semiconductor industry, China aims to secure technological leadership, find new growth sectors, create high-tech jobs, and generate healthier returns to address government debt issues. These objectives are especially critical as China faces an impending structural economic slowdown, and Beijing seeks new drivers for economic prosperity to maintain its legitimacy.

Globally, China’s aggressive investment in its semiconductor industry is likely to disrupt market dynamics. Increased production capacity in mature-node chips could lead to oversupply and price pressures, impacting countries like Taiwan, South Korea, Malaysia, and Vietnam. The United States has intensified efforts to coordinate export controls with other nations to limit China’s access to advanced technologies. This ongoing technological conflict will continue to shape global semiconductor policies and alliances.

Given the immense challenges and high stakes, the success of Big Fund 3.0 is far from assured. Its outcomes will have profound implications for the future of the semiconductor industry and global technological power dynamics, and will play a defining role in Xi Jinping’s economic and political legacy.

From Wikipedia, the free encyclopedia

Chinese National Fund

China Integrated Circuit Industry Investment Fund Co., Ltd.[![Image 4](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/b/be/China_Integrated_Circuit_Industry_Investment_Fund.png/250px-China_Integrated_Circuit_Industry_Investment_Fund.png?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:China_Integrated_Circuit_Industry_Investment_Fund.png)
Native name 国家集成电路产业投资基金股份有限公司
Type[State-owned enterprise](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/State-owned_enterprise "State-owned enterprise")
Industry[Investment management](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Investment_management "Investment management")
Founded 26 September 2014;11 years ago(2014-09-26)
Headquarters[Beijing](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beijing "Beijing"), [China](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/China "China")
Key people Zhang Xin (President)
[AUM](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Assets_under_management "Assets under management")US$95.7 billion (2024)[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/China_Integrated_Circuit_Industry_Investment_Fund#cite_note-Fortune-1)
Owners[Ministry of Finance](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ministry_of_Finance_of_the_People's_Republic_of_China "Ministry of Finance of the People's Republic of China") (36.74%)

[China Development Bank](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/China_Development_Bank "China Development Bank") (22.29%)

[China Tobacco](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/China_Tobacco "China Tobacco") (11.14%)

The **China Integrated Circuit Industry Investment Fund** (**ICF**; [Chinese](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chinese_language "Chinese language"):国家集成电路产业投资基金; [pinyin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pinyin "Pinyin"):_Guójiā Jíchéng Diànlù Chǎnyè Tóuzī Jījīn_), also known as the **National Integrated Circuit Industry Investment Fund** and the **Big Fund** ([Chinese](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chinese_language "Chinese language"):国家大基金; [pinyin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pinyin "Pinyin"):_Guójiā Dàjījīn_), is a [China Government Guidance Fund](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/China_Government_Guidance_Fund "China Government Guidance Fund").[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/China_Integrated_Circuit_Industry_Investment_Fund#cite_note-:622-2):163 The fund aims to help China reach its national goal of achieving self-sufficiency in the [semiconductor industry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Semiconductor_industry "Semiconductor industry") (as part of the [Made in China 2025](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Made_in_China_2025 "Made in China 2025") plan) by investing in domestic semiconductor companies. It has played a significant role with regards to the [semiconductor industry in China](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Semiconductor_industry_in_China "Semiconductor industry in China") by funding companies such as [SMIC](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Semiconductor_Manufacturing_International_Corporation "Semiconductor Manufacturing International Corporation"), [Hua Hong Semiconductor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hua_Hong_Semiconductor "Hua Hong Semiconductor"), and [YMTC](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yangtze_Memory_Technologies "Yangtze Memory Technologies").

The fund has three phases respectively, with Big Fund I (2014 to 2019), Big Fund II (2019 to 2024), and Big Fund III (2024 to 2039). The fund's management company is Sino IC Capital.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/China_Integrated_Circuit_Industry_Investment_Fund#cite_note-3)

## History

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=China_Integrated_Circuit_Industry_Investment_Fund&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: History")]

### Preparation

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=China_Integrated_Circuit_Industry_Investment_Fund&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Preparation")]

In June 2014, the [State Council of the People's Republic of China](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/State_Council_of_the_People's_Republic_of_China "State Council of the People's Republic of China") proposed in the National Integrated Circuit Industry Development Guidelines that a national investment fund should be set up to provide focused support for the development of the Integrated Circuit Industry.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/China_Integrated_Circuit_Industry_Investment_Fund#cite_note-SCMP-4) In August 2014, the fund management company, Sino IC Capital, was established by [China Development Bank](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/China_Development_Bank "China Development Bank"), which would own 45% of the company.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/China_Integrated_Circuit_Industry_Investment_Fund#cite_note-Caixin-5)

### Phase I (2014 - 2019)

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=China_Integrated_Circuit_Industry_Investment_Fund&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: Phase I (2014 - 2019)")]

On 26 September 2014, ICF was established.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/China_Integrated_Circuit_Industry_Investment_Fund#cite_note-SCMP-4)[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/China_Integrated_Circuit_Industry_Investment_Fund#cite_note-Caixin-5)[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/China_Integrated_Circuit_Industry_Investment_Fund#cite_note-:1-6) According to a statement on the website of the [Ministry of Industry and Information Technology](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ministry_of_Industry_and_Information_Technology "Ministry of Industry and Information Technology") (MIIT), it was set up to "invest in chip manufacturing, boost industrial production, and promote [mergers and acquisitions](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mergers_and_acquisitions "Mergers and acquisitions")".[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/China_Integrated_Circuit_Industry_Investment_Fund#cite_note-SCMP-4) The fund operates as a corporate entity under MIIT and the [Ministry of Finance](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ministry_of_Finance_of_the_People's_Republic_of_China "Ministry of Finance of the People's Republic of China").[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/China_Integrated_Circuit_Industry_Investment_Fund#cite_note-SCMP-4)[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/China_Integrated_Circuit_Industry_Investment_Fund#cite_note-:1-6) It adopted a [two tier](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dual_board "Dual board") management structure where the board set the strategy and approved major projects while Sino IC Capital carried out the investments and managed the money.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/China_Integrated_Circuit_Industry_Investment_Fund#cite_note-Caixin-5) The near-term goal was growing annual revenue of domestic semiconductor companies from 2015 to 2020 and to become a global leader in all segments of the semiconductor supply chain by 2030.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/China_Integrated_Circuit_Industry_Investment_Fund#cite_note-SCMP-4)

According to MIIT, the fund raised US$21.8 billion in its first financing round in 2014.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/China_Integrated_Circuit_Industry_Investment_Fund#cite_note-SCMP-4)[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/China_Integrated_Circuit_Industry_Investment_Fund#cite_note-Caixin-5)[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/China_Integrated_Circuit_Industry_Investment_Fund#cite_note-:2-7) At the start, it deployed at least 60% of its capital into chipmaking investments, according to [GF Securities](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/GF_Securities "GF Securities").[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/China_Integrated_Circuit_Industry_Investment_Fund#cite_note-Caixin-5)[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/China_Integrated_Circuit_Industry_Investment_Fund#cite_note-:3-8) The performance of the first phase exceeded market expectations.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/China_Integrated_Circuit_Industry_Investment_Fund#cite_note-:2-7)[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/China_Integrated_Circuit_Industry_Investment_Fund#cite_note-:3-8)

### Phase II (2019 - 2024)

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=China_Integrated_Circuit_Industry_Investment_Fund&action=edit&section=4 "Edit section: Phase II (2019 - 2024)")]

In 2019, ICF raised US$29.08 billion for its second phase.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/China_Integrated_Circuit_Industry_Investment_Fund#cite_note-Caixin-5)[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/China_Integrated_Circuit_Industry_Investment_Fund#cite_note-:1-6)[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/China_Integrated_Circuit_Industry_Investment_Fund#cite_note-:3-8) 75% of which went into [wafer fabrication](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wafer_fabrication "Wafer fabrication") projects, according to [CSC Financial](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/CSC_Financial "CSC Financial").[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/China_Integrated_Circuit_Industry_Investment_Fund#cite_note-Caixin-5) The investment approach was more conservative than the first phase, mainly focuses on the layout of the integrated circuit industry chain, focusing on chip manufacturing and equipment and materials, chip design, packaging and testing and other industry chain links, and supports the backbone of leading enterprises in the industry to grow bigger and stronger.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/China_Integrated_Circuit_Industry_Investment_Fund#cite_note-:2-7)[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/China_Integrated_Circuit_Industry_Investment_Fund#cite_note-:3-8)

In July 2022, ICF, Sino IC Capital, and several current and former executives were investigated by the [Chinese Communist Party](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chinese_Communist_Party "Chinese Communist Party")'s [Central Commission for Discipline Inspection](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Central_Commission_for_Discipline_Inspection "Central Commission for Discipline Inspection") as part of an anti-[graft](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Graft_(politics) "Graft (politics)") crackdown. The scandal raised questions over the fund's efficiency and future value.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/China_Integrated_Circuit_Industry_Investment_Fund#cite_note-Caixin-5)[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/China_Integrated_Circuit_Industry_Investment_Fund#cite_note-:2-7)[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/China_Integrated_Circuit_Industry_Investment_Fund#cite_note-:4-9)[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/China_Integrated_Circuit_Industry_Investment_Fund#cite_note-:6-10) the fund became dormant for a few months following the anti-graft investigations in July that lead to the downfall of its chief, Ding Wenwu. The fund resumed investment operations in early 2023 and on 10 March, selected Zhang Xin as its new head.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/China_Integrated_Circuit_Industry_Investment_Fund#cite_note-BBG-11)

### Phase III (2024 - 2029)

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=China_Integrated_Circuit_Industry_Investment_Fund&action=edit&section=5 "Edit section: Phase III (2024 - 2029)")]

In September 2023, it was reported that ICF for its third phase was raising money for another fund with a fundraising target of around US$40 billion.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/China_Integrated_Circuit_Industry_Investment_Fund#cite_note-12) In February 2024 it was reported the third fund would raise over US$27 billion. Investors included the [Shanghai Municipal People's Government](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shanghai_Municipal_People's_Government "Shanghai Municipal People's Government") and [State Development and Investment Corporation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/State_Development_and_Investment_Corporation "State Development and Investment Corporation").[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/China_Integrated_Circuit_Industry_Investment_Fund#cite_note-13)

On 24 May 2024, the National Integrated Circuit Industry Investment Fund III Co., Ltd. was established with a registered capital of 344 billion yuan (US$47.5 billion), larger than the first two phases.[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/China_Integrated_Circuit_Industry_Investment_Fund#cite_note-a201-14)[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/China_Integrated_Circuit_Industry_Investment_Fund#cite_note-j845-15) Phase III is expected to continue the semiconductor industry chain "neck" link investment, including large-scale manufacturing and equipment, materials and other links, in addition to the [HBM](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/High_Bandwidth_Memory "High Bandwidth Memory") industry and other key areas of artificial intelligence semiconductor is also expected to obtain the Big Fund III investment.[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/China_Integrated_Circuit_Industry_Investment_Fund#cite_note-a376-16) On 27 May, [ICBC](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/ICBC "ICBC"), [Agricultural Bank of China](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Agricultural_Bank_of_China "Agricultural Bank of China"), [Construction Bank](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/China_Construction_Bank "China Construction Bank"), [Bank of China](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bank_of_China "Bank of China"), [Bank of Communications](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bank_of_Communications "Bank of Communications"), [Postal Savings Bank of China](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Postal_Savings_Bank_of_China "Postal Savings Bank of China") proposed a total of 114 billion yuan of capital, with a shareholding of 33.14%.[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/China_Integrated_Circuit_Industry_Investment_Fund#cite_note-s971-17)

In January 2025, the National [AI](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Artificial_intelligence "Artificial intelligence") Industry Investment fund was launched with an initial capital of 60 billion yuan (US$8.2 billion). It is a joint venture between the Phase III fund and Guozhi Investment (Shanghai) Private Equity Fund Management.[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/China_Integrated_Circuit_Industry_Investment_Fund#cite_note-18)

## Operations

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=China_Integrated_Circuit_Industry_Investment_Fund&action=edit&section=6 "Edit section: Operations")]

CF deploys its capital by holding minority stakes in [publicly traded companies](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Public_company "Public company").[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/China_Integrated_Circuit_Industry_Investment_Fund#cite_note-Caixin-5)[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/China_Integrated_Circuit_Industry_Investment_Fund#cite_note-:2-7) Some of its investments are outside China.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/China_Integrated_Circuit_Industry_Investment_Fund#cite_note-:2-7) It also used to invest in investment firms such as [Oriza Holdings](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oriza_Holdings "Oriza Holdings") via a [fund of funds](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fund_of_funds "Fund of funds") strategy, which allows it to indirectly invest further into more companies such as [Ingenic Semiconductor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ingenic_Semiconductor "Ingenic Semiconductor").[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/China_Integrated_Circuit_Industry_Investment_Fund#cite_note-Caixin-5)[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/China_Integrated_Circuit_Industry_Investment_Fund#cite_note-:2-7) It has achieved success with investments in SMIC and Hua Hong Semiconductor but also has setbacks such as its investment in [Tsinghua Unigroup](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tsinghua_Unigroup "Tsinghua Unigroup"), which had to undergo bankruptcy reorganization.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/China_Integrated_Circuit_Industry_Investment_Fund#cite_note-Caixin-5)[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/China_Integrated_Circuit_Industry_Investment_Fund#cite_note-:2-7)[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/China_Integrated_Circuit_Industry_Investment_Fund#cite_note-:4-9)[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/China_Integrated_Circuit_Industry_Investment_Fund#cite_note-:6-10) The fund was a major tool in advancing the goals of Made in China 2025.[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/China_Integrated_Circuit_Industry_Investment_Fund#cite_note-19):108

The largest shareholders of the fund include the Ministry of Finance, China Development Bank, [China Tobacco](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/China_Tobacco "China Tobacco"), [China Mobile](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/China_Mobile "China Mobile"), and [China Electronics Technology Group Corporation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/China_Electronics_Technology_Group_Corporation "China Electronics Technology Group Corporation"), which are government agencies and state-owned enterprises.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/China_Integrated_Circuit_Industry_Investment_Fund#cite_note-SCMP-4)[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/China_Integrated_Circuit_Industry_Investment_Fund#cite_note-Caixin-5)[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/China_Integrated_Circuit_Industry_Investment_Fund#cite_note-:2-7)[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/China_Integrated_Circuit_Industry_Investment_Fund#cite_note-:6-10)

The fund has a very low profile and does not even have its own website. It is stated to lack transparency.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/China_Integrated_Circuit_Industry_Investment_Fund#cite_note-SCMP-4)[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/China_Integrated_Circuit_Industry_Investment_Fund#cite_note-:6-10)

## Investments

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=China_Integrated_Circuit_Industry_Investment_Fund&action=edit&section=7 "Edit section: Investments")]

The fund's official mandate covers the integrated circuit supply chain, with chip manufacturing as the priority and additional support for design, packaging and testing, equipment, and materials.[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/China_Integrated_Circuit_Industry_Investment_Fund#cite_note-CAC-Guidelines-2014-20)[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/China_Integrated_Circuit_Industry_Investment_Fund#cite_note-MOF-BigFundEstablished-2014-21) Reuters reported in 2024 that the Big Fund had provided financing to [Semiconductor Manufacturing International Corporation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Semiconductor_Manufacturing_International_Corporation "Semiconductor Manufacturing International Corporation") (SMIC), [Hua Hong Semiconductor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hua_Hong_Semiconductor "Hua Hong Semiconductor"), [Yangtze Memory Technologies](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yangtze_Memory_Technologies "Yangtze Memory Technologies") (YMTC), and smaller companies and funds.[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/China_Integrated_Circuit_Industry_Investment_Fund#cite_note-Reuters-BigFundIII-2024-22)

In foundry investments, vehicles under the Big Fund jointly made a US$2.2 billion investment in one of SMIC's plants in 2020. The deal raised the plant's registered capital from US$3.5 billion to US$6.5 billion.[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/China_Integrated_Circuit_Industry_Investment_Fund#cite_note-Reuters-SMICInvestment-2020-23) In 2023, Hua Hong said China IC Fund II would subscribe for RMB shares worth 3 billion yuan as a strategic investor in a proposed share issue.[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/China_Integrated_Circuit_Industry_Investment_Fund#cite_note-Reuters-HuaHongInvestment-2023-24) In 2025, SMIC said it would take full control of SMNC through a share issue to five shareholders, including the National Integrated Circuit Industry Investment Fund.[[25]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/China_Integrated_Circuit_Industry_Investment_Fund#cite_note-Reuters-SMNCDeal-2025-25)

The fund has also backed memory-chip projects. In 2023, registration records showed that the Big Fund had invested 14.56 billion yuan in Changxin Xinqiao, a memory-chip company, giving it 33.15% of the company's registered capital.[[26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/China_Integrated_Circuit_Industry_Investment_Fund#cite_note-Reuters-ChangxinXinqiao-2023-26) Reuters reported that the investment followed a 13 billion-yuan investment in YMTC earlier in 2023.[[26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/China_Integrated_Circuit_Industry_Investment_Fund#cite_note-Reuters-ChangxinXinqiao-2023-26) For the third phase, Reuters reported that one major focus would be equipment for chip manufacturing.[[27]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/China_Integrated_Circuit_Industry_Investment_Fund#cite_note-Reuters-PhaseIII-Planned-2023-27)[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/China_Integrated_Circuit_Industry_Investment_Fund#cite_note-Reuters-BigFundIII-2024-22)

args.summary:
The China Integrated Circuit Industry Investment Fund (ICF), also known as the "Big Fund" (国家大基金), is a Chinese state-owned enterprise established on 26 September 2014 and headquartered in Beijing. It is a China Government Guidance Fund created to achieve national self-sufficiency in the semiconductor industry as part of the "Made in China 2025" plan. The fund has played a significant role in the semiconductor industry in China by funding companies such as SMIC, Hua Hong Semiconductor, and YMTC. As of 2024, it manages US$95.7 billion in assets.

The fund had three phases: Big Fund I (2014-2019), which raised US$21.8 billion in 2014 and deployed at least 60% of capital into chipmaking investments, exceeding market expectations; Big Fund II (2019-2024), which raised US$29.08 billion with 75% going into wafer fabrication projects, but with a more conservative approach focused on the integrated circuit industry chain; and Big Fund III (2024-2029), which was established on 24 May 2024 with registered capital of 344 billion yuan (US$47.5 billion), larger than the first two phases combined. Phase III investors included the Shanghai Municipal People's Government and State Development and Investment Corporation, with six large banks (ICBC, Agricultural Bank of China, Construction Bank, Bank of China, Bank of Communications, Postal Savings Bank of China) contributing 114 billion yuan for a 33.14% stake.

In January 2025, a National AI Industry Investment fund was launched with initial capital of 60 billion yuan (US$8.2 billion), as a joint venture between Phase III and Guozhi Investment (Shanghai) Private Equity Fund Management.

Key shareholders include the Ministry of Finance (36.74%), China Development Bank (22.29%), and China Tobacco (11.14%). The fund's management company is Sino IC Capital. In July 2022, the fund and several executives were investigated by the Chinese Communist Party's Central Commission for Discipline Inspection in an anti-graft crackdown, leading to the downfall of chief Ding Wenwu. The fund became dormant for a few months and resumed operations in early 2023, with Zhang Xin selected as new head on 10 March 2023.

The fund deploys capital by holding minority stakes in publicly traded companies, and has used a fund of funds strategy. It has seen successes with SMIC and Hua Hong Semiconductor but experienced a setback with its investment in Tsinghua Unigroup, which underwent bankruptcy reorganization. The fund is known for its very low profile, lacking its own website and transparency.

Its investments include a US$2.2 billion investment in an SMIC plant in 2020, a 3 billion yuan subscription in Hua Hong shares in 2023, a 14.56 billion yuan investment in Changxin Xinqiao (33.15% stake), and a 13 billion yuan investment in YMTC. The fund has also backed companies including AMEC, ChangXin Memory Technologies, Empyrean Technology, GigaDevice, Hangzhou Changchuan Technology, Hangzhou Silan Microelectronics, Ingenic Semiconductor, JCET, National Silicon Industry Group, Oriza Holdings, Piotech, Shanghai Wanye Enterprises, Tongfu Microelectronics, Tsinghua Unigroup, UNISOC, and ZTE.

Six banks to invest in big way in IC fund

Updated: May 29, 2024 10:47 China Daily [![](/static/2023GW/images/Artical_Print.jpg)](javascript:window.print())

Six major State-owned commercial lenders in China have decided to invest big time in the third-phase State semiconductor investment fund, as Chinese financial institutions ramp up efforts to bolster sci-tech innovations.

The move is seen as part of China's overall push to increase self-reliance in science and technology.

On Monday, the six banks announced their intention to invest in the third phase of the China Integrated Circuit Industry Investment Fund, also known as the Big Fund.

Their planned investments total 114 billion yuan ($15.73 billion), or nearly one-third of the fund, which was officially established on Friday with a registered capital of 344 billion yuan, according to the National Enterprise Credit Information Publicity System, a government-run credit information agency.

Industrial and Commercial Bank of China, Agricultural Bank of China, Bank of China and China Construction Bank plan to contribute 21.5 billion yuan each to the fund within 10 years from its establishment, which will give them a 6.25 percent share each.

Bank of Communications plans to invest 20 billion yuan while Postal Savings Bank of China is looking to invest 8 billion yuan. The six banks will make up 33.14 percent of the fund's total capital.

Zeng Shengjun, a senior researcher at the Shenzhen, Guangdong province-based Greater Bay Area Financial Research Institute of Bank of China, said the move indicates major State-owned lenders are expected to play a bigger role in fostering new quality productive forces.

"The banks will likely intensify financial support while offering a range of financing services such as technology innovation loans and industrial chain finance to support specific projects," Zeng said.

"They can also leverage on their expertise in risk assessment for high-tech industries, to assist the fund better, preventing and managing project risks. In addition, they can help attract high-quality investment and introduce advanced technologies from overseas."

The banks said that all the capital for this investment will come from their own financial resources. This investment represents a strategic deployment that is in line with the nation's key policies for the development of the integrated circuit industry, their own development strategies and available business resources, they said.

Zhang Xin, a former official from the Ministry of Industry and Information Technology, will serve as the fund's legal representative.

Industry sources said the third-generation semiconductors requiring materials like silicon carbide and gallium nitride are likely to be an investment focus for the third phase of the Big Fund.

In February 2023, Zhang, then working with the MIIT, visited Shunyi district in Beijing to guide the development of third-generation semiconductor technologies, the sources said.

Zhang Yi, CEO of iiMedia Research, said the third phase of the fund has diversified its investment areas. These areas not only include equity investments and asset management, but extend to venture capital fund management services.

"This change means that the Big Fund will invest across a broader scope, significantly enhancing the flexibility and diversity of its investment strategies," Zhang said.

China Fortune Securities said in a research report that the main investment targets of the first two phases of the Big Fund focused on semiconductor equipment and materials, laying a solid foundation for the initial development of China's chip industry.

With the vigorous development of the digital economy and the artificial intelligence sector, AI chips and memory chips are becoming key parts in the industrial chain. The third phase of the Big Fund is likely to focus on high-value-added DRAM chips, in addition to continuing its support for semiconductor equipment and materials, China Fortune Securities said.

DRAM chips refer to dynamic random access memory chips, which are flash memory semiconductors widely used in smartphones, personal computers and servers.

The first phase of the Big Fund was established in 2014 with a registered capital of 138.7 billion yuan and the second phase followed in 2019 with 204 billion yuan.

# The Big Fund in Context

Written By [Nathan Picarsic](/essays?author=5e0f785e4ea7e32167e267ae)

**Understanding China’s Semiconductor Playbook**

*by Alexandra Hartman*

The third phase of China’s Big Fund — the National Integrated Circuit Industry Investment Fund — was launched on May 24. The fund’s 19 shareholders, which include China’s Ministry of Finance and the China Development Bank, have recapitalized the fund with a total of 344 billion RMB (about $47.5 billion).

Because the Big Fund invests in the PRC’s domestic chip industry, the natural impulse of many in the West is to [frame](https://fortune.com/asia/2024/05/27/beijing-biden-chips-act-big-fund-iii-chinas-semiconductor-investment-fund/) the new funding tranche as responsive to the US’ CHIPS Act or at least to [compare](https://www.morningstar.com/news/dow-jones/202405271617/china-unveils-48-billion-fund-to-bolster-chip-industry ) it to the scope of CHIPS Act funds. That framing risks misunderstanding the PRC’s comprehensive State-led technological development program. That program, which long predates the CHIPS Act and the Big Fund’s latest tranche, includes not only investment but also government direction and subsidization, preferential tax policies, and a variety of other tools to advance its aims. Understanding the full scope of those activities is crucial to any meaningful attempt by the US or its allies to compete with the PRC — in semiconductors and more broadly, across industrial and science and technology domains.

China pursues its semiconductor ambitions through a varied toolkit. On the direct funding front, the Chinese government’s capital dedicated for semiconductor companies dwarfs that of the US. The CHIPS Act directed about [$50 billion](https://spectrum.ieee.org/chips-act-funding) towards semiconductor research and development and fab construction, which is to be deployed primarily as grants and tax incentives; the [three rounds](https://baijiahao.baidu.com/s?id=1800256553043935974&wfr=spider&for=pc) of the Big Fund total to over [$95 billion](https://www.cnn.com/2024/05/27/tech/china-semiconductor-investment-fund-intl-hnk/index.html), deployed as equity investments. And that figure does not include the myriad other benefits, financial and otherwise, that the Chinese government gives its semiconductor companies.

China has also been at this longer: The first round of the Big Fund started deploying in [2014](https://www.cnn.com/2024/05/27/tech/china-semiconductor-investment-fund-intl-hnk/index.html). The latest funding round is not a response to the CHIPS Act, but rather the continuation of a long-running, systematic, and highly complex government-led financial and industrial policy program designed to foster innovative companies, capture key supply chain nodes, and dominate global semiconductor manufacturing.

The American approach is much more limited. The US has provided funding for factory construction and has implemented outbound restrictions on sales of certain advanced chips, materials, and manufacturing equipment to Chinese companies. China, on the other hand, pursues a “state led, enterprise driven” economic model, in which the Chinese government is *the* dominant market actor and shaper. In practice, this means that the PRC’s chips program includes government-controlled venture capital and other funding streams; influence over private investors; government-supported corporate-university partnerships and collaborative organizations; and preferential tax policies and government support for key emerging semiconductor companies that subsidize everything from equipment upgrading to labor.

NAURA Technology Group provides an example of that crossover. It received an investment of about [1.5 billion RMB](https://baijiahao.baidu.com/s?id=1715325687574335240&wfr=spider&for=pc) from the second phase of the Big Fund in 2021, the same year in which it was [named](https://www.naura.com/about/honor.html) a [“little giant,”](https://www.gov.cn/zhengce/zhengceku/202404/content_6946071.htm) a PRC government industrial policy program that recognizes small and medium-sized enterprises at key value chain nodes and provides [subsidies](https://zhuanlan.zhihu.com/p/451366900), business development support, and collaboration with industry leaders. NAURA is also involved in major PRC semiconductor industry associations, key hubs that facilitate collaboration among companies and inform industrial standards and policy. That support seems to have paid off; NAURA provided equipment for [SMIC’s new factory](https://www.wsj.com/tech/chinese-semiconductor-industry-smic-self-sufficient-5210abf8) outside Beijing, as part of the company and the country’s attempts to decouple semiconductor manufacturing from US inputs.

Other early Big Fund targets included [CXMT](https://www.chipriskmonitor.com/crm-cxmt) and [YMTC](https://www.chipriskmonitor.com/crm-ymtc), both of which are now major players in the PRC and international chips industry. YMTC [received](https://baijiahao.baidu.com/s?id=1759256650733024656&wfr=spider&for=pc) about 13 billion RMB in investment from Big Fund Phase 1 and over 30 billion RMB in two stages from Big Fund Phase 2. In February 2023, during Big Fund Phase 2’s second investment into YMTC, Hubei Changsheng Development Co., Ltd. also invested 30 billion RMB. One of Hubei Changsheng’s three shareholders at that time was the Hubei Integrated Circuit Industry Investment Fund, which is Hubei Province’s version of the Big Fund. In March of this year, that same Hubei Big Fund invested in [Wuhan Xinxin (XMC)](https://www.thepaper.cn/newsDetail_forward_26576973), which had been established in 2006, was a major part of the establishment of YMTC, and later became its wholly-owned subsidiary. XMC is now reportedly planning an IPO; some [commentators](https://baijiahao.baidu.com/s?id=1798748929560542374&wfr=spider&for=pc) have suggested that this move is intended to help YMTC expand and access more capital. It will also likely generate returns for at least the Hubei Big Fund, and possibly the national Big Fund as well.

This network of financial connections illustrates the complexity of the PRC’s state-led chip development program. In order to effectively respond to the challenge that the PRC’s policies create, it is critical to understand how those policies interact with each other; how they influence market and non-market actors; and the commercial, financial, and industrial realities they shape.

Accurate understanding of the full scope of the PRC’s semiconductor program can inform more comprehensive and effective approaches to countering that threat. Current US tools, like the Commerce Department’s Entity List, tend to be piecemeal and reactive, responding to entities once they are already in a position to create problems rather than anticipating developments based on a full view of the PRC system. For instance, XMC is not on the Entity List, despite its relationship with YMTC. If XMC’s planned IPO occurs, foreign investors could end up supporting a key commercial player in China’s efforts to dominate the global semiconductor supply chain. But simply subjecting that one company to restrictions will not solve the problem, because YMTC and fellow Big Fund beneficiaries can continue to create subsidiaries and find other ways around the regulations.

The last ten years have made obvious the power of Beijing’s Big Fund and the larger, comprehensive semiconductor development program of which it is a part. They have also made clear the importance of mapping and understanding the web of policies, agencies, associations, and companies in that program. Disagreement about how the US should counter that program is to be expected and can be productive. But first we need to understand what we’re actually facing.

—*Alexandra Hartman, an Analyst at* [*Horizon Advisory*](https://www.horizonadvisory.org)

args.summary:
This essay from the Chip Risk Monitor, written by Alexandra Hartman (Analyst at Horizon Advisory), analyzes China's National Integrated Circuit Industry Investment Fund ("Big Fund") and argues that Western observers mischaracterize it by viewing it primarily as a response to the US CHIPS Act. The essay contends that the Big Fund is instead part of a comprehensive, long-running State-led technological development program that predates the CHIPS Act and includes not only investment but also government direction, subsidization, preferential tax policies, and other tools.

Key facts: The third phase of the Big Fund was launched on May 24, capitalized at 344 billion RMB (about $47.5 billion) by 19 shareholders including China's Ministry of Finance and the China Development Bank. The US CHIPS Act directed about $50 billion primarily as grants and tax incentives, while China's three rounds of the Big Fund total over $95 billion deployed as equity investments — dwarfing US direct funding. The first Big Fund round began in 2014, establishing that the program long predates the CHIPS Act.

The essay describes China's "state led, enterprise driven" model, in which the government is the dominant market actor, employing controlled venture capital, influence over private investors, corporate-university partnerships, preferential taxes, and subsidies for equipment upgrading and labor.

The essay provides examples of the interconnected network: NAURA Technology Group received ~1.5 billion RMB from Big Fund Phase 2 in 2021 and was named a "little giant" (a PRC industrial policy program), and supplied equipment for SMIC's new factory near Beijing. Other early Big Fund targets include CXMT and YMTC. YMTC received ~13 billion RMB from Phase 1 and over 30 billion RMB in two stages from Phase 2, with Hubei's provincial-level fund (Hubei Integrated Circuit Industry Investment Fund) also investing. In March 2025, the Hubei Big Fund invested in Wuhan Xinxin (XMC), a YMTC subsidiary reportedly planning an IPO to help YMTC expand and raise capital.

The essay concludes that the US approach is limited and reactive — tools like the Commerce Department's Entity List respond piecemeal to entities after problems arise (XMC is not on the Entity List despite its YMTC relationship). It argues that understanding the full web of policies, agencies, associations, and companies is critical to effectively countering China's program, as restrictions on single companies are insufficient since Big Fund beneficiaries can create subsidiaries and work around regulations.

The Inflation Reduction Act (IRA) became law on August 16, 2022. Despite its name, the act was mostly designed to decarbonize the US economy by providing subsidies to producers of clean energy and consumers of low-carbon-emitting preferred products such as electric vehicles.

A contentious point of debate surrounding the passage of the IRA was its budgetary impact—how much liability American taxpayers would have to take on to subsidize clean energy. Various governmental and nongovernmental organizations estimated fiscal costs that turned out to be too low and that they later revised upward.

Using a transparent budget scoring methodology, we estimate that the energy subsidies in the act will cost between $936 billion and $1.97 trillion over the next 10 years, and between $2.04 trillion and $4.67 trillion by 2050. This estimate is substantial because several of the IRA’s largest subsidies are uncapped.
