# Norway’s oil fund shows gap between climate risk insight and action

## Action on climate by Norway fund is constrained by political mandate and uncertain policy environment

June 10, 2026|Written by [Emma Thomasson](https://greencentralbanking.com/author/emma-thomasson/ "Posts by Emma Thomasson")

![An oil refinery in the ocean off the coast of Norway.](https://greencentralbanking.com/wp-content/smush-webp/2026/06/1280px-Troll_A_Nordsjoen_28530306416-1024x798.jpg.webp)

Photo: Wikimedia Commons

## Key Points

* Norway’s oil fund, NBIM, has not applied its framework for measuring climate and nature risk into moving away from fossil fuels, a report from Carbon Tracker finds.
* The mismatch is due to a mandate limit, political expectations, and an increasingly uncertain global climate policy environment.
* The findings reveal the limits of voluntary investor action.

Norway’s oil fund (NBIM) has developed one of the most advanced frameworks for measuring climate and nature risk, but it has yet to apply those insights to shift strategy and move capital away from fossil fuels, according to a new [report](https://carbontracker.org/reports/ambition-under-pressure-analytical-leadership-vs-strategic-hesitation/) about the world’s biggest asset manager.

The report into NBIM by independent financial think tank Carbon Tracker shows that financial markets may be significantly [underestimating the true scale and immediacy of climate risk](https://greencentralbanking.com/2025/07/15/climate-risk-stocks/), with a quarter of NBIM’s equity portfolio already exposed to severe physical climate hazards.

However, Carbon Tracker highlighted a growing discrepancy between insight and action at [NBIM](https://www.nbim.no/en/investments/the-funds-value/), which has over US$2.3tn in assets and holds about 1.5% of the world’s listed companies.

“NBIM’s analysis shows that physical climate risk is already a valuation issue. But there is a gap between what the data shows and what the fund feels able to do in response. That raises important questions for investors and policymakers alike,” said Amy Owens, financial policy analyst at Carbon Tracker.

Carbon Tracker said this mismatch was due to many factors: mandate limitations, political expectations, antitrust considerations and an increasingly uncertain environment for global climate policy.

“These constraints materially influence the scope and pace of strategic  action, underscoring the financial relevance of policy risk for large, diversified, long-term investors,” the report said. “Growing climate policy uncertainty is itself becoming financially material for  long-term investors.”

## NBIM investment in fossil fuels

NBIM, which is bound by a mandate from the Norwegian parliament that focuses on maximising returns, is still a major investor in fossil fuels, although it says it is working to encourage the companies it invests in to align their operations with the goals of the Paris Agreement.

In 2024, German environment NGO [Urgewald](https://investinginclimatechaos.org/reports) said Norway’s oil fund was Europe’s largest fossil fuel investor with investments of over US$70bn.

NBIM says 23% of its equity portfolio by value is exposed to severe physical climate hazards already today. It currently has shareholdings in about 7,200 companies

Carbon Tracker noted that NBIM’s ability to influence companies it invests in is limited by its mandate from the Norwegian government and the political contexts of the countries in which it invests, compounded by the current global backlash against more ethical investing.

“Taken together, these dynamics leave NBIM operating within a narrow corridor of influence. It must balance stewardship ambitions with legal, political and market structure constraints that restrict how far it can push individual companies or broader market standards,” the report said.

Dina Rui, from the Nordic Center for Sustainable Finance, said it was up to the Norwegian parliament to steer the oil fund away from fossil fuels, noting that the fund continues to buy bonds in oil and gas companies funding new exploration like TotalEnergies.

“It’s up to the parliament to direct them to exclude fossil fuel companies,” she said.

## Limits of voluntary investor action

In April, NBIM came under [fire](https://nordsip.com/2026/04/24/nbim-backs-bp-chair-manifold-at-contested-agm/) when it said [it would vote in favour](https://www.nbim.no/no/ansvarlig-forvaltning/stemmegiving/var-stemmegivning/meeting?m=2050509) of the election of the chair of oil major BP and other board-supported resolutions, while opposing a shareholder resolution seeking extra disclosures on how BP’s capital allocation, including oil and gas spending, aligns with shareholder value.

The number of companies NBIM engaged with on climate issues fell 11% in 2025, according to its climate and nature risk [disclosures](https://www.nbim.no/contentassets/e4662a16b2e147538c1555a05e5e0935/climate-and-nature-disclosures_2025_uu.pdf). Carbon Tracker noted the fund had softened its language on the impact of its engagement on corporate practices.

Last November, the Norwegian government announced it had set up a committee to review NBIM’s [ethical framework](https://www.regjeringen.no/en/topics/the-economy/the-government-pension-fund/responsible-management/ethical-guidelines/id447009/) after a heated debate over its investments in Israeli companies and global tech giants. The committee is due to report back by Oct. 15.

That has resulted in the temporary suspension of NBIM’s powers to exclude or divest from certain companies, including on the basis of climate or nature-related concerns.

Carbon Tracker said its report into NBIM show that voluntary investor action alone is insufficient to address the scale and nature of climate risk.

“Policymakers and regulators therefore have a central role to play, especially in countries which have ambitious emissions reduction targets and climate policies,” it said. “Clearer policy signals and more robust supervisory frameworks are essential to reduce market-wide mispricing of climate and nature risks.”

args.summary:
This article from Green Central Banking (June 10, 2026, by Emma Thomasson) reports on a Carbon Tracker analysis revealing a gap between climate risk insight and action at Norway's oil fund (NBIM), the world's largest asset manager with over US$2.3tn in assets holding about 1.5% of the world's listed companies.

Key findings:
- NBIM has developed one of the most advanced frameworks for measuring climate and nature risk but has not applied these insights to shift capital away from fossil fuels.
- A quarter of NBIM's equity portfolio is already exposed to severe physical climate hazards, and 23% of its equity portfolio by value is exposed to such hazards today. It holds shares in about 7,200 companies.
- NBIM remains Europe's largest fossil fuel investor, with over US$70bn in fossil fuel investments in 2024 (per German NGO Urgewald).
- The mismatch between insight and action stems from mandate limitations (NBIM is bound by a Norwegian parliamentary mandate focused on maximizing returns), political expectations, antitrust considerations, and increasing global climate policy uncertainty.

Notable events:
- In April 2026, NBIM came under fire for voting in favor of BP board-supported resolutions (including election of the chair) while opposing a shareholder resolution seeking extra disclosures on how BP's capital allocation aligns with shareholder value.
- The number of companies NBIM engaged with on climate issues fell 11% in 2025.
- In November 2025, the Norwegian government set up a committee to review NBIM's ethical framework after debate over investments in Israeli companies and tech giants. This led to temporary suspension of NBIM's powers to exclude or divest from companies, including on climate/nature grounds. The committee reports by Oct. 15, 2026.

Expert quotes and conclusions:
- Amy Owens (Carbon Tracker financial policy analyst): "NBIM's analysis shows that physical climate risk is already a valuation issue. But there is a gap between what the data shows and what the fund feels able to do in response."
- Dina Rui (Nordic Center for Sustainable Finance): "It's up to the parliament to direct them to exclude fossil fuel companies" — noting the fund continues buying bonds in oil and gas companies funding new exploration like TotalEnergies.
- Carbon Tracker concludes that voluntary investor action alone is insufficient to address climate risk; clearer policy signals and more robust supervisory frameworks are essential to reduce market-wide mispricing of climate and nature risks.

# Observation and exclusion of companies

Until November 2025, the Executive Board of Norges Bank decided whether companies should be excluded from the fund's investment universe or placed on an observation list, in accordance with guidelines established by the Ministry of Finance.

The Executive Board's decisions on exclusion or observation of companies were based on recommendations from the Council on Ethics, which is appointed by the Ministry of Finance. For the product-based coal criterion, recommendations came from Norges Bank Investment Management.

[The Government has appointed](https://www.regjeringen.no/en/whats-new/the-government-follows-up-on-the-parliaments-decision-regarding-the-ethical-framework-for-the-pension-fund/id3136331/ "See the press release") a committee to review the ethical framework. The committee is to deliver its report by 15 October 2026. Pending a new framework, the Ministry of Finance has established temporary ethical guidelines.

Under the temporary ethical guidelines, Norges Bank shall not decide on observation or exclusion, but may revoke previous decisions on observation and exclusion. The Council on Ethics shall continue to monitor the fund's investments and inform Norges Bank about companies identified for possible exercise of ownership.

This webpage from Norges Bank provides an alphabetical overview of companies that have been excluded from, or placed on observation within, the Government Pension Fund Global's (GPFG) investment universe, as decided by Norges Bank as of November 2025.

**Decision Process and Recent Changes:**
- Until November 2025, the Executive Board of Norges Bank decided on exclusions and observations based on recommendations from the Council on Ethics (appointed by the Ministry of Finance). For the product-based coal criterion, recommendations came from Norges Bank Investment Management.
- The Government has appointed a committee to review the ethical framework, which must deliver its report by 15 October 2026. Pending the new framework, the Ministry of Finance has established temporary ethical guidelines.
- Under the temporary guidelines, Norges Bank can no longer decide on new observation or exclusion but may revoke previous decisions. The Council on Ethics continues monitoring investments and informing Norges Bank about companies for possible ownership measures.

**Categorization of Exclusions/Observations:**
The table lists roughly 170 companies with details on category (Product-based or Conduct-based), criterion, decision (Exclusion or Observation), and publishing date.

- **Product-based criteria** include: Production of coal or coal-based energy (the largest category, with dozens of companies excluded starting 14.04.2016); Production of nuclear weapons (e.g., Airbus, Boeing, BAE Systems, General Dynamics, Lockheed Martin, L3Harris, Honeywell); Production of tobacco (e.g., Altria, British American Tobacco, Philip Morris, Japan Tobacco, Imperial Brands); Production of cluster munitions (Poongsan Corp, Textron); Production of cannabis (Aurora Cannabis, Canopy Growth, Cronos, Tilray Brands).
- **Conduct-based criteria** include: Serious violations of individuals' rights in situations of war or conflict (e.g., numerous Israeli companies such as Bank Hapoalim, Bank Leumi, Elbit Systems, plus GAIL India, Korea Gas); Severe environmental damage (e.g., Vale SA, Glencore-related, Duke Energy, Norilsk Nickel, Zijin Mining); Violation of human rights (e.g., Bollore SE, Ecopetrol, Formosa Chemicals); Gross corruption (e.g., ZTE, JBS, China State Construction); Unacceptable greenhouse gas emissions (Canadian Natural Resources, Cenovus, Imperial Oil, Suncor); Sales of weapons to states in armed conflicts or to states subject to GPFG bond restrictions.

**Most recent decisions** (published in 2025-2026) include: Adani Green Energy (exclusion, 26.02.2026, gross corruption); Bollore SE, Compagnie de l'Odet SE, Ecopetrol SA (exclusion, 26.02.2026, violation of human rights); Dian Swastatika Sentosa Tbk PT (exclusion, 26.02.2026, coal); Caterpillar Inc. (exclusion, 25.08.2025); Eramet SA (exclusion, 12.09.2025); Toronto-Dominion Bank (observation, 11.06.2025, gross corruption); Paz Retail And Energy Ltd and Petroleos Mexicanos (exclusion, 11.05.2025); RWE AG (observation, 11.05.2025, coal); Fincantieri SpA (observation, 06.02.2025); RLX Technology (exclusion, 15.01.2025, tobacco).

**Note:** This is a long reference table best used as a lookup resource. Key structural facts: decisions span from 01.01.2006 through 26.02.2026, with criteria divided into product-based (tobacco, coal, nuclear weapons, cluster munitions, cannabis) and conduct-based (human rights, environmental damage, corruption, war conflict violations, greenhouse gas emissions, weapons sales) categories.

## Highlights

*   •Negative screening does not harm sovereign [wealth](https://www.sciencedirect.com/topics/social-sciences/wealth) funds’ financial performance. 
*   •Oil [divestment](https://www.sciencedirect.com/topics/economics-econometrics-and-finance/disinvestment) does not decrease the financial performance of [sovereign wealth funds](https://www.sciencedirect.com/topics/economics-econometrics-and-finance/sovereign-wealth-fund). 
*   •Negative screening decreases the risk exposure of sovereign [wealth](https://www.sciencedirect.com/topics/social-sciences/wealth) funds. 

## Abstract

This paper examines the effects of negative screening on the financial performance of [sovereign wealth funds](https://www.sciencedirect.com/topics/economics-econometrics-and-finance/sovereign-wealth-fund) (SWFs). SWFs have been under pressure to invest responsibly and divest from [fossil fuel](https://www.sciencedirect.com/topics/agricultural-and-biological-sciences/fossil-fuel) firms by their respective governments and citizens. Yet, such a strategy may reduce the financial performance of these funds. This study examines the extent to which excluding [fossil fuel](https://www.sciencedirect.com/topics/agricultural-and-biological-sciences/fossil-fuel) firms from SWF portfolios in order to comply with ethical standards reduces their financial performance. By using asset pricing models, namely the [capital asset](https://www.sciencedirect.com/topics/social-sciences/capital-assets) pricing model and the Carhart four-factor model, we find that excluding firms has a statistically insignificant impact on the financial performance of SWFs. We document similar results regarding the performance of SWF fossil fuel portfolios, suggesting that fossil fuel [divestment](https://www.sciencedirect.com/topics/economics-econometrics-and-finance/disinvestment) will not impact SWF performance. We also test for differences between “extraction and production” and “refining and integrated” fossil fuel firms to explain why some SWFs divest only from extraction and production firms. Our findings indicate that, to some extent, extraction and production companies generate lower returns. We conclude that [socially responsible investment](https://www.sciencedirect.com/topics/social-sciences/socially-responsible-investment), by negative screening of fossil fuel firms does not reduce SWF performance.

## Introduction

On October 1st, 2019, the Norwegian Ministry of Finance announced that the Government Pension Fund Global (GPFG) of Norway—the country’s sovereign wealth fund (SWF)—would divest from companies whose main core business is dedicated to oil and gas exploration and production.1 Similarly, other SWFs, such as the New Zealand Superannuation Fund (NZSF), announced their intention to reduce the carbon emissions of their portfolios to combat climate change.2 However, it seems that this campaign concerns firms mostly operating in fossil fuel extraction and production while refining companies are not affected.

Negative screening, which excludes firms from portfolios due to social, environmental, or governance issues, has been widely used by responsible SWFs since 2010 as a strategy to implement socially responsible investment (SRI). In fact, several SWFs, like the GPFG of Norway or the NZSF, have used negative screening to exclude from their portfolios firms that did not comply with their ethical guidelines or SRI policies (Jensen and Seele, 2013). The main reasons for these exclusions can be classified into two categories: norm-based and sector-based exclusions (Al Ayoubi and Enjolras, 2021). The first category concerned companies that were reported for violating specific social norms, such as child labor and human rights, while the second category concerned firms whose business is related to so-called “sin stocks,” such as alcohol, tobacco, gambling (Fabozzi et al., 2008), and other sectors such as coal extraction that may harm the environment. Because more and more investors are implementing a social and ethical strategy, SWFs are increasingly incentivized to adopt SRI.

First, although SWFs are created and owned by governments and therefore do not have explicit liabilities, such funds are nevertheless indirectly owned by the public since they serve the purpose of increasing wealth for future generations (Seele et al., 2015). Hence, institutional investors should not only act in the best interest of their beneficiaries—that is, to maximize the financial performance of their portfolios without undue risk—but also behave responsibly and ethically. In fact, as public institutional investors, SWFs have the fiduciary duty to act in the best interests of their beneficiaries in the long term, which goes beyond economic and financial considerations (Karametaxas, 2017).

Second, the sheer scale of SWF investments in recent years has raised public and legal concerns. For instance, during the financial crisis of 2008, SWFs injected significant liquidity into distressed institutions in Europe and the United States, including a capital investment in UBS Group AG of USD 11.4 billion by the Singapore Investment Corporation, or an investment in Citigroup of USD 7.5 billion by the Abu Dhabi Investment Authority.3 The investment of such significant sums has raised concerns in recipient countries over the lack of transparency about the motivations behind such financing. Such concerns have led the relevant authorities to defend their actions to protect strategic sectors related to energy, technology, and finance. Moreover, the public in the home countries of several SWFs have expressed their desire for exemplary behavior in light of reported institutional investors’ social and ethical footprint (Clark and Monk, 2010).

Following recent financial, economic, social, and environmental crises, we are witnessing the strengthening of a collective consciousness concerning environmental, social, and governance issues. This is reflected in the fact that public opinion considers investors responsible for the business behavior of the firms in which they invest (Hoepner and Schopohl, 2020, Blanc and Cozic, 2012). This is the case for many SWFs (mainly in democratic countries) that have been criticized for their investments in controversial sectors such as the nuclear and weapons industries, in addition to firms that violated human, child, and labor rights. Since those public funds manage considerable state-owned assets on behalf of the people (the implicit owners of those assets), they are constantly under public scrutiny (Richardson, 2011).

In response to public pressure, some SWFs (with the approval of regulatory authorities) have shifted toward a more responsible investment strategy. In order to implement SRI and reassure the public, several funds—the GPFG of Norway, the NZSF, the French Pension Reserve fund (FRR), the Ireland Strategic Investment Fund (ISIF), and the Future Fund of Australia (FFA)—have adopted negative screening and excluded from their portfolios companies that conducted the abovementioned sin activities, companies that damaged the environment (e.g., the GPFG and the FRR excluded coal-based companies), and firms reported to have violated human and labor rights. Moreover, with increasing awareness of climate change, public opinion has become increasingly skeptical about the environmental impact of the oil and gas industry, and campaigns have emerged to encourage SWFs to sell their stakes in this sector. This is the case in Norway, New Zealand, and Alaska 4 where public and political pressure is mounting for the respective funds of these states to exclude firms related to oil and gas production and extraction.

From the investors’ point of view, there are concerns about the effect on financial performance of such exclusionary strategies. Withholding investment from some industries can be expected to have a financial cost due to the reduction in opportunities for portfolio diversification (Barnett and Salomon, 2006). An important stream of the literature analyzing the impact of exclusions on financial performance found that investors could suffer from an opportunity cost insofar as screened portfolios do not benefit from the superior profitability offered by sin stocks (Hong and Kacperczyk, 2009, Trinks and Scholtens, 2017). A dilemma might then exist in choosing between financial performance or favoring ethical and responsible behavior since it seems that being responsible (by employing negative screening) comes with a cost. SWFs that implemented or are considering implementing SRI are also affected, especially since they are more sensitive to their beneficiaries’ claims as public investors and may be urged to adopt SRI.

This study aims to examine the validity of the apparent dilemma between financial performance and ethical requirements. We investigate the case of SWFs that apply an exclusionary strategy and discuss the effects on their financial returns of excluding firms from their portfolios. Although this issue has been addressed in previous research related to sin stocks and the effect of exclusions on sustainable indexes and SRI private funds (Endrikat, 2016), little is known about how negative screening may impact the financial performance of SWFs. To the best of our knowledge, one study examined the case of the GPFG as well as the Swedish AP-Funds (Hoepner and Schopohl, 2018) and found that negative screening did not harm fund performance, meaning that the Norwegian fund “can meet the ethical objectives of their beneficiaries without compromising financial returns.”

The first novelty in our study is that we include other SWFs with an exclusion strategy and examine if their financial performance is affected, namely the FRR, the NZSF, the Alaska Permanent Fund (APF), the ISIF, and the GPFG. These five SWFs have excluded firms that did not respect their ethical policies even though their proprietary criteria for exclusion may differ. The scope of excluded industries, as well as the intensity of screening, depends on the funds and so there is some divergence. For instance, the GPFG excludes from its investment portfolio companies involved in the production of coal, which is not the case for the other SWFs considered. This paper examines whether the nature and intensity of screening by SWFs has affected their financial performance.

We distinguish between the so-called “common” exclusions and fossil fuel exclusions (as referred to in the literature). Common exclusions refer to businesses that are considered to be non-compliant with certain social standards, such as the production of conventional and nuclear weapons, the sale of alcohol and tobacco, use of child labor, etc. This type of exclusion dominates the literature on the relationship between negative screening and financial performance. Fossil fuel exclusions refer to companies operating in the fossil fuel sector. This type of exclusion has been largely ignored in the negative screening literature since the fossil fuel sector is not necessarily considered “sinful”.5 However, this sector has a significant impact on the environment, which explains the recent wave of divestment from this sector. A review of the negative screening literature shows that several industries and activities are regularly considered sinful. By contrast, operating in the fossil fuel industry—more specifically, gas and oil firms—is rarely considered a reason for divestment, despite the emergence of divestment campaigns in developed countries. To date, no SWF has effectively divested from all fossil fuel firms; the main exception concerns coal and coal-based firms, which have been partially excluded from the portfolio of several SWFs such as the GPFG of Norway or the ISIF. For instance, the GPFG excludes firms that derive at least 30% of their income from the production of thermal coal or coal-based power production.6 Nevertheless, responsible SWFs—including the GPFG and the ISIF—have expressed their intention to divest from other fossil fuel firms related to oil and gas production, and other SWFs are seriously examining the issue. For instance, in 2018, the FRR affirmed its commitment to reduce its carbon emissions and invest more in a low-carbon economy by excluding companies whose thermal coal mining activity or production of electricity, heat, or steam from coal exceeds 10% of their turnover.7 Similarly, the NZSF aims to reduce by 80% its ownership of fossil fuel reserves by 2025.8 Hence, we both expand the field of screens applied by some SWFs by adding the oil and gas sectors and analyze their impact on the financial performance of considered funds.

The third novelty of this paper is to distinguish between extraction and production firms and refining and integrated firms. (It should be noted that SWFs willing to divest from the fossil fuel industry have expressed their intention to keep stakes in refining, downstream, and some integrated oil firms.) One of the reasons given for the distinction between “oil and gas extraction and production” and “refining and integrated” firms is that the second category has the financial and technological capacities to shift toward renewable energy, and therefore has a lower environmental negative impact.9 One could question the real motives behind the distinction, but we distinguish between “fossil fuel extraction and production” and “refining and integrated” firms to identify any differences between the two groups in terms of financial returns which might explain the distinction made by SWFs.

Moreover, this study aims to enrich the negative screening literature, especially on oil and gas divestment, by means of real-world-based portfolio analyses. While much of the literature on exclusionary strategies uses hypothetical or “fictive” portfolios to examine the financial impact of the exclusions, we consider real-world-based SWF portfolios. This allows to examine the impact of negative screening on the financial performance of those funds, and therefore account for real-world investment restrictions (Adamsson and Hoepner, 2015).

This study proposes to combine several fields of literature, namely negative screening, oil divestments, and responsible SWF investments. By focusing on responsible SWFs, we analyze the impact of one of their main SRI strategies (i.e., negative screening) on financial performance. We refine the general framework of sinful issues considered in the negative screening literature by including the fossil fuel sector. Examining whether exclusionary strategies harm the financial returns of SWFs is challenging given that these funds are public institutional investors with no explicit liabilities. This means that SWFs are supposed to allocate their assets in the best interests of the people, not only in terms of financial performance but also in terms of social and environmental performance. Because contemporary public opinion seems to favor fossil fuel divestment and a transition toward renewable energies, SWFs could play an important role in achieving these objectives: as state-owned companies, they may be used by authorities as a tool to reduce the social and environmental impact of their investments and encourage private stakeholders to follow suit in the long term.

Through developing various asset pricing models, namely the capital asset pricing model and the Carhart four-factor model, we assess the impact of negative screening on the financial performance of five SWFs. Data on exclusions from these funds was collected from their websites as well as from various reports they publish. We distinguish between the so-called “common” exclusions and fossil fuel exclusions. We do not observe a significant impact of “common” exclusions, implying that negative screening does not hurt the returns of SWFs. Regarding fossil fuel exclusions, we distinguish between “extraction and production” and “refining and integrated” fossil fuel firms’ exclusions. Our results suggest that, to some extent, extraction and production firms generate lower returns, implying that excluding these firms should be beneficial for SWFs. To ensure the validity of our results, we also control for regional factors by developing a two-level Carhart model and examine the risk implication of negative screening. Besides this work’s academic contribution to the negative screening and SWF literature, the main novelty of this study rests in addressing the recent disinvestment campaign from fossil fuel firms undertaken by responsible SWFs. The findings suggest that it is possible for these funds not to suffer from an opportunity cost for meeting their ethical standards, which should encourage other SWFs and institutional investors to engage in negative screening.

This paper is organized as follows. An overview of the literature regarding responsible SWFs and negative screening is presented in the next section. Thereafter, Section 3 presents development of the hypotheses being tested in the paper. In Section 4, we present the data and methodology used in this paper. The empirical results are presented in Section 5, and we present our conclusions in Section 6.

args.summary:
This research article, published in the Journal of Multinational Financial Management (Vol. 64, June 2022) by Khalil Al Ayoubi and Geoffroy Enjolras, examines whether disinvestment from fossil fuels reduces the financial performance of responsible sovereign wealth funds (SWFs). The study investigates the effects of negative screening on SWF financial performance, driven by public and governmental pressure on SWFs to divest from fossil fuel firms.

Key findings from the study:
- Negative screening does not harm SWFs' financial performance
- Oil divestment does not decrease SWF financial performance
- Negative screening actually decreases the risk exposure of SWFs

Methodology: The researchers used the capital asset pricing model and the Carhart four-factor model to analyze the impact of negative screening on five SWFs over the period 2005-2019: the GPFG of Norway, the French Pension Reserve Fund (FRR), the New Zealand Superannuation Fund (NZSF), the Alaska Permanent Fund (APF), and the Ireland Strategic Investment Fund (ISIF). The study used real-world-based SWF portfolios rather than hypothetical portfolios common in the literature.

The study distinguished between "common" exclusions (weapons, alcohol, tobacco, child labor, etc.) and fossil fuel exclusions, further dividing fossil fuel firms into "extraction and production" and "refining and integrated" categories. Results showed that extraction and production companies generate lower returns to some extent, suggesting that excluding these firms could be beneficial for SWFs.

Background context: On October 1, 2019, the Norwegian Ministry of Finance announced that the GPFG would divest from companies primarily engaged in oil and gas exploration and production. Other SWFs like the NZSF announced intentions to reduce carbon emissions. The study notes that at the end of 2019, there were 88 SWFs worldwide managing over USD 8 trillion in assets.

The article's novelties include: expanding the negative screening field to include oil and gas sectors, examining five SWFs with exclusion strategies (rather than just one), distinguishing between extraction/production and refining/integrated fossil fuel firms, and using real-world portfolios. The conclusion supports that SWFs can meet ethical objectives without compromising financial returns, encouraging other SWFs and institutional investors to engage in negative screening.

--- SOURCE 8: Sovereign wealth fund ---
URL: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sovereign_wealth_fund

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is the Wikipedia article on sovereign wealth funds (SWFs), which are state-owned investment funds that invest in real and financial assets such as stocks, bonds, real estate, precious metals, private equity funds, or hedge funds. SWFs invest globally, and most are funded by commodity export revenues or foreign exchange reserves held by central banks.

**Key definitions and characteristics:** SWFs can be held by central banks (typically of major economic and fiscal importance) or be state savings invested for returns. Their assets may include foreign currency deposits, gold, special drawing rights (SDRs), IMF reserve positions, pension investments, oil funds, and other national holdings. SWFs aim for long-term returns, unlike foreign exchange reserves which serve short-term currency stabilization.

**History:** The term "sovereign wealth fund" was first used in 2005 by Andrew Rozanov in the Central Banking Journal. China's SWFs entered global markets in 2007. SWFs were the first institutions to use sovereign capital to contain financial damage in the early stages of the 2008 financial crisis. SWF assets under management grew from approximately $4 trillion to over $10 trillion between 2008 and 2021. The first SWFs were non-federal U.S. state funds from the mid-19th century, starting with Texas's Permanent School Fund (1854) and Permanent University Fund (1876). The first sovereign-state SWF was the Kuwait Investment Authority (1953), worth $853 billion as of July 2023. The Revenue Equalization Reserve Fund of Kiribati (1956) grew to over $1.5 billion.

**Nature and purpose:** SWFs are typically created when governments have budgetary surpluses and little international debt, especially for nations dependent on raw material exports. SWFs are primarily commodity-based (many from oil-rich states), with China's SWFs being a notable exception. Other reasons include strategic "war chests" and boosting international financial standing. As of 2025, a 2014 study suggests SWF creation often follows a "fad" model where governments imitate peers. SWFs have also been proposed as tools for managing AI-driven social and economic disruption, including supporting AI leadership through strategic investment and distributing returns through universal basic dividends.

**Concerns:** Key concerns include potential impacts on asset markets, national security issues (e.g., U.S. Foreign Investment and National Security Act of 2007 and the Exon-Florio Amendment as administered by CFIUS), inadequate transparency, and their heterogeneity compared to central banks or pension funds. Governments commit to accumulation, withdrawal, and investment rules.

**Recent governmental interest:** Key events include a March 2008 U.S. House hearing on foreign government investment; Germany's August 2008 law requiring parliamentary approval for foreign investments over 25% of voting shares; a February 3, 2025 executive order by President Donald Trump directing creation of a U.S. sovereign wealth fund; Indonesia's Danantara fund announced February 23, 2025 (expected to manage $900 billion); SWFs from Gulf states and Singapore acquiring stakes in AI companies like OpenAI, Anthropic, and xAI; Canada's SWF announced by Prime Minister Mark Carney on April 27, 2026; and a July 2026 CNBC report that 69% of Americans support requiring AI companies to transfer half their stock to a public SWF.

**Santiago Principles:** On September 2-3, 2008, major SWFs met in Santiago, Chile, under IMF leadership and drafted 24 Santiago Principles addressing transparency, independence, and accountability. As of 2016, 30 funds representing 80% of global SWF assets (US$5.5 trillion) had signed up. Natural resource-rich developing economies are encouraged to adopt these standards over local content policies.

**Size:** SWF assets under management amounted to $13–15 trillion as of 2025. Oil and gas-funded SWFs held $5.4 trillion as of 2020. Middle East and Asian countries account for 77% of all SWFs.

**Depletion:** Numerous SWFs have gone bankrupt, including Algeria's FRR, Brazil's FSB, Ecuador's funds, Papua New Guinea's MRSF, and Venezuela's FIEM and FONDEN, primarily due to political instability. Highly stable countries are less likely to experience depletion.

**Largest funds (assets in billions):** Government Pension Fund Global (Norway, $2,117, 1990, Oil & Gas); SAFE Investment Company (China, $1,952, 1997, Non-commodity); China Investment Corporation ($1,567, 2007, Non-commodity); Abu Dhabi Investment Authority (UAE, $1,128, 1976, Oil & Gas); Kuwait Investment Authority ($1,072, 1953, Oil & Gas); GIC Private Limited (Singapore, $936, 1981, Non-commodity); Public Investment Fund (Saudi Arabia, $925, 1971, Oil & Gas); Danantara (Indonesia, $900, 2025, Minerals/Non-commodity); Qatar Investment Authority ($557, 2005, Oil & Gas); and the Exchange Fund (Hong Kong, $533, 1935, Non-commodity). The table also lists dozens of other funds including Temasek Holdings, Future Fund, Korea Investment Corporation, Alaska Permanent Fund, and Texas Permanent School Fund.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"A sovereign wealth fund (SWF), or sovereign investment fund, is a state-owned investment fund that invests in real and financial assets such as stocks, bonds, real estate, precious metals, or in alternative investments such as private equity funds or hedge funds."
</key_excerpts>

The fund's value at the end of 2025 was 21,268 billion kroner, with investments comprising 71.3% equities, 26.5% fixed income, 1.7% unlisted real estate, and 0.4% unlisted renewable energy infrastructure.

**Results:** The fund returned 15.1% in 2025 (2,362 billion kroner in accounting terms, the fund's second-highest return in krone terms), 0.28 percentage points below the benchmark index. --- SOURCE 5: The Portfolio Construction of the Norwegian Sovereign Wealth Fund: Strategy, Structure, and Stewardship - Finance ---
URL: https://sites.duke.edu/finance/2025/06/06/norwegian-sovereign-wealth-fund

SUMMARY:
<summary>
The Norwegian Government Pension Fund Global (GPFG), known as the "Norwegian oil fund," is the world's largest sovereign wealth fund with over $1.5 trillion in assets. Established in 1990 to responsibly manage Norway's petroleum revenues and avoid the "resource curse," the fund transforms volatile oil/gas income into stable long-term financial wealth for intergenerational stewardship. By law, only about 3% annual real return can be used in the national budget; the principal is preserved for future generations.

The fund's strategic asset allocation (determined by the Norwegian Ministry of Finance, with NBIM handling operational management) is: 70% equities, 25% fixed income, and 5% unlisted real estate and renewable infrastructure. The equity portfolio spans over 9,000 companies in 70+ countries, covering nearly 1.5% of the global stock market. It invests only in public companies, is largely passive (mirroring the FTSE Global All Cap Index and Bloomberg Global Aggregate Bond Index), with heavy technology exposure (Apple, Microsoft, Alphabet) and minor active positions. Fixed income plays a stabilizing role with sovereign and high-quality corporate bonds diversified across USD, EUR, JPY, and GBP. Real assets (added 2011 for real estate, 2020 for renewable infrastructure) focus on prime urban centers and offshore wind/solar projects, serving as inflation hedges.

Governance features high transparency, low management costs (~0.05% of AUM), annual parliamentary review, and clear separation between policy-setting (Ministry of Finance) and implementation (NBIM). The fund's Ethical Guidelines (established 2004) exclude weapons companies, human rights violators, environmental damage firms, coal, and tobacco — with over 180 companies excluded as of 2025, guided by the independent Council on Ethics. Risk management employs factor-based analysis, stress testing, and scenario analysis, while maintaining high liquidity. The fund has delivered ~4% annualized real returns since inception against a 3% above-inflation goal.

The GPFG serves as a global model for sovereign, pension, and endowment funds, demonstrating that transparency, diversification, and ethical investing can coexist with strong financial performance, with its divestments carrying systemic market influence.
</summary>

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is the Executive Summary of Meld. St. 22 (2024–2025), the Norwegian Government's White Paper on the Government Pension Fund 2025, recommended by the Ministry of Finance on 10 April 2025 by the Council of State (Government Støre). 

**Fund Overview & Fiscal Framework:** The Government Pension Fund consists of the Government Pension Fund Global (GPFG) and Government Pension Fund Norway (GPFN). Its purpose is to fund National Insurance Scheme pension expenditure and facilitate long-term management of petroleum revenues. The investment objective is the highest possible return at an acceptable risk level, with responsible management within that financial objective. The Fund is integrated into the fiscal policy framework; net petroleum cash flows are transferred to the GPFG, while funds are drawn annually to cover the non-oil budget deficit. The fiscal guideline links spending to an estimated 3 percent real rate of return, with withdrawals in normal years to remain well below 3 percent. For 2025, about 24 percent of the fiscal budget will be funded by transfers from the Fund. Historically, more than 99 percent of return fluctuations are explained by the benchmark index set by the Ministry and endorsed by the Storting.

**Governance:** The Ministry of Finance holds formal responsibility, with Norges Bank and Folketrygdfondet conducting operational management of the GPFG and GPFN respectively. The Fund is not a political instrument, with investment decisions made at arm's length from political authorities. There's a risk that geopolitical developments (democratic erosion, protectionism, economic decoupling) could weaken global growth and returns; broad diversification remains the best strategy.

**Investment Strategy:** The GPFG equity share is 70 percent; GPFN is 60 percent. Broad diversification across asset classes and companies reduces risk. Managers may deviate from benchmark indices within defined risk limits; the GPFG may invest in unlisted real estate and renewable energy infrastructure.

**2024 Performance:** The GPFG value rose by NOK 3,985 billion to NOK 19,742 billion, with a return of 13.1 percent (NOK 2,511 billion) before costs. Net transfers were NOK 409 billion; NOK depreciation increased the NOK value by 1,072 billion. The GPFN market value rose about NOK 27 billion to NOK 381 billion, with a 7.6 percent return. In 2024, Norges Bank underperformed its benchmark by 0.45 percentage points, while Folketrygdfondet outperformed by 1.15 points. Average annual excess return was 0.19 points over 20 years for GPFG and 1.00 point since 2007 for GPFN. Management costs were 4.1 basis points for GPFG and 6.5 basis points for GPFN — very low by international comparisons.

**Responsible Investment:** Environmental, social, and corporate governance factors are integral to management, based on UN and OECD standards. The framework includes corporate governance advocacy, expectations documents, ownership dialogue, and voting. The Ministry's ethically motivated Guidelines for Observation and Exclusion include product-based criteria (tobacco, recreational cannabis, coal, certain weapons) and conduct-based criteria (war/conflict rights violations, severe environmental damage, unacceptable GHG emissions, serious human rights violations). An independent Council on Ethics makes recommendations to Norges Bank's Executive Board. In 2024, the Council assessed companies linked to Israeli settlements/occupation on the West Bank (ten companies excluded) and Myanmar, and considered weapons sales criteria regarding the Gaza war. The settlements are assessed on the basis of being unlawful under international law.

**Key Decisions:**
- <b>Small-cap benchmark reduction (GPFG):</b> Emerging market small-cap companies will be removed from the equity benchmark, reducing the number of companies by about 22 percent (less than 1 percent of market value). This follows the 2021 decision to reduce benchmark complexity.
- <b>Expert council (GPFG):</b> An external expert council is being established to examine issues affecting GPFG management (per recommendation in the Sverdrup Commission, NOU 2022: 12).
- <b>Russia investments:</b> On 3 December 2024, the Ministry lifted the freeze (imposed 28 February 2022) on GPFG Russian investments, allowing sales within the applicable sanctions regime. Russia remains excluded from the investment universe; Russian securities held as of 28 February 2022 stay in the universe until divestments complete.
- <b>Climate risk (GPFN):</b> The Ministry added provisions to the GPFN mandate to strengthen climate risk management, mirroring 2022 amendments to the GPFG mandate.
</summary>

SUMMARY:
<summary>
The SIPRI Fact Sheet (April 2026) reports that world military expenditure rose by 2.9 per cent in real terms to $2,887 billion in 2025, marking the 11th consecutive year of growth and the highest level ever recorded by SIPRI. Total military expenditure accounted for 2.5 per cent of global GDP. The five biggest spenders—the United States ($954 billion), China ($336 billion), Russia ($190 billion), Germany ($114 billion), and India ($92.1 billion)—accounted for 58 per cent of world military spending.

Key trends: The USA's military spending fell by 7.5 per cent to $954 billion, mainly due to the end of supplemental appropriations for financial military assistance to Ukraine and Israel. China's spending rose by 7.4 per cent (its 31st consecutive year of growth), Russia increased spending by 5.9 per cent (7.5 per cent of GDP), and Ukraine's spending rose by 20 per cent to $84.1 billion (40 per cent of GDP). Military expenditure grew in all world regions except the Americas. European spending rose by 14 per cent to $864 billion, and Asian/Oceanian spending rose by 8.1 per cent to $681 billion.

Regional highlights: NATO members (32) spent $1,581 billion (55 per cent of global spending), with European NATO members spending $559 billion; 23 of the 32 NATO members met the 2.0 per cent GDP target. In June 2025, NATO agreed to raise its spending target to 5.0 per cent of GDP by 2035, prompting concerns about "creative accounting" and blurred definitions of military-related spending. Germany's spending exceeded 2.0 per cent of GDP for the first time since 1990. Spain recorded the largest increase among top spenders (up by 50 per cent). Algeria's military burden (8.8 per cent of GDP) was the second largest globally after Ukraine.

Notable country developments: Taiwan's military spending rose by 14 per cent (largest increase since 1988) amid rising tensions in the Taiwan Strait, with a pledge to reach 5.0 per cent of GDP by 2030. Japan reached its highest military burden (1.4 per cent of GDP) since 1958. Ukraine received $52.2 billion in partner support in 2025. The Middle East's spending was roughly flat (+0.1 per cent) at $218 billion, with Israel's spending falling 4.9 per cent following the Gaza ceasefire. The global military burden rose to its highest level since 2009 at 2.5 per cent of GDP, with the Middle East having the highest regional burden (3.8 per cent of GDP).

This is an official NATO webpage (updated 29 June 2026) detailing NATO's defence investment commitments and spending data. The core content covers:

**The 5% Hague Defence Commitment:** At the 2025 NATO Summit in The Hague, Allies committed to investing 5% of GDP annually on defence by 2035, strengthening armed forces and ensuring fairer burden-sharing. --- SOURCE 4: Government Spending ---
URL: https://ourworldindata.org/government-spending

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This page from Our World in Data provides a comprehensive analysis of government spending worldwide, examining historical trends, cross-country comparisons, and spending composition.

**Historical trends in early-industrialised countries:**
- Government spending as a share of GDP evolved through four broad periods: low spending until WWI; volatile spending between 1915-1945 (driven by war-related defense spending); rapid growth between 1945-1980 (driven by social spending growth); and slowing growth since 1980.
- At the end of the 19th century, European governments spent around 10% of GDP; in the 21st century, this figure is closer to 50% in many European countries.
- Growth in the mid-20th century was largely driven by expansion of public funding for healthcare and education.

**Cross-country differences:**
- Government spending varies widely between world regions; high-income countries (particularly in Europe) spend much more relative to their economies than low-income countries. France spends multiple times as much as Ethiopia as a share of GDP.
- Spending per person also varies dramatically - Mexico's government spends a fraction per person compared to Norway.
- High-income countries have higher levels of social spending than lower-income countries.

**Composition of spending:**
- On average, OECD countries spend about half of total government spending on social protection and health.
- Social protection spending varies substantially across OECD countries.
- Across OECD countries, spending on old age (pensions and elderly care) receives the largest social spending allocation, followed by health, with family or incapacity-related benefits third.
- Employee compensation ranges from 5-20% of central government spending in Europe, but 30-50% throughout most of Africa.

**Public procurement:**
- Governments rely on private sector for goods and services through "public procurement."
- Procurement includes both large infrastructure projects and routine purchases ("outsourcing" or "contracting out").
- Public-private partnerships in low and middle-income countries have grown markedly over recent decades, driven mainly by electricity and roads projects in South Asia and Latin America, with the total value of projects in these countries more than doubling in 2005-2010.

**Correlates of government spending:**
- Government spending as a share of GDP correlates positively with GDP per capita (higher-income countries spend more), likely reflecting greater capacity to raise revenues.
- Taxes and transfers reduce income inequality by about one-quarter on average across 45 OECD countries.

Data sources include the IMF (for general government spending), OECD (Social Expenditure Database, COFOG classifications), and the World Bank's Private Participation in Infrastructure Database. The page was first published in October 2016 with minor text changes in April 2025.

--- SOURCE 1: World Investment Report 2026 ---
URL: https://unctad.org/system/files/official-document/wir2026_en.pdf

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This webpage presents the United Nations Conference on Trade and Development (UNCTAD) World Investment Report 2026, titled "International Investment in a Turbulent Era," published in Geneva in 2026 (UNCTAD/WIR/2026, ISBN: 978-92-1-154998-0).

KEY HEADLINE FINDINGS:
- Global foreign direct investment (FDI) rose by 6% to $1.6 trillion in 2025, following two consecutive years of decline, but growth remains fragile and uneven. Excluding conduit flows through major European financial centres, global FDI increased 4%.
- Inflows rose 11% in developed economies (to $723 billion) but only 2% in developing economies (to just over $901 billion).
- Investment activity is increasingly concentrated in a few capital- and technology-intensive sectors—data centres, semiconductors, oil and gas, clean energy, and critical minerals. These strategic sectors now represent almost half of all announced greenfield projects in 2025. Most other sectors, including renewable energy and manufacturing, registered significant declines.
- FDI in least developed countries (LDCs) rose 21% but remained highly concentrated in a small number of resource-rich economies. LDCs and lower-middle-income countries attract barely 10% of strategic sector projects, versus more than 20% in other industries.
- The top 20 recipients accounted for more than 80% of global FDI inflows. The United States remained the largest recipient ($277 billion), followed by Singapore, Hong Kong (China), and China. Developing economies represent half of the top 20.
- Global FDI outflows: the US remained largest source ($263 billion), followed by Japan ($186 billion) and China ($174 billion). Developing Asia accounts for one third of global outflows. Gulf Cooperation Council economies are increasingly prominent outward investors, including through sovereign wealth funds.
- The global investor landscape has become more diverse: more than a quarter of the top 100 MNEs are State-owned, and private equity international acquisitions account for about 20% of global M&As.
- Cross-border M&A values declined 7%. Greenfield project values remained near 2024 levels but were driven mainly by megaprojects. International project finance rose only 3%, remaining about 25% below its 2021 peak.
- FDI remains the largest source of external finance for developing economies (about 50% of total), ahead of remittances, ODA, and portfolio flows.

POLICY AND GOVERNANCE CONTEXT:
- Governments are becoming increasingly active in shaping investment flows, with new investment policy measures reaching a record high in 2025—strongly supporting strategic sectors, industrial upgrading, digital transformation, and green transition.
- The report emphasizes that investment is shifting from following cost and efficiency (where developing countries competed) to following strategic calculation, industrial policy, subsidies, economic security, and technological advantage—a logic that rewards deep pockets and established ecosystems.
- New opportunities exist for developing economies in supply-chain reconfiguration: alternative manufacturing locations, processing hubs for critical minerals, and gateways to regional markets.
- At UNCTAD 16 in October 2025, 170 countries adopted the Geneva Consensus, renewing commitment to an open, equitable, and development-oriented investment environment.
- The report references the Sevilla Commitment's global call to address limited access to finance for developing countries.

OUTLOOK (2026):
- Global FDI prospects remain uncertain with significant downside risks from trade policy uncertainty, geopolitical tensions (including the 2026 Middle East conflict), and conflicts. The geopolitical risk index rose sharply to 230.8 in the 2026 forecast from 145.1, while energy prices are forecast to rise significantly. However, moderating interest rates and foreign exchange volatility provide some positive signals.

The report was prepared by an UNCTAD team led by Nan Li Collins, Director of the Division on Investment and Enterprise, with a preface by UN Secretary-General António Guterres and foreword by UNCTAD Acting Secretary-General Pedro Manuel Moreno. The report contains three main chapters covering international investment trends, investment policy trends, and the theme chapter on "International investment in a turbulent era: Trends and policy response."
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"In 2025, global foreign direct investment rose by 6 per cent to reach $1.6 trillion. But this growth masks underlying fragility and disparities across countries, regions and sectors." - António Guterres, UN Secretary-General
</key_excerpts>

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This webpage from the UN Audiovisual Library documents a video news story (asset d3414524, MAMS ID 3414524) about the launch of the UNCTAD World Investment Report 2025, released on 19 June 2025, in Geneva, Switzerland (UNTV CH source). The 2-minute-58-second English-language video features UN Trade and Development (UNCTAD) Secretary-General Rebeca Grynspan presenting key findings.

Key findings from the report and storyline:
- Global foreign direct investment (FDI) fell by 11% in 2024, marking the second consecutive year of decline and confirming a deepening slowdown in productive capital flows.
- Although global FDI rose by 4% in 2024 to $1.5 trillion, the increase was driven partly by volatile financial conduit flows through several European economies that serve as transfer points for investments.
- Investment dropped sharply across developed economies, particularly in Europe. In developing countries, inflows appeared broadly stable but concealed a deeper crisis, with capital stagnating or bypassing critical sectors like infrastructure, energy, technology, and job-creating industries.
- The report was released ahead of the Fourth International Conference on Financing for Development (FFD4), where leaders will address the widening gap between capital flows and development needs.

In her soundbites, Secretary-General Grynspan attributed the decline to growing geopolitical tensions, rising trade barriers, and increasing screening measures on foreign investment, especially in developed countries. She emphasized the real consequences—jobs not created, infrastructure not built, and sustainable development delayed—and called for embedding sustainability in investment decisions, combating greenwashing, supporting policy reform, directing capital toward the real economy (energy, industry, tech, infrastructure), modernizing international investment governance, protecting public interest, ensuring fair treatment for investors, and preserving national policy space. She concluded: "The time to act is now. Investment is not just about money. It is about trust. It is about fairness. It is about a future that includes everyone."

The webpage also lists related content, including previous UNCTAD World Investment Report news stories (2019, 2023, 2026) and World Chronicle features with Karl P. Sauvant of UNCTAD.

URL: https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/statistics-explained/SEPDF/cache/65097.pdf?v=4582848109069452

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This Eurostat article (data extracted January 2026, from the "Statistics Explained" publication) analyzes global foreign direct investment (FDI) patterns for 2014–2024, based on UNCTAD data. Key findings:

**FDI Stocks (2024):** Global FDI stock was valued at €45.5 trillion. Europe was the largest source of outward FDI (39.8% of world total, €16.7 trillion) and second largest destination of inward FDI (31.4%, €15.4 trillion). Europe was the only continent that was a net investor. EU-held stocks: 14.4% share of global inward investment and 22.2% of global outward investment (second highest, behind the US which accounted for 30.6% of inward and 22.4% of outward FDI). China ranked third in both.

**Trends (2014–2024):** Europe's share of global inward FDI stocks fell by 7.8 percentage points (the largest decline of any continent), reaching 31.4% in 2024. Northern America's share rose 9.7 pp, Asia rose 1.0 pp, while Latin America & Caribbean (−1.2 pp), Africa (−0.9 pp) and Oceania (−0.8 pp) fell. Europe's share of outward stocks declined 5.3 pp (lowest at 39.8% in 2024), while Asia's rose 5.1 pp (to 26.9%) and North America's rose 0.5 pp (28.8%).

**FDI relative to GDP (2024):** World outward stocks/GDP ratio was 39.5%, inward stocks/GDP was 46.1%. Hong Kong (5.7x GDP) and Singapore (4.1x GDP) were most "open" economies. EU inward FDI stocks equaled 39.1% of GDP. Low ratios: Japan (5.5%), Russia (10.3%), Türkiye (13.6%), India (14.1%), South Korea (15.4%), China (20.0%). Japan's outward stocks/GDP ratio (53.6%) was almost 10 times its inward ratio.

**Multinational Enterprises:** In 2024, half of the world's top 10 non-financial multinational groups by foreign assets were HQ'd in the EU (Volkswagen Group, Stellantis NV, Deutsche Telekom AG, TotalEnergies SE, Anheuser-Busch InBev NV). Of the top 20, 9 were in the EU (4 German). Foreign assets exceeded 90% for CK Hutchison, British American Tobacco, Shell and Stellantis.

**FDI Flows (2024):** Global FDI flows totaled €1,440 billion. In 2024, the US was both the world's largest host (18.5% of inward flows) and largest outward investor (16.6% of outward flows). Singapore (9.5%), Hong Kong (8.4%) and China (7.7%) received significant inward flows; Japan (12.7%) and China (10.1%) were the next largest outward investors after the US. Inward FDI into the EU was negative (−14.7% of world total), while EU outward flows were 4.0%. Europe's share of world inward flows fell from 40.5% in 2015 to 12.6% by 2024, while Asia's rose to a peak of 55.0% in 2022 (43.6% in 2024).

**Growth 2014–2024:** China's inward FDI stocks grew 3.9x (highest growth, along with US, UAE and Singapore at 3x+). Chinese and UAE outward stocks grew 4.1x. Between 2014–2024, largest absolute increases in inward flows: US (+€105.8bn), Singapore (+€77.3bn), UAE (+€33.8bn). Largest outward flow increases: Japan (+€90.3bn) and China (+€57.7bn).

**Methodology/Context:** Data follows IMF BPM6 and OECD BD4 standards. A notable caveat: EU data includes special purpose entities (SPEs) while the rest of the world excludes them, which may distort geographic distribution of FDI. Four broad types of FDI are defined: greenfield investment, brownfield investment (acquisitions/mergers), capital extension, and financial restructuring. Geopolitical factors affected flows, notably sanctions leading to decreased Russian investment flows (inward flows turned negative in 2022).
</summary>

--- SOURCE 16: The Budgetary Cost of the Inflation Reduction Act’s Energy Subsidies ---
URL: https://www.cato.org/policy-analysis/budgetary-cost-inflation-reduction-acts-energy-subsidies

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is a Cato Institute Policy Analysis (No. 992, published March 11, 2025) by Travis Fisher and Joshua L. Loucks examining the true budgetary cost of the Inflation Reduction Act's (IRA) energy subsidies. The paper argues that the IRA, signed into law August 16, 2022, despite its name, was mostly designed to decarbonize the US economy through subsidies for clean energy producers and EV consumers. Using a transparent, replicable scoring methodology based on EIA and NREL projections, the authors estimate IRA energy subsidies will cost between $936 billion and $1.97 trillion over the next 10 years, and between $2.04 trillion and $4.67 trillion by 2050. They apply a 3% discount rate reducing the 2050 present value by approximately 30%.

Key context: When passed, the CBO and JCT estimated IRA energy subsidies at approximately $369-383 billion over 10 years. However, estimates have been revised upward multiple times—the CBO/JCT later found ~$786 billion (2024-2033 window), Penn Wharton estimated over $1 trillion by 2032, Brookings roughly $800 billion, and Goldman Sachs $1.2 trillion. Early IRS tax return data shows rapid cost overruns: the residential clean energy credit cost $6.3 billion in 2023 (vs. $459 million estimated), and the energy-efficient home-improvement credit cost $2.1 billion in 2023 (vs. $273 million estimated, nearly eight times higher).

Major spending drivers include: the production tax credit (PTC, section 45Y) at $27.50/MWh in 2023, the investment tax credit (ITC, section 48E) typically reimbursing 30% of up-front investment costs, and the uncapped advanced manufacturing tax credit (section 45X) that indefinitely subsidizes 50 critical minerals including aluminum, lithium, nickel, and cobalt. The PTC and ITC (for clean electricity under sections 45Y/48E) could cost $70-180 billion per year. Many IRA subsidies phase down only when electricity sector GHG emissions fall to 25% of 2022 levels—a target unlikely to be met by 2050 due to growing electricity demand from electrification, which extends subsidy duration. Wood Mackenzie estimated clean electricity portions could cost nearly $3 trillion by 2060.

The authors estimate $600 billion difference between lower- and upper-bound estimates is driven by nuclear deployment (zero vs. 200 GW by 2050). They assume ITCs at 30%, model EIA as lower bound and NREL projections as upper bound, and include 80/20 rule repowering assumptions in upper bounds.

Policy recommendations: Congress should repeal all IRA energy subsidies, or at minimum cap total energy subsidy spending and require CBO, JCT, and other government bodies to publish transparent, updated long-term cost estimates.
</summary>

Supporters note it helps equalize tax treatment between buybacks and dividends, since buybacks allow foreign investors to avoid US taxation.

**Clean Energy Tax Breaks:** Original JCT estimates put environmental tax credits at about $260 billion over 10 years, with subsequent estimates roughly two-thirds higher due to greater-than-anticipated demand. The final legislation differed from the original version (which was estimated to save over $300 billion through 2031), with changes including removal of the inflation cap on commercial drug prices and the carried interest provision, modifications to the corporate book income minimum tax, inclusion of a 1 percent tax on stock buybacks, more generous Medicare coverage of insulin, extension of limits on loss deductibility for pass-through entities, and removal of IRS pay/hiring flexibilities.

The legislation includes approximately $738 billion of offsets to fund roughly $499 billion of new spending and tax breaks. Key components include: Energy and Climate provisions (-$391 billion, including $161 billion for clean electricity tax credits); Health Care spending (-$108 billion, including -$64 billion for a three-year extension of expanded ACA subsidies); Health Savings of $281 billion (repeal of Trump-era drug rebate rule at $122 billion, drug price negotiation at $96 billion, and drug price inflation cap at $63 billion); and Revenue of $457 billion (15 percent corporate minimum tax at $222 billion, IRS tax enforcement funding at $101 billion, 1 percent excise tax on stock buybacks at $74 billion, and a 2-year extension on limitations of excess business losses at $53 billion).

The IRS funding provision involves an $80 billion expenditure over ten years, estimated to yield $180 billion in additional revenue for a net savings of $100 billion. If the temporary ACA subsidy extension were made permanent without offsets, the deficit reduction would drop to roughly $90 billion over a decade. The page also links to related articles on rising National Health Expenditures, Medicare Part D costs rising due to the IRA's benefit redesign, and Social Security solvency.

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This article from the Center for American Progress argues that the Inflation Reduction Act (IRA), signed into law by President Biden nearly two years ago (around 2022), still reduces the federal deficit despite higher-than-expected costs for clean energy tax credits. Key points:

- The most recent CBO and JCT estimates put the cost of the IRA's climate provisions at about $730 billion, excluding EPA emissions rule costs.
- The IRA offsets costs through: IRS funding ($80 billion) to catch wealthy tax cheats (the top 1 percent of taxpayers owe roughly $215 billion in unpaid taxes annually), a corporate alternative minimum tax (15% tax on about 80 large corporations with over $1 billion in revenue, raising more than $200 billion over 10 years), a 1% excise tax on stock buybacks (raising about $75 billion over 10 years), and Medicare prescription drug price negotiations and inflation rebates.

--- SOURCE 21: Egil Matsen: Climate change, climate risks and Norges Bank ---
URL: https://www.bis.org/review/r191108a.htm

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This speech by Egil Matsen, Deputy Governor of Norges Bank (Central Bank of Norway), delivered in Oslo on 8 November 2019, addresses climate change, climate risks, and their implications for Norway's central bank operations, monetary policy, banking sector, and the Government Pension Fund Global (GPFG).

**Climate Change Background:** The global average temperature has risen about 1 degree Celsius above pre-industrial levels, and climate change is widely accepted as largely human-induced. Matsen identifies two types of climate risk: physical climate risk (economic consequences of higher temperatures and extreme weather) and transition risk (economic effects of shifting to a low-carbon economy through climate policy, changing attitudes, and new technologies). While poor countries in the Global South will likely be hardest hit by physical risks, Norway has experienced about five times higher annual insurance payouts for climate-related flood and storm damage over the past decade compared to the 1980s.

**Monetary Policy Implications:** Extreme weather acts as negative supply shocks—lowering output while raising inflation. Under Norway's flexible inflation targeting regime, Norges Bank typically does not adjust policy rates for transient supply shocks (e.g., agricultural production fell 40% in Q3 2018 due to a hot, dry summer without a rate change). However, policy rate changes may occur if such events cause persistent inflation. Prices for European CO2 emission allowances rose nearly 500 percent over two years, affecting coal, gas, and Norwegian electricity prices.

**Norwegian Economy and Transition Risk:** Norway's large oil and gas sector exposes the economy to transition risk, a concern raised by then-Governor Hermod Skånland as early as 1989. Norway has converted oil wealth into financial wealth via the GPFG since 1996 (with a fiscal rule since 2001), reducing overall risk. Oil stock price-to-book ratios have declined relative to the market average, partly attributed to increased investor climate risk awareness. If the oil sector declined abruptly, monetary policy could support activity and employment, though structural restructuring responsibility lies elsewhere.

**Banking Sector:** Climate risks, particularly transition risk, may become a source of credit risk for Norwegian banks, which have reduced (but not eliminated) oil industry exposure. Banks should correctly price climate risk, rely on relevant company disclosures, and prepare for investors demanding improved climate disclosure (the TCFD recommendations are becoming normative). Transition risk can contribute to financing risk and systemic risk, and should be included in assessments of bank capitalization and funding.

**Government Pension Fund Global (GPFG):** The GPFG invests in over 9,000 companies in 73 countries (70% equities) with the goal of maximizing return within acceptable risk while integrating responsible investment. Its responsible investment work rests on three pillars: (1) setting standards (supporting international standards, with climate expectations published since 2009); (2) exercising ownership (voting rights and dialogue); and (3) portfolio composition (environment-related mandates). The environment-related mandate limit will increase from NOK 60 billion to NOK 120 billion, with expansion in 2020 to include unlisted renewable energy infrastructure (primarily wind and solar), targeting about 1% of the GPFG (≈NOK 100 billion). Notably, 82 companies have been excluded based on a coal criterion, though a conduct-based climate criterion has yet to result in exclusions.

**Conclusion:** In 2018, extreme weather affected about 60 million people, though fatalities from storms and flooding have decreased due to better disaster risk management. Norges Bank participates in the NGFS (Central Banks and Supervisors Network for Greening the Financial System) with Finanstilsynet to build expertise, aiming to strengthen the resilience of the Norwegian economy to climate change and climate risk.
</summary>

--- SOURCE 23: Norway’s oil fund shows gap between climate risk insight and action ---
URL: https://greencentralbanking.com/2026/06/10/norways-oil-fund-climate-risk-gap-and-action

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This article from Green Central Banking (June 10, 2026, by Emma Thomasson) reports on a Carbon Tracker analysis revealing a gap between climate risk insight and action at Norway's oil fund (NBIM), the world's largest asset manager with over US$2.3tn in assets holding about 1.5% of the world's listed companies.

Key findings:
- NBIM has developed one of the most advanced frameworks for measuring climate and nature risk but has not applied these insights to shift capital away from fossil fuels.
- A quarter of NBIM's equity portfolio is already exposed to severe physical climate hazards, and 23% of its equity portfolio by value is exposed to such hazards today. It holds shares in about 7,200 companies.
- NBIM remains Europe's largest fossil fuel investor, with over US$70bn in fossil fuel investments in 2024 (per German NGO Urgewald).
- The mismatch between insight and action stems from mandate limitations (NBIM is bound by a Norwegian parliamentary mandate focused on maximizing returns), political expectations, antitrust considerations, and increasing global climate policy uncertainty.

Notable events:
- In April 2026, NBIM came under fire for voting in favor of BP board-supported resolutions (including election of the chair) while opposing a shareholder resolution seeking extra disclosures on how BP's capital allocation aligns with shareholder value.
- The number of companies NBIM engaged with on climate issues fell 11% in 2025.
- In November 2025, the Norwegian government set up a committee to review NBIM's ethical framework after debate over investments in Israeli companies and tech giants. This led to temporary suspension of NBIM's powers to exclude or divest from companies, including on climate/nature grounds. The committee reports by Oct. 15, 2026.

Expert quotes and conclusions:
- Amy Owens (Carbon Tracker financial policy analyst): "NBIM's analysis shows that physical climate risk is already a valuation issue. But there is a gap between what the data shows and what the fund feels able to do in response."
- Dina Rui (Nordic Center for Sustainable Finance): "It's up to the parliament to direct them to exclude fossil fuel companies" — noting the fund continues buying bonds in oil and gas companies funding new exploration like TotalEnergies.
- Carbon Tracker concludes that voluntary investor action alone is insufficient to address climate risk; clearer policy signals and more robust supervisory frameworks are essential to reduce market-wide mispricing of climate and nature risks.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"NBIM's analysis shows that physical climate risk is already a valuation issue. But there is a gap between what the data shows and what the fund feels able to do in response. That raises important questions for investors and policymakers alike," said Amy Owens, financial policy analyst at Carbon Tracker.
</key_excerpts>

--- SOURCE 25: Does disinvestment from fossil fuels reduce the financial performance of responsible sovereign wealth funds? ---
URL: https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/abs/pii/S1042444X22000032

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This research article, published in the Journal of Multinational Financial Management (Vol. 64, June 2022) by Khalil Al Ayoubi and Geoffroy Enjolras, examines whether disinvestment from fossil fuels reduces the financial performance of responsible sovereign wealth funds (SWFs). The study investigates the effects of negative screening on SWF financial performance, driven by public and governmental pressure on SWFs to divest from fossil fuel firms.

Key findings from the study:
- Negative screening does not harm SWFs' financial performance
- Oil divestment does not decrease SWF financial performance
- Negative screening actually decreases the risk exposure of SWFs

Methodology: The researchers used the capital asset pricing model and the Carhart four-factor model to analyze the impact of negative screening on five SWFs over the period 2005-2019: the GPFG of Norway, the French Pension Reserve Fund (FRR), the New Zealand Superannuation Fund (NZSF), the Alaska Permanent Fund (APF), and the Ireland Strategic Investment Fund (ISIF). The study used real-world-based SWF portfolios rather than hypothetical portfolios common in the literature.

The study distinguished between "common" exclusions (weapons, alcohol, tobacco, child labor, etc.) and fossil fuel exclusions, further dividing fossil fuel firms into "extraction and production" and "refining and integrated" categories. Results showed that extraction and production companies generate lower returns to some extent, suggesting that excluding these firms could be beneficial for SWFs.

Background context: On October 1, 2019, the Norwegian Ministry of Finance announced that the GPFG would divest from companies primarily engaged in oil and gas exploration and production. Other SWFs like the NZSF announced intentions to reduce carbon emissions. The study notes that at the end of 2019, there were 88 SWFs worldwide managing over USD 8 trillion in assets.

The article's novelties include: expanding the negative screening field to include oil and gas sectors, examining five SWFs with exclusion strategies (rather than just one), distinguishing between extraction/production and refining/integrated fossil fuel firms, and using real-world portfolios. The conclusion supports that SWFs can meet ethical objectives without compromising financial returns, encouraging other SWFs and institutional investors to engage in negative screening.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
Using asset pricing models, namely the capital asset pricing model and the Carhart four-factor model, we find that excluding firms has a statistically insignificant impact on the financial performance of SWFs. We conclude that socially responsible investment, by negative screening of fossil fuel firms does not reduce SWF performance, "Negative screening decreases the risk exposure of sovereign wealth funds, To some extent, extraction and production companies generate lower returns, The findings suggest that it is possible for these funds not to suffer from an opportunity cost for meeting their ethical standards, which should encourage other SWFs and institutional investors to engage in negative screening.
</key_excerpts>
