# Investment mandate Government Pension Fund Global

Issued by Norges Bank's Executive Board to the Chief Executive Officer of Norges Bank Investment Management. Last amended 9 December 2025.

The Chief Executive Officer of Norges Bank Investment Management (NBIM CEO) is through this investment mandate (the “Investment Mandate”) granted the responsibility for management of the Government Pension Fund Global (the “fund”). The fund shall be managed in accordance with the Management Mandate for the Government Pension Fund Global, issued by the Ministry of Finance, (the “Ministry Mandate”) as published on [www.lovdata.no](https://eur02.safelinks.protection.outlook.com/?url=http%3A%2F%2Fwww.lovdata.no%2F&data=04%7C01%7Clli%40nbim.no%7C5cb90f3a5e3b4e33f42d08d916aeb7e7%7C4a653e38cdfe40468620e0fa13765079%7C0%7C0%7C637565761921497943%7CUnknown%7CTWFpbGZsb3d8eyJWIjoiMC4wLjAwMDAiLCJQIjoiV2luMzIiLCJBTiI6Ik1haWwiLCJXVCI6Mn0%3D%7C1000&sdata=u0dmBUPMOL04VQ7K%2FQwE8HlwIHdHVcHAjqv2XD0QA3w%3D&reserved=0) and as in force at all times. The Investment Mandate supplements and set out additional risk limits as required in the Ministry Mandate. References to applicable provisions from the Ministry Mandate are incorporated to the right of each section. In the case of inconsistencies between this Investment Mandate and the Ministry Mandate the latter will prevail.

## 1.  Management assignment and objective

### 1.1 General provisions

NBIM CEO shall manage the Government Pension Fund Global and make investment decisions in accordance with Ministry Mandate and the provisions set by the Executive Board in this mandate (the “Investment Mandate”).

Investment activities shall be carried out in accordance with the strategy as approved by the Executive Board and its principles for management of the fund.

Investment activities shall at all times comply with relevant laws and regulations in the markets where the fund is invested.

The Executive Board shall review this Investment Mandate at least annually.

### 1.2 Objective

The fund shall be managed with an objective to generate the highest possible return, net of costs, measured in the currency basket of the fund, subject to the applicable investment framework.

### 1.3 Delegation of investment mandate

Authority for investment decisions may be delegated.

Formal investment mandates are to be issued for all internally and externally managed portfolios. These mandates must, as a minimum, contain a specification of the investment universe and risk limits. The overall mandate structure shall ensure the diversification of the fund.

## 2. Investment universe

### 2.1 Investment universe

The investment universe is as set out in the Ministry Mandate.

### 2.2 Approval of instruments, markets and issuers of government bonds

The fund may only be invested in financial instruments, markets and issuer government bonds from issuers approved by the Executive Board.

NBIM CEO shall inform the Executive Board without undue delay and recommend measures to be taken in situations where markets, instruments or government bond issuers no longer fulfil the requirements in the Executive Board’s framework for such approvals.

NBIM CEO shall facilitate regular Executive Board reviews of already approved instruments, markets and issuers of government bonds and instruments.

## 3. Benchmark

The strategic and actual benchmark indices for the Government Pension Fund Global are as set out in the Ministry Mandate.

## 4. Investment restrictions

The fund shall be invested in accordance with the risk limits set by the Ministry of Finance in the Ministry Mandate.

### 4.1 Executive Board investment restrictions for listed investments

*4.1.1*  
The overlap between actual portfolio and actual benchmark index must be at least 60 per cent for the equity portfolio and at least 60 per cent for issuers in the fixed income portfolio.

*4.1.2*  
NBIM CEO shall organize the management with the aim that the maximum holding of a single issuer non-investment grade government bonds does not exceed 2 per cent and that the maximum holding of other single issuer non-investment grade bonds does not exceed 0.5 per cent of the net asset value of the fixed income portfolio.

NBIM CEO shall organise the management with the aim that high yield bonds (credit rating lower than “investment grade”) does not exceed 5 per cent of the market value of the fixed income portfolio.

*4.1.3*  
NBIM CEO shall organise the management with the aim that a minimum of 7.5 per cent of the net asset value of the fund shall be held in treasury bonds issued by the governments of France, Germany, Japan, the United Kingdom and the United States of America and supranationals issued by the European Union.

*4.1.4*  
Potential future counterparty exposure shall not exceed 0.75 per cent of the net asset value of the fund for any single counterparty.

Counterparts to unsecured deposits shall have a minimum long-term rating of minimum “A” or the equivalent. Counterparts to collateralised instruments or contracts shall have a minimum long-term rating of at least “BBB” or the equivalent. Counterparts to collateralised instruments or contracts not meeting the minimum rating requirements may be approved by the CEO for exposure up to 1 per cent of the net asset value of the fund, and not exceeding 0.2 per cent of the net asset value of the fund for any single counterparty.

All securities financing transactions and trading in OTC derivatives shall be subject to adequate collateral criteria reflecting the credit quality of the counterparty. Netting agreements shall be in place before trading takes place.

*4.1.5*  
Leveraging the equity and fixed income portfolio is not permitted beyond what is necessary to minimise transaction costs or a normal part of investment management, and not in excess of 5 per cent of the net asset value of the combined equity and fixed income portfolios.

*4.1.6*  
Cash collateral received can only be invested in cash equivalent instruments.

*4.1.7*  
The borrowing of securities may not exceed 5 per cent of the net asset value of the fund.

*4.1.8*NBIM CEO shall organise the management with the aim that the annualised expected shortfall measured at 97.5 per cent confidence level for the relative return between the fund and the benchmark index does not exceed 3.75 per cent.

The methodology for calculation of the expected shortfall shall be approved by the Executive Board.

In situations with extreme market volatility which may provoke a breach of the limit, NBIM CEO shall without undue delay recommend measures to be decided upon by the Executive Board.

*4.1.9*  
Lending of securities is permitted, provided that NBIM CEO ensures that adequate security is provided for the loan, reflecting the credit quality of the counterparty. Securities lent, including obligations to lend, shall not exceed 20 per cent of the net asset value of the fund.

*4.1.10*  
Gross exposure of contracts for difference (CfD) shall not exceed 7 per cent of the net asset value of the fund.

*4.1.11*Gross exposure of index contract for difference (index CfD) shall not exceed 5 percent of the net asset value of the fund.

*4.1.12*  
When lending securities from the fund, one voting share in each company shall, as a minimum, always be retained on any Annual or Extraordinary General Meeting record date to ensure that we can express our views as a shareholder.

*4.1.13*  
The issue of call options on individual securities that are not held in the fund is not permitted. Issuing of put and call options (measured as notional value) is limited to 2.5 per cent of the net asset value of the fund.

*4.1.14*  
Ownership in a single listed real estate company shall not exceed 30 per cent.

*4.1.15*  
Investment with a single external manager shall not exceed 0.5 per cent of the net asset value of the fund.

*4.1.16*  
Agreements with external managers shall contain provisions to ensure that the total annual fee paid per year per external mandate does not exceed a maximum amount, which shall not be above USD 30 million. Performance fees accrued above the maximum amount may be paid the following years, subject to the maximum annual pay out limit and excess return over the relevant time period.

### 4.2 Executive Board investment restrictions for unlisted real estate

*4.2.1*Investments in unlisted real estate above USD 2 500 million, or of an unusual nature or major importance in the context of Norges Bank’s management of the fund, shall be approved by the Executive Board.

Transactions that include acquisition of operating subsidiaries with employees shall be approved by the Executive Board.

*4.2.2*All weights shall be calculated by the use of net asset value of the unlisted real estate portfolio, unless otherwise is specified below.

*4.2.3*The unlisted real estate portfolio shall be diversified in accordance with the following regional allocation:  
a. North America: 30-70 per cent  
b. Europe: 20-60 per cent  
c. Asia Pacific:0-10 per cent

4.2.4  
The unlisted real estate portfolio shall be diversified in accordance with the following sector allocation:  
a. Office: 20-60 per cent  
b. Retail: 0-30 per cent  
c. Logistics: 0-40 per cent  
d. Living: 0-20 per cent  
e. Other: 0-10 per cent

4.2.5  
Investments in emerging markets shall not exceed 10 per cent.

*4.2.6*The debt ratio of the unlisted real estate portfolio shall not exceed 25 per cent. No single investment shall be financed with more than 70 per cent debt measured against the value of the asset at acquisition or when refinanced.

*4.2.7*  
Co-investment with a single investment partner in unlisted real estate in the logistics sector shall not exceed 1 per cent of the net asset value of the fund. Co-investments with a single investment partner in unlisted real estate in other sectors (cf. section 4.2.4) shall not exceed 0.5 per cent of the net asset value of the fund.

*4.2.8*  
Counterparts used for real estate daily cash management can be approved with a minimum rating requirement of BBB. Counterparts related to the acquisition of unlisted real estate needs separate approval. Guidelines shall be in place to ensure that a documented credit and operational risk assessment has been performed.

*4.2.9*  
Investment in interest bearing instruments shall not exceed 25 per cent.

*4.2.10 Limits for direct investments*

a. Investments in property under development shall not exceed 20 per cent of the net asset value of the unlisted real estate portfolio, of which more than 50 per cent should have forward lease

b. The average economic vacancy rate shall not exceed 15 per cent. Properties under development shall be excluded from this calculation.

c. Agreements with real estate asset management organisations or investment partners shall, as a general rule, contain provisions to ensure that the total performance related annual fee paid per year does not exceed a maximum amount, which shall not be above USD 30 million. Performance fees accrued above the maximum amount may be paid the following years, subject to the maximum annual pay out limit and excess return over the relevant time period.

*4.2.11 Limits for indirect investments*

a. Investments in real estate funds shall not exceed 10 per cent of the maximum allocation to unlisted real estate. Smaller co-investments, offered as part of the fund investment and leading to a total ownership share of less than 20 per cent in a single investment, is defined as part of the fund investment.

b. Investments in real estate platforms shall not exceed 15 percent of the maximum allocation to unlisted real estate.

c. Committed capital for each fund investment shall as a general rule not exceed 20 per cent of total committed fund capital at final fund close. In closed funds with a focussed strategy offered to only a few selected known investors, committed capital should not exceed 50 per cent of total committed fund capital at final fund close. Ownership stakes in platforms should not exceed 50 percent.

d. Agreements related to fund and platform investments shall, as a general rule, contain provisions to ensure that the management ee and performance fee shall not exceed certain limits. Reference in made to Annex A.

### 4.3 Executive Board investment restrictions for unlisted infrastructure for renewable energy

*4.3.1*  
Investments in infrastructure for renewable energy above USD 2 500 million, or of an unusual nature or major importance in the context of Norges Bank’s management of the fund, shall be approved by the Executive Board.

Transactions that include acquisition of operating subsidiaries with employees shall be approved by the Executive Board.

*4.3.2*   
Limits for direct investments

a. Direct investments in unlisted infrastructure for renewable energy can only be undertaken in developed markets in Europe and North America.  
  
b. Investments in projects in the construction phase shall not exceed 40 per cent of the maximum allocation to unlisted infrastructure for renewable energy.  
  
c. Direct investments in projects in the development phase, must not exceed 2 per cent of the maximum allocation to unlisted infrastructure for renewable energy.  
  
d. The fund may only be invested in unlisted companies or other legal entities where unlisted infrastructure for renewable energy represents a minimum of 80 per cent of the activities. For investments in unlisted companies or other legal entities in transmission and distribution, renewable energy must represent more than 50 per cent of the electricity produced in the country the grid operates in on an annual basis.    
  
e. The management of the portfolio for unlisted infrastructure for renewable energy shall be organised with the aim that the debt ratio of the portfolio over time shall not exceed 60 per cent. The debt ratio for single investments in unlisted infrastructure for renewable energy shall not exceed 70 per cent.  
  
f. Co-investment with a single investment partner in unlisted infrastructure for renewable energy shall, as a general rule, not exceed 0.5 per cent of the net asset value of the fund. The Executive Board may grant exemptions from this general rule.  
  
g. Counterparts used for renewable infrastructure daily cash management can be approved with a minimum rating requirement of BBB. Counterparts related to the acquisition of renewable infrastructure needs separate approval. Guidelines shall be in place to ensure that a documented credit and operational risk assessment has been performed.

h. Agreements with investment partners shall, as a general rule, contain provisions to ensure that the total performance related annual fee paid per year does not exceed a maximum amount, which shall not be above USD 30 million. Performance fees accrued above the maximum amount may be paid the following years, subject to the maximum annual pay out limit and excess return over the relevant time period.

i. Ownership stakes in unlisted companies with employees (operating companies) shall not exceed 50 percent.  

*4.3.3*  
Limits for indirect investments:  
a. Investments in funds for renewable energy shall not exceed 15 per cent of the maximum allocation to unlisted infrastructure for renewable energy. Smaller co-investments, offered as part of the fund investment and leading to a total ownership share of less than 20 per cent of a single project, is defined as part of the fund investment.  
  
b. The fund may only be invested in funds that target a minimum of 70 per cent of their investments to be in unlisted infrastructure for renewable energy,  with the exception of funds that aim to accelerate the energy transition (transition funds), where the target must be a minimum of 60 per cent.  
  
c. A minimum of 70 per cent of underlying investments in funds shall be in OECD countries.

d.  Committed capital for each fund investment shall not exceed 10 per cent of total committed fund capital at final fund close.

e.  Ownership in a single project (sum of fund investment and co-investment) shall not exceed 50 per cent.

f. Agreements related to fund investments shall, as a general rule, contain provisions to ensure that the management fee and the performance fee shall not exceed certain limits. Reference is made to Annex A.

### 4.4 Executive Board investment restrictions for pre-IPOs

a. Investments in unlisted companies where the board has expressed an intention to seek a listing on a regulated and recognised exchange (pre-IPOs) above USD 500 million shall be approved by the Executive Board.

b. If an expected listing on a recognised and regulated exchange fails to materialise, NBIM CEO shall decide on a plan for how the stocks in the unlisted companies shall be disposed. The plan shall include assessments of how the stocks can be disposed in an appropriate and cost-efficient manner, how the investment shall be followed up on through ownership activities and ensure that relevant risks are monitored and managed

c. Counterparts for pre-initial public offerings (pre-IPO) and central clearing counterparties shall not be subject to the minimum rating requirements above but require a separate risk assessment and CEO approval.

### 4.5 Executive Board limit for operational risk

Operational risk tolerance for NBIM is defined and set in the Executive Board Principles for Risk Management in NBIM.

## 5. Duties in the event of limits being exceeded

In the event that investment restrictions in section 2 and section 4 are exceeded, NBIM CEO shall notify the Executive Board and assess how the portfolio may be brought within the limits in an appropriate and cost-effective manner. In the event that restrictions in sections 4.2, 4.3 or 4.4 are exceeded primarily due to market development, NBIM may make decisions that immaterially increase the exposure above the exceeded limit to protect the financial interest of the fund.

args.summary:
This is the official Investment Mandate for the Government Pension Fund Global (GPFG), issued by Norges Bank's Executive Board to the CEO of Norges Bank Investment Management (NBIM), last amended 9 December 2025. The mandate grants the NBIM CEO responsibility for managing the fund in accordance with the Ministry of Finance's Management Mandate, which prevails in case of inconsistency.

**Management and objective:** The fund aims to generate the highest possible return, net of costs, measured in the fund's currency basket, subject to the applicable investment framework. The Executive Board reviews this Investment Mandate at least annually. Investment authority may be delegated, and formal mandates specifying investment universes and risk limits must be issued for all internally and externally managed portfolios.

**Benchmark and investment universe:** The strategic and actual benchmark indices are set by the Ministry Mandate. The fund may only invest in financial instruments, markets, and government bonds from issuers approved by the Executive Board.

**Key investment restrictions for listed investments (Section 4.1):**
- Portfolio/benchmark overlap must be at least 60% for equities and 60% for fixed income issuers.
- Maximum holding of a single issuer non-investment grade government bond is 2% (other non-investment grade bonds: 0.5%) of fixed income NAV; high yield bonds limited to 5% of fixed income market value.
- Minimum 7.5% of fund NAV must be held in treasury bonds of France, Germany, Japan, UK, US, and EU supranationals.
- Counterparty exposure limited to 0.75% of NAV per counterparty; unsecured deposit counterparts need minimum "A" rating, collateralized counterparts minimum "BBB".
- Leveraging limited to 5% of combined equity/fixed income portfolio NAV; securities borrowing capped at 5%; securities lending capped at 20% of NAV.
- Annualized expected shortfall (97.5% confidence) must not exceed 3.75% relative to benchmark.
- Gross exposure for contracts for difference capped at 7% and index CfDs at 5% of NAV.
- Options issuance on non-held individual securities prohibited; put/call options limited to 2.5% of NAV; single listed real estate company ownership capped at 30%; single external manager investment capped at 0.5% of NAV; annual external manager fees capped at USD 30 million.

**Unlisted real estate (Section 4.2):** Investments above USD 2,500 million require Executive Board approval. Regional allocation: North America 30-70%, Europe 20-60%, Asia Pacific 0-10%. Sector allocation: office 20-60%, retail 0-30%, logistics 0-40%, living 0-20%, other 0-10%. Emerging market investments capped at 10%; portfolio debt ratio capped at 25% (70% per single investment); co-investments with single partners capped at 1% (logistics) or 0.5% (other sectors) of fund NAV; property under development capped at 20% of real estate portfolio; average economic vacancy rate capped at 15%.

**Unlisted renewable energy infrastructure (Section 4.3):** Investments above USD 2,500 million require board approval; direct investments only in developed European and North American markets; construction-phase projects capped at 40% (development-phase at 2%) of maximum allocation; portfolio debt ratio capped at 60% (70% per single investment); co-investment with single partner capped at 0.5% of fund NAV; funds must target minimum 70% (60% for transition funds) in renewable infrastructure; minimum 70% of fund investments in OECD countries; committed capital per fund capped at 10%; single project ownership capped at 50%.

**Pre-IPOs (Section 4.4):** Investments above USD 500 million require board approval; disposal plans required if listings fail; pre-IPO counterparts require separate risk assessment and CEO approval.

**Operational risk:** Tolerance defined in the Executive Board Principles for Risk Management in NBIM. When limits are exceeded, the NBIM CEO must notify the Executive Board and assess how to bring the portfolio back within limits; immaterial increases above limits may be permitted to protect the fund's financial interests during market-driven breaches (primarily in real estate and infrastructure sections).

# After Rollercoaster Year, Japan’s GPIF Ekes Out 0.71% Gain in Fiscal 2024

*The $1.7 trillion pension giant also increased its domestic bond holdings by $28 billion during the fourth quarter.*

By [Michael Katz](mailto:cioeditors@strategic-i.com)

[![Add as a preferred source on Google](https://www.ai-cio.com/wp-content/themes/cio/images/preferred-source-badge.png)](https://www.google.com/preferences/source?q=ai-cio.com)

![](https://si-interactive.s3.amazonaws.com/prod/ai-cio-com/wp-content/uploads/2025/07/24131014/CIO-72425-GPIF-Returns-1202949737-web.jpg)  
  
A rollercoaster year that produced wild quarterly swings evened out for Japan’s Government Pension Investment Fund, which eked out a 0.71% return in fiscal 2024. The gain, led by foreign equities, raised the pension giant’s asset value to approximately 250 trillion yen ($1.7 trillion). [[Source](https://www.gpif.go.jp/en/performance/32821257gpif/annual_report_summary_2024_en.pdf)]   
  
During the year, the GPIF swung from a 3.65% gain in the first quarter to a 3.57% loss in the second quarter, back to a 4.31% return in the third quarter, and back again to a 3.41% loss in the fourth quarter.  

All four of the pension fund’s asset classes—domestic and foreign equities and bonds—saw losses in the final quarter. The GPIF’s foreign equities portfolio performed the worst, losing 6% for the quarter, while domestic equities lost 3.5%, and domestic and foreign bonds fell back 2.2% and 2%, respectively.  

Despite the dismal fourth quarter performance, foreign equities were the top-performing asset class for the year with a 6.6% return, followed by a 1.7% gain for the fund’s investments in foreign bonds. Meanwhile, the GPIF’s domestic bond portfolio lost 4.5% for the year, while its domestic equities portfolio was down 1.5%. 

As of March 31, the pension fund’s asset allocation was 27.64% to domestic bonds, 24.37% to foreign bonds, 24.05% to foreign equities and 23.94% to domestic equities. For the quarter that ended December 31, the allocation was 25.51% to domestic bonds, 24.99% to domestic equities, 24.93% to foreign equities and 24.58% to foreign bonds.  

[***For more stories like this, sign up for the CIO Alert newsletter.*** ](https://www.ai-cio.com/alert-shortform/?pk=CIOTEXT2024A)

The GPIF’s domestic bond holdings increased by more than 2% during its fiscal fourth quarter, which amounts to approximately $28 billion. The shift comes after Japanese lawmakers [called for the GPIF](https://www.ai-cio.com/news/japans-gpif-urged-to-boost-domestic-pe-vc-investments/) to increase its investments in domestic assets. However, the fund’s domestic equities allocation was down nearly 1% from the fiscal third quarter.

The remark sparked gains in the yen and bonds as investors bet billions of dollars could ​be channeled into Japanese markets through GPIF, the world's largest pension fund, which manages 293.6 trillion yen ($1.81 trillion) in assets ​as of March.

While the government is exploring ways to boost such investments within the existing allowable ranges ⁠of the benchmark portfolio, the initiative won't lead to immediate revisions to GPIF's medium-term objectives, two government sources said.

"Markets reacted much more ​than we expected," the first source said, while acknowledging that Katayama's remarks were not intended to imply a change in the asset allocation. ​The sources spoke on condition of anonymity due to the sensitivity of the matters.

Advertisement · Scroll to continue

Katayama's comments came after a draft of the government's economic blueprint triggered a sell-off in yen and bonds by giving markets the impression dovish premier Sanae Takaichi's administration would pressure the central bank to delay rate hikes. A [minister](https://www.reuters.com/world/asia-pacific/japan-will-not-convey-advance-preference-boj-policy-minister-says-2026-07-10/) ​in charge of the blueprint was later forced to admit the government will tweak language to soothe market jitters.

GPIF is mandated to ​invest solely in the interests of pension beneficiaries and cannot deploy its assets to advance government policy goals.

Under its current medium-term management plan, GPIF allocates ‌25% ⁠each to domestic bonds, foreign bonds, domestic equities and foreign equities. For domestic bonds, it allows a six percentage point deviation range around its target allocation.

The first source did not rule out the possibility of directing more of GPIF's funds into domestic bonds within that allowable range.

But he stressed that investment decisions of the pension funds needed to be cautious and that even shifts within the permitted deviation ​band required convincing justifications.

"Even if ​it doesn't lead to a ⁠review of its basic portfolio, it's possible for GPIF to increase domestic investment within the scope of existing discretion," said Takahide Kiuchi, executive economist at Nomura Research Institute, adding the government could nudge GPIF ​to make such increases.

"Given the rise in long-term interest rates, Japanese government bonds have become relatively ​attractive safe assets ⁠offering higher returns," he said.

Oversight of the fund rests with the Ministry of Health, Labour and Welfare. The ministry declined to comment when asked whether the government is considering changes to GPIF's asset allocation.

"GPIF reviews the policy portfolio annually, managing risk in light of market developments and ⁠assessing whether ​the investment environment assumed when the portfolio was established has changed materially," said ​Chief Cabinet Secretary Minoru Kihara.

"My understanding is that the portfolio will be revised if such changes make adjustments necessary," he told a news briefing on Monday.

args.summary:
Reuters article (July 13, 2026) reporting that Japan has no immediate plans to overhaul the target asset allocations of its state pension funds, particularly the Government Pension Investment Fund (GPIF), the world's largest pension fund managing 293.6 trillion yen ($1.81 trillion) in assets as of March.

Finance Minister Satsuki Katayama stated on Friday that the government would seek ways to encourage pension funds, including GPIF, to make "substantially greater investments in Japanese financial assets." This remark sparked gains in the yen and bonds as investors bet billions could be channeled into Japanese markets through GPIF.

However, two government sources said the initiative won't lead to immediate revisions to GPIF's medium-term objectives, though the government could work within existing allowable ranges to direct more investment to domestic assets. One source acknowledged "Markets reacted much more than we expected," noting Katayama's remarks were not intended to imply a change in asset allocation.

GPIF is mandated to invest solely in the interests of pension beneficiaries and cannot deploy assets to advance government policy goals. Under its current plan, GPIF allocates 25% each to domestic bonds, foreign bonds, domestic equities and foreign equities, with a six percentage point deviation range allowed for domestic bonds. Shifts within the permitted deviation band require convincing justifications.

The comments came after a draft of the government's economic blueprint triggered sell-offs in yen and bonds by giving markets the impression dovish Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi's administration would pressure the central bank to delay rate hikes. A minister later admitted the government would tweak language to soothe market jitters.

Nomura Research Institute executive economist Takahide Kiuchi noted that "Given the rise in long-term interest rates, Japanese government bonds have become relatively attractive safe assets offering higher returns." Chief Cabinet Secretary Minoru Kihara said GPIF reviews its policy portfolio annually and would revise it if changes make adjustments necessary.

# Japan weighs greater investment flexibility for GPIF as fund reports Q1 results

By Makiko Yamazaki and Takahiko Wada

TOKYO, Aug 7 (Reuters) – Japan’s GPIF will announce its performance for April-June on Friday as the government debates whether the world’s largest pension fund should rethink its investment strategy.

The Government Pension Investment Fund is likely to report comfortable returns from ​its investments, helped by gains in domestic and overseas equities during much of the quarter.

A ‌strong showing would emphasise the resilience of GPIF’s portfolio, which is divided equally among domestic bonds, foreign bonds, domestic equities and foreign equities.

It could also complicate the case for a major overhaul only a year after the fund completed its latest five-year review.

The first major debate over GPIF’s investment strategy in more than a decade began last month after Minister of Finance ‌Satsuki ​Katayama said the government aims to steer state pension funds to increase ⁠domestic asset investments as domestic bond ⁠yields rise and stocks offer stronger returns.

Nearly a month after the remarks, however, government officials said there has been no major policy action towards an imminent change to GPIF’s benchmark portfolio.

A more practical option, they said, would be to allow the fund greater freedom to move within permissible ranges ​around existing targets, without embarking on a strategic review.

GPIF’s basic portfolio sets a 25% target for each of four asset classes, with permissible deviations of five to six percentage points.

But GPIF has made limited use ⁠of that flexibility, partly because its institutional evaluation places emphasis ⁠on keeping holdings and investment performance close to its benchmarks, said executive researcher ​Koji Okuda at Dai-ichi Life Research Institute.

“That focus may have led GPIF to rebalance its portfolio more frequently ​than necessary,” he said.

With $1.8 trillion under management, GPIF is so large that even a ‌modest shift towards domestic bonds or equities could reverberate through currency, stock and debt markets far beyond Japan.

A formal change to its basic portfolio would be a lengthy and highly institutionalised process.

The fund reviews its medium-term investment strategy every five years in conjunction with the health ministry’s actuarial review of the public pension system.

That exercise ⁠reassesses long-term pension finances and provides the basis for determining GPIF’s required return and benchmark allocation.

Although rising domestic bond yields could warrant another review, an overhaul in 2014 showed that major change requires strong political leadership. ⁠At that time, GPIF cut its ‌domestic bond target to 35% from 60% and raised its domestic equity ⁠target to 25% from 12%, while increasing foreign assets.

The shift gained momentum only ​after Shinzo ‌Abe began his second term as prime minister in 2012 and made ​GPIF reform part ⁠of his economic agenda. His government established expert panels and built support across ministries, including the health ministry, which oversees the fund.

Dai-ichi Life’s Okuda said the 2014 overhaul was underpinned by a clear political goal of reshaping Japan’s post-deflation economy.

“While the shift to inflation could provide a rationale for change today, the government has yet to embrace it with comparable political commitment,” Okuda said.

(Reporting by Makiko Yamazaki, Takahiko Wada, Tamiyuki Kihara and Anton ​Bridge; Editing by Christopher Cushing)

# Japan gov’t signals greater domestic pension allocation to Japan

## Comments from finance minister spur yen to rise

![Japan presents both uncertainty and macro resilience notes Amova](https://funds-europe.com/wp-content/themes/jnews/assets/img/jeg-empty.png)

Japan’s finance minster Satsuki Katayama surprised markets on Friday 10 July by using a regular scheduled press conference to launch a surprise policy announcement calling for the country’s pension funds, including the giant GPIF, to invest more in Japanese assets.

The Government Pension Investment Fund holds some $1.8trn of assets. And because it is overseen by a different ministry to Katayama’s, the comments were additionally interpreted as implying broader cabinet agreement on the policy objective.

Naoya Oshikubo, chief market economist at Mitsubishi UFJ Trust and Banking Co., who took part in [*Funds Europe’*s roundtable on Japan](https://funds-europe.com/how-macro-and-micro-factors-are-creating-an-equity-hothouse/) earlier in 2026, responded: “On the 10th of July, finance minister Katayama stated: ‘I want to pursue measures to encourage pension funds, including the GPIF, to invest more in Japanese financial assets.’ She added: ‘I intend to promote this through a new package aimed at creating a virtuous cycle of growth and asset accumulation for the public.'”

“Currently, the GPIF manages its basic portfolio so that domestic bonds, foreign bonds, domestic stocks, and foreign stocks each account for 25% of the total. Although the domestic investment ratio stands at around 50%, the government appears to be moving toward increasing this ratio in the future, as expected returns on domestic bonds have risen against the backdrop of recent interest rate hikes. In response to these remarks, long-term interest rates fell and the yen strengthened.”

“Against the backdrop of the draft of ‘Basic Policies on Economic and Fiscal Management and Reform’, the Takaichi administration’s opposition to the Bank of Japan’s interest rate hikes, coupled with growing concerns over expansionary fiscal policy, had caused long-term interest rates to rise and left the market facing a situation where the yen’s depreciation showed no signs of abating.”

“However, with the revision of “Basic Policies on Economic and Fiscal Management and Reform” – which will include a reference to the Bank of Japan’s independence – and Katayama’s mention of the GPIF actively increasing its investments in Japanese financial assets, we expect the trends of rising long-term interest rates and yen weakness to pause. In the near term, we anticipate a ‘triple rise’ in the Japanese market.”

Commenting further, Masahiko Loo, senior fixed income strategist at State Street Investment Management, said: “Katayama’s comment on potential pension funds’ investments increasing in Japanese financial assets is constructive for both JGBs and the yen over the medium to long-term.”

“While any strategic asset allocation shift is likely to be gradual rather than immediate, pension funds historically have had a small deviation range around their strategic domestic bond target, suggesting there remains a modest amount of flexibility to increase domestic bond exposure over time.”

“The announcement is also a smart policy signal from the administration at a time when markets have increasingly questioned how much firepower the Ministry of Finance has left from an FX intervention perspective. With over $1trn in FX reserves, intervention remains an option, but encouraging domestic institutional capital to stay invested at home is a more durable and structural way to support the yen over time.”

“We continue to hold a constructive medium to long-term view on both JGBs and the yen. As the BOJ approaches its terminal rate and yields become more attractive, domestic investors – including banks sitting on roughly ¥400trn of excess cash – are likely to deploy a greater portion of liquidity back into JGBs, helping improve the demand-supply backdrop. A gradual reduction in structural capital outflows could also provide increasing support for the yen.”

“More broadly, the policy direction fits the growing ‘Japan is Back’ narrative. Higher domestic yields, stronger corporate governance, improving growth prospects, and rising strategic investment into AI, semiconductors, robotics and advanced manufacturing should support both portfolio flows and FDI over time. The result is likely to be a structurally more supportive backdrop for both the yen and Japanese financial assets, even if the adjustment process is unlikely to be a straight line.”

David Mitchinson, partner & CIO at Zennor Asset Management, commented: “The backdrop to this is the GPIF’s upcoming mid term strategy plan for their investment mandate. In part this also reflects the rise in the market that has taken Japanese equity weightings towards the top of the current strategy bands at GPIF. The government is keen to encourage these funds to hold on to their positions and compound through time. A higher limit gives GPIF room to do this.”

“Secondly the government wants Japanese investors – including funds – to take more equity risk to generate higher long term returns. The overall asset allocation remains much more conservative than the US or even Europe. Steps such as the NISA [Nippon Individual Savings Account] and broader market reforms all promote this.”

“Despite higher domestic real yields and strong equity markets Japanese funds still have around 50% international exposure. The government wants to encourage Japanese overseas capital back into Japan – helping strengthen the yen – or at a minimum stop continued outflows. The sense is that if adopted repatriation/less outflows would strengthen the yen, support equities and reduce yields.”

“Politically, The government highlights Japan is growing and investing in new capacity and wants the Japanese population to benefit from this growth through wages and asset ownership.”

# Japan's $1.7 trillion GPIF to keep portfolio composition unchanged

By [Anton Bridge](https://www.reuters.com/authors/anton-bridge/)

March 31, 2025 8:16 AM UTC Updated March 31, 2025

The sign of Japan's Government Pension Investment Fund (GPIF) is seen at its reception in Tokyo, Japan, November 16, 2018. REUTERS/Toru Hanai/File Photo [Purchase Licensing Rights, opens new tab](https://www.reutersconnect.com/item/sign-of-japans-gpif-is-seen-at-its-reception-in-tokyo/dGFnOnJldXRlcnMuY29tLDIwMTg6bmV3c21sX1JDMTkwMzA1QTFDMA%3D%3D/?utm_medium=rcom-article-media&utm_campaign=rcom-rcp-lead)

TOKYO, March 31 (Reuters) - Japan's Government Pension Investment Fund (GPIF) will retain its existing portfolio composition, an equal split between domestic stocks and bonds, and foreign stocks and bonds in 2025 and beyond, it said on Monday.

Over the fund's five year mid-term plan period to the end of the 2029 financial year, the GPIF has raised its investment return target to 1.9% from 1.7% above nominal wage growth. The 1.7% target had been in place since April 2015.

The return target could be more easily achieved by increasing the proportion of stocks in the portfolio but it would still be possible to hit the target with lower risk bonds, the fund said.

Since its inception in 2001 to the end of the 2023 financial year, the fund has made an average annual actual rate of return of 4.24%.

The announcement dispels speculation that it would increase its allocation to stocks that built up after the government last December proposed raising the investment return target to 1.9% from 1.7% above nominal wage growth.

The GPIF's movements are closely watched by markets as it is one of the world's largest institutional investors with 258 trillion yen ($1.73 trillion) in total assets as of the end of December 2024.

Advertisement · Scroll to continue

The fund also maintained the 5% the upper limit of its total portfolio that can be made up of alternative assets, including infrastructure, private equity and real estate.

At its last review in 2020 the GPIF raised its allocation of foreign bonds to 25% from 15% and cut its allocation of domestic bonds to 25% from 35%.

Last week Japan's health ministry said former MUFG Bank executive Kazuto Uchida will be the fund's next head, replacing Masataka Miyazono, a former executive of Norinchukin Bank.

args.summary: Japan's Government Pension Investment Fund (GPIF), one of the world's largest institutional investors with 258 trillion yen ($1.73 trillion) in total assets as of end of December 2024, announced on March 31, 2025 that it will retain its existing portfolio composition—an equal split between domestic stocks and bonds, and foreign stocks and bonds—in 2025 and beyond. This announcement dispels speculation that the fund would increase its stock allocation following the government's December proposal to raise the investment return target to 1.9% from 1.7% above nominal wage growth over the five-year mid-term plan period to end of the 2029 financial year (the 1.7% target had been in place since April 2015). The fund noted the higher return target could be more easily achieved by increasing stock proportion, but could still be hit with lower risk bonds. Since its 2001 inception through the 2023 financial year, the GPIF has averaged a 4.24% annual actual rate of return. The fund also maintained the 5% upper limit for alternative assets (infrastructure, private equity, real estate). At its last review in 2020, the GPIF raised foreign bonds to 25% (from 15%) and cut domestic bonds to 25% (from 35%). Additionally, Japan's health ministry announced last week that former MUFG Bank executive Kazuto Uchida will succeed Masataka Miyazono as the fund's next head.

# Japan’s bond meltdown spurs speculation of GPIF portfolio shift

John Cheng & Masaki Kondo / Bloomberg

4 min read

* [JPY=X

  -0.16%](/quote/JPY%3DX/ "JPY=X")

[![](data:image/gif;base64,R0lGODlhAQABAIAAAAAAAP///ywAAAAAAQABAAACAUwAOw==)](https://s.yimg.com/lo/mysterio/api/CEC02CED3D44FDAFAE75C4FC69DDC7573BAFEF16DE1DE62A120744711A86569D/subgraphmysterio/resizefit_w960;quality_80;format_webp/https:%2F%2Fmedia.zenfs.com%2Fen%2Fthe_edge_961%2F9f9165445d757172ebe6f3f4b2088602)

Investors gaming out how Japan can calm its volatile bond market and prop up the yen see a possible answer in the US$1.8 trillion Government Pension Investment Fund (GPIF).

(Jan 27): Investors gaming out how Japan can calm its volatile bond market and prop up the yen see a possible answer in the US$1.8 trillion Government Pension Investment Fund (GPIF).

As one of the world's largest pension funds — and a trendsetter for other Japanese institutions — the GPIF could help arrest the spike in yields by increasing its asset allocation to the country's government bonds, they say. The shift would be coupled with a reduced target for holdings of foreign bonds, notably US Treasuries, in the process easing selling pressure on the Japanese currency.

The fund, which takes a long-term perspective on its portfolio structure, declined to comment on the prospect of any change. While GPIF completed a five-yearly review of its portfolio in 2025, an early rethink is being raised by market participants after last week's meltdown in Japanese government bonds (JGBs) and indications of potential government intervention to support the yen.

"The clear solution is for GPIF to sell foreign bonds and buy JGBs," Brent Donnelly, the president of Spectra Markets and a former currency trader, said in a note. "GPIF currently holds around US$400 billion of foreign bonds and a change in allocation there would send a strong signal for the start of a Japanese repatriation theme. This would be enormously bullish for JGBs and the yen at the same time."

[![](data:image/gif;base64,R0lGODlhAQABAIAAAAAAAP///ywAAAAAAQABAAACAUwAOw==)](https://myassets.theedgemalaysia.com/pics/2026/20260127_japan_bond_1_20260127125637_ezqlmf.jpg)

The talk of such a shift gained traction after last week's bond rout propelled long-term yields to historical peaks and sent ripples across global markets.

The scale of the move has put officials on alert in Tokyo and Washington, with the yen rebounding sharply after sliding to an 18-month low as traders cited signs the US may join Japan to defend the beleaguered currency.

Japanese public pension funds have increasingly become the steady domestic buyer of government bonds as the Bank of Japan steps back. They have bought a net ¥28.2 trillion of sovereign debt since the fourth quarter of 2022, based on central bank data adjusted for redemptions. By contrast, the BOJ has fallen behind, with slowing purchases failing to offset bonds rolling off its balance sheet.

The GPIF reviews its model portfolio once every five years. At its latest review in 2025, effective from April 1, the fund said it would keep assets evenly split between stocks and bonds.

[![](data:image/gif;base64,R0lGODlhAQABAIAAAAAAAP///ywAAAAAAQABAAACAUwAOw==)](https://myassets.theedgemalaysia.com/pics/2026/20260127_japan_bond_2_20260127125705_v2bs09.jpg)

Between those cycles, however, the fund may assess its strategic allocation and can make revisions when deemed necessary, GPIF says. In 2014, the GPIF unveiled a major portfolio shift outside its regular review timetable following the BOJ's expansion of quantitative easing.

A GPIF spokesperson said investments are conducted in line with the basic portfolio from a long-term perspective.

Under pressure to improve long-term returns amid Japan's ageing population, the GPIF gradually raised its exposure to overseas assets over the past decade. The move, combined with the BOJ's massive easing, added to downward pressure on the yen.

As per its current investment plan, the fund which is one of the world's largest retirement pools, allocates assets evenly across Japanese and foreign stocks and bonds — 25% each — and targets returns of 1.9 percentage points above nominal wage growth.

The potential diversion has significant implications for US Treasuries with GPIF among its biggest investors globally.

GPIF held 51.8% of its foreign bond holdings in Treasuries at the end of March 2025, the highest since data became available in 2015, according to data compiled by *Bloomberg*, as elevated global yields and a weak yen spurred outbound flows.

"It is not our base case but we think it is a risk we should be considering into the end of March," said Stephen Spratt, a rates strategist at Societe Generale SA. "From a political perspective, this would help solve two major issues for the administration. There would be less net buying of overseas assets from this community, removing some pressure on the yen. This would also support long-end JGBs."

Still, market experts are reining in hopes of aggressive buying of JGBs, citing an agreement between the two nations which says, "Government investment vehicles such as pension funds continue to invest abroad for risk-adjusted return and diversification purposes, not targeting exchange rates for competitive purposes."

Public pensions' JGB holdings at ¥67.6 trillion remain far smaller than the BOJ's ¥522.2 trillion as of the third quarter of 2025. But strategists say even a modest shift — or a clear signal — could help steady sentiment in a market where investors have been wary of the heightened volatility at the super-long end.

"An emphatic backstop in the JGB market means that those afraid of 'catching falling knives' could find the confidence to get back in," said Vishnu Varathan, head of macro research, Asia ex-Japan at Mizuho Securities. "JGB yields are already turning increasingly attractive," he said while the market moves were "daunting".

* *Q*How does GPIF construct its portfolio?

GPIF makes investment based on the policy asset mix. The current policy asset mix formed by the target allocation to each asset class, and manages portfolio within deviation limits.

The current policy asset mix, which started in April 2025, shall meet the investment objective, a real investment return (net investment yields on the pension reserve fund less the nominal wage growth rate) of 1.9% with minimal risks.

Japan’s equity investors see a limited impact from the [Government Pension Investment Fund](https://www.bloomberg.com/quote/GPIVFZ:JP)’s reported decision to keep its asset allocation unchanged in the next fiscal year from April.

--- SOURCE 1: World Investment Report 2026 ---
URL: https://unctad.org/system/files/official-document/wir2026_en.pdf

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This webpage presents the United Nations Conference on Trade and Development (UNCTAD) World Investment Report 2026, titled "International Investment in a Turbulent Era," published in Geneva in 2026 (UNCTAD/WIR/2026, ISBN: 978-92-1-154998-0).

KEY HEADLINE FINDINGS:
- Global foreign direct investment (FDI) rose by 6% to $1.6 trillion in 2025, following two consecutive years of decline, but growth remains fragile and uneven. Excluding conduit flows through major European financial centres, global FDI increased 4%.
- Inflows rose 11% in developed economies (to $723 billion) but only 2% in developing economies (to just over $901 billion).
- Investment activity is increasingly concentrated in a few capital- and technology-intensive sectors—data centres, semiconductors, oil and gas, clean energy, and critical minerals. These strategic sectors now represent almost half of all announced greenfield projects in 2025. Most other sectors, including renewable energy and manufacturing, registered significant declines.
- FDI in least developed countries (LDCs) rose 21% but remained highly concentrated in a small number of resource-rich economies. LDCs and lower-middle-income countries attract barely 10% of strategic sector projects, versus more than 20% in other industries.
- The top 20 recipients accounted for more than 80% of global FDI inflows. The United States remained the largest recipient ($277 billion), followed by Singapore, Hong Kong (China), and China. Developing economies represent half of the top 20.
- Global FDI outflows: the US remained largest source ($263 billion), followed by Japan ($186 billion) and China ($174 billion). Developing Asia accounts for one third of global outflows. Gulf Cooperation Council economies are increasingly prominent outward investors, including through sovereign wealth funds.
- The global investor landscape has become more diverse: more than a quarter of the top 100 MNEs are State-owned, and private equity international acquisitions account for about 20% of global M&As.
- Cross-border M&A values declined 7%. Greenfield project values remained near 2024 levels but were driven mainly by megaprojects. International project finance rose only 3%, remaining about 25% below its 2021 peak.
- FDI remains the largest source of external finance for developing economies (about 50% of total), ahead of remittances, ODA, and portfolio flows.

POLICY AND GOVERNANCE CONTEXT:
- Governments are becoming increasingly active in shaping investment flows, with new investment policy measures reaching a record high in 2025—strongly supporting strategic sectors, industrial upgrading, digital transformation, and green transition.
- The report emphasizes that investment is shifting from following cost and efficiency (where developing countries competed) to following strategic calculation, industrial policy, subsidies, economic security, and technological advantage—a logic that rewards deep pockets and established ecosystems.
- New opportunities exist for developing economies in supply-chain reconfiguration: alternative manufacturing locations, processing hubs for critical minerals, and gateways to regional markets.
- At UNCTAD 16 in October 2025, 170 countries adopted the Geneva Consensus, renewing commitment to an open, equitable, and development-oriented investment environment.
- The report references the Sevilla Commitment's global call to address limited access to finance for developing countries.

OUTLOOK (2026):
- Global FDI prospects remain uncertain with significant downside risks from trade policy uncertainty, geopolitical tensions (including the 2026 Middle East conflict), and conflicts. The geopolitical risk index rose sharply to 230.8 in the 2026 forecast from 145.1, while energy prices are forecast to rise significantly. However, moderating interest rates and foreign exchange volatility provide some positive signals.

The report was prepared by an UNCTAD team led by Nan Li Collins, Director of the Division on Investment and Enterprise, with a preface by UN Secretary-General António Guterres and foreword by UNCTAD Acting Secretary-General Pedro Manuel Moreno. The report contains three main chapters covering international investment trends, investment policy trends, and the theme chapter on "International investment in a turbulent era: Trends and policy response."
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"In 2025, global foreign direct investment rose by 6 per cent to reach $1.6 trillion. But this growth masks underlying fragility and disparities across countries, regions and sectors." - António Guterres, UN Secretary-General
</key_excerpts>

--- SOURCE 2: UNCTAD / WORLD INVESTMENT REPORT | UN Audiovisual Library ---
URL: https://media.un.org/avlibrary/en/asset/d341/d3414524

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This webpage from the UN Audiovisual Library documents a video news story (asset d3414524, MAMS ID 3414524) about the launch of the UNCTAD World Investment Report 2025, released on 19 June 2025, in Geneva, Switzerland (UNTV CH source). The 2-minute-58-second English-language video features UN Trade and Development (UNCTAD) Secretary-General Rebeca Grynspan presenting key findings.

Key findings from the report and storyline:
- Global foreign direct investment (FDI) fell by 11% in 2024, marking the second consecutive year of decline and confirming a deepening slowdown in productive capital flows.
- Although global FDI rose by 4% in 2024 to $1.5 trillion, the increase was driven partly by volatile financial conduit flows through several European economies that serve as transfer points for investments.
- Investment dropped sharply across developed economies, particularly in Europe. In developing countries, inflows appeared broadly stable but concealed a deeper crisis, with capital stagnating or bypassing critical sectors like infrastructure, energy, technology, and job-creating industries.
- The report was released ahead of the Fourth International Conference on Financing for Development (FFD4), where leaders will address the widening gap between capital flows and development needs.

In her soundbites, Secretary-General Grynspan attributed the decline to growing geopolitical tensions, rising trade barriers, and increasing screening measures on foreign investment, especially in developed countries. She emphasized the real consequences—jobs not created, infrastructure not built, and sustainable development delayed—and called for embedding sustainability in investment decisions, combating greenwashing, supporting policy reform, directing capital toward the real economy (energy, industry, tech, infrastructure), modernizing international investment governance, protecting public interest, ensuring fair treatment for investors, and preserving national policy space. She concluded: "The time to act is now. Investment is not just about money. It is about trust. It is about fairness. It is about a future that includes everyone."

The webpage also lists related content, including previous UNCTAD World Investment Report news stories (2019, 2023, 2026) and World Chronicle features with Karl P. Sauvant of UNCTAD.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"Productive global foreign direct investment continues to be weak, with a further negative outlook for 2025 and with consequences most sharply felt in the developing world." - Rebeca Grynspan, UNCTAD Secretary-General
</key_excerpts>

--- SOURCE 3: [PDF] World direct investment patterns Statistics Explained - Europa.eu ---
URL: https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/statistics-explained/SEPDF/cache/65097.pdf?v=4582848109069452

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This Eurostat article (data extracted January 2026, from the "Statistics Explained" publication) analyzes global foreign direct investment (FDI) patterns for 2014–2024, based on UNCTAD data. Key findings:

**FDI Stocks (2024):** Global FDI stock was valued at €45.5 trillion. Europe was the largest source of outward FDI (39.8% of world total, €16.7 trillion) and second largest destination of inward FDI (31.4%, €15.4 trillion). Europe was the only continent that was a net investor. EU-held stocks: 14.4% share of global inward investment and 22.2% of global outward investment (second highest, behind the US which accounted for 30.6% of inward and 22.4% of outward FDI). China ranked third in both.

**Trends (2014–2024):** Europe's share of global inward FDI stocks fell by 7.8 percentage points (the largest decline of any continent), reaching 31.4% in 2024. Northern America's share rose 9.7 pp, Asia rose 1.0 pp, while Latin America & Caribbean (−1.2 pp), Africa (−0.9 pp) and Oceania (−0.8 pp) fell. Europe's share of outward stocks declined 5.3 pp (lowest at 39.8% in 2024), while Asia's rose 5.1 pp (to 26.9%) and North America's rose 0.5 pp (28.8%).

**FDI relative to GDP (2024):** World outward stocks/GDP ratio was 39.5%, inward stocks/GDP was 46.1%. Hong Kong (5.7x GDP) and Singapore (4.1x GDP) were most "open" economies. EU inward FDI stocks equaled 39.1% of GDP. Low ratios: Japan (5.5%), Russia (10.3%), Türkiye (13.6%), India (14.1%), South Korea (15.4%), China (20.0%). Japan's outward stocks/GDP ratio (53.6%) was almost 10 times its inward ratio.

**Multinational Enterprises:** In 2024, half of the world's top 10 non-financial multinational groups by foreign assets were HQ'd in the EU (Volkswagen Group, Stellantis NV, Deutsche Telekom AG, TotalEnergies SE, Anheuser-Busch InBev NV). Of the top 20, 9 were in the EU (4 German). Foreign assets exceeded 90% for CK Hutchison, British American Tobacco, Shell and Stellantis.

**FDI Flows (2024):** Global FDI flows totaled €1,440 billion. In 2024, the US was both the world's largest host (18.5% of inward flows) and largest outward investor (16.6% of outward flows). Singapore (9.5%), Hong Kong (8.4%) and China (7.7%) received significant inward flows; Japan (12.7%) and China (10.1%) were the next largest outward investors after the US. Inward FDI into the EU was negative (−14.7% of world total), while EU outward flows were 4.0%. Europe's share of world inward flows fell from 40.5% in 2015 to 12.6% by 2024, while Asia's rose to a peak of 55.0% in 2022 (43.6% in 2024).

**Growth 2014–2024:** China's inward FDI stocks grew 3.9x (highest growth, along with US, UAE and Singapore at 3x+). Chinese and UAE outward stocks grew 4.1x. Between 2014–2024, largest absolute increases in inward flows: US (+€105.8bn), Singapore (+€77.3bn), UAE (+€33.8bn). Largest outward flow increases: Japan (+€90.3bn) and China (+€57.7bn).

**Methodology/Context:** Data follows IMF BPM6 and OECD BD4 standards. A notable caveat: EU data includes special purpose entities (SPEs) while the rest of the world excludes them, which may distort geographic distribution of FDI. Four broad types of FDI are defined: greenfield investment, brownfield investment (acquisitions/mergers), capital extension, and financial restructuring. Geopolitical factors affected flows, notably sanctions leading to decreased Russian investment flows (inward flows turned negative in 2022).
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
In 2024, the global stock of FDI was valued at €45.5 trillion (€45,482 billion), based on an average of inward and outward positions. Europe was the largest source and second largest destination of FDI stocks in the world.
</key_excerpts>

URL: https://www.facebook.com/theOECD/posts/in-2025-the-united-states-the-peoples-republic-of-china-china-and-brazil-receive/1436394911866279

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is an OECD Facebook post from May 14, 2025, announcing findings from its new "FDI in Figures" report on global foreign direct investment trends. Key data points include: In 2025, the United States, China, and Brazil received the most FDI, while the US, Japan, and China were the largest investors abroad. SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is a Cato Institute Policy Analysis (No. 992, published March 11, 2025) by Travis Fisher and Joshua L. Loucks examining the true budgetary cost of the Inflation Reduction Act's (IRA) energy subsidies. The paper argues that the IRA, signed into law August 16, 2022, despite its name, was mostly designed to decarbonize the US economy through subsidies for clean energy producers and EV consumers. Using a transparent, replicable scoring methodology based on EIA and NREL projections, the authors estimate IRA energy subsidies will cost between $936 billion and $1.97 trillion over the next 10 years, and between $2.04 trillion and $4.67 trillion by 2050. They apply a 3% discount rate reducing the 2050 present value by approximately 30%.

Key context: When passed, the CBO and JCT estimated IRA energy subsidies at approximately $369-383 billion over 10 years. Major spending drivers include: the production tax credit (PTC, section 45Y) at $27.50/MWh in 2023, the investment tax credit (ITC, section 48E) typically reimbursing 30% of up-front investment costs, and the uncapped advanced manufacturing tax credit (section 45X) that indefinitely subsidizes 50 critical minerals including aluminum, lithium, nickel, and cobalt. The PTC and ITC (for clean electricity under sections 45Y/48E) could cost $70-180 billion per year. Many IRA subsidies phase down only when electricity sector GHG emissions fall to 25% of 2022 levels—a target unlikely to be met by 2050 due to growing electricity demand from electrification, which extends subsidy duration. Wood Mackenzie estimated clean electricity portions could cost nearly $3 trillion by 2060.

The authors estimate $600 billion difference between lower- and upper-bound estimates is driven by nuclear deployment (zero vs. 200 GW by 2050). They assume ITCs at 30%, model EIA as lower bound and NREL projections as upper bound, and include 80/20 rule repowering assumptions in upper bounds.

Policy recommendations: Congress should repeal all IRA energy subsidies, or at minimum cap total energy subsidy spending and require CBO, JCT, and other government bodies to publish transparent, updated long-term cost estimates.

This speech by Egil Matsen, Deputy Governor of Norges Bank (Central Bank of Norway), delivered in Oslo on 8 November 2019, addresses climate change, climate risks, and their implications for Norway's central bank operations, monetary policy, banking sector, and the Government Pension Fund Global (GPFG).

**Climate Change Background:** The global average temperature has risen about 1 degree Celsius above pre-industrial levels, and climate change is widely accepted as largely human-induced. Matsen identifies two types of climate risk: physical climate risk (economic consequences of higher temperatures and extreme weather) and transition risk (economic effects of shifting to a low-carbon economy through climate policy, changing attitudes, and new technologies). While poor countries in the Global South will likely be hardest hit by physical risks, Norway has experienced about five times higher annual insurance payouts for climate-related flood and storm damage over the past decade compared to the 1980s.

**Monetary Policy Implications:** Extreme weather acts as negative supply shocks—lowering output while raising inflation. Under Norway's flexible inflation targeting regime, Norges Bank typically does not adjust policy rates for transient supply shocks (e.g., agricultural production fell 40% in Q3 2018 due to a hot, dry summer without a rate change). However, policy rate changes may occur if such events cause persistent inflation. Prices for European CO2 emission allowances rose nearly 500 percent over two years, affecting coal, gas, and Norwegian electricity prices.

**Norwegian Economy and Transition Risk:** Norway's large oil and gas sector exposes the economy to transition risk, a concern raised by then-Governor Hermod Skånland as early as 1989. Norway has converted oil wealth into financial wealth via the GPFG since 1996 (with a fiscal rule since 2001), reducing overall risk. Oil stock price-to-book ratios have declined relative to the market average, partly attributed to increased investor climate risk awareness. If the oil sector declined abruptly, monetary policy could support activity and employment, though structural restructuring responsibility lies elsewhere.

**Banking Sector:** Climate risks, particularly transition risk, may become a source of credit risk for Norwegian banks, which have reduced (but not eliminated) oil industry exposure. Banks should correctly price climate risk, rely on relevant company disclosures, and prepare for investors demanding improved climate disclosure (the TCFD recommendations are becoming normative). Transition risk can contribute to financing risk and systemic risk, and should be included in assessments of bank capitalization and funding.

**Government Pension Fund Global (GPFG):** The GPFG invests in over 9,000 companies in 73 countries (70% equities) with the goal of maximizing return within acceptable risk while integrating responsible investment. Its responsible investment work rests on three pillars: (1) setting standards (supporting international standards, with climate expectations published since 2009); (2) exercising ownership (voting rights and dialogue); and (3) portfolio composition (environment-related mandates). The environment-related mandate limit will increase from NOK 60 billion to NOK 120 billion, with expansion in 2020 to include unlisted renewable energy infrastructure (primarily wind and solar), targeting about 1% of the GPFG (≈NOK 100 billion). Notably, 82 companies have been excluded based on a coal criterion, though a conduct-based climate criterion has yet to result in exclusions.

**Conclusion:** In 2018, extreme weather affected about 60 million people, though fatalities from storms and flooding have decreased due to better disaster risk management. Norges Bank participates in the NGFS (Central Banks and Supervisors Network for Greening the Financial System) with Finanstilsynet to build expertise, aiming to strengthen the resilience of the Norwegian economy to climate change and climate risk.
</summary>

--- SOURCE 25: Does disinvestment from fossil fuels reduce the financial performance of responsible sovereign wealth funds? ---
URL: https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/abs/pii/S1042444X22000032

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This research article, published in the Journal of Multinational Financial Management (Vol. 64, June 2022) by Khalil Al Ayoubi and Geoffroy Enjolras, examines whether disinvestment from fossil fuels reduces the financial performance of responsible sovereign wealth funds (SWFs). The study investigates the effects of negative screening on SWF financial performance, driven by public and governmental pressure on SWFs to divest from fossil fuel firms.

Key findings from the study:
- Negative screening does not harm SWFs' financial performance
- Oil divestment does not decrease SWF financial performance
- Negative screening actually decreases the risk exposure of SWFs

Methodology: The researchers used the capital asset pricing model and the Carhart four-factor model to analyze the impact of negative screening on five SWFs over the period 2005-2019: the GPFG of Norway, the French Pension Reserve Fund (FRR), the New Zealand Superannuation Fund (NZSF), the Alaska Permanent Fund (APF), and the Ireland Strategic Investment Fund (ISIF). The study used real-world-based SWF portfolios rather than hypothetical portfolios common in the literature.

The study distinguished between "common" exclusions (weapons, alcohol, tobacco, child labor, etc.) and fossil fuel exclusions, further dividing fossil fuel firms into "extraction and production" and "refining and integrated" categories. Results showed that extraction and production companies generate lower returns to some extent, suggesting that excluding these firms could be beneficial for SWFs.

Background context: On October 1, 2019, the Norwegian Ministry of Finance announced that the GPFG would divest from companies primarily engaged in oil and gas exploration and production. Other SWFs like the NZSF announced intentions to reduce carbon emissions. The study notes that at the end of 2019, there were 88 SWFs worldwide managing over USD 8 trillion in assets.

The article's novelties include: expanding the negative screening field to include oil and gas sectors, examining five SWFs with exclusion strategies (rather than just one), distinguishing between extraction/production and refining/integrated fossil fuel firms, and using real-world portfolios. The conclusion supports that SWFs can meet ethical objectives without compromising financial returns, encouraging other SWFs and institutional investors to engage in negative screening.
</summary>

--- SOURCE 1: World Investment Report 2026 ---
URL: https://unctad.org/system/files/official-document/wir2026_en.pdf

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This webpage presents the United Nations Conference on Trade and Development (UNCTAD) World Investment Report 2026, titled "International Investment in a Turbulent Era," published in Geneva in 2026 (UNCTAD/WIR/2026, ISBN: 978-92-1-154998-0).

KEY HEADLINE FINDINGS:
- Global foreign direct investment (FDI) rose by 6% to $1.6 trillion in 2025, following two consecutive years of decline, but growth remains fragile and uneven. Excluding conduit flows through major European financial centres, global FDI increased 4%.
- Inflows rose 11% in developed economies (to $723 billion) but only 2% in developing economies (to just over $901 billion).
- Investment activity is increasingly concentrated in a few capital- and technology-intensive sectors—data centres, semiconductors, oil and gas, clean energy, and critical minerals. These strategic sectors now represent almost half of all announced greenfield projects in 2025. Most other sectors, including renewable energy and manufacturing, registered significant declines.
- FDI in least developed countries (LDCs) rose 21% but remained highly concentrated in a small number of resource-rich economies. LDCs and lower-middle-income countries attract barely 10% of strategic sector projects, versus more than 20% in other industries.
- The top 20 recipients accounted for more than 80% of global FDI inflows. The United States remained the largest recipient ($277 billion), followed by Singapore, Hong Kong (China), and China. Developing economies represent half of the top 20.
- Global FDI outflows: the US remained largest source ($263 billion), followed by Japan ($186 billion) and China ($174 billion). Developing Asia accounts for one third of global outflows. Gulf Cooperation Council economies are increasingly prominent outward investors, including through sovereign wealth funds.
- The global investor landscape has become more diverse: more than a quarter of the top 100 MNEs are State-owned, and private equity international acquisitions account for about 20% of global M&As.
- Cross-border M&A values declined 7%. Greenfield project values remained near 2024 levels but were driven mainly by megaprojects. International project finance rose only 3%, remaining about 25% below its 2021 peak.
- FDI remains the largest source of external finance for developing economies (about 50% of total), ahead of remittances, ODA, and portfolio flows.

POLICY AND GOVERNANCE CONTEXT:
- Governments are becoming increasingly active in shaping investment flows, with new investment policy measures reaching a record high in 2025—strongly supporting strategic sectors, industrial upgrading, digital transformation, and green transition.
- The report emphasizes that investment is shifting from following cost and efficiency (where developing countries competed) to following strategic calculation, industrial policy, subsidies, economic security, and technological advantage—a logic that rewards deep pockets and established ecosystems.
- New opportunities exist for developing economies in supply-chain reconfiguration: alternative manufacturing locations, processing hubs for critical minerals, and gateways to regional markets.
- At UNCTAD 16 in October 2025, 170 countries adopted the Geneva Consensus, renewing commitment to an open, equitable, and development-oriented investment environment.
- The report references the Sevilla Commitment's global call to address limited access to finance for developing countries.

OUTLOOK (2026):
- Global FDI prospects remain uncertain with significant downside risks from trade policy uncertainty, geopolitical tensions (including the 2026 Middle East conflict), and conflicts. The geopolitical risk index rose sharply to 230.8 in the 2026 forecast from 145.1, while energy prices are forecast to rise significantly. However, moderating interest rates and foreign exchange volatility provide some positive signals.

The report was prepared by an UNCTAD team led by Nan Li Collins, Director of the Division on Investment and Enterprise, with a preface by UN Secretary-General António Guterres and foreword by UNCTAD Acting Secretary-General Pedro Manuel Moreno. The report contains three main chapters covering international investment trends, investment policy trends, and the theme chapter on "International investment in a turbulent era: Trends and policy response."
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"In 2025, global foreign direct investment rose by 6 per cent to reach $1.6 trillion. But this growth masks underlying fragility and disparities across countries, regions and sectors." - António Guterres, UN Secretary-General
</key_excerpts>

--- SOURCE 3: UNCTAD / WORLD INVESTMENT REPORT | UN Audiovisual Library ---
URL: https://media.un.org/avlibrary/en/asset/d341/d3414524

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This webpage from the UN Audiovisual Library documents a video news story (asset d3414524, MAMS ID 3414524) about the launch of the UNCTAD World Investment Report 2025, released on 19 June 2025, in Geneva, Switzerland (UNTV CH source). The 2-minute-58-second English-language video features UN Trade and Development (UNCTAD) Secretary-General Rebeca Grynspan presenting key findings.

Key findings from the report and storyline:
- Global foreign direct investment (FDI) fell by 11% in 2024, marking the second consecutive year of decline and confirming a deepening slowdown in productive capital flows.
- Although global FDI rose by 4% in 2024 to $1.5 trillion, the increase was driven partly by volatile financial conduit flows through several European economies that serve as transfer points for investments.
- Investment dropped sharply across developed economies, particularly in Europe. In developing countries, inflows appeared broadly stable but concealed a deeper crisis, with capital stagnating or bypassing critical sectors like infrastructure, energy, technology, and job-creating industries.
- The report was released ahead of the Fourth International Conference on Financing for Development (FFD4), where leaders will address the widening gap between capital flows and development needs.

In her soundbites, Secretary-General Grynspan attributed the decline to growing geopolitical tensions, rising trade barriers, and increasing screening measures on foreign investment, especially in developed countries. She emphasized the real consequences—jobs not created, infrastructure not built, and sustainable development delayed—and called for embedding sustainability in investment decisions, combating greenwashing, supporting policy reform, directing capital toward the real economy (energy, industry, tech, infrastructure), modernizing international investment governance, protecting public interest, ensuring fair treatment for investors, and preserving national policy space. She concluded: "The time to act is now. Investment is not just about money. It is about trust. It is about fairness. It is about a future that includes everyone."

The webpage also lists related content, including previous UNCTAD World Investment Report news stories (2019, 2023, 2026) and World Chronicle features with Karl P. Sauvant of UNCTAD.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"Productive global foreign direct investment continues to be weak, with a further negative outlook for 2025 and with consequences most sharply felt in the developing world." - Rebeca Grynspan, UNCTAD Secretary-General
</key_excerpts>
