Just six years ago, IHC reported total assets of around $1bn, a figure that had soared to $119bn as of end June this year[1].” Behind the number sits a shift in global capital behavior: GCC institutions are no longer [#funding](https://www.linkedin.com/signup/cold-join?session_redirect=https%3A%2F%2Fwww.linkedin.com%2Ffeed%2Fhashtag%2Ffunding&trk=public_post-text) global [#growth](https://www.linkedin.com/signup/cold-join?session_redirect=https%3A%2F%2Fwww.linkedin.com%2Ffeed%2Fhashtag%2Fgrowth&trk=public_post-text); they’re designing it. 🆔From our managing partner [Rudi Schmidt](https://ae.linkedin.com/in/rudi-schmidt?trk=public_post-text) Call it a strategy or a financial philosophy — either way, it redefines how GCC investors think about time and speed. „Finance and philosophy may seem to be worlds apart. But they share at least one common ancestor: Thales of Miletus - who was a very wise man. Thales is typically regarded as the first philosopher, but he was also a financial innovator[2].” ➡️That shift isn’t theoretical - it’s visible in how the region’s investors deploy capital. With this philosophy, “the Middle East has become a new global hub of wealth and investment. This is, [for example], the case in the six member states of the Gulf Cooperation Council (GCC) - The United Arab Emirates (UAE), Saudi Arabia, Qatar, Kuwait, Bahrain and Oman - and the region’s six largest Sovereign Wealth Funds (SWF) by assets under management (AUM), listed below in alphabetical order: 🔹Abu Dhabi Developmental Holding Company ([ADQ](https://ae.linkedin.com/company/adqofficial?trk=public_post-text)) 🔹[Abu Dhabi Investment Authority (ADIA)](https://ae.linkedin.com/company/adia?trk=public_post-text) 🔹Kuwait Investment Authority (KIA) 🔹[Mubadala](https://ae.linkedin.com/company/mubadala?trk=public_post-text) Investment Company (Abu Dhabi) 🔹Public Investment Fund (PIF) (Saudi Arabia) 🔹Qatar Investment Authority (QIA)[3]” This six SWFs, three of which are based in Abu Dhabi, currently manage a pool of $4 trillion. ➡️With this background, the IHC $36bn-strategy makes perfect sense. Nevertheless, an expansion on this scale still faces a familiar test: How much of that speed converts into durable, trusted enterprise value? Even the [Novo Nordisk](https://dk.linkedin.com/company/novo-nordisk?trk=public_post-text) Foundation that has invested >$40 billion since 2020 in R&D, manufacturing, and M&A is in a different weight class. However, the patterns are worth studying. Capital in biotech and healthcare may not yet move at this velocity - but the blueprint from Abu Dhabi can be a guiding North Star. args.key_excerpts: "Abu Dhabi's sovereign wealth machine is firing on all cylinders - now at US$1.7 trillion AUM."
args.summary:
Global SWF's analysis of Mubadala Investment Company's 2024 performance highlights a record-breaking year for Abu Dhabi's sovereign wealth machine. Key findings include: US$32.4bn deployed in 2024 (a 34% jump), US$326.7bn in assets under management with a 10.1% 5-year return. However, Mubadala's share of Abu Dhabi's total sovereign wealth dropped to 19%, down from 24% in 2019. Meanwhile, ADQ surged 28% in 2024 alone, converging fast with US$251 billion in AUM, and Abu Dhabi Investment Authority (ADIA) represents two-thirds of Abu Dhabi's total SWF AUM, down from 71% in 2019.

Notable strategic moves in 2024 include: (1) AI Power Play - MGX (backed by Mubadala, G42, and the UAE's AI Council) co-led a US$30bn infrastructure fund and joined a US$100bn AI megaproject with OpenAI, SoftBank, and Microsoft; (2) Private Credit Push - a US$20bn portfolio with Fortress Investment Group, Apollo, KKR, and The Carlyle Group, making Mubadala an anchor lender in global markets; (3) Resilience Investing - large moves in healthcare, semiconductors, and aluminum to de-risk supply chains and align with national industrial policy; (4) Space42 - formed MENA's largest spacetech firm and expanded logistics and real estate via a US$30bn JV with ALDAR.

The report notes risks including Mubadala's growing geopolitical exposure and illiquid bets as global markets fragment. The deeper analysis was published in Global SWF's "Mubadala in 2024: Big Capital, Bolder Bets, and the Strategic Tightrope" report.

The page also includes related commentary and posts about Abu Dhabi's broader sovereign wealth landscape, including the IHC's plan to invest $36bn every 18 months (planning to double its $119bn asset base over five years), the six largest GCC SWFs managing a combined $4 trillion, and various other UAE capital markets developments.

# Mubadala Investment Company Reports 2024 Financial Results

Press Releases

Mubadala Investment Company Reports 2024 Financial Results

08 May 2025

Abu Dhabi

![Image 28: facebook sharing button](https://platform-cdn.sharethis.com/img/facebook.svg)

![Image 29: twitter sharing button](https://platform-cdn.sharethis.com/img/twitter.svg)

![Image 30: email sharing button](https://platform-cdn.sharethis.com/img/email.svg)

![Image 31: whatsapp sharing button](https://platform-cdn.sharethis.com/img/whatsapp.svg)

*   Significant investments in AI, healthcare and advanced manufacturing underpin future-focused sectors strategy
*   Assets Under Management grew to AED 1.2 trillion
*   10.1% annualized returns over the last five years
*   Alongside G42, backed a new national champion: MGX

![Image 32: Mubadala Investment Company Reports 2024 Financial Results](https://www.mubadala.com/~/media/Images/M/mubadala/corp/templates/news/thumbnails/mubadalaar2024-prl.jpg)

**Abu Dhabi – May 8th, 2025:**Mubadala Investment Company (“Mubadala”), the Abu Dhabi–based sovereign investor, today reported strong performance in its 2024 financial results, reinforcing the focus and resilience of its strategy. Assets under management grew 9.1% year-on-year to AED 1.2 trillion, with annualized returns of 10.1% over five years.

 “This year marked two decades of disciplined financial performance as an investor central to the UAE’s long-term competitiveness. Our 2024 results and portfolio growth reflect Mubadala’s focused and resilient strategy, with risk-adjusted returns in sectors where we have conviction,” said **Khaldoon Khalifa Al Mubarak, Managing Director and Group CEO**. “Our portfolio has been constructed to navigate market cycles and scale future-focused sectors—from AI and clean energy to life sciences, semiconductors, and advanced manufacturing—all aligned with our national priorities.”

**Al Mubarak further commented:** “A highlight of 2024 was the creation of MGX by the Artificial Intelligence and Advanced Technology Council - the new AI investment champion for Abu Dhabi - with G42 and Mubadala as co-founding partners.

 A growing number of best-in-class investors also continued to partner with Mubadala across key geographies and sectors, reflecting confidence in our approach and long-term strategy. We will work to deepen these partnerships, invest in advancing innovation and create new entities in Abu Dhabi and around the world.”

**Key Financial Highlights:**

 Mubadala’s 2024 results underscore its continued success as a trusted guardian of the nation’s wealth:

*   Delivered a five-year rate of return of 10.1%
*   Assets under management grew 9.1% year-over-year to AED 1.2 trillion
*   Capital deployed grew 33.7% year-over-year to AED 119 billion
*   Proceeds, including monetizations, grew 10% year-over-year to AED 109 billion
*   Portfolio mix remained broadly consistent year-over-year: 40% in private equity, 23% in public markets, and 17% in infrastructure and real estate
*   Raised AED 30.5 billion through a range of capital market instruments, including:
o The world’s first AA-rated sovereign Sukuk

o A bond with the tightest credit spread ever issued in emerging markets

o Mubadala’s first dirham-denominated global Sukuk

o The first Euro-denominated 6- and 7-year corporate facilities in the EMEA region

 “Mubadala’s 10.1% return over the last five years reflects our disciplined capital allocation strategy, resilient execution and consistent focus on long-term value creation,” said **Carlos Obeid, Group Chief Financial Officer.**

 “We continue to grow and diversify across sectors and geographies, supported by a strong balance sheet, a low cost of debt, and a conservative gearing ratio of 7.8%, which positions us well for future investments.”

**UAE Value Creation Highlights:**

 In 2024, Mubadala continued to be a key driver of innovation, economic diversification, and job creation in the UAE, reinforcing the country’s position as a global hub for capital and future-focused industries.

*   The establishment of MGX, alongside G42, was transformational for the UAE’s emergence as a global leader in artificial intelligence and advanced technologies.
*   The creation of Space42, the MENA region’s largest publicly listed space technology company, formed through the merger of Yahsat and Bayanat.
*   Mubadala supported the growth of the life sciences industry in the UAE through acquisitions along the value chain focusing on manufacturing and distribution to support national drug security and address the global need for essential medicines.
*   Emirates Global Aluminium (EGA) expanded its global aluminum recycling capacity to 140,000 tonnes, with another 225,000 tonnes under construction, through the acquisition of 80% of Spectro Alloys Corporation in the United States, the acquisition of Leichtmetall in Europe and the ongoing development of the UAE’s largest recycling plant.
*   Mubadala and Aldar extended their long-standing strategic partnership to support the sustainable economic growth and transformation of Abu Dhabi by developing and managing joint ventures in prime residential, commercial, retail and logistics assets with a combined value of more than AED 30 billion (US$8.2 billion).

**Global Portfolio Highlights:**
Mubadala’s portfolio continued to expand across North America, Europe, and Asia, guided by long-term investment horizons and aligned with global growth trends and Abu Dhabi’s economic vision.

*   Operating as Mubadala’s indirect investments arm and working alongside the best-in-class asset managers globally, Abu Dhabi Investment Council (ADIC) continued to invest through funds and co-investments that supported the diversification of our portfolio.
*   Mubadala Capital, now managing US$30 billion (AED 110.2 billion), two-thirds on behalf of global investors, grew its international footprint by acquiring Fortress Investment Group and establishing a US$1 billion (AED 3.6 billion) partnership with Silver Rock Financial.
*   Mubadala Capital closed Private Equity Fund IV with total commitments of US$3.1 billion (AED 11.4 billion), surpassing its original target by more than US$1 billion (AED 3.6 billion).
*   Mubadala’s private credit portfolio grew to US$20 billion (AED 73.5 billion), supported by deep, trusted partnerships with institutions including Apollo, Ares, Carlyle, Goldman Sachs, and KKR.
*   Masdar, the UAE’s clean energy champion, doubled its portfolio capacity during 2024 from 16.5 gigawatts to 32.6 gigawatts, including through a partnership with Greece’s TERNA to develop one of Europe’s most ambitious renewable energy projects, pioneering 3 gigawatts of clean energy capacity and supporting the EU’s energy transition.
*   A significant investment was made in Manipal Health Enterprises, one of India’s largest multi-specialty hospital networks.
*    A strategic investment in Zelis, a leading U.S. healthcare payments platform, reinforced Mubadala’s commitment to technology-driven businesses transforming essential services.
*   Mubadala made a cornerstone investment in PAG REN I, PAG’s Asia-Pacific renewable energy platform—its first renewable energy investment in Japan.
*   MGX co-led the US$30 billion (AED 110.2 billion) AI Infrastructure Partnership alongside Microsoft, BlackRock, GIP, NVIDIA and xAI and invested in companies such as OpenAI, Anthropic, and Databricks.

Financial Reporting

 Mubadala focuses on long-term value creation and, in line with its sovereign investment mandate, reports multi-year performance metrics that reflect the nature of its strategy. Since 2021 the company has not disclosed annual financial figures such as revenue or net income but has disclosed its rolling 5-year IRR and, in 2024, has begun publishing its 10-year rolling IRR which in 2024 was 8.7%.

 The Annual Review 2024 can be viewed [here](https://annual2024.mubadala.com/).

About Mubadala

 Mubadala Investment Company is a sovereign investor managing a global portfolio, aimed at generating sustainable financial returns for the Government of Abu Dhabi. Mubadala’s US$330 billion (AED 1,212 billion) portfolio spans six continents with interests in multiple sectors and asset classes. We leverage our deep sectoral expertise and long-standing partnerships to drive sustainable growth and profit, while supporting the continued diversification and global integration of the economy of the United Arab Emirates. For more information about Mubadala Investment Company, please visit: [www.mubadala.com](https://www.mubadala.com/)

**Mubadala Investment Company PJSC** ([Arabic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arabic_language "Arabic language"): شركة مبادلة للاستثمار), or simply **Mubadala**, is a state-owned global investment firm that acts as one of the [sovereign wealth funds](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sovereign_wealth_funds "Sovereign wealth funds") of the government of [Abu Dhabi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abu_Dhabi "Abu Dhabi"). The company was established in 2017 when then-named Mubadala Development Company (now Mamoura Diversified Global Holding) and the International Petroleum Investment Company (IPIC) merged. Headquartered in [Abu Dhabi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abu_Dhabi "Abu Dhabi"), Mubadala also has offices in [London](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/London "London"), [Rio de Janeiro](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rio_de_Janeiro "Rio de Janeiro"), [New York](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_York_City "New York City"), [San Francisco](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/San_Francisco "San Francisco") and [Beijing](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beijing "Beijing").

## History

[[edit source](/w/index.php?title=Mubadala_Investment_Company&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section's source code: History")]

Established in 1984, the International Petroleum Investment Company (IPIC) was created to advance Abu Dhabi's natural petroleum wealth for the development of the emirate. Mubadala Development Company followed in 2002 to further diversify the economy. In June 2016, it was announced that Mubadala Development Company would merge with the International Petroleum Investment Company.[[2]](#cite_note-:1-2)[[3]](#cite_note-3)[[4]](#cite_note-4) In 2017, ownership of both MDC and IPIC was transferred to a newly created parent company, Mubadala Investment Company.[[5]](#cite_note-5) The company is a wholly owned investment vehicle of the government of Abu Dhabi, and Sheikh [Mansour bin Zayed Al Nahyan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mansour_bin_Zayed_Al_Nahyan "Mansour bin Zayed Al Nahyan"), vice-president and deputy prime minister of the United Arab Emirates, is chairman of the company.[[6]](#cite_note-6)[[7]](#cite_note-7)[[8]](#cite_note-8)

## Investments

[[edit source](/w/index.php?title=Mubadala_Investment_Company&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section's source code: Investments")]

Mubadala has invested in [logistics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Logistics "Logistics") software [startup](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Startup_company "Startup company") Turvo,[[9]](#cite_note-9) [Alphabet](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alphabet_Inc. "Alphabet Inc.")-owned self-driving technology company [Waymo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Waymo "Waymo"),[[10]](#cite_note-10) Reliance [Jio Platforms](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jio_Platforms "Jio Platforms"),[[11]](#cite_note-11) UK life sciences company Envision,[[12]](#cite_note-12) and [Telegram](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Telegram_(software) "Telegram (software)").[[13]](#cite_note-13) Mubadala is a parent company of [GlobalFoundries](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/GlobalFoundries "GlobalFoundries"), a [semiconductor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Semiconductor "Semiconductor") foundry company.[[14]](#cite_note-thenational-14)

Mubadala owns stakes in numerous companies, including a 7.5 percent share in the [Carlyle Group](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carlyle_Group "Carlyle Group").[[15]](#cite_note-15)

In 2007 Mubadala announced an initial investment in [AMD](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/AMD "AMD").[[16]](#cite_note-16) As of 2017 Mubadala had a stake of 12.9 percent in the chipmaker.[[17]](#cite_note-17) In 2019 Mubadala sold its entire stake in AMD.[[18]](#cite_note-18)

In 2019, Mubadala and Falcon Edge Capital established Abu Dhabi Catalyst Partners, a $1 billion joint venture to invest in financial institutions.[[19]](#cite_note-19)[[20]](#cite_note-20) In November 2020, Mubadala transferred ownership of two information technology companies it previously owned, Injazat and Khazna, to artificial intelligence company, [G42](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/G42_(company) "G42 (company)"), and took a stake in G42.[[21]](#cite_note-21)

In 2021, Mubadala purchased a 2.6% stake in [En+ Group](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/En+_Group "En+ Group"), a manufacturer of green aluminum, from Polina Yumasheva, the former wife of Russian businessman [Oleg Deripaska](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oleg_Deripaska "Oleg Deripaska").[[22]](#cite_note-22) The same year, Mubadala purchased MetrôRio, the company that holds the operations for the [Rio de Janeiro](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rio_de_Janeiro "Rio de Janeiro") metro, from [Invepar](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Invepar "Invepar"). In 2016, Mubadala became the biggest external shareholder at [Investcorp](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Investcorp "Investcorp"), after acquiring 20% stakes in the [Bahraini](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bahrain "Bahrain") firm.[[23]](#cite_note-Parasie-23) In 2023, a former UK minister, [Gerry Grimstone](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gerry_Grimstone,_Baron_Grimstone_of_Boscobel "Gerry Grimstone, Baron Grimstone of Boscobel") was criticized for conducting and not declaring 13 meetings with Mubadala and Khaldoon al-Mubarak, after acquiring the role as an adviser and the chair of planned climate fund at Investcorp. In March 2021, Grimstone finalized a deal between the UK and Mubadala, allowing it to oversee investment of around £10 billion in the [UK](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_Kingdom "United Kingdom") from the UAE. A senior research officer at Transparency International UK, Rose Whiffen said if a minister is working for a firm and meeting its shareholder several times while in office, it should be declared or assessed before approval.[[23]](#cite_note-Parasie-23)

A unit of the company, Mubadala Capital, invested €50 million in the Novalpina Capital [private equity fund](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Private_equity_fund "Private equity fund") of €1 billion, which bought the Israeli security company [NSO Group](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NSO_Group "NSO Group") in 2019. Reports revealed that the UAE targeted human rights activists, journalists, and [Princess Haya](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Princess_Haya "Princess Haya") using the [Pegasus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pegasus_(spyware) "Pegasus (spyware)") spyware, during the same time. Mubadala Capital got a seat on Novalpina's committee of largest investors.[[24]](#cite_note-24)

In 2021, Mubadala invested in wefox, a German digital insurance platform, through a $650 million funding round[[25]](#cite_note-25) and led another $400 million round in 2022.[[26]](#cite_note-26)

In May 2022, Mubadala Investment Company signed a preliminary agreement with French utility [Engie](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Engie "Engie") for the development of a digital platform to charge [electric vehicles](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Electric_vehicle "Electric vehicle") in the UAE and across the Middle East. The two companies would also explore areas related to sustainable mobility.[[27]](#cite_note-27)

In 2022, Mubadala sold the Anglo-Trade Bank, which it funded together with AGTB Holdings in 2018, to Gulf Islamic Investments.[[28]](#cite_note-28)[[29]](#cite_note-29) In April 2023 Mubadala, together with Stone Point Capital and other partners, acquired 20% of [Truist Insurance Holdings](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Truist#Insurance_services "Truist") for $1.95 billion.[[30]](#cite_note-30) The fund bought the remaining 80% of Truist, together with Stone Point Capital, Clayton, Dubilier & Rice and other investors, for $15.5 billion in 2024.[[31]](#cite_note-31)[[32]](#cite_note-32)

In May 2023, Mubadala agreed to buy a majority stake in a New York–based [Fortress Investment Group](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fortress_Investment_Group "Fortress Investment Group") from the [SoftBank Group](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SoftBank_Group "SoftBank Group"). The $3 billion takeover was intended to be closed in the first quarter of 2024. However, the deal that would give Mubadala 70% stakes in Fortress was being scrutinized by the U.S. national security officers. The deal, which raised concerns for the US over the UAE's ties with China, was being closely reviewed by the Committee on Foreign Investment in the US ([Cfius](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cfius "Cfius")).[[33]](#cite_note-33)[[34]](#cite_note-34) In May 2024, the regulatory body approved of the sale.[[35]](#cite_note-35) A year later in April 2025, Mubadala and [Fortress Investment](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fortress_Investment_Group "Fortress Investment Group") started a $1 billion investment partnership.[[36]](#cite_note-36)[[37]](#cite_note-37)

Mubadala increased its partnership with [Aldar Properties](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aldar_Properties "Aldar Properties") in September 2024 with four joint ventures amounting to more than $8.2 billion across Abu Dhabi.[[38]](#cite_note-38)

In September 2024, [Turkish Competition Authority](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Turkish_Competition_Authority "Turkish Competition Authority") confirmed that Mubadala applied to acquire [Getir](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Getir "Getir") in entirety.[[39]](#cite_note-39) In June 2024, Getir founders, Nazim Salur and Serkan Borancili, opposed Mubadala's restructuring plan that would separate profitable local grocery delivery operations with noncore businesses. Under the proposed plan, Mubadala was to acquire grocery delivery operations in exchange for $250 million investment. However, in January 2025, Salur alleged Mubadala of an “illegal coup” and vowed to take legal action against the Emirati firm. He claimed that Mubadala attempted to take over all shares of the founders, and “intentionally delayed” transferring units to them. Getir's founders also stated that Mubadala attempted to back off from the deal at the end of 2024. They appealed to the Enterprise Chamber of the Amsterdam Court of Appeal, and said to take a legal action in [Turkey](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Turkey "Turkey") and the UK as well. Mubadala was planning to propose an alternative plan, which it said was already approved by Getir's independent directors. But Salur expressed his intent to “continue fighting” the restructuring plan.[[40]](#cite_note-40)[[41]](#cite_note-41) On 30 January 2025, Salur removed Getir's CEO Batuhan Gultakan from his position without giving specific reasons. Sources revealed that the move was taken due to Gultakan's full support towards Mubadala.[[42]](#cite_note-42)

In December 2024, Mubadala announced a partnership with Silver Rock Financial LP in which Mubadala Capital acquired a 42% stake in the company.[[43]](#cite_note-43)[[44]](#cite_note-44)

Mubadala Capital acquired the Canadian asset manager CI Financial Corp. in August 2025 for $8.9 billion.[[45]](#cite_note-45)[[46]](#cite_note-46) Also in August 2025, Mubadala invested $35 million for a 12.8% stake into Paragraf, a British technology company.[[47]](#cite_note-47)

Mubadala Capital acquired the outdoor advertising company [Clear Channel Outdoor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Clear_Channel_Outdoor "Clear Channel Outdoor") in February 2026 for $6.2 billion.[[48]](#cite_note-48)

## Mubadala Technology

[[edit source](/w/index.php?title=Mubadala_Investment_Company&action=edit&section=4 "Edit section's source code: Mubadala Technology")]

Mubadala Technology

| Founded | 2014 (2014) |
| Successor | Advanced Technology Investment Company (ATIC) |
| Headquarters | [Abu Dhabi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abu_Dhabi "Abu Dhabi") , [UAE](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/UAE "UAE") |
| Key people | [Ibrahim Ajami](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ibrahim_Ajami?action=edit&redlink=1 "Ibrahim Ajami (page does not exist)") (CEO) |
| [Parent](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Parent_company "Parent company") | Mubadala Investment Company |

The company's Advanced Technology Investment Company (ATIC) in 2008, is an investment company[[2]](#cite_note-:1-2) in the [high-technology](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/High-technology "High-technology") sector.[[50]](#cite_note-50) ATIC owns the [semiconductor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Semiconductor "Semiconductor") foundry companies [GlobalFoundries](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/GlobalFoundries "GlobalFoundries"),[[14]](#cite_note-thenational-14) and [Chartered Semiconductor Manufacturing](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chartered_Semiconductor_Manufacturing "Chartered Semiconductor Manufacturing") (which later merged with GlobalFoundries).[[51]](#cite_note-51)[[52]](#cite_note-52) ATIC has invested in [Calxeda](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Calxeda "Calxeda"), a start-up company for producing [ARM architecture](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/ARM_architecture "ARM architecture")–based computers for the server market.[[53]](#cite_note-53) In 2011, ATIC announced investments of $5.5 billion to expand chip manufacturing in Singapore, Dresden, and New York.[[54]](#cite_note-54)[[55]](#cite_note-55) It also announced a $6–$8 billion computer chip factory in Abu Dhabi for completion in 2012.[[56]](#cite_note-56) The company supports research initiatives in [Khalifa University](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Khalifa_University "Khalifa University"), UAE University, American University of Sharjah, Masdar Institute and [New York University Abu Dhabi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_York_University_Abu_Dhabi "New York University Abu Dhabi"). In 2014, ATIC became Mubadala Technology.[[57]](#cite_note-:0-57)

## Mubadala Energy

[[edit source](/w/index.php?title=Mubadala_Investment_Company&action=edit&section=5 "Edit section's source code: Mubadala Energy")]

Mubadala Energy (formerly Mubadala Petroleum) plans to expand into liquefied natural gas, blue hydrogen, and carbon capture. Mubadala Energy works in eleven markets and employs over 500 people.[[58]](#cite_note-58) In April 2025, Mubadala Energy acquired a 24.1% stake in Kimmeridge SoTex HoldCo.[[59]](#cite_note-59)[[60]](#cite_note-60)

args.summary:
Mubadala Investment Company PJSC is a state-owned global investment firm and one of the sovereign wealth funds of the Abu Dhabi government. Established in 2017 through the merger of Mubadala Development Company (now Mamoura Diversified Global Holding) and the International Petroleum Investment Company (IPIC, founded 1984), the company is headquartered in Abu Dhabi with offices in London, Rio de Janeiro, New York, San Francisco, and Beijing. As of 2024, it manages US$330 billion in assets under management (AUM).

Key leadership includes Chairman Sheikh Mansour bin Zayed Al Nahyan (UAE Vice-President and Deputy Prime Minister) and CEO & Managing Director Khaldoon Khalifa Al Mubarak. Key subsidiaries include Abu Dhabi Investment Council, Clear Channel Outdoor, Dolphin Energy, Fortress Investment Group, GlobalFoundries, International Petroleum Investment Company, Masdar, Nova Chemicals, and Mamoura Diversified Global Holding.

**History:** IPIC was established in 1984 to advance Abu Dhabi's petroleum wealth. Mubadala Development Company followed in 2002 for economic diversification. The June 2016 merger announcement led to the 2017 formation of Mubadala Investment Company as the parent entity.

**Major Investments and Transactions:**
- Invested in Turvo, Waymo, Reliance Jio Platforms, Envision, and Telegram
- Owns a 7.5% stake in Carlyle Group; was a 12.9% shareholder in AMD (2007-2019, sold remaining stake in 2019)
- 2019: Established Abu Dhabi Catalyst Partners ($1 billion JV with Falcon Edge Capital)
- 2020: Transferred Injazat and Khazna to AI firm G42 and took stake in G42
- 2021: Purchased 2.6% stake in En+ Group; acquired MetrôRio; invested in wefox ($650M round, led $400M round in 2022)
- 2016: Became largest external shareholder at Investcorp (20% stake)
- 2023: Acquired 70% of Fortress Investment Group ($3 billion takeover from SoftBank, approved by CFIUS in May 2024), followed by a $1 billion investment partnership in April 2025
- 2024: Acquired Truist Insurance Holdings remaining 80% stake ($15.5 billion, with partners); announced $8.2 billion+ Aldar Properties JVs; partnered with Silver Rock Financial LP (42% stake)
- 2025: Acquired CI Financial Corp for $8.9 billion; invested $35 million in Paragraf (12.8% stake); Mubadala Energy acquired 24.1% stake in Kimmeridge SoTex HoldCo
- 2026: Acquired Clear Channel Outdoor for $6.2 billion (in partnership with TWG Global)

**Notable Controversies:**
- Mubadala Capital invested €50 million in Novalpina Capital fund which bought Israeli security firm NSO Group (maker of Pegasus spyware), linked to UAE surveillance of activists and journalists
- The contentious Getir acquisition saw founder Nazim Salur allege an "illegal coup" by Mubadala (January 2025), with ongoing legal disputes and CEO removal
- Former UK minister Gerry Grimstone was criticized for undeclared meetings with Mubadala officials (2023)

**Platforms:** Operates through four investment platforms: Direct Investments, UAE Investments, Disruptive Investments, and Real Estate & Infrastructure Investments.

**Subsidiary Entities:** 
- Mubadala Technology (formerly ATIC, founded 2008/2014) - owns GlobalFoundries semiconductor foundry, invested in Calxeda, supports university research
- Mubadala Energy (formerly Mubadala Petroleum) - operates in eleven markets, employs 500+ people, expanding into LNG, blue hydrogen, and carbon capture

BENGALURU/ABU DHABI, April 9 (Reuters) - Mubadala Investment Company, among the biggest sovereign wealth funds globally, said on Thursday its assets under management rose 17% to $385 billion in 2025.

The company, based in Abu Dhabi, ​credited the strong performance of its portfolio in the United Arab Emirates for ​its growth last year.

“The strength of Mubadala’s performance in 2025 reflects the ⁠long-term strategy to invest in key sectors of growth in the UAE and abroad," ​Khaldoon Khalifa Al Mubarak, managing director and group CEO said in a statement.

"That strategy and ​our portfolio performance over the last five and ten years mean Mubadala remains resilient and well positioned to weather the current challenges facing the regional and global economy."

Annualised five- and 10-year rates of ​return were over 10%. Capital deployment rose 20% from the previous year to 143 ​billion dirhams, while proceeds increased 27% to 138 billion dirhams, according to the company statement.

Mubadala, along with ‌the ⁠Abu Dhabi Investment Authority and L'Imad Holding, the oil-rich emirate's newest sovereign investment fund, plays a significant role in supporting efforts to diversify the UAE economy away from its reliance on hydrocarbons.

Advertisement · Scroll to continue

It has built up a sizeable domestic portfolio of assets along with its ​international investments, with almost ​a quarter of ⁠its investments in the UAE.

U.S. investments made up 44% of Mubadala's portfolio last year, the largest proportion globally.

The fund is targeting opportunities ​in [artificial intelligence and robotics](https://www.reuters.com/world/middle-east/mubadala-targets-opportunities-ai-robotics-ceo-says-2026-01-20/), viewing the sectors as a major source ​of industrial ⁠growth and a guide for future investments, and it has expanded its technology portfolio in recent years, taking stakes in companies spanning semiconductors, data centres and AI infrastructure.

It recently increased ⁠its shareholding ​in Abu Dhabi's biggest real estate developer, Aldar Properties [(ALDAR.AD), opens new tab](https://www.reuters.com/markets/companies/ALDAR.AD).

Private investments ​made up 42% of Mubadala's portfolio by asset class, while 20% was public investment, followed by real estate ​and infrastructure at 17% in 2025.

Reuters article (April 9, 2026): Mubadala Investment Company, one of the world's largest sovereign wealth funds based in Abu Dhabi, announced its assets under management rose 17% to $385 billion in 2025. The growth was credited to strong portfolio performance in the UAE and abroad.

Key details:
- Annualised five- and 10-year rates of return exceeded 10%.
- Capital deployment rose 20% year-over-year to 143 billion dirhams; proceeds increased 27% to 138 billion dirhams.
- Nearly a quarter (about 25%) of Mubadala's investments are allocated within the UAE.
- U.S. investments accounted for 44% of the portfolio, the largest share globally.
- The fund is targeting opportunities in artificial intelligence and robotics as future growth sectors, having expanded its technology portfolio (semiconductors, data centres, AI infrastructure).
- Recently increased its shareholding in Abu Dhabi's biggest real estate developer, Aldar Properties.
- Portfolio breakdown by asset class: 42% private investments, 20% public investment, 17% real estate and infrastructure.
- Alongside the Abu Dhabi Investment Authority and L'Imad Holding (the emirate's newest sovereign fund), Mubadala plays a significant role in diversifying the UAE economy away from hydrocarbons.
- Quote from Khaldoon Khalifa Al Mubarak, managing director and group CEO: "The strength of Mubadala's performance in 2025 reflects the long-term strategy to invest in key sectors of growth in the UAE and abroad... That strategy and our portfolio performance over the last five and ten years mean Mubadala remains resilient and well positioned to weather the current challenges facing the regional and global economy."

The **Public Investment Fund** (PIF) of **Saudi Arabia** closed 2025 with strong growth, confirming its role as one of the key drivers of the Kingdom’s economic transformation. According to the financial statements, revenue rose by 9 per cent to **120 billion** dollars, whilst net profit more than doubled, reaching 17 billion. This surge reflects the greater maturity of the fund’s portfolio and the growing contribution from companies and projects developed in recent years. On a negative note, the return to shareholders was 5.8 per cent, compared with 7.2 per cent in 2024, although this is in line with the annualised average since 2017. The most impressive figure, however, remains that relating to the fund’s overall size. Assets under management by PIF have now exceeded **900 billion** dollars, compared with around 530 billion in 2021 and just 150 billion in 2015. Over the course of a decade, the fund’s assets have therefore increased approximately sixfold, thanks to expansion across both the Saudi and international markets.

On the domestic front, the fund has strengthened its role as a driving force behind Saudi Arabia’s economic diversification. Since 2021, cumulative investment in the country’s priority sectors has reached **199 billion** dollars. Tourism, entertainment, technology, artificial intelligence, mobility, industry and infrastructure are at the heart of this strategy. According to the fund led by **Yasir Al-Rumayyan**, these activities contributed over 342 billion dollars to Saudi Arabia’s real non-oil GDP between 2021 and 2025. Among the most significant moves of the past year, the acceleration of artificial intelligence stands out. PIF has launched HUMAIN, a wholly-owned subsidiary that will operate across the entire AI value chain, from data centres to the cloud, right through to advanced models and applications. At the same time, PIF and Aramco have finalised the terms for the energy group’s entry as a significant minority shareholder. The objective is clear: to build domestic digital infrastructure and position Saudi Arabia as a leading player in the global AI economy.

Loading...

As for flagship projects, the **NEOM Green Hydrogen Project** is now more than 90 per cent complete, marking a decisive step forward in one of the Kingdom’s most ambitious energy initiatives. In **Qiddiya City**, Six Flags Qiddiya City has opened, marking the first Six Flags park outside North America. Red Sea Global has continued to expand its tourism portfolio with developments on Shura Island. Overall, these developments show that part of the portfolio is moving from the design and construction phase to the operational and revenue-generating phase. According to the official financial statements, the PIF has also continued to diversify its sources of funding. In 2025, it placed its first **euro-denominated green bond**, raising €1.65 billion with demand exceeding supply by more than six times. It also launched its first commercial paper programme, adding a short-term funding instrument to a financial structure that already includes bonds, sukuk and loans. Finally, the report marks the conclusion of the 2021–2025 strategy and the start of the new 2026–2030 cycle. After ten years of rapid expansion, the challenge for the PIF will no longer be merely to grow, but to transform the enormous volume of accumulated investments into sustainable returns, greater private-sector participation and a structural contribution to the Saudi non-oil economy.

args.summary:
The Saudi Arabian Public Investment Fund (PIF) closed 2025 with significant growth, confirming its role as a key driver of the Kingdom's economic transformation. According to its financial statements, revenue rose by 9% to $120 billion, while net profit more than doubled to $17 billion. However, the return to shareholders declined to 5.8% (from 7.2% in 2024), though this is in line with the annualized average since 2017.

The most striking figure is the fund's overall size: assets under management have exceeded $900 billion, up from approximately $530 billion in 2021 and just $150 billion in 2015—a roughly sixfold increase over a decade, driven by expansion in both Saudi and international markets.

Domestically, the fund has been a driving force for economic diversification. Since 2021, cumulative investment in Saudi Arabia's priority sectors has reached $199 billion, targeting tourism, entertainment, technology, AI, mobility, industry, and infrastructure. These activities contributed over $342 billion to Saudi Arabia's real non-oil GDP between 2021 and 2025, according to fund leadership.

Key developments in the past year include:
- PIF launched HUMAIN, a wholly-owned subsidiary operating across the entire AI value chain (data centers, cloud, advanced models, and applications).
- PIF and Aramco finalized terms for the energy group's entry as a significant minority shareholder, aiming to build domestic digital infrastructure and position Saudi Arabia as a global AI leader.
- The NEOM Green Hydrogen Project is now over 90% complete.
- Six Flags Qiddiya City opened in Qiddiya, marking the first Six Flags park outside North America.
- Red Sea Global expanded its tourism portfolio with developments on Shura Island.

The PIF has also diversified its funding sources: in 2025 it placed its first euro-denominated green bond, raising €1.65 billion with demand exceeding supply by more than six times, and launched its first commercial paper programme.

The report marks the conclusion of the 2021–2025 strategy and the start of the new 2026–2030 cycle. Going forward, the challenge for the PIF will shift from growth alone to transforming accumulated investments into sustainable returns, greater private-sector participation, and a structural contribution to Saudi Arabia's non-oil economy.

Saudi Arabia’s Public Investment Fund saw its assets under management fall by $10 billion in 2025 to around $900 billion.  
  
It’s a relatively small decline for one of the world’s biggest sovereign wealth funds — but it’s significant because it marks PIF’s first annual drop in a decade.  
  
PIF attributed the decline to wider market conditions, while the value of its domestic equity investments also fell.  
  
The fund has also scaled back some major projects, including The Line and LIV Golf.  
  
Still, PIF remains central to Saudi Arabia’s diversification strategy, with its portfolio companies contributing 11% of the Kingdom’s non-oil GDP last year.

This is an Instagram post from the account "smashibusiness" (Smashi Business / سماشي أعمال), based in Riyadh, Saudi Arabia, dated around August 19, 2026. The post reports that Saudi Arabia's Public Investment Fund (PIF) saw its assets under management decline by $10 billion in 2025, falling to approximately $900 billion. This marks the first annual drop for the sovereign wealth fund in nearly a decade. PIF attributed the decline to broader market conditions, and the value of its domestic equity investments also fell. The fund has scaled back some major projects, including The Line and LIV Golf. Despite the decline, PIF remains central to Saudi Arabia's diversification strategy (Vision 2030), with its portfolio companies contributing 11% of the Kingdom's non-oil GDP last year.

The post includes several comments from users. One commenter (as_nomaan) claims PIF has agreed to provide about $10 billion backing for the Paramount Skydance takeover and merger deal with Warner Bros., criticizing the investment as "haram" and suggesting the funds could benefit the local defense industry. Another commenter (thameralbuainain) disputes the graphic, saying it should show $910bn. The post also displays additional recent posts from the same account on other business topics, including a WIO Bank CEO statement about the UAE reaching a certain level.

## The Most Aggressive Sports Investment Campaign in Sovereign Wealth History

No sovereign wealth fund in history has pursued athletic capital with the velocity, scale, and strategic ambition of the Public Investment Fund. In less than five years, the PIF has transformed Saudi Arabia from a country with virtually no global sports presence into the most consequential new entrant in international athletics since the United States professionalized its major leagues in the twentieth century. The fund’s sports portfolio spans football, golf, combat sports, tennis, motorsport, and esports — a deliberately diversified approach that mirrors the PIF’s broader investment philosophy of multi-sector dominance rather than single-asset concentration.

The numbers tell part of the story. The PIF’s sports-related investments exceed $6 billion in direct capital deployment, with indirect economic activity — stadium development, broadcast rights, tourism impact, sponsorship ecosystems — pushing the total figure considerably higher. But the financial metrics alone miss the strategic architecture. Every sports investment the PIF makes serves at least three simultaneous objectives: financial returns through asset appreciation and revenue growth, soft power projection that repositions Saudi Arabia’s global brand, and domestic entertainment infrastructure that supports the Kingdom’s quality-of-life transformation under Vision 2030.

This page examines each vertical of the PIF’s sports portfolio in detail. For related analysis of the fund’s entertainment strategy, see [tourism and entertainment](/pif/tourism-entertainment/). For the broader investment framework that governs capital allocation to sports, see [investment strategy](/pif/investment-strategy/).

---

## Newcastle United — The Premier League as a Platform

The PIF’s October 2021 acquisition of Newcastle United Football Club for approximately £305 million ($375 million) represents the most strategically significant sports acquisition in the fund’s portfolio. Not because of the price — which was modest by sovereign wealth standards — but because of what the asset represents. Newcastle United gave the PIF a permanent seat at the table of the English Premier League, the most commercially valuable and globally watched domestic football competition on earth.

### The Acquisition Structure

The deal was structured through a consortium in which the PIF holds an 80% stake, with PCP Capital Partners (Amanda Staveley’s firm) and RB Sports & Media (the Reuben brothers) each holding 10%. This structure was deliberate. The Premier League’s Owners’ and Directors’ Test required separation between the PIF and the Saudi state to satisfy broadcasting and competition concerns, particularly given the piracy dispute involving beoutQ that had complicated earlier acquisition attempts.

The Premier League ultimately approved the takeover after receiving legally binding assurances that the Kingdom of Saudi Arabia would not control or direct the club’s operations. The PIF’s position is that of a financial investor, with club governance handled by the appointed board. Whether this separation is observed in practice has been the subject of continuous media scrutiny, but the formal structure has withstood regulatory challenge.

### Capital Deployment and Squad Investment

Since the acquisition, Newcastle United has received substantial investment in playing squad, coaching infrastructure, training facilities, and commercial operations. Transfer spending exceeded £400 million in the first three full transfer windows under PIF ownership. Key signings — Alexander Isak, Sandro Tonali, Anthony Gordon, Bruno Guimarães — were targeted to move the club from a relegation-threatened side to a Champions League qualifier, which was achieved in the 2022–23 season.

The club’s wage bill has increased commensurately, rising from approximately £100 million per year pre-acquisition to over £180 million. This level of investment is sustainable only because the PIF views Newcastle not as a standalone financial asset but as a platform for broader strategic objectives — brand exposure, tourism marketing, commercial partnerships that extend into Saudi Arabia’s domestic economy.

### Stadium and Infrastructure Plans

St James’ Park, the club’s 52,000-capacity stadium in Newcastle city center, is the subject of expansion and modernization plans. The PIF has explored both in-situ expansion and the construction of a new stadium on the nearby Town Moor site. Either option would increase capacity to 60,000–65,000 seats and add hospitality, conferencing, and commercial space that transforms the venue from a matchday facility into a year-round commercial hub.

The training ground at Darsley Park has already received significant upgrades, with plans for a new state-of-the-art training complex that would rival the facilities at Manchester City’s Etihad Campus or Liverpool’s AXA Training Centre.

### Strategic Value Beyond Football

Newcastle United’s value to the PIF extends well beyond matchday revenue and broadcasting rights. The club provides a platform for Saudi Arabia to engage with British and European business communities, a visible brand asset that generates media coverage worth hundreds of millions annually, and a tourism marketing channel that connects Tyneside to Riyadh in ways that no advertising campaign could replicate.

The PIF has been careful to position Newcastle’s success as evidence of professional sports management rather than state-directed sportswashing. Whether this framing succeeds depends on continued on-pitch performance and the degree to which the club integrates into its local community — an area where early results have been mixed but improving.

---

## LIV Golf — Disrupting the PGA Tour and Reshaping Professional Golf

If Newcastle United was a strategic acquisition of an existing asset, LIV Golf was something far more audacious: the creation of an entirely new competitive league designed to challenge and ultimately reshape the global golf ecosystem. Backed by an estimated $2 billion in PIF capital, LIV Golf launched in 2022 under the leadership of Greg Norman and immediately disrupted a professional golf landscape that had been dominated by the PGA Tour for decades.

### The Disruption Model

LIV Golf’s competitive model was deliberately designed to address what the PIF and its advisors identified as structural weaknesses in the PGA Tour format. LIV events are 54 holes rather than 72, feature shotgun starts for faster play, include team-based competition alongside individual scoring, guarantee appearance fees for contracted players, and offer purses that dwarf traditional PGA Tour events.

The financial model was simple: deploy sovereign capital at a scale that no privately funded competitor could match, sign the world’s best players to exclusive or semi-exclusive contracts, create a media product that appeals to younger and more casual golf audiences, and force the PGA Tour into a negotiating position.

### Player Recruitment and Contracts

LIV Golf recruited players through guaranteed contracts worth between $25 million and $200 million per player for the top tier. Phil Mickelson, Dustin Johnson, Brooks Koepka, Cameron Smith, Bryson DeChambeau, and Jon Rahm were among the highest-profile signings. These contracts guaranteed compensation regardless of performance — a radical departure from the PGA Tour’s purse-based model where only tournament participants who make the cut earn prize money.

The total player compensation committed by LIV Golf through its initial contracts exceeded $2 billion, with the majority funded directly from the PIF’s balance sheet. This level of investment was explicitly designed to be loss-making in the short term, with profitability projected only after LIV Golf secured domestic television rights, international broadcasting deals, and sponsorship revenues at scale.

### The PGA Tour Merger Framework

In June 2023, the PGA Tour and LIV Golf announced a framework agreement to merge their commercial operations under a new entity, with the PIF as a significant investor. This announcement stunned the golf world, as it suggested that the PGA Tour’s leadership had concluded that competing against sovereign capital was unsustainable.

The merger negotiations have proven extraordinarily complex. As of early 2026, a definitive agreement has not been finalized, though the parties continue to negotiate terms that would see the PIF invest approximately $1.5 billion into a combined entity in exchange for a minority equity stake and board representation. The key sticking points have included player release clauses, governance rights, content distribution, and the PGA Tour’s tax-exempt status.

Whatever the final structure, LIV Golf has already achieved its primary strategic objective: it has permanently increased the economic value of professional golf, redirected global attention to Saudi Arabia as a sports destination, and demonstrated the PIF’s willingness to deploy capital aggressively in pursuit of market-shaping outcomes.

### Broadcasting and Media Strategy

LIV Golf’s media strategy has evolved through several phases. Initially, events were streamed on YouTube and LIV Golf’s own platforms. The league subsequently secured a deal with The CW Network in the United States and various international broadcasters. The media rights have not yet achieved the per-event value of PGA Tour broadcasts, but the trajectory is positive, and the merger framework, if completed, would likely integrate LIV events into the PGA Tour’s existing broadcast agreements with CBS, ESPN, and NBC.

---

## Boxing and Combat Sports — Saudi Arabia as the Fight Capital of the World

Saudi Arabia’s emergence as a premium destination for world championship boxing began before the PIF’s formal involvement but has been turbocharged by sovereign capital. The Kingdom hosted its first major boxing event in December 2019 — the Anthony Joshua vs. Andy Ruiz Jr. rematch at the Diriyah Arena — and has since become the preferred venue for the sport’s highest-profile contests.

### The Riyadh Season Boxing Program

Under the Riyadh Season entertainment umbrella (managed by the General Entertainment Authority but closely aligned with PIF strategic objectives), Saudi Arabia has hosted a series of blockbuster boxing events. The Tyson Fury vs. Oleksandr Usyk undisputed heavyweight championship fight in May 2024 was the first undisputed heavyweight title fight in 25 years, generating global pay-per-view revenue exceeding $150 million and positioning Riyadh as the fight capital of the world.

The economic model for these events is straightforward: Saudi Arabia pays site fees of $40–80 million per event to secure hosting rights, generates tourism revenue as tens of thousands of international visitors travel to the Kingdom for fight week, and captures media exposure worth multiples of the site fee in equivalent advertising value.

### Matchroom and Promotional Partnerships

The PIF’s sports investment ecosystem includes relationships with major boxing promoters, particularly Eddie Hearn’s Matchroom Boxing and Turki Alalshikh’s role as chairman of the General Entertainment Authority. These partnerships ensure a pipeline of premium events and exclusive content rights that support both the live event economy and the Kingdom’s emerging sports broadcasting infrastructure.

### Mixed Martial Arts and Combat Sports Expansion

Beyond boxing, Saudi Arabia has explored hosting UFC events and has invested in combat sports training infrastructure. The Kingdom’s interest in MMA aligns with the demographic profile of Vision 2030’s target audience — young Saudi nationals for whom combat sports represent the fastest-growing segment of global sports entertainment.

---

## Tennis — ATP and WTA Investment

The PIF’s tennis investments operate on two levels: hosting rights for premium tournaments and potential equity investment in professional tennis infrastructure.

### The Saudi Tennis Federation and Event Hosting

Saudi Arabia has hosted ATP exhibition events and has been in discussions regarding hosting an ATP Masters 1000 event or a season-ending championship. The construction of dedicated tennis facilities in NEOM, Riyadh, and Jeddah supports a long-term play for permanent tournament hosting.

The Kingdom’s climate presents challenges for outdoor tennis during summer months, but the development of climate-controlled indoor and semi-indoor venues — several of which are under construction as part of giga-project entertainment districts — addresses this constraint.

### Strategic Partnerships with Tennis Governing Bodies

Saudi Arabia’s engagement with the ATP and WTA has included sponsorship agreements, hosting discussions, and exploratory conversations about equity investment in the tours’ commercial operations. The model would parallel the PIF’s approach in golf: use sovereign capital to acquire influence over the sport’s governance and commercial direction, then leverage that influence to ensure Saudi Arabia occupies a permanent position in the global tennis calendar.

Professional tennis has historically been dominated by European and American venues, with the Australian Open as the sole Grand Slam outside those continents. Saudi Arabia’s ambition to host a fifth Grand Slam-tier event — while speculative at this stage — would represent one of the most transformative developments in tennis history if realized.

---

## Formula 1 — The Saudi Arabian Grand Prix and Beyond

The Saudi Arabian Grand Prix, held on the Jeddah Corniche Circuit since 2021, represents the PIF’s most visible motorsport investment. The race is part of a ten-year hosting agreement reportedly worth $900 million total, making it one of the most expensive Formula 1 hosting contracts ever signed.

### The Jeddah Corniche Circuit

The street circuit in Jeddah is one of the fastest on the F1 calendar, with average speeds exceeding 250 km/h. The circuit was designed by Tilke Engineers and constructed in record time for its inaugural race. While the Jeddah circuit has produced exciting racing, it has also been the subject of safety concerns due to its high-speed blind corners — concerns that have prompted circuit modifications in subsequent seasons.

### The Qiddiya Permanent Circuit

Saudi Arabia’s long-term F1 plans center on the construction of a permanent circuit at Qiddiya, the entertainment mega-project south of Riyadh. The Qiddiya circuit, designed by Tilke with input from F1 drivers and the FIA, will feature state-of-the-art facilities including a 40,000-seat main grandstand, a motorsport academy, and a surrounding entertainment district.

The move from Jeddah to Qiddiya is expected to occur in 2028 or 2029, aligning with the broader Qiddiya development timeline. The permanent circuit will eliminate the logistical complexity and cost of street circuit construction while providing a purpose-built venue capable of hosting F1, FIA World Endurance Championship, and other premier motorsport events.

### F1 Team Ownership Ambitions

Beyond race hosting, there have been persistent reports of PIF interest in acquiring or investing in a Formula 1 team. The most frequently cited targets have included Williams Racing, Aston Martin (in which the PIF already holds an indirect stake through Lucid Group’s association with Lawrence Stroll), and potential new team entries under F1’s expansion framework.

F1 team ownership would give the PIF a permanent, year-round presence in one of the world’s most commercially valuable sports properties, with brand exposure across 23+ races per season, a global television audience exceeding 1.5 billion, and commercial partnerships with some of the world’s most prestigious luxury and technology brands.

---

## Esports — Digital Sports and the Youth Demographic

The PIF’s esports investments target what may be the most strategically important sports demographic of all: the under-30 population that represents Saudi Arabia’s demographic majority and the primary audience for Vision 2030’s entertainment economy.

### Savvy Gaming Group

The PIF established Savvy Gaming Group in 2022 as its dedicated gaming and esports investment vehicle. Savvy has deployed over $7.5 billion in gaming investments, including the acquisition of ESL Gaming and FACEIT (merged into ESL FACEIT Group), a $3.3 billion investment in a diversified portfolio of gaming company stakes, and ongoing investments in game development studios.

ESL FACEIT Group is the world’s largest esports tournament organizer, running competitions across Counter-Strike, Dota 2, League of Legends, Valorant, and other titles. The acquisition gives the PIF control over the infrastructure layer of competitive gaming — the tournament platforms, broadcasting production, player ranking systems, and commercial partnerships that generate revenue from the esports ecosystem.

### Esports World Cup

Saudi Arabia launched the Esports World Cup (EWC) in Riyadh in 2024, positioning the event as the premier multi-game esports tournament in the world. The EWC featured competitions across more than 20 game titles, with a total prize pool exceeding $60 million — making it the richest esports event ever staged.

The EWC is designed to be an annual fixture, with Riyadh as the permanent host city. The event serves the same strategic function as the Kingdom’s boxing and motorsport investments — tourism revenue, global media exposure, youth engagement — but targets a demographic that traditional sports events may not fully reach.

### Gaming Infrastructure and Content Development

Beyond tournaments, the PIF’s gaming strategy includes investments in game development studios, cloud gaming infrastructure, and gaming content creation. The goal is to establish Saudi Arabia not merely as a host of gaming events but as a creator and distributor of gaming content — a significantly more valuable position in the gaming value chain.

The Kingdom’s young, digitally native population provides a domestic market for gaming content, while the PIF’s capital enables investments in international studios that develop content for global audiences. This dual approach — domestic consumption and international production — mirrors the PIF’s strategy in film and entertainment.

---

## The Strategic Logic — Why Sports, Why Now, Why This Much

The PIF’s sports portfolio is not a vanity project. It is a calculated deployment of sovereign capital in pursuit of objectives that span economics, geopolitics, and domestic social transformation.

### Economic Returns and Asset Appreciation

Sports assets have demonstrated strong long-term value appreciation. Premier League clubs have increased in value by 500–1,000% over the past two decades. F1 team valuations have tripled since Liberty Media’s acquisition of the sport in 2017. Gaming companies have delivered venture-style returns in a market growing at 8–10% annually.

The PIF’s entry into these markets at the scale it has deployed positions the fund to capture substantial appreciation as the global sports economy continues to grow. Newcastle United, purchased for £305 million, is now valued at over £1.2 billion by multiple independent assessments. LIV Golf’s merged entity with the PGA Tour could generate returns that justify the initial $2 billion investment several times over.

### Soft Power and National Brand

Sports provide the most efficient mechanism for national brand transformation available to any country. The PIF’s sports investments have generated more international media coverage of Saudi Arabia — and more of it positive or neutral rather than negative — than any diplomatic initiative, business conference, or advertising campaign in the Kingdom’s history.

This brand transformation has tangible economic value. It supports Saudi Arabia’s tourism ambitions (target: 150 million visits by 2030), facilitates business relationships by normalizing engagement with the Kingdom, and creates cultural touchpoints that make Saudi Arabia familiar and accessible to international audiences who might never visit the country.

### Domestic Entertainment and Quality of Life

Vision 2030’s social transformation requires domestic entertainment options that keep Saudi nationals — particularly young Saudis — engaged and spending within the Kingdom rather than traveling abroad for leisure. Before the current investment cycle, Saudi households spent an estimated $20 billion annually on international leisure travel, much of it driven by the absence of entertainment options at home.

The PIF’s sports investments directly address this outflow. Premier League matches broadcast from a Saudi-owned club, LIV Golf events hosted in Saudi Arabia, boxing championships in Riyadh, F1 races in Jeddah, esports tournaments with massive local attendance — each of these creates domestic entertainment value that reduces outbound leisure spending and strengthens the Kingdom’s internal economy.

### Talent Development and Knowledge Transfer

Each sports investment creates pathways for Saudi nationals to develop expertise in sports management, event operations, broadcast production, sponsorship sales, athlete management, and sports technology. The PIF has established training programs, scholarship pathways, and employment pipelines through its sports portfolio companies that are building a generation of Saudi sports professionals.

This knowledge transfer dimension is critical. The PIF’s end state is not permanent dependence on international expertise but the development of Saudi capabilities that can eventually manage and grow these assets without external support.

---

## Risk Factors and Controversies

The PIF’s sports portfolio is not without risk. Political opposition to Saudi sports investments — often framed as “sportswashing” — has created reputational challenges for portfolio companies, particularly Newcastle United and LIV Golf. Human rights organizations have consistently criticized the use of sports to improve Saudi Arabia’s international image without corresponding improvements in domestic human rights practices.

Regulatory risk is also present. The European Super League ruling by the European Court of Justice, while not directly related to PIF investments, established principles about the relationship between governing bodies and breakaway competitions that could affect LIV Golf’s legal position and any future efforts to create Saudi-affiliated league structures.

Financial risk exists in the short term. Many of the PIF’s sports investments are currently loss-making, with profitability dependent on revenue growth, media rights appreciation, and successful integration of acquired assets. The PIF’s balance sheet can absorb these losses indefinitely, but the fund’s governance framework requires portfolio companies to demonstrate credible pathways to self-sustaining profitability.

---

## Outlook and Future Investments

The PIF’s sports portfolio will continue to expand. Expected areas of investment include potential F1 team acquisition, additional football club investments (La Liga and Serie A clubs have been mentioned as targets), expanded combat sports hosting through purpose-built arenas, Olympic bid infrastructure (Saudi Arabia’s 2034 Asian Games hosting sets the stage for a future Olympic bid), and continued growth in gaming and esports through Savvy Gaming Group.

The fund’s sports investment allocation is expected to grow from $6 billion to $10–12 billion by 2028, with increasing emphasis on revenue-generating assets rather than event hosting. The shift from consumption (paying site fees to host events) to ownership (owning teams, leagues, and platforms that generate recurring revenue) represents the maturation of the PIF’s sports strategy from brand-building to portfolio-building.

For investors and partners, the PIF’s sports portfolio represents one of the most dynamic opportunity sets in global sports finance. The fund’s willingness to deploy capital at scale, its long-term investment horizon, and its strategic alignment with Saudi Arabia’s national transformation create conditions that are unlikely to be replicated by any other investor.

The PIF, managing $930 billion in assets, has launched what the article calls "the most aggressive sports investment campaign in sovereign wealth history," pursuing athletic capital across football, golf, boxing, tennis, motorsport, and esports.

Key investments detailed include:

The club achieved Champions League qualification in 2022-23. The club's wage bill rose from ~£100 million to over £180 million annually. St James' Park (52,000 capacity) is slated for expansion to 60,000-65,000 seats. The club is now valued at over £1.2 billion.

2. **LIV Golf**: Backed by an estimated $2 billion in PIF capital, launched 2022 under Greg Norman to challenge the PGA Tour. Uses a 54-hole, shotgun-start format with guaranteed player contracts between $25-$200 million per player. Top signings include Phil Mickelson, Dustin Johnson, Brooks Koepka, Cameron Smith, Bryson DeChambeau, and Jon Rahm. Total player compensation exceeded $2 billion. A June 2023 framework agreement with the PGA Tour proposed a merger with PIF investing ~$1.5 billion for a minority stake, though a definitive agreement remains uncompleted as of early 2026.

3. **Boxing/Combat Sports**: Saudi Arabia hosts premium boxing events under the Riyadh Season umbrella, paying site fees of $40-80 million per event. The Fury vs. Usyk undisputed heavyweight championship (May 2024) generated PPV revenue exceeding $150 million. Partnerships exist with Matchroom Boxing (Eddie Hearn) and the GEA (Turki Alalshikh).

4. **Tennis**: PIF engaged in ATP/WTA sponsorship, hosting discussions, and exploratory equity investment conversations. Saudi Arabia ambitions include a potential fifth Grand Slam-tier event.

5. **Formula 1**: Saudi Arabian Grand Prix at Jeddah Corniche Circuit (since 2021) under a 10-year hosting deal reportedly worth $900 million. A permanent circuit at Qiddiya (40,000-seat grandstand) is expected to host from 2028-2029. PIF has shown interest in F1 team ownership (Williams, Aston Martin).

6. **Esports**: Savvy Gaming Group (established 2022) has deployed over $7.5 billion in gaming investments, including acquisition of ESL Gaming and FACEIT (merged into ESL FACEIT Group, the world's largest esports tournament organizer). The Esports World Cup launched in Riyadh 2024 with a $60+ million prize pool across 20+ game titles.

Strategic logic behind the portfolio includes three simultaneous objectives per investment: financial returns, soft power projection, and domestic entertainment infrastructure supporting Vision 2030. The portfolio is projected to grow from $6 billion to $10-12 billion by 2028, shifting from event hosting (consumption) to asset ownership (revenue generation).

Risks include "sportswashing" criticism, regulatory challenges (including the European Super League ruling implications for LIV Golf), and short-term financial losses. # Saudi PIF ‘seeks’ external investment to fund Newcastle stadium plans

##### Talks are 'ongoing' regarding the sale of a minority stake in the club.

![](https://www.sportspro.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/05/Nick-Woltemade-Newcastle-United.jpg?x58376)

Getty Images

**Saudi Arabia’s [Public Investment Fund](https://www.sportspro.com/company/public-investment-fund-pif/) (PIF) is in discussions to sell a minority stake in [Newcastle United](https://www.sportspro.com/company/newcastle-united/), according to [Reuters](https://www.reuters.com/sports/soccer/saudi-pif-talks-with-potential-investors-fund-newcastle-united-plans-sources-say-2026-05-18/).**

The sovereign wealth fund has owned Newcastle since 2021 and is currently debating whether to expand St James’ Park or build a new city centre venue. To raise funds for either venture, PIF is considering issuing new shares to an external investor.

Reuters reports that another option under consideration is to use future commercial revenue as security for a loan. The Magpies generated a club record of UK£335.3 million (US$449.5 million) in revenue last year, which included a 44 per cent increase in commercial income to UK£120.1 million (US$161 million).

A renovation of St James’s Park would cost hundreds of millions of pounds, while a new stadium would require over UK£1 billion (US$1.34 billion) in financing. The club is also building an expanded training facility that has cost millions of pounds.

#### RELATED POSTS

##### Inside Newcastle’s business plan to challenge for the Premier League by 2030

![](https://www.sportspro.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/04/Bryson-DeChambeau-LIV-Golf-150x150.jpg?x58376)

##### What next for LIV Golf and sport’s relationship with Saudi Arabia?

Greater matchday income from an expanded stadium is seen as crucial if Newcastle are to achieve their ambition of regularly challenging for the [Uefa](https://www.sportspro.com/company/uefa/) Champions League and [Premier League](https://www.sportspro.com/company/premier-league/) by 2030. This will require further investment in their playing squad, which will be made easier by the introduction of a new squad cost ratio (SCR) system for next season.

Speaking at [SportsPro London](https://london.sportspro.com/) last month, Newcastle chief executive David Hopkinson acknowledged that resolving the future of St James’ Park was a priority issue during recent meetings with the PIF, with “more [stadium] capacity to drive revenue”.

He has set a target of increasing the team’s revenue by more than UK£100 million (US$134.1 million), by raising more income in areas such as matchday, sponsorship and merchandise.

“If we execute superbly, there might be UK£100 million in annual run-rate revenue that could be unlocked,” Hopkinson said. “Our revenue is worth about UK£400 million, that could become UK£500 million and stretched further to UK£550 million.

“Then we’d enter the conversation [of competing at the top]. That’s our ambition and it’s our job now to go unlock this [income].”

![Newcastle United annual revenue (Column Chart)](https://datawrapper.dwcdn.net/fKLFo/full.png)

Hopkinson’s strategy to deliver more revenue for Newcastle comes as the PIF reevaluates its investment strategy. While it remains committed to the Premier League club, it has however decided to scale back funding commitments in other sports such as tennis and snooker.

Most notably, the sovereign wealth fund plans to withdraw its financial support for [LIV Golf](https://www.sportspro.com/company/liv-golf/) at the end of the ongoing 2026 campaign. It has invested heavily in LIV, spending more than US$5.3 billion on operating the breakaway golf circuit since it launched in 2021 and currently spends US$100 million a month to fund the venture’s ongoing operations.

LIV is now in search of new investors, with investment bank Ducera Partners appointed to lead the process. A report from [Axios](https://www.axios.com/2026/05/18/liv-golf-investment) now suggests it will target raising up to US$250 million from new backers, with the full amount projected to help the competition reach profitability within around 20 months.

Should it raise US$100 million less than its target, the circuit will focus on banking more funds through selling its teams, as well as securing a more lucrative media rights deal. Axios reports LIV needs to secure its new investment by the start of October, and will consider seeking bridge financing if it fails to do so.

Saudi Arabia's Public Investment Fund (PIF), which has owned Newcastle United since 2021, is in discussions to sell a minority stake in the club to raise funds for stadium plans. According to Reuters, talks are "ongoing" regarding issuing new shares to an external investor, with an alternative option of using future commercial revenue as security for a loan. The sovereign wealth fund is debating whether to expand St James' Park (which would cost hundreds of millions of pounds) or build a new city centre venue (requiring over UK£1 billion/US$1.34 billion in financing).

Newcastle generated a club record UK£335.3 million (US$449.5 million) in revenue last year, including a 44 per cent increase in commercial income to UK£120.1 million (US$161 million). Club CEO David Hopkinson, speaking at SportsPro London, set a target of increasing revenue by more than UK£100 million (US$134.1 million) through matchday, sponsorship, and merchandise income, potentially raising annual revenue from ~UK£400 million to UK£500-550 million. Greater matchday income from an expanded stadium is seen as crucial for Newcastle's ambition to regularly challenge for the Champions League and Premier League by 2030, aided by a new squad cost ratio (SCR) system.

The PIF is simultaneously scaling back funding in other sports. It plans to withdraw financial support for LIV Golf at the end of the 2026 campaign after investing over US$5.3 billion in the circuit since 2021 and currently spending US$100 million a month. LIV is seeking new investors via investment bank Ducera Partners, targeting up to US$250 million to reach profitability within around 20 months, with a deadline to secure investment by the start of October. The club is also building an expanded training facility costing millions of pounds.

*   Nearly a quarter of Mubadala's investments are allocated within the UAE
*   U.S. assets accounted for 44% of Mubadala's portfolio
*   Mubadala aims to expand in ​AI and robotics, targeting these as future growth sectors
*   Annualised five- and 10-year ‌returns exceeded 10%

BENGALURU/ABU DHABI, April 9 (Reuters) - Mubadala Investment Company, among the biggest sovereign wealth funds globally, said on Thursday its assets under management rose 17% to $385 billion in 2025.

The company, based in Abu Dhabi, ​credited the strong performance of its portfolio in the United Arab Emirates for ​its growth last year.

“The strength of Mubadala’s performance in 2025 reflects the ⁠long-term strategy to invest in key sectors of growth in the UAE and abroad," ​Khaldoon Khalifa Al Mubarak, managing director and group CEO said in a statement.

Advertisement · Scroll to continue

"That strategy and ​our portfolio performance over the last five and ten years mean Mubadala remains resilient and well positioned to weather the current challenges facing the regional and global economy."

Annualised five- and 10-year rates of ​return were over 10%. Capital deployment rose 20% from the previous year to 143 ​billion dirhams, while proceeds increased 27% to 138 billion dirhams, according to the company statement.

Mubadala, along with ‌the ⁠Abu Dhabi Investment Authority and L'Imad Holding, the oil-rich emirate's newest sovereign investment fund, plays a significant role in supporting efforts to diversify the UAE economy away from its reliance on hydrocarbons.

Advertisement · Scroll to continue

It has built up a sizeable domestic portfolio of assets along with its ​international investments, with almost ​a quarter of ⁠its investments in the UAE.

U.S. investments made up 44% of Mubadala's portfolio last year, the largest proportion globally.

The fund is targeting opportunities ​in [artificial intelligence and robotics](https://www.reuters.com/world/middle-east/mubadala-targets-opportunities-ai-robotics-ceo-says-2026-01-20/), viewing the sectors as a major source ​of industrial ⁠growth and a guide for future investments, and it has expanded its technology portfolio in recent years, taking stakes in companies spanning semiconductors, data centres and AI infrastructure.

It recently increased ⁠its shareholding ​in Abu Dhabi's biggest real estate developer, Aldar Properties [(ALDAR.AD), opens new tab](https://www.reuters.com/markets/companies/ALDAR.AD).

Private investments ​made up 42% of Mubadala's portfolio by asset class, while 20% was public investment, followed by real estate ​and infrastructure at 17% in 2025.
