These regional patterns reflect a growing fragmentation in global investment flows. Investment is increasingly shaped by geopolitical considerations, industrial policies and supply chain realignment. While some regions and sectors continue to attract significant capital, others face tightening constraints.
b. FDI outflows In 2024, FDI outflows from developed countries increased by 8 per cent, reaching $1.1 trillion. As with inflows, outflows were significantly influenced by corporate restructuring activities and intrafirm financial flows in Europe. Several major conduit economies recorded substantial increases in outflows.2 However, when these countries are excluded, FDI outflows from developed countries declined by 24 per cent. The decline occurred despite an increase in the value of cross-border M&As, normally a key driver of FDI outflows from developed economies. The value of transactions rose by 26 per cent, largely due to major deals involving MNEs from the United Kingdom of Great Britain and Northern Ireland. 2 The Netherlands and Luxembourg alone reported a combined net increase in outward FDI flows of $380 billion (from -$217 billion to $163 billion), or almost a quarter of global FDI flows.
Announced greenfield projects by investors from developed countries remained stable across both Europe and North America.
The United States remained the largest home country of FDI outflows despite a 26 per cent decline. Cross-border M&As by United States–based investors held steady at $118 billion, still about 30 per cent below the five-year average. Their overseas asset purchases were heavily concentrated in the information and communication sector, which accounted for half of all cross-border M&A deals and announced greenfield projects in 2024. Companies from the United States allocated more than 60 per cent of the total value of their greenfield projects to domestic (interstate) investment – the highest share ever recorded. This increased domestic focus reflected a relatively strong economy, policy measures aimed at encouraging investment at home and stricter controls on outbound investment (chapter II). FDI outflows from companies in Japan rose by 4 per cent, driven primarily by a 27 per cent increase in investment in the United States. Outward FDI from investors in Europe (excluding conduit jurisdictions) declined by nearly 30 per cent, with sharp decreases from major investor home countries such as France and Germany (figure I.4), where cross-border M&A activity dropped significantly. Among other home countries of major investors, seven were in developing Asia. Notably, India and Saudi Arabia rose in the rankings compared with the previous year. The number of greenfield projects announced by Indian investors increased by 20 per cent, placing India among the world’s top 10 investor countries. FDI outflows from investors in the United Arab Emirates also rose by 5 per cent, supported by a 46 per cent surge in the value of cross-border acquisitions.

The drop was particularly pronounced in Latin America and the Caribbean, where outflows fell by 33 per cent, largely due to a halving of investment by Brazilian investors. In Asia, FDI outflows decreased slightly, by 3 per cent, yet the region still accounted for 28 per cent of global FDI outflows. The value of announced greenfield projects dropped sharply, to $86 billion – half the level recorded in 2023, which had seen a significant surge. However, the number of greenfield projects announced by Chinese MNEs increased by 6 per cent, ranking China sixth globally. Notably, 70 per cent of these projects were focused on the manufacturing sector, particularly in the European Union and South-East Asia. In early 2025, the number of greenfield projects announced by Chinese firms was below the quarterly average of 2023 and 2024, as investors appeared to be waiting for greater clarity on tariff policies.
c. FDI prospects The outlook for global FDI in 2025 is negative. Although at the start of the year expectations were for modest growth, these have been overtaken by rising economic and policy uncertainty. The escalation of a new tariff war, along with deteriorating investor sentiment, has led to downward revisions in key FDI determinants: global GDP growth, capital formation, trade and exchange rate stability (table I.1). Financial market volatility has also increased. These trends contributed to a sharp drop in investment activity in early 2025, with first-quarter data showing record lows in both deal volumes and project announcements.

Forecasts for global GDP growth have been revised downward since the beginning of the year. Projections for capital formation and trade – critical to value chain–driven investment – have also weakened. Persistent high debt levels in several countries, coupled with political instability and fluctuating exchange rates, are reducing the attractiveness of FDI across many regions. Investor confidence indicators such as the Purchasing Managers’ Index have softened in key capital-exporting countries.
The M&A market has been particularly affected. Despite optimism in January for a continued recovery in dealmaking, activity dropped sharply in the first quarter of 2025, reaching the lowest levels since the global financial crisis. Importantly, even if global M&A rebounds later in 2025, this may not translate into an equivalent rise in cross-border transactions. Policy-driven fragmentation, growing regulatory scrutiny of foreign acquisitions and geopolitical factors are reshaping corporate acquisition strategies.
Nevertheless, there are some mitigating factors. The anticipated start of an interest rate–cutting cycle in major economies may ease borrowing conditions, which could help stabilize IPF and capital-intensive FDI. In addition, the profit levels of large multinational corporations remain strong (figure I.5), suggesting continued capacity for reinvestment. Reinvested earnings are an important and stable component of FDI flows, especially in times of uncertainty.

Sectors such as artificial intelligence (AI), cloud computing and cybersecurity have attracted substantial investment. This document is the World Investment Report 2025, published by UNCTAD (United Nations Conference on Trade and Development), focused on "International investment in the digital economy." The report was prepared under the leadership of UNCTAD Secretary-General Rebeca Grynspan, with a preface by UN Secretary-General António Guterres.

**Key Findings:**

**Global FDI Trends (2024):**
- Global FDI fell by 11 per cent in 2024 to $1.5 trillion (when excluding volatile conduit economy flows; headline figure of 4 per cent increase was inflated by conduit flows through Ireland, Luxembourg, the Netherlands, and Switzerland).
- This marks the second consecutive year of double-digit contraction.
- International project finance (IPF) fell by 26 per cent in value, following a steep drop in 2023.
- Cross-border M&As increased 14 per cent to $443 billion but remained below the decade average.
- Greenfield project announcements rose 3 per cent in number (over 19,000 projects) but fell 5 per cent in value.

**Regional Performance:**
- Europe saw FDI decline by 58 per cent; China inflows fell 29 per cent; South America declined 18 per cent.
- North America increased 23 per cent (US up 20 per cent); Africa rose 75 per cent (record high, driven by a $35 billion megaproject in Egypt); ASEAN grew 10 per cent.
- Developing countries received $867 billion (57 per cent of global FDI).
- FDI to LDCs increased 9 per cent; SIDS rose 11 per cent; LLDCs declined 10 per cent.

**SDG Investment Crisis:**
- Goals investment in developing countries dropped by a quarter to a third across infrastructure, renewable energy, water/sanitation, and agrifood systems.
- Energy and gas supply investment fell 28 per cent; renewable energy project finance declined 16 per cent.
- Only the health sector saw positive growth in 2024.
- IPF value fell more than 40 per cent between 2021 and 2024, disproportionately affecting LDCs.

**Digital Economy Focus:**
- Digital economy is the only growth sector, expanding at an annual rate of 10-12 per cent, outpacing global GDP growth.
- Digital sectors saw a doubling of project values; technology firms now account for more than 20 per cent of revenues of the top 100 MNEs.
- Despite $500+ billion in greenfield investment in the digital economy into developing countries over the past five years, investment is heavily concentrated in a few countries.
- Among top 10 highest-value greenfield projects in 2024, 4 were in semiconductor manufacturing (3 in the US); AI, cloud computing, and cybersecurity attracted substantial investment.

**Policy Recommendations:**
- The report proposes a Policy Toolkit for Investment in the Digital Economy.
- Highlights the catalytic role of development finance institutions, multilateral development banks, sovereign wealth funds, and blended finance mechanisms.
- Aligns with the Global Digital Compact and Pact for the Future (adopted 2024).
- Supports calls to triple multilateral lending capacity ahead of the Fourth International Conference on Financing for Development.

**2025 Outlook:**
- Negative outlook for 2025 due to tariff escalation, rising economic and policy uncertainty, and record lows in deals and project announcements in early Q1 2025.
- M&A activity in Q1 2025 reached lowest levels since the global financial crisis.
- Mitigating factors: anticipated interest rate cuts, strong MNE profit levels supporting reinvestment, and continued digital economy growth.

![](https://globalbusiness.org/wp-content/uploads/2022/11/transparent-logo.png)

# Global Investment Fuels U.S. Innovation

## Overview of Foreign Direct Investment in the United States 2025

### Cumulative FDIUS Reaches $5.7 Trillion

Annual foreign direct investment flows over the past few  
years brought total FDIUS to $5.7 trillion through yearend  
2024, measured on a historical-cost basis. This was  
an increase of 30 percent since 2019. The United States  
was the world’s largest investment destination at the end  
of 2024.

International companies often prefer the United States  
to other overseas investment locations because it has  
offered many advantages. For decades, the United States  
has had one of the most open markets and investment  
climates in the world. Other benefits have included:

• an unrivaled consumer market;  
• a world-class system of higher education;  
• a skilled and productive workforce;  
• an entrepreneurial culture of innovation and risk-taking;  
• a transparent regulatory environment; and,  
• the world’s largest capital market.

### Cumulative FDIUS 2019-2024

![](https://globalbusiness.org/wp-content/uploads/2025/09/Screenshot-2025-09-10-152357.jpg)

### Worldwide Inward Stock of Foreign Direct Investment, 2004 and 2024

![](https://globalbusiness.org/wp-content/uploads/2025/09/Screenshot-2025-09-10-154009.jpg)

### United States Faces Intense Competition

The United States faces stiff global competition  
for investment dollars; it accounted for 31  
percent of the world’s inward stock of foreign  
direct investment in 2024, up from 26 percent  
in 2004 and 21 percent in 2014. Despite this  
recent rebound, the United States’ share of  
inward investment remains behind developing  
countries. The European Union’s share of  
worldwide FDI shrank considerably from 33  
percent in 2004 to 23 percent in 2024.

International companies are investing more  
in developing economies, with their share  
increasing more than 10 percentage points  
since 2004 to 31 percent in 2024. Large  
developing economies, including China, Hong  
Kong, Indonesia, and Singapore, were among  
the beneficiaries. International investment in  
China jumped from two percent of worldwide  
investment in 2004 to seven percent last year.

## 2024 Foreign Direct Investment Inflows Below Decade Average

International companies invested more than  
$290 billion in the United States last year, less  
than average over the past decade, and down  
two percent from 2023. In 2024, reinvested  
earnings came to more than $200 billion,  
representing close to 70 percent of total inward  
direct investment in the United States.

During the COVID-19 pandemic, FDIUS flows  
dropped to $112 billion in 2020, the lowest  
level of the past decade. They then rebounded  
to $406 billion the next year. Multinational  
companies headquartered abroad invested  
more than $480 billion in the United States in  
2015 and 2016, well above the annual average  
over this past decade.

### Foreign Direct Investment Flows in the U.S., 2014-2024

![](https://globalbusiness.org/wp-content/uploads/2025/09/Screenshot-2025-09-10-154239.jpg)

## Cumulative FDIUS by Country Through 2024

![](https://globalbusiness.org/wp-content/uploads/2025/09/Untitled-design-12-819x1024.png)

## Four Countries Account for More Than Half of Cumulative FDIUS

Four countries provided the majority of the  
$5.7 trillion in cumulative direct investment  
in the United States through the end of 2024.  
Japan and Canada were the largest investors,  
each constituting 14 percent of total cumulative  
foreign direct investment holdings. Germany was  
the third-largest investor in the United States,  
accounting for 12 percent of cumulative FDIUS.  
Until 2018, the United Kingdom was the largest  
investor in the United States, but it has since  
dropped to fourth position.

The eight countries shown in the pie chart  
accounted for some three-quarters of total FDI  
stock in the United States in 2024. More than 100  
other countries represented the remainder.

This report shows country data by ultimate  
beneficial owner, which reflects the actual  
ownership of a foreign firm in the United States.

## More Than Half of FDIUS Comes from European Investors for Foreign Investment

Europe is the largest regional investor in the  
United States. It made up 56 percent of all foreign  
investment through 2024. These figures include the  
27 European Union (EU) countries and others, such  
as the United Kingdom, Switzerland, Norway, and  
Monaco.

The Asia and Pacific region was the second largest,  
accounting for just over one-fifth of FDI stock in the  
United States. Canada held 14 percent through 2024,  
which was a larger share than several world regions.

Last year, South and Central America, as well as the  
Caribbean and Atlantic Islands each held just two  
percent of FDI stock in the United States. The Middle  
East held one percent. Investment from Africa  
remained tiny at $7 billion. South Africa accounted  
for the majority of the continent’s cumulative  
investments in the United States.

## Cumulative FDIUS by Region 2024

![](https://globalbusiness.org/wp-content/uploads/2025/09/Screenshot-2025-09-10-154826.jpg)

## Denmark and Sweden Lead in Investment Growth in the United States Over

Of the top 20 countries by cumulative direct investment in the United States at year-end 2024, Denmark and Sweden both more than doubled their investment stock since 2019. During that time, the two Scandinavian countries substantially increased their investments in the U.S. wholesale trade sector.

With 70 percent growth, South Korea was the third  
fastest-growing country by FDIUS between 2019 and  
2024. Nearly three-quarters of its FDIUS position is  
in wholesale trade. Mexico, Italy, and Canada each  
increased their FDIUS stock by more than 40 percent  
during the same period.

If recent trends continue, Canada will soon replace Japan as the largest investor in the United States. In stark contrast, China’s FDIUS position shrank nearly 25 percent between 2019 and 2024.

## Cumulative FDIUS from Leading Countries 2019-2024

![](https://globalbusiness.org/wp-content/uploads/2025/09/Screenshot-2025-09-10-155121.jpg)

## China, Largest BRICS Investor in United States, Is Also Largest Divestor

Brazil, Russia, India, China, and South Africa are  
known collectively as BRICS. Despite the size of  
their respective economies, combined BRICS’  
investment registered less than two percent  
of all foreign investment stock in the United  
States through the end of 2024; as a group, its  
investment dropped 15 percent from 2019. China  
was the largest BRICS investor at $40 billion  
through 2024. However, its investment plunged  
23 percent from 2019. Russia’s small cumulative  
direct investment of $3 billion in the United States  
shrank more than 20 percent during the same  
period.

Brazil’s FDIUS also fell more than 20 percent  
from 2019, though it was the second-largest  
BRICS investor in the United States, totaling $38  
billion through 2024. South Africa’s cumulative  
investment registered $5 billion by the end of last  
year, rising about 35 percent since 2019.

## Cumulative FDIUS from BRICS 2019-2024

![](https://globalbusiness.org/wp-content/uploads/2025/09/Untitled-design-14-819x1024.png)

## Manufacturing Accounts for 42 Percent of Inward Investment for Foreign Investment

International companies invest in all sectors  
of the U.S. economy. At $2.4 trillion in 2024,  
manufacturing accounted for 42 percent of total  
foreign direct investment stock. Because the  
United States has the largest and most liquid  
financial markets, international companies, on a  
cumulative basis, have invested heavily in the U.S.  
finance and insurance industries at some $600  
billion by year-end 2024.  
Wholesale trade accounted for 9 percent of total  
foreign direct investment at the end of 2024.

The information sector received $272 billion in  
cumulative foreign direct investment through  
2024, followed by professional, scientific, and  
technical services. The inward investment stock  
position for banking and retail each totaled  
more than $200 billion last year. International  
companies had invested close to $190 billion in  
real estate and rental and leasing through 2024.

International companies invested $324 billion in  
America’s broad petroleum sector\* by the end of  
2024.

## Cumulative FDIUS by Industry 2024

![](https://globalbusiness.org/wp-content/uploads/2025/09/Screenshot-2025-09-10-155511.jpg)
![](https://globalbusiness.org/wp-content/uploads/2024/09/Screenshot-2024-09-18-141516.png)

## Retail Trade Is Fastest-Growing Industry Segment

Speaking of the largest industries, cumulative  
FDIUS in America’s retail trade sector grew the  
fastest, up nearly 55 percent to $213 billion last  
year from 2019. Food and beverage stores was  
its largest subsector, whose FDIUS stock more  
than doubled over the past five years. Likewise,  
inward stock in clothing and accessories stores  
more than doubled between 2019 and 2024.

Up 33 percent over the past five years, inward  
investment stock in the information sector was  
the second fastest-growing industry. Software  
publishing was its largest and fastest-growing  
subsector (see p. 7 for more analysis).

Manufacturing, the largest industry sector by  
FDIUS, also continues to be one of the fastest  
growing, rising 32 percent between 2019 and  
2024.

## Cumulative FDIUS by Industry 2019-2024

![](https://globalbusiness.org/wp-content/uploads/2025/09/Screenshot-2025-09-10-152731.jpg)

## Chemicals Represents A Third of Manufacturing FDIUS

International firms invest heavily in the U.S.  
manufacturing industry. Chemicals attracted  
close to $830 billion in total FDI stock by the  
end of 2024, representing 34 percent of all  
foreign investment in domestic manufacturing  
International companies spend billions annually  
in the U.S. chemicals industry because it boasts a  
highly educated workforce, world-class research  
centers, strong intellectual property protections,  
and a robust regulatory system. Two-thirds of all  
FDI stock in chemicals was in pharmaceuticals  
and medicines.

Multinational companies invested nearly $270  
billion in the U.S. transportation equipment sector  
by year-end 2024, mostly in motor vehicles, bodies  
and trailers, and parts.

International investment in the computers and  
electronic products segment was the third-highest  
in manufacturing, at $210 billion. Beverages and  
tobacco products was the fourth-largest sector by  
international investment stock with nearly $190  
billion through 2024.

## Cumulative FDIUS in Manufacturing 2024

![](https://globalbusiness.org/wp-content/uploads/2025/09/Untitled-design-15-768x960.png)

## Cumulative FDIUS by Largest Manufacturing Sectors, 2019-2024

![](https://globalbusiness.org/wp-content/uploads/2025/09/Screenshot-2025-09-16-124833.png)

## FDIUS in Machinery Posts Fastest Manufacturing Growth Rate Five Years

Total foreign direct investment in America’s machinery sector doubled between 2019 and 2024, the fastest rate of growth among manufacturing sectors. Machinery’s largest subsector, ventilation, heating, air-conditioning, and commercial refrigeration equipment, surged almost 450 percent over those five years.

Investment from international firms nearly doubled in beverages and tobacco products over the past five years. Transportation equipment was the third fastest-growing manufacturing sector by FDIUS stock, rising 67 percent from 2019.

International investment stock in primary and fabricated metals rose 48 percent between 2019 and 2024, followed by computers and electronic products, which grew close to 40 percent.

## FDIUS in Software Publishing More Than Doubles Since 2019

International investors added $56 billion to FDIUS  
stock in software publishing over the past fi ve  
years, translating to a growth rate of nearly 150  
percent. These companies design and sell a variety  
of computer software applications.

Although U.S. software companies lead the world’s  
software market, international investors are eager to  
invest in this lucrative industry, with annual revenues  
in the hundreds of billions of dollars and estimates  
of strong future growth. International software firms have shown a keen interest in the U.S. market  
because of its strong intellectual property rights laws  
and enforcement.

In 2022, international software companies employed  
88,400 American workers and generated $42 billion  
in sales. These companies include British-owned  
Sage and Sophos, and German-owned SAP AG.  
Canadian, French, and Japanese software companies  
also have a strong presence in the United States.

## Cumulative FDIUS in Software Publishing 2019-2024

Research Note 

# China's Global Investment Grew in 2025, But Exports Outpaced Offshoring

Feb 04, 2026 Thilo Hanemann, Armand Meyer, Danielle Goh

The China Cross-Border Monitor (CBM) recorded a total of $124 billion of new FDI transactions announced by Chinese firms in 2025, an 18% increase from 2024. Completed investment also edged up 14% to $73 billion, hitting the highest level since 2019 as China's FDI continued to recover from its pandemic lows. Greenfield projects continued to drive overall investment, but the value of acquisitions almost doubled since 2022. Automotive investment lost steam while data centers, materials, and consumer goods were the top sectors attracting Chinese capital. Investment in overseas manufacturing facilities remains elevated compared to pre-pandemic levels but is trending downward, while China’s exports reached new record highs: Chinese companies may be localizing some of their production through FDI, but China’s globalization approach remains dominated by exports.

![copper mine](/sites/default/files/styles/square_large_desktop/public/2026-02/900681089_0.jpg?h=e5aec6c8&itok=WKwn0ScH)

## China’s outbound FDI continued to grow but verifiable investment lags official statistics

The value of announced FDI transactions by Chinese firms increased to $124 billion in 2025 (Figure 1). This reflects the highest level of new investment since 2018 but remains well below the 2016 high. The value of completed FDI transactions increased to $73 billion, reflecting both a time lag between announcement and completion as well as project cancellations. The value of verifiable FDI transactions continues to stay well below China’s official outbound FDI data, although that gap, which represents Chinese firms holding USD at overseas subsidiaries rather than bringing them back into onshore CNY assets, has shrunk for the third year in a row.

## Greenfield investment continues to dominate but M&A has almost doubled since 2022

Newly announced greenfield investment by Chinese firms reached $100 billion in 2025, driven by capital intensive projects in mining, data centers, and energy (Figure 2). The value of M&A transactions dropped every year from 2016 through 2022 but has since trended upwards and totaled $26 billion in 2025. Our dataset shows nine multibillion-dollar acquisitions in 2025, compared with an average of three per year in 2022–2024. Acquisitions were focused on mining, consumer goods, and entertainment assets.

## Manufacturing FDI remains elevated, but China is not yet meaningfully offshoring production capacity

Overseas investment by Chinese firms in manufacturing facilities remained elevated compared to pre-pandemic patterns but slowed for the second year in a row (Figure 3). Except for North Africa, newly announced investment in manufacturing facilities fell across all regions, with a particularly significant drop in Central and Eastern Europe. Chinese firms have used the greater availability of domestic capital resulting from the property sector deleveraging to build up significant manufacturing capacities at home, and domestic manufacturing investment continues to far outpace overseas investment.

Even though Chinese firms are investing more in overseas production than in the past, exports continue to be the dominant channel for serving markets abroad (Figure 4). Big greenfield projects by companies like BYD have captured headlines, but the reality is that Chinese firms have built out manufacturing capacity at home at a much faster pace than production outside of China since the pandemic. Beijing’s growing concern about the leakage of home-grown technology through FDI creates additional headwinds for Chinese firms planning to set up advanced manufacturing operations in key overseas markets. Slower than anticipated localization will likely create disappointment in nations who have been betting on Chinese capital for industrial revitalization.

## Auto investment drops further while materials, energy and data centers drive new activity

The **automotive** industry remains a major driver of investment at 13% of the total, but its share has plummeted to the lowest level since 2020, reflecting a slowdown in electric vehicle (EV) value chain manufacturing. Investment in battery materials and EV assembly has plateaued since 2024, with new battery investments nearly vanishing in 2025. However, this downturn was somewhat cushioned by a shift toward vehicle parts manufacturing, which accounted for roughly half of all automotive-related investment.

In contrast, **basic materials** and **energy** have surged to represent nearly half of all Chinese outbound investment, signaling a return to strategic asset purchases seen in the 2010s. Basic materials investment hit an all-time high of $36 billion, fueled by capital intensive processing projects like the Simandou iron ore mine in Guinea and a flurry of acquisitions. Rising market prices have also pulled Chinese capital back into gold and lithium mining and processing. Meanwhile, the energy sector continued to see investment growth across both traditional fossil fuels and renewables, with a notable uptick in wind turbine investment offsetting a decline in solar manufacturing investment.

Beyond commodities, **data centers**and **consumer goods** recorded the largest marginal growth. The information and communications technology (ICT) sector recorded the second-highest year on record, driven by a data center boom primarily concentrated in Southeast Asia. The consumer goods sector is seeing a resurgence driven by M&A activity, particularly within Europe, where Chinese firms are targeting established European brands and retail networks to expand their market share and capture higher margins in mature markets.

## Asia remains the biggest attraction, with growth in MENA, Latin America, and Africa

The geographic composition of China's FDI further shifted away from high-income economies toward low- and middle-income economies (Figure 6). In 2025, **Asia** remained the primary recipient with around $40 billion of new transactions, driven by a mix of manufacturing investments, data centers, and raw materials mining and processing. Investment in **Sub-Saharan Africa** jumped due to investments in energy and materials processing for things like steel, hydrogen, ammonia, and titanium. However, Africa historically shows lower completion rates so completed investment may turn out significantly smaller than that. Investment in the **MENA** region also reached a new record driven by investments in Egypt, Morocco, and several individual Gulf countries. **Latin American** investment was also strong, mostly in mining and infrastructure projects. **North America, Europe, and Oceania**together attracted less than 20% of total announced FDI, down from 70% in 2016.

URL: https://www.sipri.org/sites/default/files/2026-04/2604_milex_2025.pdf

SUMMARY:
<summary>
The SIPRI Fact Sheet (April 2026) reports that world military expenditure rose by 2.9 per cent in real terms to $2,887 billion in 2025, marking the 11th consecutive year of growth and the highest level ever recorded by SIPRI. Total military expenditure accounted for 2.5 per cent of global GDP. The five biggest spenders—the United States ($954 billion), China ($336 billion), Russia ($190 billion), Germany ($114 billion), and India ($92.1 billion)—accounted for 58 per cent of world military spending.

Key trends: The USA's military spending fell by 7.5 per cent to $954 billion, mainly due to the end of supplemental appropriations for financial military assistance to Ukraine and Israel. China's spending rose by 7.4 per cent (its 31st consecutive year of growth), Russia increased spending by 5.9 per cent (7.5 per cent of GDP), and Ukraine's spending rose by 20 per cent to $84.1 billion (40 per cent of GDP). Military expenditure grew in all world regions except the Americas. European spending rose by 14 per cent to $864 billion, and Asian/Oceanian spending rose by 8.1 per cent to $681 billion.

Regional highlights: NATO members (32) spent $1,581 billion (55 per cent of global spending), with European NATO members spending $559 billion; 23 of the 32 NATO members met the 2.0 per cent GDP target. In June 2025, NATO agreed to raise its spending target to 5.0 per cent of GDP by 2035, prompting concerns about "creative accounting" and blurred definitions of military-related spending. Germany's spending exceeded 2.0 per cent of GDP for the first time since 1990. Spain recorded the largest increase among top spenders (up by 50 per cent). Algeria's military burden (8.8 per cent of GDP) was the second largest globally after Ukraine.

Notable country developments: Taiwan's military spending rose by 14 per cent (largest increase since 1988) amid rising tensions in the Taiwan Strait, with a pledge to reach 5.0 per cent of GDP by 2030. Japan reached its highest military burden (1.4 per cent of GDP) since 1958. Ukraine received $52.2 billion in partner support in 2025. The Middle East's spending was roughly flat (+0.1 per cent) at $218 billion, with Israel's spending falling 4.9 per cent following the Gaza ceasefire. The global military burden rose to its highest level since 2009 at 2.5 per cent of GDP, with the Middle East having the highest regional burden (3.8 per cent of GDP).
</summary>

- Europe: Spending rose 14% to $864 billion, the main contributor to global growth. Russia spent $190 billion (up 5.9%, 7.5% of GDP); Ukraine spent $84.1 billion (up 20%, 40% of GDP). The 29 European NATO members spent $559 billion, with 22 meeting the 2.0% of GDP threshold. Germany was the largest spender at $114 billion (up 24%, burden of 2.3% of GDP, first time above 2% since 1990). Spain rose 50% to $40.2 billion (above 2% for the first time since 1994). European NATO spending rose faster than at any time since 1953.
- Middle East: Spending was stable at ~$218 billion. Israel fell 4.9% to $48.3 billion (still 97% higher than in 2022); Türkiye rose 7.2% to $30.0 billion; Iran fell 5.6% to $7.4 billion in real terms due to 42% inflation (though it understates off-budget spending).
- Asia and Oceania: Spending rose 8.1% to $681 billion, the largest rise since 2009. China increased 7.4% to $336 billion (31st consecutive annual increase); Japan rose 9.7% to $62.2 billion (1.4% of GDP, highest since 1958); Taiwan rose 14% to $18.2 billion.
- Other: UK fell 2.0% to $89.0 billion; France rose 1.5% to $68.0 billion; India rose 8.9% to $92.1 billion; Pakistan rose 11% to $11.9 billion; Saudi Arabia rose 1.4% to $83.2 billion; Africa rose 8.5% to $58.2 billion (Nigeria up 55% to $2.1 billion); Guyana rose 16% to $248 million due to tensions with Venezuela over Essequibo.

The release also notes SIPRI's methodology (military expenditure includes salaries, operations, equipment, construction, R&D, and administration) and that SIPRI data may differ from NATO's methodology. Contact for media: Stephanie Blenckner.
</summary>

'Given the range of current crises, as well as many states' long-term military spending targets, this growth will probably continue through 2026 and beyond.', 'The decline in US military expenditure in 2025 is likely to be short-lived,' said Nan Tian, Programme Director of the SIPRI Military Expenditure and Arms Production Programme. SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is a SIPRI Fact Sheet titled "Trends in World Military Expenditure, 2025," published in April 2026 in Stockholm by the Stockholm International Peace Research Institute (SIPRI). The document reports that world military expenditure rose by 2.9 per cent in real terms to reach $2887 billion in 2025, marking the 11th consecutive year of growth. Global spending has increased by 41 per cent over the past decade (2016–25). The 2025 year-on-year increase was considerably smaller than the 9.7 per cent rise recorded in 2024 and was the lowest annual rate of growth since 2021.

Key figures: The world's military burden (share of global GDP devoted to military expenditure) rose from 2.4 per cent in 2024 to 2.5 per cent in 2025. The global average military expenditure as a share of government expenditure was 6.9 per cent in 2025 (down from 7.0 per cent in 2024), and world spending per person stood at $352 in 2025.

Notably, global military expenditure rose in 2025 despite a drop in spending by the United States (the world's biggest spender), as a sharp increase in European spending and continued growth in Asia and Oceania more than offset the decrease in US spending. World military expenditure excluding the USA grew by 9.2 per cent in 2025.

The Fact Sheet examines regional and national military expenditure data for 2025 and trends over the decade 2016–25. The data comes from the updated SIPRI Military Expenditure Database and replaces all military spending data previously published by SIPRI. The authors include researchers Xiao Liang, Dr Nan Tian, Dr Diego Lopes da Silva, Lorenzo Scarazzato, Zubaida A. Karim, and Jade Guiberteau Ricard from the SIPRI Military Expenditure and Arms Production Programme. The report is available at DOI: https://doi.org/10.55163/ZLHQ1057.

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is an official NATO webpage (updated 29 June 2026) detailing NATO's defence investment commitments and spending data. The core content covers:

**The 5% Hague Defence Commitment:** At the 2025 NATO Summit in The Hague, Allies committed to investing 5% of GDP annually on defence by 2035, strengthening armed forces and ensuring fairer burden-sharing. European Allies and Canada increased combined defence expenditure by nearly 20% in real terms in 2025 compared to 2024 — over USD 90 billion (in 2021 prices, or close to USD 139 billion in nominal terms). Over the past decade, their collective investment rose from 1.4% of combined GDP in 2014 to 2.3% in 2025, when they invested a combined total of more than USD 571 billion (in 2021 prices). The trajectory and balance of spending will be reviewed in 2029.

**What counts as NATO defence expenditure:** NATO defines defence expenditure as payments by Allied national governments (excluding regional/local/municipal authorities) to meet the needs of its own armed forces, those of other Allies, or the Alliance as a whole. This includes NATO common funding and NATO-managed trust funds. Included items: Ministry of Defence-budgeted armed forces (land, maritime, air, plus joint formations such as Special Operations Forces, Medical Service, Logistic Command, Space Command, Cyber Command, and proportionally certain Interior/coast guard/police forces); government-paid retirement pensions; stockpiling of war reserves; operations/missions under defence budgets; peacekeeping and humanitarian operations; the military component of mixed civilian-military activities (when specifically accountable); all R&D costs (including unsuccessful projects); and military/financial assistance from one Ally to another (counted under the donor nation). Excluded: war damage payments, civil defence spending, and non-MoD money via other international organizations. NATO uses USD as the common denominator, applying the IMF average annual exchange rate.

**2014 Wales Summit 2% Commitment:** Previously, the 2014 Wales Summit committed Allies to 2% of GDP on defence (building on a 2006 guideline agreed by Defence Ministers), in response to Russia's illegal annexation of Crimea and broader Middle East instability. The pledge also required that at least 20% of defence expenditure go toward major equipment and related R&D. The 2023 Vilnius Summit renewed this pledge—enduring commitment to at least 2% of GDP annually and 20% on major equipment—while affirming many cases require spending beyond 2% to remedy shortfalls, paving the way for the 2025 commitment of 5% by 2035.

**Historical data:** NATO publishes an annual compendium of financial, personnel, and economic data for all member countries (since 1963 providing a consistent basis of comparison based on the common definition). The page provides downloadable PDF/Excel compendia covering 1949 to the present (e.g., 2026, 2025, 2024 down to 1963). Figures represent payments actually made during the fiscal year and may diverge from nationally quoted figures. The page also includes links to related contents, official texts (summits from 2014 to 2025), a PDF library, and newsletter subscription options, as well as a multimedia account system for downloading NATO broadcast-quality video content.
</summary>

--- SOURCE 4: Government Spending ---
URL: https://ourworldindata.org/government-spending

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This page from Our World in Data provides a comprehensive analysis of government spending worldwide, examining historical trends, cross-country comparisons, and spending composition.

**Historical trends in early-industrialised countries:**
- Government spending as a share of GDP evolved through four broad periods: low spending until WWI; volatile spending between 1915-1945 (driven by war-related defense spending); rapid growth between 1945-1980 (driven by social spending growth); and slowing growth since 1980.
- At the end of the 19th century, European governments spent around 10% of GDP; in the 21st century, this figure is closer to 50% in many European countries.
- Growth in the mid-20th century was largely driven by expansion of public funding for healthcare and education.

**Cross-country differences:**
- Government spending varies widely between world regions; high-income countries (particularly in Europe) spend much more relative to their economies than low-income countries. France spends multiple times as much as Ethiopia as a share of GDP.
- Spending per person also varies dramatically - Mexico's government spends a fraction per person compared to Norway.
- High-income countries have higher levels of social spending than lower-income countries.

**Composition of spending:**
- On average, OECD countries spend about half of total government spending on social protection and health.
- Social protection spending varies substantially across OECD countries.
- Across OECD countries, spending on old age (pensions and elderly care) receives the largest social spending allocation, followed by health, with family or incapacity-related benefits third.
- Employee compensation ranges from 5-20% of central government spending in Europe, but 30-50% throughout most of Africa.

**Public procurement:**
- Governments rely on private sector for goods and services through "public procurement."
- Procurement includes both large infrastructure projects and routine purchases ("outsourcing" or "contracting out").
- Public-private partnerships in low and middle-income countries have grown markedly over recent decades, driven mainly by electricity and roads projects in South Asia and Latin America, with the total value of projects in these countries more than doubling in 2005-2010.

**Correlates of government spending:**
- Government spending as a share of GDP correlates positively with GDP per capita (higher-income countries spend more), likely reflecting greater capacity to raise revenues.
- Taxes and transfers reduce income inequality by about one-quarter on average across 45 OECD countries.

Data sources include the IMF (for general government spending), OECD (Social Expenditure Database, COFOG classifications), and the World Bank's Private Participation in Infrastructure Database. The page was first published in October 2016 with minor text changes in April 2025.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"In early-industrialized countries, specifically, the historical data shows that public spending increased remarkably in the 20th century, as governments started spending more resources on social protection, education, and healthcare."
</key_excerpts>

--- SOURCE 7: After the Fall: China's Economy in 2025 - Rhodium Group ---
URL: https://rhg.com/research/after-the-fall-chinas-economy-in-2025

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This Rhodium Group research article, "After the Fall: China's Economy in 2025," by Daniel H. Rosen, Logan Wright, Jeremy Smith, Matthew Mingey, and Rogan Quinn, argues that China's official GDP figures are unreliable due to "authority bias." The authors estimate China's actual 2024 GDP growth was approximately 2.4-2.8%, well below official claims of nearly 5%, despite Beijing's economic stimulus measures (including aggressive rate cuts, a 10 trillion yuan local government debt refinancing program, new liquidity facilities for the stock market, and a first-time shift to "appropriately easing" monetary policy since the global financial crisis). They project China could reach 3-4.5% growth in 2025 with urgent domestic demand stimulation, but warn this is the top of or above the potential growth ceiling until structural problems are fixed.

The analysis breaks down 2024 growth by expenditure components: Investment likely shrank (flat at best), dragged by property and local government infrastructure decline (new starts down 23%, completions down 26.2%, cement output down 10.1%); government consumption was weakly positive (~0.2pp); household consumption was likely 3.5-4% (contribution of 1.3-1.6pp, well below official figures suggesting 2+pp) with CPI at just 0.2% and consumer confidence at an all-time low; and net exports contributed a large positive ~1.2pp (export volumes up 11.6% y/y in November, with imports weak).

For 2025, the authors project: investment stabilizing and expanding 2-3% (0.5-1.0pp contribution); government consumption contributing 0.5-1pp (supported by a reported 4% fiscal deficit target and 3 trillion RMB in special treasury bonds, but capped by weak tax revenues—down 3.3% over 12 months—and LGFV debt management priorities); household consumption growth of 3.5-4.5% (1.5-2.0pp contribution) despite trade-in subsidy programs; and net exports contributing ~0.5pp, though deeply uncertain due to potential US tariffs (Trump's possible 60% tariffs), possible yuan depreciation, and the response of other trading partners.

The authors conclude that 2024 was a turning point as Beijing conceded it needed to use all tools to support domestic consumption, but a cyclical 2025 improvement (3-4%, possibly 4.5%) should not be mistaken for long-term recovery given overinvestment in manufacturing and the need for deeper economic liberalization.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"By our estimates, China's GDP growth in 2024 improved modestly to around 2.4% to 2.8%, well below official claims of nearly 5%. If it stimulates domestic demand with some urgency and ramps up debt, we think China could get to 3-4.5% growth in 2025, reaching the high end of that range only if everything falls in Beijing's favor."

--- SOURCE 9: 2025 Investment Climate Statements: China ---
URL: https://www.state.gov/reports/2025-investment-climate-statements/china

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is the U.S. State Department's 2025 Investment Climate Statement for China, published in February 2026. It provides a comprehensive assessment of China's investment environment, concluding that China remains one of the world's most closed major economies. Key findings include: Inbound FDI fell 27.1% to $114.8 billion in 2024 (MOFCOM data), and China ranked 17th most restrictive out of 104 countries on the OECD's December 2024 FDI Regulatory Restrictiveness Index, and last among major economies on the Atlantic Council's 2024 Pathfinder Scorecard.

The report details China's discriminatory investment regime favoring domestic firms, including negative lists (Market Access Negative List reduced from 117 to 106 industries in April 2025; Foreign Investment Negative List reduced from 31 to 29 areas in September 2024), onshoring requirements, equity caps, JV requirements, and politicized licensing. Despite rhetoric about openness, foreign investors face nontransparent regulation, restricted data sharing, and pressure from authorities. The 2023 amended Counter-Espionage Law broadened espionage definitions, leading to raids on foreign consultancies and arrests of Chinese staff, significantly reducing investor confidence. Chinese regulators pressured economists to limit negative commentary, and the MSS intensified campaigns against foreign firms.

The Chinese government courted foreign investment in 2024 with specific supports (e.g., the February 2025 "2025 Action Plan for Stabilizing Foreign Investment" with 20 measures) rather than structural reforms. Notable legal developments include the September 2024 Foreign Investment Negative List update removing manufacturing restrictions, the November 2024 revised Anti-Money Laundering Law (effective January 2025), and March 2025 State Council implementing guidance strengthening enforcement of the 2021 Anti-Foreign Sanctions Law. China's net FDI position decreased by $168 billion in 2024, the largest capital outflow since 1990.

On legal and regulatory matters: China lacks judicial independence (courts cannot operate independently of the CCP, described as "rule by law" rather than "rule of law"). The 1993 Company Law requires Communist Party organizations in companies. Security reviews on foreign investments expanded in 2021 without public comment. SAMR launched targeted antitrust investigations against U.S. tech firms, with CSIS noting only three deals (less than 0.01%) prohibited. China has 109 BITs in force, no BIT with the U.S.; has a 1987 tax treaty with the U.S. China is party to ICSID and New York Conventions but enforcement of arbitral awards is opaque.

On trade/industrial policy: FTZs expanded to 22 zones; Hainan is China's only free trade port (independent customs by end of 2025). Outbound direct investment reached $163 billion in 2024 (up 10.1%), driven by the Belt and Road Initiative. China's outbound investment is categorized as prohibited, restricted, or encouraged to guide capital to strategic sectors. Data localization requirements force foreign firms to partner with Chinese entities. China signed the WTO Investment Facilitation for Development Agreement in 2023. Despite WTO commitments, China continues to impose performance requirements, technology transfer demands, and local content requirements for government procurement, and fails to properly notify draft technical regulations to the WTO TBT Committee. A December 2024 MOF draft policy on defining "domestic" products proposed a 20% price advantage for domestic content, concerning foreign stakeholders.
</summary>

The report assesses China's economic resilience amid multiple shocks (pandemic, property crisis, trade tensions), noting that China contributed ~30% of global growth over the last three years.

**Key findings:**
- China's historic growth model (heavy investment/state direction) faces mounting challenges: prolonged domestic demand weakness, deflationary pressures, elevated vulnerabilities, and rising reliance on external demand.
- Real GDP growth moderated to 4.5% y/y in Q4 2025 (from 5.2% in first three quarters), with full-year 2025 growth of 5.0%. Net exports contributed 1.6 percentage points to annual growth in 2025.

- Banking sector: Tier 1 ratio 12.4%, CAR 15.4% (2025Q3); NPL ratio stable at 1.5%; profitability pressures and rising vulnerabilities in some segments.
- The 2025 FSAP found significant vulnerabilities related to property correction and LGFV debt overhang.

**Outlook and projections:**
- Growth expected to slow to 4.5% in 2026, and progressively to ~3.5% by 2030 absent concerted reforms.
- Headline inflation projected to rise from 0% (2025) to 0.9% (2026), approaching 2% over medium term.
- Current account surplus projected to decline to 2.8% of GDP by 2027 and ~2% over medium term.
- Augmented debt projected to rise from 126.6% of GDP (2025) to 153.7% by 2030.

- A 1 percentage point decrease in Chinese growth lowers growth in key trading partners by 0.2-0.3 percentage points.

**Policy recommendations:**
The IMF recommends a comprehensive and more forceful policy response, including expansionary macroeconomic policies (greater consumption-focused fiscal support, further monetary easing) and stepped-up structural reforms to boost consumption and tackle imbalances. The authorities broadly agreed with the near-term outlook but viewed external environment as the main downside risk, expressed concerns about the external sector assessment, envisioned faster medium-term growth, and highlighted the financial sector's soundness.
</summary>

URL: https://www.ecb.europa.eu/press/economic-bulletin/articles/2026/html/ecb.ebart202602_01~7989f7715e.en.html

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This ECB Economic Bulletin article (Issue 2/2026) examines how boosting efficiency in public investment can address Europe's massive strategic investment needs (digitalisation, infrastructure, climate, defence) amid limited fiscal space. The EU faces annual public funding needs of approximately €510 billion for defence, green and digital transitions (Bouabdallah et al., 2025), while aggregate public debt-to-GDP stood at 80.7% in 2024 and nearly half of Member States exceed the 3% deficit threshold.

Key findings on public investment: Public investment accounts for ~17% of total EU investment (2024), ranging from ~30% in Luxembourg to ~13% in Belgium, and is expected to average 3.8% of GDP in 2025 (rising from 3.1% in 2019) and ~4% by 2027. Transport infrastructure is the largest component, averaging 27% of public investment (0.9% of GDP in 2023).

Using Data Envelopment Analysis (DEA) and Stochastic Frontier Analysis (SFA) methodologies on EU transport infrastructure investment, the analysis finds significant efficiency gaps. The median DEA efficiency score is ~50% when measured against transport network density (slightly lower for non-euro area and high fiscal-risk countries) and ~65% when measured against public transport quality. SFA results show lower median scores: 38% for railway investment and 43% for motorway investment — considerably lower than efficiency scores above 90% reported for health and education spending.

Closing the efficiency gap could yield potential savings of approximately €46-50 billion annually, though results carry high uncertainty. The article recommends improved public investment management frameworks, reducing red tape, streamlining regulatory requirements, strengthening administrative capacity, and conducting spending reviews (as done in Denmark, Spain and the Netherlands). The Germany case study (Box 1) demonstrates that shifting spending composition toward productive investment has significant positive macroeconomic effects, with scenario modeling showing a ten-year cumulative multiplier of ~1 when all public investment is productive.

--- SOURCE 12: After the Fall: China's Economy in 2025 - Rhodium Group ---
URL: https://rhg.com/research/after-the-fall-chinas-economy-in-2025

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This Rhodium Group research article, "After the Fall: China's Economy in 2025," by Daniel H. Rosen, Logan Wright, Jeremy Smith, Matthew Mingey, and Rogan Quinn, argues that China's official GDP figures are unreliable due to "authority bias." The authors estimate China's actual 2024 GDP growth was approximately 2.4-2.8%, well below official claims of nearly 5%, despite Beijing's economic stimulus measures (including aggressive rate cuts, a 10 trillion yuan local government debt refinancing program, new liquidity facilities for the stock market, and a first-time shift to "appropriately easing" monetary policy since the global financial crisis). They project China could reach 3-4.5% growth in 2025 with urgent domestic demand stimulation, but warn this is the top of or above the potential growth ceiling until structural problems are fixed.

The analysis breaks down 2024 growth by expenditure components: Investment likely shrank (flat at best), dragged by property and local government infrastructure decline (new starts down 23%, completions down 26.2%, cement output down 10.1%); government consumption was weakly positive (~0.2pp); household consumption was likely 3.5-4% (contribution of 1.3-1.6pp, well below official figures suggesting 2+pp) with CPI at just 0.2% and consumer confidence at an all-time low; and net exports contributed a large positive ~1.2pp (export volumes up 11.6% y/y in November, with imports weak).

For 2025, the authors project: investment stabilizing and expanding 2-3% (0.5-1.0pp contribution); government consumption contributing 0.5-1pp (supported by a reported 4% fiscal deficit target and 3 trillion RMB in special treasury bonds, but capped by weak tax revenues—down 3.3% over 12 months—and LGFV debt management priorities); household consumption growth of 3.5-4.5% (1.5-2.0pp contribution) despite trade-in subsidy programs; and net exports contributing ~0.5pp, though deeply uncertain due to potential US tariffs (Trump's possible 60% tariffs), possible yuan depreciation, and the response of other trading partners.

The authors conclude that 2024 was a turning point as Beijing conceded it needed to use all tools to support domestic consumption, but a cyclical 2025 improvement (3-4%, possibly 4.5%) should not be mistaken for long-term recovery given overinvestment in manufacturing and the need for deeper economic liberalization.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"By our estimates, China's GDP growth in 2024 improved modestly to around 2.4% to 2.8%, well below official claims of nearly 5%. If it stimulates domestic demand with some urgency and ramps up debt, we think China could get to 3-4.5% growth in 2025, reaching the high end of that range only if everything falls in Beijing's favor."

--- SOURCE 15: Unpacking China's GDP | ChinaPower Project ---
URL: https://chinapower.csis.org/tracker/china-gdp

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This webpage from the CSIS ChinaPower Project provides a comprehensive breakdown of China's GDP, offering 10 charts with up-to-date data to compare key aspects of China's economy. It begins by defining GDP and noting that while China's official economic figures are known to be distorted, GDP remains the most cited macroeconomic indicator.

The article explains that for centuries, China and India each accounted for one-fourth to one-third of global GDP, but China's share shrank in the 19th century until market reforms began in the late 1970s. As of 2024, China's share of global GDP stood at about 19 percent when adjusted for price differences—the largest share of any country. The page distinguishes between nominal GDP (where China ranks second after the United States) and GDP at Purchasing Power Parity (PPP), where China's GDP surpasses the United States.

China is presented as an outlier among large economies in several ways: it received a Freedom Score of 9 in 2025 (one of the lowest in the world, indicating "not free"), while other top-five economies scored above 80. China also continues to label itself a developing economy despite uneven development—Beijing's per capita GDP was about $31,760 in 2024 (on par with advanced economies), while Gansu province, the poorest, had about $7,358 (similar to Jamaica and Thailand).

On growth, China has averaged nearly 9 percent GDP growth per year since 1990, peaking at over 14 percent. Growth slowed to 2.2 percent in 2020 due to Covid-19 and fell to 3 percent in 2022—below the world average for the first time in decades—before recovering to approximately 5 percent in 2023 and 2024. The IMF projected in April 2025 that China's GDP would reach $23.1 trillion by 2030 (revised down from $27.5 trillion forecast in April 2023), while U.S. GDP was projected at nearly $37 trillion by 2030.

The article notes that China's official GDP figures are known to be padded due to political motivations, leading to alternative tracking tools like the Federal Reserve Bank of San Francisco's China Cyclical Activity Tracker (CCAT), which uses eight non-GDP indicators.

In breaking down China's GDP composition, industrial output accounted for nearly 37 percent of GDP in 2024 (more than double the U.S. at 17.3 percent), while the service sector was 56.7 percent of GDP (compared to 79.7 percent in the U.S.). China remains heavily reliant on exports—the trade surplus reached a record $1.2 trillion in 2025, with net exports accounting for 32.7 percent of GDP growth, the highest since 1997. Consumption-driven growth has rebounded to nearly 57 percent of GDP since 2023, but consumer confidence remains tepid and China remains well behind the U.S. and UK, where consumption contributes over 80 percent of GDP.
</summary>

--- SOURCE 1: Main Science and Technology Indicators, March 2026 ---
URL: https://stats.oecd.org/wbos/fileview2.aspx?IDFile=58d4a7cd-e15d-449f-8012-7cff548b52c5

SUMMARY:
<summary>
## OECD Main Science and Technology Indicators (MSTI), March 2026 Edition

### General Description & Purpose
This webpage describes the OECD's Main Science and Technology Indicators (MSTI), a statistical publication prepared by the OECD Science and Technology Policy (STP) Division under the aegis of the OECD Working Party of National Experts on Science and Technology Indicators (NESTI). MSTI provides indicators reflecting the level and structure of R&D efforts by OECD member countries and selected non-member economies. Data draws primarily on financial and human resources devoted to research and experimental development (R&D) as defined in the OECD Frascati Manual, supplemented by patent data and international trade in goods from R&D-intensive industries.

### Territorial Coverage
- Reports indicators for all 38 OECD Member countries, with most recent data typically reaching up to 2024 (2025 for some R&D budgets)
- Also covers the OECD aggregate zone, EU-27 zone, and non-member economies: Argentina, Bulgaria, China, Croatia, Romania, Russia, Singapore, South Africa, and Chinese Taipei
- Due to Russia's aggression against Ukraine, the OECD suspended solicitation of R&D statistics from Russian authorities (March 8, 2022 decision), so recent Russian data is absent from the database
- Mexico's R&D estimates have been suppressed from reference year 2018 onward because its National Survey on Research and Technological Development (ESIDET) has not been conducted since 2017

### Key R&D Indicators and Methodologies
- **GERD** (Gross Domestic Expenditure on R&D) is the flagship measure, capturing all spending on R&D carried out within each economy annually, with sectoral breakdowns by performing and funding sectors
- R&D data collected per the **OECD "Frascati Manual 2015"** methodology
- Data comes from two types: retrospective performer surveys (GERD, R&D personnel in FTE/headcount) and budgetary sources (GBARD - Government Budget Allocations for R&D from a funder perspective)
- Four sectors of performance: Business Enterprise, Higher Education, Government, and Private Non-Profit (PNP); sources of funds include Business Enterprises, Government, Higher Education, PNPs, and rest of world
- Currency conversions use PPP (purchasing power parity) series; constant-dollar series deflated using implicit GDP deflator
- Industry breakdowns use ISIC Rev.4 classification (pharmaceuticals, computer/electronic/optical, aerospace)
- Statistics footnote conventions: e (estimated), p (provisional), b (time series break), etc.

### Notable Caveats and Notes
- The 2008 update to the System of National Accounts raised GDP levels in many countries (recognizing R&D as asset-creating activity), which reduced R&D-to-GDP ratios
- EU-27 zone totals exclude the UK (following its withdrawal on February 1, 2020) for the entire time series
- OECD totals exclude Colombia for R&D personnel indicators and Costa Rica for GBARD indicators

### Patents
- Presents triadic patent families (filed at EPO, JPO, and USPTO) as proxy for R&D output inventions
- Also presents PCT (Patent Co-operation Treaty) applications, including in ICT and biotechnology sectors
- Priority date (earliest filing date) used as reference; from 2022 onward, patent families for individual countries are Secretariat estimates
- Sources: EPO's PATSTAT (Autumn 2025 database)

### Trade Indicators
- Trade balances and export market shares for three R&D-intensive product groups: pharmaceutical products, computer/electronic/optical products, and aerospace products
- Data from OECD's Bilateral Trade in Goods by End-Use (BTIGE) database, converted from Harmonised System to CPA 2.1 classification

### Indicator List
The publication includes 148 indicators covering:
- GERD, BERD, HERD, GOVERD (in current PPP$, national currency, constant prices, as % of GDP, growth rates)
- R&D financing by source sector
- R&D personnel in FTE and headcount, including researchers and women researchers by sector
- GBARD by socio-economic objective (Defence, Civil, Economic Development, Health/Environment, Education/Society, Space, Non-oriented Research, General University Funds)
- Triadic patent families and PCT applications
- Trade indicators for pharmaceutical, computer/electronic/optical, and aerospace products
- Economic background indicators (GDP, PPP, population, employment)
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"The flagship measure is the Gross Domestic Expenditure on Research and Experimental Development (GERD), which captures all spending on R&D carried out within each economy each year, comprising sectoral breakdowns by performing and funding sectors."

"In response to Russia's large-scale aggression against Ukraine, the OECD Council decided on 8 March 2022 to immediately suspend the participation of Russia and Belarus in OECD bodies. In view of this decision, the OECD suspended its solicitation of official statistics on R&D from Russian authorities, leading to the absence of more recent R&D statistics for this country in the OECD database."

"The R&D data used in MSTI have been collected and presented in line with the standard OECD methodology for R&D statistics as laid out in the OECD 'Frascati Manual 2015: Guidelines for Collecting and Reporting Data on Research and Experimental Development'"

"Readers are warned that GBARD data vary in coverage compared to government-financed GERD series and that these two types of data should not be combined."

"One key change was recognising the role of R&D as an activity leading to the creation of knowledge assets. One implication of recognising R&D as an asset-creating activity is that the level of GDP was, in many countries, revised upwards by a magnitude close to the value of domestic business investment in R&D. This reduced the R&D to GDP ratio, as the numerator stayed constant while the denominator increased to incorporate an element that was previously missing from the GDP estimate."
</key_excerpts>

--- SOURCE 3: Global Innovation Index 2025 - Global Innovation Tracker ---
URL: https://www.wipo.int/web-publications/global-innovation-index-2025/en/global-innovation-tracker.html

SUMMARY:
<summary>
The Global Innovation Index (GII) 2025 Tracker, published by WIPO, analyzes global innovation performance across four stages of the innovation cycle: science and innovation investment, technological progress, technology adoption, and socioeconomic impact. The overall picture for 2024 shows uneven but across-the-board growth, with only three indicators in decline (VC deal counts, drug launches, and global warming) — an improvement over the GII 2024 (five declining indicators) and GII 2023 (seven).

**Key Findings by Stage:**

**1. Science and Innovation Investment**
- Science and innovation investment showed only partial, uneven recovery in 2024 after a sharp 2023 downturn. Only scientific publications were above trend; R&D, VC, and patents fell below.
- Global R&D growth slowed to 2.9% in 2024, projected to fall to 2.3% in 2025 — the weakest expansion in over a decade. Top firms' R&D spending rose only 3% nominally (below decade average of 8%). Software and ICT services more than doubled 2018 R&D by 2024, while automotive, construction, and consumer goods saw declining R&D.
- Scientific publications rose 5.6% in 2024 to nearly 2 million (a new record), driven by China (14% increase, 26% global share) and India (7.7% growth).
- Corporate R&D reached nearly USD 1.3 trillion (historic high) but with slowest nominal growth since 2010; R&D intensity rose to 5.5%.
- VC deal values rose 7.7% to USD 384 billion (still well below 2021's USD 750 billion peak), but deal counts fell 4.4% to ~43,000 — third consecutive year of decline. VC is reconcentrating in the US (72% share by 2025) and AI/software sectors (software hit 50% of VC funding in 2025). AI megadeals (OpenAI, Anthropic, xAI, Databricks, Waymo) totaled ~USD 40 billion in 2024.
- International patent filings rose a modest 0.5% to 273,900 (PCT), recovering from 2023's 1.9% decline, but below the 2.5% decade average. China remained top filer; Korea grew 7.1% (27-year streak); US, Japan, and Germany declined.

**2. Technological Progress**
- Supercomputer efficiency of top 50 "greenest" supercomputers rose 65% (well above 35% decade rate), but overall supercomputer performance growth slowed (from 85%/year in 2003–2013 to 37%/year in 2013–2024).
- Microchip transistor count grew 37% (slightly below Moore's Law's 42%, but 10-year average aligns at 42%).
- Solar PV costs fell 90% since 2010 (now 56% cheaper than fossil fuels); onshore wind down 67% cheaper; offshore wind 25% lower.
- Lithium-ion battery prices fell 20% to a record low of USD 115/kWh in 2024 (85% drop since 2013, while lithium production rose 550%).
- Genome sequencing costs declined 11.1% annually (slower than the 21.5% long-term rate); cost dropped from ~USD 100 million in 2001 to just over USD 500 in 2023. Chinese firms may bring costs to USD 10/genome within 3 years.
- Drug launches fell ~19% to 65 new drugs in 2024 (vs. 80 in 2023, peak of 93 in 2021); median development timeline was 14 years.

**3. Technology Adoption**
- Global EV stock grew 45% in 2024 (18 million units), but this was below the 55% decade rate. Western markets slowed sharply (France: 49%→11%; US: 59%→35%; Germany: 34%→24%), while China held at 55% and emerging economies (Russia, Vietnam, India, Türkiye, Brazil) exceeded 100% growth. As of 2025, 4.5 per 100 cars are electric.
- Industrial robots grew just under 10% (down 5+ percentage points from earlier years); China holds 41% of global stock.
- 5G reached half the global population by 2024, but 84% of high-income populations had access vs. just 4% in low-income economies.
- High-speed rail (new indicator) expanded 5% in 2023 (below 9% decade rate); China accounts for ~70% of global high-speed rail (adding ~45,400 km since 2008).
- Safe sanitation reached 58% of global population (up from 47% in 2014); cancer radiotherapy equipment (LINACs) grew 1.3% per capita, with persistent divides in lower-income countries.

**4. Socioeconomic Impact**
- Labor productivity rose 2.5% (near the 2.2% decade average), reaching ~USD 55,000 PPP per worker. Fastest growth in China (5.9%), Vietnam (5.4%), and Ethiopia (5%).
- Extreme poverty fell 0.6% to 817 million people (under half of 20 years ago). South Asia cut poverty by 84% and East Asia/Pacific by 93%, but Eastern/Southern Africa saw poverty rise 50%.
- Life expectancy rose 0.7% in 2023 to 73 years (up from 63 in 1988), a record high, though healthy life expectancy growth (0.1%/year) lags life expectancy growth (0.3%/year).
- Global temperatures hit a record 1.29°C above the 1951–1980 baseline in 2024, near the 1.5–2°C Paris Agreement limits, following a 15-month streak of record monthly temperatures. CO2 emissions rose 0.8% (below the 1.7% average since 1994), with most major emitters declining except India (+4.6%).

**Conclusion:** Innovation demonstrated overall resilience in 2024 with all four stages recording progress, though gains were uneven and sector-specific, with persistent slowdowns in R&D growth, VC contraction, and climate concerns.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
Only three indicators were in decline in GII 2025: venture capital (VC) deal counts, drug launches and global warming. Global R&D growth continued to slow – down to 2.9 percent in 2024 and projected to fall further to 2.3 percent in 2025 – marking the weakest expansion in over a decade. In 2024, VC deal values rose by 7.7 percent... the number of VC deals continued to decline in 2024, falling by 4.4 percent to around 43,000 deals. Global temperatures in 2024 reached 1.29°C above the 20th-century baseline (1951–1980)... surpassing the record set in 2023.
</key_excerpts>

**Global R&D Overview:**

--- SOURCE 9: Federal R&D funding ---
URL: https://emergingtechpolicy.org/policy-levers/federal-rd-funding

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This webpage is a comprehensive policy guide on US Federal R&D funding, explaining how and why the government invests in scientific and technological research. Federal R&D is described as one of the strongest policy tools for shaping national innovation, with the US government spending roughly $200 billion annually (approximately $210 billion in FY2024) across more than 30 federal agencies and hundreds of thousands of researchers.

**Reasons for government R&D investment include:**
1. Addressing market failures (private sector underinvests in basic/high-risk research)
2. De-risking emerging technologies (bridging the "valley of death" between discovery and commercialization)
3. Advancing national priorities (defense, pandemic preparedness, energy security)
4. Steering technology toward public values (safety, privacy, openness)
5. Responding to crises (e.g., Operation Warp Speed, which invested $18 billion to deliver 300 million vaccine doses in under a year)
6. Workforce development

**Funding categories span:** Basic research, applied research, development, and commercialization/technology transition. The Department of War (DOW) organizes its R&D through Budget Activity 6 (RDT&E), which is divided into eight activity codes (6.1–6.8) commonly referenced in defense circles.

**Key agencies:** DOW and HHS (primarily NIH) account for ~75% of total federal R&D spending, with the remaining 25% going to DOE, NASA, and NSF. Federal R&D has risen from about $90 billion in 1976 to ~$190 billion in 2023 (constant 2022 dollars), though it has declined from nearly 12% of the federal budget in the 1960s to under 3% today.

**Funding models:** Traditional programs (peer-reviewed grants, dominant at NIH/NSF), ARPA-style programs ("high-risk, high-reward" with hands-on program managers, e.g., DARPA, IARPA, ARPA-E, ARPA-H), translation/commercialization programs (e.g., BARDA, Defense Innovation Unit, In-Q-Tel), and moonshot programs (e.g., Cancer Moonshot, moon landing).

**Funding mechanisms include:** Grants, contracts, cooperative agreements, prize competitions, advance market commitments, resource provision, loans/loan guarantees, Other Transaction Authorities (OTAs), and milestone-based funding.

**Emerging technology impact:** Many defining technologies began as federal R&D initiatives, including the Internet (ARPANET), GPS, smartphone components (multi-touch screens, microprocessors, lithium-ion batteries, voice assistants), AI/neural networks, Google's search algorithm (PageRank), self-driving cars (DARPA Grand Challenges), semiconductors, and the Human Genome Project. Over 70% of US Nobel Laureates were funded by NSF during their careers.

**Recent policy timeline highlights:**
- Nov 2025: White House OSTP issues RFI on "Accelerating the American Scientific Enterprise"
- Sep 2025: NSF solicits proposals for a $35M NAIRR operations center
- Jun 2025: Senate adds $150M for DOE AI R&D; Trump FY2026 budget proposes significant R&D cuts (65% cut to NSF CISE, 43% to TIP)
- Oct 2023: Biden Executive Order launches National AI Research Resource (NAIRR) pilot
- Aug 2022: CHIPS and Science Act provides $36B new NSF funding including $20B for TIP directorate
- Mar 2022: ARPA-H established with $1B
- Jan 2021: National AI Initiative Act formalizes coordinated national AI R&D strategy
- Sep 2018: DARPA launches AI Next campaign with $2B+ commitment
- May 2020: Operation Warp Speed launched

**Career considerations:** Working in R&D funding offers upstream influence on emerging technologies, incentives-based policy, long-term bet support, and leveraged impact. Program managers can oversee hundreds of millions in funding; ARPA PMs typically lead 2-5 programs with budgets of $20-80M each. Tradeoffs include high risk of failure, slow feedback loops (~20-year average lag from funding to application), limited downstream control, bureaucratic complexity, low political salience, and institutional bottlenecks.

**Funding process stages:** (1) Budget and policy direction setting (White House via OMB/OSTP, plus Congress's authorization and appropriations processes), (2) Grant-making and program execution, (3) Conducting the actual R&D, (4) Coordination (OSTP, NSTC, interagency working groups), (5) Oversight (Congress, OMB, GAO). In FY2025, seven agencies received ~97% of total federal R&D funding, led by DOW at 46%.
</summary>

The Congressional Budget Office noted DOD has shifted focus from counterinsurgency weapons procurement to developing new weapons for potential conflicts against adversaries with advanced military capabilities.
- The DOD increase was partially offset by declines at the Department of Health and Human Services (HHS), which fell 7.1% ($52.5 billion to $48.8 billion). - Data comes from the Survey of Federal Funds for Research and Development, a census of all federal agencies funding R&D (excluding CIA and NSA), covering 29 federal agencies (571 total respondents at various levels).
- Beginning FY 2016, development obligations were redefined as "experimental development" per OMB Circular A-11, excluding DOD Budget Activities 7 and 8, so data are not directly comparable with earlier years.
- FY 2020-22 obligations include COVID-19 supplemental appropriations; FYs 2022-24 obligations include Infrastructure Investment and Jobs Act, CHIPS and Science Act, and Inflation Reduction Act funding.
- FY 2025 data are preliminary and subject to revision.
- The report is cited as: NCSES. 2026. Federal R&D Obligations Increased 4.4% in FY 2024; Most Agencies Estimate Declines in FY 2025. NSF 26-317.

--- SOURCE 16: Expenditure on research and development (R&D) in Germany has grown considerably since 2005 | KfW ---
URL: https://www.kfw.de/About-KfW/Newsroom/Latest-News/Pressemitteilungen-Details_729344.html

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This KfW press release (2022-10-05) reports on a ZEW Mannheim study analyzing Germany's research and development (R&D) growth. Real R&D expenditure grew at an average of 3.4% per annum from 2005 to 2019, up from 1.4% per annum between 1991 and 2005. Germany's R&D-to-GDP ratio rose from 2.1% in 1994 to 3.17% in 2019, placing Germany sixth among comparison countries, on par with the US and ahead of China and similar-sized European countries. German R&D growth surpassed Japan (0.7%), France (1.6%), and the UK (2.2%), but lagged China (13.0%), South Korea (8.0%), and Israel (6.0%). The positive trend is attributed to a broad realignment of research policy from 2006 and economic upswing; Germany targets 3.5% of GDP by 2025 (EU target: 3.0%).

Key findings: (1) The private sector funded 64% of German R&D in 2019 (up from 62% in 1991), while public share dropped from 36% to 28%; comparison countries saw a steeper shift (private 59%→69%, public 35%→21%). (2) Private R&D is concentrated in automotive (37.3%), electronics/measuring/optics (18.5%), mechanical engineering (10.3%), pharmaceuticals (6.7%), and chemicals (5.9%), totaling ~79%; ICT services are not a German R&D priority, and sectoral concentration has increased since 2009 unlike in comparison countries. (3) Large enterprises (500+ employees) account for 88% of R&D expenditure (2018), second only to Japan (90%). (4) Germany's overall private sector R&D intensity is below what its economic structure suggests; raising below-average sectors to comparison-country averages could increase private R&D expenditure by nearly 30%.

KfW Chief Economist Dr Fritzi Köhler-Geib stressed the importance of continuing the Federal Government's high-tech strategy, providing R&D incentives for SMEs, integrating R&D and digitalization into support schemes, and addressing the skilled worker shortage through expanded education, training, and skilled migration policy.
</summary>
