--- SOURCE 3: [PDF] World direct investment patterns Statistics Explained - Europa.eu ---
URL: https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/statistics-explained/SEPDF/cache/65097.pdf?v=4582848109069452

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This Eurostat article (data extracted January 2026, from the "Statistics Explained" publication) analyzes global foreign direct investment (FDI) patterns for 2014–2024, based on UNCTAD data. Key findings:

**FDI Stocks (2024):** Global FDI stock was valued at €45.5 trillion. Europe was the largest source of outward FDI (39.8% of world total, €16.7 trillion) and second largest destination of inward FDI (31.4%, €15.4 trillion). Europe was the only continent that was a net investor. EU-held stocks: 14.4% share of global inward investment and 22.2% of global outward investment (second highest, behind the US which accounted for 30.6% of inward and 22.4% of outward FDI). China ranked third in both.

**Trends (2014–2024):** Europe's share of global inward FDI stocks fell by 7.8 percentage points (the largest decline of any continent), reaching 31.4% in 2024. Northern America's share rose 9.7 pp, Asia rose 1.0 pp, while Latin America & Caribbean (−1.2 pp), Africa (−0.9 pp) and Oceania (−0.8 pp) fell. Europe's share of outward stocks declined 5.3 pp (lowest at 39.8% in 2024), while Asia's rose 5.1 pp (to 26.9%) and North America's rose 0.5 pp (28.8%).

**FDI relative to GDP (2024):** World outward stocks/GDP ratio was 39.5%, inward stocks/GDP was 46.1%. Hong Kong (5.7x GDP) and Singapore (4.1x GDP) were most "open" economies. EU inward FDI stocks equaled 39.1% of GDP. Low ratios: Japan (5.5%), Russia (10.3%), Türkiye (13.6%), India (14.1%), South Korea (15.4%), China (20.0%). Japan's outward stocks/GDP ratio (53.6%) was almost 10 times its inward ratio.

**Multinational Enterprises:** In 2024, half of the world's top 10 non-financial multinational groups by foreign assets were HQ'd in the EU (Volkswagen Group, Stellantis NV, Deutsche Telekom AG, TotalEnergies SE, Anheuser-Busch InBev NV). Of the top 20, 9 were in the EU (4 German). Foreign assets exceeded 90% for CK Hutchison, British American Tobacco, Shell and Stellantis.

**FDI Flows (2024):** Global FDI flows totaled €1,440 billion. In 2024, the US was both the world's largest host (18.5% of inward flows) and largest outward investor (16.6% of outward flows). Singapore (9.5%), Hong Kong (8.4%) and China (7.7%) received significant inward flows; Japan (12.7%) and China (10.1%) were the next largest outward investors after the US. Inward FDI into the EU was negative (−14.7% of world total), while EU outward flows were 4.0%. Europe's share of world inward flows fell from 40.5% in 2015 to 12.6% by 2024, while Asia's rose to a peak of 55.0% in 2022 (43.6% in 2024).

**Growth 2014–2024:** China's inward FDI stocks grew 3.9x (highest growth, along with US, UAE and Singapore at 3x+). Chinese and UAE outward stocks grew 4.1x. Between 2014–2024, largest absolute increases in inward flows: US (+€105.8bn), Singapore (+€77.3bn), UAE (+€33.8bn). Largest outward flow increases: Japan (+€90.3bn) and China (+€57.7bn).

**Methodology/Context:** Data follows IMF BPM6 and OECD BD4 standards. A notable caveat: EU data includes special purpose entities (SPEs) while the rest of the world excludes them, which may distort geographic distribution of FDI. Four broad types of FDI are defined: greenfield investment, brownfield investment (acquisitions/mergers), capital extension, and financial restructuring. Geopolitical factors affected flows, notably sanctions leading to decreased Russian investment flows (inward flows turned negative in 2022).
</summary>

The Inflation Reduction Act of 2022 (IRA) is a landmark United States federal budget reconciliation law, Pub. L. 117–169, signed by President Joe Biden on August 16, 2022. The law aimed to reduce the federal deficit, lower prescription drug prices, and invest in domestic energy production while promoting renewable energy. It originated from the Build Back Better Act, a $3.5 trillion bill that was opposed by Senator Joe Manchin and reworked into a smaller package through secret negotiations between Manchin and Senate Majority Leader Chuck Schumer in July 2022. It was passed by the Senate 51–50 (Vice President Kamala Harris broke the tie) and by the House 220–207, with all Democrats voting in favor and all Republicans opposed. The legislation represents the largest investment in addressing greenhouse gas emissions in U.S. history.

According to the CBO and Joint Committee on Taxation, the law raises $738 billion from tax reform and prescription drug reform, and authorizes $891 billion in total spending—including $391 billion on energy and climate change, and $64 billion on three years of Affordable Care Act subsidies. Key revenue provisions include: Medicare drug price negotiation ($281 billion), a 15% corporate minimum tax on companies with over $1 billion in annual income ($222 billion), increased tax enforcement ($181 billion), and a 1% excise tax on stock buybacks ($74 billion). Key spending provisions span $391 billion for energy security and climate (including clean energy tax incentives, a green bank, solar/nuclear investments, EV incentives, home energy upgrades, and advanced manufacturing), $64 billion for ACA subsidy extension, $44 billion for Medicare Part D changes, and $80 billion for IRS modernization including up to 87,000 new employees. The law caps insulin costs at $35/month, caps out-of-pocket drug costs at $2,000 for Medicare recipients, and requires oil/gas auctions on federal lands before wind/solar leasing while raising royalty rates from 12.5% to 16.7%. In 2026, negotiated prices for the first group of 10 high-cost Medicare drugs take effect.

The act is generally not believed to have reduced inflation in 2022 and 2023, although some economists predict renewable energy investments will lower long-term inflation. The IRS expansion led to over $1 billion collected in past-due taxes from millionaires by July 2024. Major amendments include the Fiscal Responsibility Act of 2023 and the One Big Beautiful Bill Act. The act faced implementation criticisms regarding environmental justice, EV rules, clean hydrogen rules, sustainable aviation fuel rules, and labor rules, and was subject to actions by the Trump administration and the courts.
</summary>

--- SOURCE 21: Egil Matsen: Climate change, climate risks and Norges Bank ---
URL: https://www.bis.org/review/r191108a.htm

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This speech by Egil Matsen, Deputy Governor of Norges Bank (Central Bank of Norway), delivered in Oslo on 8 November 2019, addresses climate change, climate risks, and their implications for Norway's central bank operations, monetary policy, banking sector, and the Government Pension Fund Global (GPFG).

**Climate Change Background:** The global average temperature has risen about 1 degree Celsius above pre-industrial levels, and climate change is widely accepted as largely human-induced. Matsen identifies two types of climate risk: physical climate risk (economic consequences of higher temperatures and extreme weather) and transition risk (economic effects of shifting to a low-carbon economy through climate policy, changing attitudes, and new technologies). While poor countries in the Global South will likely be hardest hit by physical risks, Norway has experienced about five times higher annual insurance payouts for climate-related flood and storm damage over the past decade compared to the 1980s.

**Monetary Policy Implications:** Extreme weather acts as negative supply shocks—lowering output while raising inflation. Under Norway's flexible inflation targeting regime, Norges Bank typically does not adjust policy rates for transient supply shocks (e.g., agricultural production fell 40% in Q3 2018 due to a hot, dry summer without a rate change). However, policy rate changes may occur if such events cause persistent inflation. Prices for European CO2 emission allowances rose nearly 500 percent over two years, affecting coal, gas, and Norwegian electricity prices.

**Norwegian Economy and Transition Risk:** Norway's large oil and gas sector exposes the economy to transition risk, a concern raised by then-Governor Hermod Skånland as early as 1989. Norway has converted oil wealth into financial wealth via the GPFG since 1996 (with a fiscal rule since 2001), reducing overall risk. Oil stock price-to-book ratios have declined relative to the market average, partly attributed to increased investor climate risk awareness. If the oil sector declined abruptly, monetary policy could support activity and employment, though structural restructuring responsibility lies elsewhere.

**Banking Sector:** Climate risks, particularly transition risk, may become a source of credit risk for Norwegian banks, which have reduced (but not eliminated) oil industry exposure. Banks should correctly price climate risk, rely on relevant company disclosures, and prepare for investors demanding improved climate disclosure (the TCFD recommendations are becoming normative). Transition risk can contribute to financing risk and systemic risk, and should be included in assessments of bank capitalization and funding.

**Government Pension Fund Global (GPFG):** The GPFG invests in over 9,000 companies in 73 countries (70% equities) with the goal of maximizing return within acceptable risk while integrating responsible investment. Its responsible investment work rests on three pillars: (1) setting standards (supporting international standards, with climate expectations published since 2009); (2) exercising ownership (voting rights and dialogue); and (3) portfolio composition (environment-related mandates). The environment-related mandate limit will increase from NOK 60 billion to NOK 120 billion, with expansion in 2020 to include unlisted renewable energy infrastructure (primarily wind and solar), targeting about 1% of the GPFG (≈NOK 100 billion). Notably, 82 companies have been excluded based on a coal criterion, though a conduct-based climate criterion has yet to result in exclusions.

**Conclusion:** In 2018, extreme weather affected about 60 million people, though fatalities from storms and flooding have decreased due to better disaster risk management. Norges Bank participates in the NGFS (Central Banks and Supervisors Network for Greening the Financial System) with Finanstilsynet to build expertise, aiming to strengthen the resilience of the Norwegian economy to climate change and climate risk.
</summary>

This webpage presents the United Nations Conference on Trade and Development (UNCTAD) World Investment Report 2026, titled "International Investment in a Turbulent Era," published in Geneva in 2026 (UNCTAD/WIR/2026, ISBN: 978-92-1-154998-0).

KEY HEADLINE FINDINGS:
- Global foreign direct investment (FDI) rose by 6% to $1.6 trillion in 2025, following two consecutive years of decline, but growth remains fragile and uneven. Excluding conduit flows through major European financial centres, global FDI increased 4%.
- Inflows rose 11% in developed economies (to $723 billion) but only 2% in developing economies (to just over $901 billion).
- Investment activity is increasingly concentrated in a few capital- and technology-intensive sectors—data centres, semiconductors, oil and gas, clean energy, and critical minerals. These strategic sectors now represent almost half of all announced greenfield projects in 2025. Most other sectors, including renewable energy and manufacturing, registered significant declines.
- FDI in least developed countries (LDCs) rose 21% but remained highly concentrated in a small number of resource-rich economies. LDCs and lower-middle-income countries attract barely 10% of strategic sector projects, versus more than 20% in other industries.
- The top 20 recipients accounted for more than 80% of global FDI inflows. The United States remained the largest recipient ($277 billion), followed by Singapore, Hong Kong (China), and China. Developing economies represent half of the top 20.
- Global FDI outflows: the US remained largest source ($263 billion), followed by Japan ($186 billion) and China ($174 billion). Developing Asia accounts for one third of global outflows. Gulf Cooperation Council economies are increasingly prominent outward investors, including through sovereign wealth funds.
- The global investor landscape has become more diverse: more than a quarter of the top 100 MNEs are State-owned, and private equity international acquisitions account for about 20% of global M&As.
- Cross-border M&A values declined 7%. Greenfield project values remained near 2024 levels but were driven mainly by megaprojects. International project finance rose only 3%, remaining about 25% below its 2021 peak.
- FDI remains the largest source of external finance for developing economies (about 50% of total), ahead of remittances, ODA, and portfolio flows.

POLICY AND GOVERNANCE CONTEXT:
- Governments are becoming increasingly active in shaping investment flows, with new investment policy measures reaching a record high in 2025—strongly supporting strategic sectors, industrial upgrading, digital transformation, and green transition.
- The report emphasizes that investment is shifting from following cost and efficiency (where developing countries competed) to following strategic calculation, industrial policy, subsidies, economic security, and technological advantage—a logic that rewards deep pockets and established ecosystems.
- New opportunities exist for developing economies in supply-chain reconfiguration: alternative manufacturing locations, processing hubs for critical minerals, and gateways to regional markets.
- At UNCTAD 16 in October 2025, 170 countries adopted the Geneva Consensus, renewing commitment to an open, equitable, and development-oriented investment environment.
- The report references the Sevilla Commitment's global call to address limited access to finance for developing countries.

OUTLOOK (2026):
- Global FDI prospects remain uncertain with significant downside risks from trade policy uncertainty, geopolitical tensions (including the 2026 Middle East conflict), and conflicts. The geopolitical risk index rose sharply to 230.8 in the 2026 forecast from 145.1, while energy prices are forecast to rise significantly. However, moderating interest rates and foreign exchange volatility provide some positive signals.

The report was prepared by an UNCTAD team led by Nan Li Collins, Director of the Division on Investment and Enterprise, with a preface by UN Secretary-General António Guterres and foreword by UNCTAD Acting Secretary-General Pedro Manuel Moreno. The report contains three main chapters covering international investment trends, investment policy trends, and the theme chapter on "International investment in a turbulent era: Trends and policy response."
</summary>

--- SOURCE 4: Global Investment Trends Monitor, No. 50 | UN Trade and Development (UNCTAD) ---
URL: https://unctad.org/publication/global-investment-trends-monitor-no-50

SUMMARY:
<summary>
UNCTAD's Global Investment Trends Monitor No. 50 (published 20 Jan 2026) reports that global foreign direct investment (FDI) rose 14% in 2025 to $1.6 trillion, but this headline growth overstates the recovery. More than $140 billion of the increase came from global financial centres ("conduit flows"); excluding these, global FDI rose only about 5%. Real investment activity weakened: international mergers and acquisitions fell 10%, international project finance declined for the fourth consecutive year (-16% in value, -12% in deal numbers) to 2019 levels, and greenfield project announcements dropped 16% despite high total values from a few mega-projects.

Regional divides widened: FDI to developed economies jumped 43% to $728 billion (EU up 56%, driven by Germany, France, Italy), while flows to developing economies fell 2% to $877 billion (55% of global FDI). Three quarters of least developed countries saw stagnant or declining flows.

Data centres reshaped investment: they accounted for over one fifth of global greenfield project values in 2025 (announced investment exceeding $270 billion, driven by AI infrastructure), while semiconductor project values rose 35%. Tariff-exposed, GVC-intensive sectors saw project numbers fall sharply (-25%) in textiles, electronics, and machinery. France, the US, and the Republic of Korea led as host countries; Brazil, India, Thailand and Malaysia also attracted major projects.

International infrastructure projects fell 10% largely due to a sharp pullback in renewable energy amid regulatory uncertainty, with domestic investors increasingly filling the gap. The 2026 outlook is highly uncertain: modest FDI growth is possible if financing conditions ease and cross-border M&A picks up, but real investment is likely to remain subdued due to geopolitical tensions, policy uncertainty, and economic fragmentation.

The Inflation Reduction Act of 2022 (IRA) is a landmark United States federal budget reconciliation law, Pub. L. 117–169, signed by President Joe Biden on August 16, 2022. The law aimed to reduce the federal deficit, lower prescription drug prices, and invest in domestic energy production while promoting renewable energy. It originated from the Build Back Better Act, a $3.5 trillion bill that was opposed by Senator Joe Manchin and reworked into a smaller package through secret negotiations between Manchin and Senate Majority Leader Chuck Schumer in July 2022. It was passed by the Senate 51–50 (Vice President Kamala Harris broke the tie) and by the House 220–207, with all Democrats voting in favor and all Republicans opposed. The legislation represents the largest investment in addressing greenhouse gas emissions in U.S. history.

According to the CBO and Joint Committee on Taxation, the law raises $738 billion from tax reform and prescription drug reform, and authorizes $891 billion in total spending—including $391 billion on energy and climate change, and $64 billion on three years of Affordable Care Act subsidies. Key revenue provisions include: Medicare drug price negotiation ($281 billion), a 15% corporate minimum tax on companies with over $1 billion in annual income ($222 billion), increased tax enforcement ($181 billion), and a 1% excise tax on stock buybacks ($74 billion). Key spending provisions span $391 billion for energy security and climate (including clean energy tax incentives, a green bank, solar/nuclear investments, EV incentives, home energy upgrades, and advanced manufacturing), $64 billion for ACA subsidy extension, $44 billion for Medicare Part D changes, and $80 billion for IRS modernization including up to 87,000 new employees. The law caps insulin costs at $35/month, caps out-of-pocket drug costs at $2,000 for Medicare recipients, and requires oil/gas auctions on federal lands before wind/solar leasing while raising royalty rates from 12.5% to 16.7%. In 2026, negotiated prices for the first group of 10 high-cost Medicare drugs take effect.

The act is generally not believed to have reduced inflation in 2022 and 2023, although some economists predict renewable energy investments will lower long-term inflation. The IRS expansion led to over $1 billion collected in past-due taxes from millionaires by July 2024. Major amendments include the Fiscal Responsibility Act of 2023 and the One Big Beautiful Bill Act. The act faced implementation criticisms regarding environmental justice, EV rules, clean hydrogen rules, sustainable aviation fuel rules, and labor rules, and was subject to actions by the Trump administration and the courts.

The central argument is that common projections underestimate the IRA's benefits and overstate its true costs to the U.S. economy.

Key points:
- The IRA is the largest U.S. investment to date in fighting climate change, and the economic case for it is stronger than sometimes realized.

- The OMB's Circular A-4 guidance (both 2003 and 2023 versions) explicitly states transfer payments are not economic resource costs.
- Goldman Sachs calculated the IRA would cost the government $52 per ton of greenhouse gas abated, and Brookings projected $36-$87 per ton for power sector subsidies - both far below the EPA's social cost of carbon, meaning benefits far exceed costs.

--- SOURCE 25: Government Pension Fund of Norway ---

SUMMARY:
<summary>
The Government Pension Fund of Norway (Statens pensjonsfond) is the sovereign wealth fund collectively owned by the Government of Norway, consisting of two entirely separate funds: the Government Pension Fund Global (known as the Oil Fund or Oljefondet) and the Government Pension Fund Norway.

**Government Pension Fund Global (Oil Fund):**
- Established in 1990 to invest surplus revenues from the Norwegian petroleum sector (taxes, license payments, State's Direct Financial Interest, and Equinor dividends).
- As of July 2026, it held over US$2.2 trillion in assets, equivalent to 1.5% of the world's listed companies' value, making it the world's largest sovereign wealth fund by assets under management (~US$390,000 per Norwegian citizen).
- Invested in 8,763 companies across 71 countries (as of 2024); holds portfolios of real estate and fixed-income investments, with the majority in equities (65% as of 2017).
- Managed by Norges Bank Investment Management (NBIM), part of the Norwegian Central Bank.
- Surpassed US$1 trillion in September 2017 (a thirteen-fold increase since 2002); Norway can withdraw up to 3% of the fund's value annually.
- Received a perfect score of 100 on the Peterson Institute's Sovereign Wealth Fund Transparency and Accountability Scoreboard in 2019 (first among 64 funds).

**Government Pension Fund Norway:**
- Established in 1967 as a national insurance fund; smaller, managed by Folketrygdfondet, limited to domestic and Nordic investments, predominantly via the Oslo Stock Exchange.

**Ethical Framework and Divestments:**
- The Petroleum Fund's Advisory Council on Ethics was established in 2004; the fund cannot invest in companies contributing to killing, torture, human rights violations, or production of nuclear arms (though some arms producers are permitted).
- In January 2010, 17 tobacco companies were excluded ($2 billion divestment). In 2014, the fund divested from 53 coal companies (including Peabody Energy, Arch Coal, Alpha Natural Resources, Coal India) and sold stakes in many oil and gas companies. In 2015, parliament endorsed ~$945 million in coal divestments (over $8 billion total agreed).
- In March 2019, the Ministry of Finance recommended divesting from oil and gas exploration-production holdings; new guidelines prohibit investment in companies producing over 20 million tons of coal annually (planned over $10 billion in fossil fuel stock sales).
- On 11 August 2025, the fund terminated contracts with asset managers in Israel and divested Israeli-related portfolio portions; it also divested Caterpillar shares on ethical grounds.
- Works with RepRisk ESG Business Intelligence for ethical screening since 2009.

**Debate and Sovereignty:**
- The fund is a major political issue in Norway, with debates on: (1) whether to spend more petroleum revenues on the state budget (inflation concerns), (2) whether ~71% stock market exposure is financially safe, and (3) investment ethics.
- Global debates concern sovereign wealth funds' potential destabilizing or protectionist effects, though experts note funds like Norway's are unlikely to gain board seats and may increase global financial stability through diversification.

**Excluded Companies:** A comprehensive list of excluded companies includes those involved in tobacco production (Altria, British American Tobacco, Philip Morris, Japan Tobacco, Imperial Brands, Reynolds American, etc.), cluster munitions/nuclear weapons (Alliant Techsystems, Lockheed Martin, Northrop Grumman, General Dynamics, Raytheon, Boeing, Honeywell, Airbus, Safran, Serco), severe environmental damage (Barrick Gold, Freeport-McMoRan, Norilsk Nickel, Duke Energy, Vedanta, Zijin Mining), human rights violations (G4S, Li-Ning), Israeli settlement activity (Africa Israel Investments, Danya Cebus, Elbit Systems, Shikun UVinui), Western Sahara phosphate production (Potash Corporation), and others. Recent July 2025 exclusions include Bank Hapoalim, Bank Leumi, First International Bank of Israel, Mizrahi Tefahot Bank, and Caterpillar (US$2.1 billion divestment). Some previously excluded companies have been reinstated when the grounds for exclusion no longer applied.
</summary>

URL: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Public_Investment_Fund

SUMMARY:
<summary>
The Public Investment Fund (PIF) is the sovereign wealth fund of Saudi Arabia, headquartered in Riyadh at the Public Investment Fund Tower. It was established on August 17, 1971, by King Faisal bin Abdulaziz via Royal Decree M/24. As of May 2026, the fund holds approximately US$900 billion in assets under management, making it among the largest sovereign wealth funds globally. It is chaired by Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman (de facto ruler of Saudi Arabia since 2015), with Yasir Al-Rumayyan serving as Governor. Ownership rests with the Government of Saudi Arabia, and more than 60% of fund activities are domestic.

HISTORY: Originally a passive entity overseeing state equity in listed firms, the PIF expanded its staff from 50 in 2015 to nearly 500 in 2018. In July 2014, the Council of Ministers granted PIF authority to fund new companies independently. In March 2015, oversight moved from the Ministry of Finance to the Council of Economic and Development Affairs (CEDA). The fund is aligned with Saudi Vision 2030, aiming to diversify the economy. In 2022 and 2023, 4% stakes in Saudi Aramco were transferred to the fund (the 2023 transfer valued at ~$78 billion) as part of plans to exceed $1 trillion in assets by 2025. A 2021 Global SWF report scored PIF's Governance, Sustainability, and Resilience at 40%, with annual returns around 8% between 2018-2022.

MAJOR INVESTMENT PROJECTS: The fund holds stakes in numerous global companies including a 38% stake in POSCO Engineering & Construction, 5% of Uber (purchased for $3.5 billion), 5% stakes in Capcom and Nexon, a 5.7% stake in Live Nation, a 2.32% stake in Jio Platforms (worth $1.5 billion), and stakes in Boeing ($713.7M), Citigroup ($522M), Meta/Facebook ($522M), Disney ($495.8M), Bank of America ($487.6M), BP ($827.7M), and Berkshire Hathaway. In 2020, it disclosed investments of over $700 million in major US companies. Domestically, PIF owns Qiddiya City, the Red Sea Project, and Neom.

KEY PARTNERSHIPS: In 2016, PIF and SoftBank established the SoftBank Vision Fund (up to $45 billion over five years), which later suffered $17.7 billion in losses (fiscal 2019-2020) related to WeWork and Uber, resulting in SoftBank's worst-ever losses. In 2017, during the Saudi–US CEO Forum, PIF pledged $40 billion for infrastructure projects mostly in the US, with Blackstone committing $20 billion. PIF opened offices in London, New York, and San Francisco in 2019.

FORMER TRUMP ADMINISTRATION OFFICIALS: In 2021, PIF invested $2 billion in Affinity Partners, a private equity firm formed by Jared Kushner (Trump's son-in-law) shortly after he left the White House, despite internal concerns about the merits. The investment raised ethics concerns about potential payback for Kushner. PIF also invested $1 billion in the fund of former Treasury Secretary Steven Mnuchin. In May 2022, Affinity Partners directed Saudi money to Israeli startups—the first known Saudi PIF investment in Israel—viewed as groundwork for Israel–Saudi normalization.

NEWCASTLE UNITED: On April 14, 2020, a £300 million agreement sold Newcastle United F.C. from Mike Ashley to a consortium led by PIF. The Premier League initially blocked the deal, but on October 7, 2021, the acquisition was completed after "legally binding assurances" that Saudi Arabia wouldn't control the club. The sale drew criticism from Amnesty International ("an extremely bitter blow for human rights defenders") and other human rights advocates, who called it "a blatant example of Saudi sportswashing." In April 2021, Mohammed bin Salman reportedly urged UK PM Boris Johnson to influence the Premier League amid a proposed $30 billion Saudi investment in the UK.

LIV GOLF: In October 2021, PIF division Golf Saudi funded LIV Golf Investments with Greg Norman as CEO. The LIV Golf Invitational Series launched in June 2022 with $255 million in total prize money, backed by $2 billion in PIF funds. Notable players joining included Phil Mickelson ($200 million contract), Dustin Johnson (allegedly $150 million), and others, while Tiger Woods reportedly turned down a near-$1 billion offer. The league was condemned as a "sportswashing" tool. Mickelson controversially stated the Saudis "killed Khashoggi and have a horrible record on human rights" yet joined anyway. On June 6, 2023, LIV Golf and PGA Tour announced a merger of commercial businesses with PIF investing billions. In April 2026, PIF announced it was reevaluating priorities against mounting financial pressures from hosting World Expo 2030 and the 2034 FIFA World Cup.

CREDIT SUISSE: In 2022, PIF invested $1.5 billion in Credit Suisse and connected it to Saudi National Bank (making it largest shareholder under 10% to avoid regulatory requirements). In March 2023, Saudi National Bank's chairman publicly refused to supply more capital, causing Credit Suisse shares to drop 25%, contributing to the bank's acquisition by UBS on March 19, 2023.

TENNIS: In 2024, PIF announced partnerships with the ATP and WTA tours, including a $2 billion offer to buy and merge both professional tours into a single PIF-led tour (excluding grand slams); whether the offer was accepted remains unclear.

CURRENT PORTFOLIO (as of May 2025): Giga-projects include Neom, Red Sea Global, Qiddiya City, Roshn, and Diriyah Company. International investments include Electronic Arts (93.4%), LIV Golf, Newcastle United (85%), Lucid Motors (58%), Heathrow Airport Holdings (15%), Uber, Jio Platforms, Magic Leap, Accor, Reliance Retail, and Minerva Foods (34%). Additional entertainment holds include ATP Media, DAZN, Kings League, Professional Fighters League, and Professional Triathletes Organisation. Middle East and North Africa holdings span dozens of companies across sectors including Saudi Telecom Company (STC), Ma'aden, Riyad Bank, Alinma Bank, Saudi National Bank, ACWA Power, Riyadh Air, Saudi Arabian Military Industries, and many more covering real estate, financial services, utilities, automotive, construction, healthcare, and entertainment.
</summary>

--- SOURCE 2: What Is the CHIPS Act? | Council on Foreign Relations ---
URL: https://www.cfr.org/articles/what-chips-act

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This article from the Council on Foreign Relations explains the CHIPS and Science Act, a major U.S. industrial policy initiative signed into law in August 2022 to bring semiconductor manufacturing back to the United States. The U.S. produced nearly 40% of the world's semiconductor supply in 1990 but now produces only 12%, and produces none of the higher-end chips, while Taiwan produces more than 60% of the world's semiconductors and over 90% of the most advanced chips.

The Act allocated $53 billion in federal incentives for domestic semiconductor manufacturing and R&D, including $39 billion set aside for the CHIPS for America Fund administered by the Department of Commerce, plus a 25% tax credit for eligible companies (both U.S. and foreign firms with U.S. facilities qualify).

Effects so far: Hundreds of companies have requested more than $70 billion in subsidies (nearly double the available amount), and companies have announced over $200 billion in private sector investments. New chip facilities cost $5-20 billion each—more than a nuclear power plant. The first CHIPS grant ($35 million) went to BAE Systems in December 2023 for F-15 and F-35 fighter jet chips. Intel was approved in March 2024 for $8.5 billion in grants and $11 billion in loans (the largest grant), after announcing $100 billion in planned investments over five years. TSMC will receive $6.6 billion in grants and $5 billion in loans for three Arizona fabrication plants, with $65 billion in planned investment—the largest foreign direct investment in a greenfield project in U.S. history. The Biden administration says these investments put the U.S. on track to manufacture 20% of the world's most advanced chips by 2030.

Challenges ahead: Experts suggest CHIPS Act II or III may be needed to fully revitalize the industry. The EU passed its own European Chips Act (€43 billion), and China has invested billions annually in the sector. TSMC and Intel have already delayed facility openings due to higher construction costs and supplier issues, and there is a current lack of a trained semiconductor workforce in the U.S. Some U.S. partners, including South Korea, have criticized the requirements attached to CHIPS incentives (e.g., submitting business management information and childcare plans), and recipients are restricted from expanding facilities in China and other "countries of concern" for ten years.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"The CHIPS Act allocated $53 billion in federal incentives for domestic semiconductor manufacturing and research and development, of which $39 billion is set aside for a financial assistance program—also called the CHIPS for America Fund."
</key_excerpts>

--- SOURCE 3: CHIPS and Science Act of 2022 Summary - BGR Group ---
URL: https://bgrdc.com/chips-and-science-act-of-2022-summary

SUMMARY:
<summary>
The CHIPS and Science Act of 2022 is a landmark bipartisan piece of legislation passed by both chambers of Congress (Senate 64-34, House 243-187) and sent to President Biden for signature on July 29, 2022. The act provides $54.2 billion in supplemental funding for the semiconductor and wireless industry, including $52 billion in grants and incentives specifically for the American semiconductor industry, plus a 25% investment tax credit for semiconductor manufacturing.

KEY COMPONENTS:

**CHIPS Act ($54.2 billion):**
- Commerce Department Incentives Program: $39 billion to incentivize investment in semiconductor facilities (up to $6 billion for direct loans and loan guarantees)
- Advanced Microelectronics R&D: $11 billion for the National Semiconductor Technology Center (NSTC), National Advanced Packaging Manufacturing Program, and other R&D programs
- CHIPS for America Workforce and Education Fund: $200 million
- CHIPS for America Defense Fund: $2 billion
- CHIPS for America International Technology Security and Innovation Fund: $500 million
- Public Wireless Supply Chain Innovation Fund: $1.5 billion for open-architecture, software-based wireless technologies
- 25% Advanced Manufacturing Investment Credit for semiconductor manufacturing investments (begins after December 21, 2022, for construction before January 1, 2027)

**National Science Foundation Authorization ($81 billion over 5 years; +$36 billion over baseline):**
- $20 billion for new TIP Directorate (Technology, Innovation, and Partnerships) focusing on AI, quantum computing, advanced manufacturing, 6G, energy, and material science
- $13 billion for STEM workforce development including AI scholarship-for-service, microelectronics education network, and cybersecurity programs
- Funding for basic research, minority-serving institutions, and rural STEM education expansion

**Department of Commerce Technology Hubs ($11 billion over 5 years):**
- $10 billion to create 20 geographically-distributed "regional technology hubs"
- $1 billion "Recompete Pilot Program" for distressed communities

**NIST Authorization ($9 billion; +$4 billion over baseline):**
- Triples Manufacturing Extension Partnership funding ($2 billion)
- Creates National Supply Chain Database ($131 million)
- Manufacturing USA institutes ($829 million)

**NASA Authorization:**
- Authorizes Artemis Moon program and Moon-to-Mars campaign
- Extends International Space Station through 2030
- Codifies Planetary Defense Coordination Office and Near-Earth Object Surveyor telescope
- Supports Nancy Grace Roman Space Telescope development

**Research Security Provisions:**
- Requires NSF Research Security and Policy Office
- Prohibits federal research agency personnel from foreign talent recruitment programs
- Requires annual disclosures for NSF award recipients regarding foreign financial arrangements (China, Russia, North Korea, Iran)

**Department of Energy Provisions:**
- Funding for basic energy sciences, fusion energy research, high energy physics, nuclear physics (Facility for Rare Isotope Beams and Electron-Ion Collider)
- Establishes Foundation for Energy Security and Innovation (FESI)
- MICRO Act: Dedicated DOE microelectronics research program and four Microelectronics Science Research Centers
- Nuclear research infrastructure: $55M/year (2023-2027) for university reactor infrastructure; $390M over 5 years for new research reactors
- SUPER Act: Low-emissions steel manufacturing R&D
- Fission for the Future: Federal financial assistance for advanced nuclear reactor demonstration
</summary>

"The bipartisan CHIPS and Science Act has been sent to President Biden for his signature after passing both chambers. After passing the Senate 64-34, the U.S. House voted 243-187, with 24 Republicans, to pass legislation that will provide $54.2 billion in supplemental funding for the semiconductor and wireless industry, including $52 billion in grants and incentives specifically for the American semiconductor industry."

## Overview of the European Chips Act

This webpage provides a comprehensive, chronological overview of the European Chips Act, its evolution, and its implementation timeline from its initial proposal in February 2022 through planned updates scheduled for 2026-2027.

### What is the European Chips Act?
The European Chips Act (Regulation (EU) 2023/1781) is a Regulation establishing a framework to strengthen the EU's semiconductor ecosystem through three pillars:
1. **Pillar 1 – Chips for Europe Initiative:** Reinforces Europe's technological leadership by transferring knowledge from lab to fab, bridging research and industrial activities. It includes five operational objectives: a Design Platform (cloud-based virtual environment with EDA tools and IP libraries), advanced pilot lines (including sub-2nm GAA process technology, FD-SOI at 10nm and below, and heterogeneous integration), quantum chip development, a network of competence centres, and a Chips Fund for start-ups and SMEs. Supported by €3.3 billion in EU funds (matched by Member States), primarily implemented through the Chips Joint Undertaking.
2. **Pillar 2 – Security of Supply:** Creates a framework for Integrated Production Facilities and Open EU Foundries that are "first-of-a-kind" in the Union, incentivizing public and private investments in manufacturing.
3. **Pillar 3 – Coordination Mechanism:** Establishes Member State-Commission coordination for monitoring semiconductor supply, estimating demand, anticipating shortages, and activating a crisis stage. A semiconductor alert system was set up on 18 April 2023.

### Key Timeline of Events
- **8 February 2022:** The Commission proposed the European Chips Act as a comprehensive package (Communication, Regulation proposal, Joint Undertaking amendments, and a Recommendation).
- **1 December 2022:** The Council formalized its negotiating position; Dan Nica appointed as Parliament rapporteur.
- **18 April 2023:** Political agreement reached between Parliament and Member States; semiconductor alert system established.
- **21 September 2023:** The European Chips Act entered into force.
- **30 November 2023:** Official inauguration of the Chips Joint Undertaking (Chips JU), the main implementer of the Chips for Europe Initiative (expected total budget €15.8 billion until 2030; nearly €11 billion managed by the JU). Chips JU establishes pilot lines, a cloud-based Design Platform, quantum chip capacities, and competence centres.
- **12 March 2025:** Nine EU Member States (Austria, Belgium, Finland, France, Germany, Italy, Poland, Spain, Netherlands) launched the Semiconductor Coalition.
- **20 October 2025:** Commission work programme 2026 planned a new Chips Act proposal for Q1 2026 (legal basis: Articles 114 and 173 TFEU).
- **23 April 2026:** European institutions agreed a Joint Roadmap; European Chips Act 2 scheduled for Q2/Q4 2027 (note: timeline is indicative, not a formal legal schedule).
- **3 June 2026:** The Commission adopted a proposal for Chips Act 2.0, which would repeal Regulation (EU) 2023/1781, continue the Chips for Europe Initiative 2.0, and enhance the coordination mechanism.

### Context and Rationale
- Europe holds less than 10% of global semiconductor production market share and is heavily dependent on third-country suppliers (Taiwan and Southeast Asia for manufacturing, US for design).
- The EU aims to double its global market share to 20% by 2030.
- The Chips Act has mobilized over €80 billion in investments for semiconductor manufacturing and R&D.
- Global chip shortages resulted from COVID-19 demand surges, fab closures, logistics dislocations, and lean inventory approaches; recovery takes 2-3 years.
- Geopolitical tensions (China's "Made in China 2025" plan, US export controls) have exacerbated supply chain vulnerabilities.
- European-headquartered semiconductor firms account for ~10% (~$40 billion) of global sales; STMicroelectronics, Infineon, and NXP rank among the world's top 15 firms.
- Edge computing presents a major opportunity: 80% of data currently processed in cloud (dominated by US firms) is expected to shift to edge processing within 5 years.
- Building a leading-edge fab requires at least €15 billion upfront investment and three years to achieve production-readiness.

### Five Strategic Objectives of the European Chips Strategy
1. Strengthen research and technology leadership.
2. Build capacity to innovate in design, manufacturing, and packaging of advanced chips.
3. Establish a framework to substantially increase production capacity by 2030.
4. Address skills shortage and attract new talent.
5. Develop in-depth understanding of global semiconductor supply chains.

SUMMARY:
<summary>
The European Chips Act (ECA), also known as the Chips Act (Regulation (EU) 2023/1781), is an EU legislative package adopted in September 2023 to encourage semiconductor production in the European Union and reduce dependence on dominant producers like TSMC. First announced in February 2022 as part of the "Chips for Europe" plan, it aims to raise Europe's global semiconductor market share from under 10% to 20% by 2030 with an investment of at least €43 billion in public funds (matched by private investment for a total of €86 billion). The Act is built on three pillars: (1) research, development and innovation; (2) state aid exemptions for "first-of-a-kind" semiconductor manufacturing; and (3) supply chain monitoring and crisis response mechanisms. Its primary governance body is the European Semiconductor Board (ESB).

The Act has been extensively criticized and analyzed. A 2025 European Court of Auditors (ECA) Special Report found the Commission made "reasonable progress" on Pillar I but that the 20% target is very unlikely to be met—the Commission's own forecast projects only 11.7% market share by 2030. The ECA noted the Act was drafted under urgency following COVID supply disruptions, without a full impact assessment or public consultation, and lacks clearly defined operational targets. The Commission directly controls only ~€4.5 billion of the funding; the rest depends on fragmented Member State aid decisions. A Bruegel analysis (May 2026) concluded the Act "has underdelivered," with only €13.75 billion in State aid approved by early 2026 versus $33.7 billion in grants under the US CHIPS Act.

Key implementation developments include: the Chips Joint Undertaking (Chips JU) launching four pilot line calls in December 2023 and a fifth for photonics in July 2024; the €120 million DARE project (2025) supporting RISC-V open-source architecture for exascale supercomputing; and the October 2025 deployment of Europe's first out-of-order RISC-V processor silicon on 22nm process (eProcessor project). The EU has strategically emphasized RISC-V open-source ISA to reduce reliance on proprietary ARM/x86 architectures. Pillar II has seen slow uptake—only four FOAK investments approved (€10.2 billion State aid, €21 billion private) at time of audit. A major setback occurred in July 2025 when Intel cancelled its planned ~€30 billion Magdeburg, Germany fab. Some projects progressed, including the ESMC joint venture (TSMC, Bosch, Infineon, NXP) Dresden plant approved August 2024 (~$11 billion) and STMicroelectronics' Catania silicon carbide plant (€293 million, due 2026). Pillar III crisis mechanisms were still in "very early stages" at audit time.

Structural challenges include: EU demand concentrated in mature chips (65-90nm) with a €6 billion trade deficit in mainstream chips (30%+ imported from China); intense global subsidy competition (China €135.2 billion equity, US $37.1 billion grants, Japan €16.7 billion); high EU energy costs (new processes need up to 10x more power); geopolitical pressure on ASML's EUV lithography monopoly exports to China (33% of ASML's 2025 sales); and a projected global skilled labor shortage of one million workers by 2030. Academic analysis (Charles University) warned of deepening core-periphery divides and "national industrial champions" competition, while Jan-Peter Kleinhans argued the Act is "not a long-term semiconductor strategy... but a collection of ideas and initiatives."

Calls for revision have emerged: DigitalEurope (November 2025 and March 2026 papers) urged a centralised €20 billion EU semiconductor budget; Bruegel proposed a "sovereignty through indispensability" strategy focused on chokepoints (lithography, chemicals, specialised design) rather than self-sufficiency; and the ECA recommended a "reality check" and a successor strategy for post-2030. On June 3, 2026, the European Commission adopted a proposal for Chips Act 2.0 with new measures to boost the industry, reduce strategic dependencies, and support advanced chip production.

North America, Europe, and Oceania together attracted less than 20% of announced FDI, down from 70% in 2016, reflecting a continued shift toward low- and middle-income economies.

This data includes military and civil personnel, operation and maintenance, procurement, military research and development, infrastructure, and aid. Civil defense and current expenditures for previous military activities are excluded.

#### How is this data described by its producer?

Although the lack of sufficiently detailed data makes it difficult to apply a common definition of military expenditure on a worldwide basis, SIPRI has adopted a definition as a guideline. Where possible, SIPRI military expenditure data includes all current and capital expenditure on: (a) the armed forces, including peacekeeping forces; (b) defence ministries and other government agencies engaged in defence projects; (c) paramilitary forces, when judged to be trained and equipped for military operations; and (d) military space activities. This should include expenditure on: i. personnel, including: a. salaries of military and civil personnel; b. retirement pensions of military personnel, and; c. social services for personnel; ii. operations and maintenance; iii. procurement; iv. military research and development (R&D); v. military infrastructure spending, including military bases; and vi. military aid (in the military expenditure of the donor country). SIPRI’s estimate of military aid includes financial contributions, training and operational costs, replacement costs of the military equipment stocks donated to recipients and payments to procure additional military equipment for the recipient. However, it does not include the estimated value of military equipment stocks donated. Civil defence and current expenditures on previous military activities, such as veterans' benefits, demobilization, conversion and weapon destruction are excluded. In practice it is not possible to apply this definition for all countries, and in many cases SIPRI is confined to using the national data provided. Priority is then given to the choice of a uniform definition over time for each country in order to achieve consistency over time, rather than to adjusting the figures for single years according to a common definition. In the light of these difficulties, military expenditure data is most appropriately used for comparisons over time, and may be less suitable for close comparison between individual countries. Reference should always be made, when comparing data for different countries, to the footnotes and special notes attached to the data for these countries, which indicate deviations from the SIPRI definition, where these are known.

<webpage_content>
Featured:

[Coverage: Farnborough Airshow](https://www.defensenews.com/digital-show-dailies/farnborough/)

[2026 Strategic Architects List](https://defensenewsindex.com/2026-strategic-architects/)

[40 Years of Defense News](https://www.defensenews.com/home/2026/06/02/celebrating-40-years-of-defense-news/)

#### [Asia Pacific](/global/asia-pacific)

# Japan’s Cabinet OKs record defense budget that aims to deter China

By Mari Yamaguchi, The Associated Press

A Philippine Navy member looks at the Japanese destroyer Takanami during an exercise in the South China Sea, June 2025. (STR/JIJI Press/AFP via Getty Images)

Japan’s Cabinet on Friday approved a record [defense budget](https://www.defensenews.com/news/your-military/2025/12/22/dod-needs-more-consistent-indo-pacific-deterrence-funding-gao-says/ "https://www.defensenews.com/news/your-military/2025/12/22/dod-needs-more-consistent-indo-pacific-deterrence-funding-gao-says/") plan exceeding 9 trillion yen ($58 billion) for the coming year, aiming to fortify its strike-back capability and coastal defense with cruise missiles and unmanned arsenals as tensions rise in the region.

The draft budget for fiscal 2026, beginning April, is up 9.4% from 2025 and marks the fourth year of Japan’s ongoing five-year program to [double annual arms spending](https://www.defensenews.com/global/asia-pacific/2025/01/16/japans-passes-record-defense-budget-while-still-playing-catch-up/ "https://www.defensenews.com/global/asia-pacific/2025/01/16/japans-passes-record-defense-budget-while-still-playing-catch-up/") to 2% of gross domestic product.

“It is the minimum needed as [Japan](https://www.defensenews.com/news/your-military/2025/12/02/us-marine-corps-stands-up-3-new-combat-logistics-companies-in-japan/ "https://www.defensenews.com/news/your-military/2025/12/02/us-marine-corps-stands-up-3-new-combat-logistics-companies-in-japan/") faces the severest and most complex security environment in the postwar era,” Defense Minister Shinjiro Koizumi said, stressing his country’s determination to pursue military buildup and protect its people.

“It does not change our path as a peace-loving nation,” he said.

The increase comes as Japan faces elevated tension from [China](https://www.defensenews.com/news/pentagon-congress/2025/12/24/chinas-military-buildup-makes-us-increasingly-vulnerable-dod-says/ "https://www.defensenews.com/news/pentagon-congress/2025/12/24/chinas-military-buildup-makes-us-increasingly-vulnerable-dod-says/"). Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi said in November that her country’s military could get involved if China were to take action against [Taiwan](https://www.militarytimes.com/global/asia-pacific/2025/12/18/us-preps-massive-weapons-package-for-taiwan-valued-at-over-10-billion/ "https://www.militarytimes.com/global/asia-pacific/2025/12/18/us-preps-massive-weapons-package-for-taiwan-valued-at-over-10-billion/"), the self-governing island that Beijing says must come under its rule.

Takaichi’s government, under U.S. pressure for a military increase, pledged to achieve the 2% target by March, two years earlier than planned. Japan also plans to revise its ongoing security and defense policy by December 2026 to further strengthen its military.

### **Missiles and drones will add to southwestern island defense**

Japan has been bolstering its offensive capability with long-range missiles to attack enemy targets from a distance, a major break from its post-World War II principle limiting the use of force to its own self-defense.

The current security strategy, adopted in 2022, names China as the country’s biggest strategic challenge and calls for a more offensive role for Japan’s Self-Defense Force under its security alliance with the U.S.

The new budget plan allocates more than 970 billion yen ($6.2 billion) to bolster Japan’s “standoff” missile capability. It includes a 177 billion-yen ($1.13 billion) purchase of domestically developed and upgraded Type-12 surface-to-ship missiles with a range of about 1,000 kilometers (620 miles).

The first batch of the Type-12 missiles will be deployed in Japan’s southwestern Kumamoto prefecture by March, a year earlier than planned, as Japan accelerates its missile buildup in the region.

In part due to Japan’s aging and declining population and its struggles with an understaffed military, the government believes unmanned weapons are essential.

To defend the coasts, Japan will spend 100 billion yen ($640 million) to deploy “massive” unmanned air, sea-surface and underwater drones for surveillance and defense under a system called “SHIELD” planned for March 2028, defense ministry officials said.

For speedier deployment, Japan initially plans to rely mainly on imports, possibly from Turkey or Israel.

### **Tension with China grows**

The budget announcement comes as Japan’s row with China escalates following Takaichi’s remark in November about Taiwan.

The disagreement escalated this month when Chinese aircraft carrier drills near southwestern Japan prompted Tokyo to protest when Chinese aircraft locked their radar on Japanese aircraft, which is considered possible preparation for firing missiles.

The Defense Ministry, already alarmed by China’s rapid expansion of operations in the Pacific, will open a new office dedicated to studying operations, equipment and other necessities for Japan to deal with China’s Pacific activity.

Two Chinese aircraft carriers were spotted in June almost simultaneously operating near the southern Japanese island of Iwo Jima for the first time, fueling Tokyo’s concern about Beijing’s rapidly expanding military activity far beyond its borders and areas around the disputed East China Sea islands.

In Beijing, China’s Foreign Ministry spokesperson Lin Jian said the Takaichi government has “noticeably accelerated its pace of military buildup and expansion” since taking office.

“Japan is deviating from the path of peaceful development it has long claimed to uphold and is moving further and further in a dangerous direction,” Lin said.

### **Japan plans joint development of frigates and jets**

Japan is pushing to strengthen its largely domestic defense industry by participating in joint development with friendly nations and promoting foreign sales after drastically easing arms export restrictions in recent years.

For 2026, Japan plans to spend more than 160 billion yen ($1 billion) to jointly develop a next-generation fighter jet with Britain and Italy for deployment in 2035. There are also plans for research and development of Artificial Intelligence-operated drones designed to fly with the jet.

In a major boost to the country’s defense industry, Australia selected Mitsubishi Heavy Industries in August to upgrade the Mogami-class frigate to replace its fleet of 11 ANZAC-class ships.

Japan’s budget allocates nearly 10 billion yen ($64 million) to support industry base and arms sales.

### **Meeting targets but future funding uncertain**

The budget plan requires parliamentary approval by March to be implemented as part of a 122.3 trillion yen ($784 billion) national budget bill.

The five-year defense buildup program would bring Japan’s annual spending to around 10 trillion yen ($64 billion), making it the world’s third-largest spender after the U.S. and China. Japan will clear the 2% target by March as promised, the Finance Ministry said.

Takaichi’s government plans to fund its growing military spending by raising corporate and tobacco taxes and recently adopted a plan for an income tax increase beginning 2027. Prospects for future growth at a higher percentage of GDP remain unclear.

# Japan Accelerates Defense Buildup With Record Budget and Expanded Unmanned Capabilities

The draft defense budget sets a new spending record for the 12th straight year amid mounting regional threats and U.S. alliance pressure.

By [Takahashi Kosuke](https://thediplomat.com/authors/kosuke-takahashi/)

December 26, 2025



![Japan Accelerates Defense Buildup With Record Budget and Expanded Unmanned Capabilities](https://thediplomat.com/wp-content/uploads/2025/12/sizes/td-story-s-1/thediplomat_2025-12-26-204118.jpeg "Japan Accelerates Defense Buildup With Record Budget and Expanded Unmanned Capabilities")

The Japan Maritime Self-Defense Force’s second Izumo-class helicopter carrier JS Kaga, whose bow has been modified to a rectangular shape to enable operations of the stealth F-35B fighter.

Credit: JMSDF

Japan is accelerating its defense buildup amid rising geopolitical tensions, driven by mounting military pressure from three nuclear-armed neighbors — China, North Korea, and Russia — and calls from the United States for higher defense spending.

On December 26, the cabinet of Prime Minister Takaichi Sanae approved a draft defense budget for fiscal year 2026 totaling 9.04 trillion yen ($58 billion), including expenditures related to the realignment of U.S. forces in Japan. The nation’s fiscal year begins in April.

The budget represents a 3.8 percent increase from the previous year, marking the first time Japan’s defense spending has exceeded 9 trillion yen and extending its record-high trajectory to a 12th consecutive year. Compared with the initial budget request submitted in August, which stood at 8.85 trillion yen, the total was increased by about 190 billion yen. The move underscores the Takaichi administration’s policy emphasis on accelerating Japan’s defense buildup. 

Japan’s fiscal year 2026 budget plan, expected to be approved by the country’s bicameral legislature in the coming months, marks the fourth year of the Defense Buildup Program — a five-year framework covering fiscal years 2023 through 2027 that allocates a total of 43 trillion yen ($275 billion) in defense-related spending. Under the program, the Japanese government has set a goal of raising defense-related expenditures to 2 percent of gross domestic product (GDP) by fiscal year 2027, including not only the Ministry of Defense’s budget but also defense-related outlays by other government agencies.

However, under the Takaichi administration, the supplementary budget for the current fiscal year 2025 — the first compiled during her tenure and passed and enacted by the Diet earlier this month — includes roughly 1.1 trillion yen in additional security-related spending, including defense expenditures.

As a result, Japan is on track to reach its 2 percent-of-GDP defense spending target two years ahead of schedule. This front-loading of defense outlays underscores the administration’s determination to accelerate the country’s defense buildup amid a deteriorating regional security environment, in line with demands from the Trump administration in the United States for allies to boost defense spending.

As in the past three years, the budget plan lists seven key pillars of “necessary efforts to drastically strengthen Japan’s defense capabilities.”

These include (1) “stand-off defense capabilities,” such as mass production of longer-range missiles; (2) “comprehensive air and missile defense capabilities” to respond to increasingly diverse and complex airborne threats, including missiles; (3) “unmanned asset defense capabilities,” such as the use of drones; (4) “cross-domain operational capabilities” in space, cyberspace, and electromagnetic domains; (5) “command and control and intelligence-related functions”; (6) “maneuvering and deployment capability” to send troops and supplies to the front line of a conflict; and (7) “sustainability and resiliency.”

Of these seven pillars, the latest draft defense budget places a strong emphasis on the third pillar: strengthening unmanned asset defense capabilities.

The Defense Ministry was allocated 100.1 billion yen to establish an overall coastal defense system called “SHIELD” by fiscal year 2027, utilizing a massive fleet of unmanned vehicles in the air, sea, and underwater. The name stands for “Synchronized, Hybrid, Integrated and Enhanced Littoral Defense.”

The ministry said that it will acquire an unspecified number of small attack unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs), surface ship-launched UAVs, small ship-based UAVs, small multirole unmanned surface vessels (USVs), and small multirole unmanned underwater vessels (UUVs) for the three branches of the Self-Defense Forces (SDF) – Ground (GSDF), Maritime (MSDF), and Air (ASDF) – to build SHIELD.

Defense officials said the plan would involve purchasing existing UAVs and USVs, primarily from foreign manufacturers. Most notably, the Defense Ministry secured 76.5 billion yen to acquire four more MQ-9B SkyGuardian UAVs, which have already been decided for deployment to the MSDF. 

In addition, the Defense Ministry was allocated 2.2 billion yen to conduct demonstration tests for simultaneous control of a large number of various unmanned assets.

As one of the major projects, the ministry also secured 104.3 billion yen to build the sixth ship of the upgraded Mogami-class multirole frigate of the MSDF, known in Tokyo as the “New FFM” or 06FFM. The lead ship of the New FFM class is scheduled to be laid down in fiscal year 2025 and commissioned in fiscal year 2028. According to Mitsubishi Heavy Industries, if construction proceeds smoothly, all 12 vessels are expected to be in service by fiscal year 2032.

On stand-off defense capabilities, the Defense Ministry was allocated 177 billion yen to acquire a new upgraded ground-based version of the Type 12 surface-to-ship missile (SSM) and its related ground equipment. The SSM is part of the country’s development of counterstrike capabilities – formerly known as “enemy base strike capabilities.”

The ministry announced it will start to deploy the new missile, which has an extended range of about 1,000 km, to the GSDF 5th Surface-to-Ship Missile Regiment at Camp Kengun in Kumamoto Prefecture on Kyushu Island during fiscal 2025 and 2026, and to the GSDF Fuji Artillery School Unit at Camp Fuji in Shizuoka Prefecture during fiscal 2027.

The ministry also secured 35.7 billion yen to acquire the long-range, ship-launched, improved version of the Type 12 SSM. 

Japan began mass production of the improved Type 12 ship-launched SSM in the current fiscal year. It said the JMSDF will begin operating this new missile on the refurbished JS Teruzuki (DD-116) in fiscal 2027.

In addition, the Defense Ministry said the upgraded air-launched version of the Type 12 SSM is scheduled to enter service in fiscal 2027 at ASDF Hyakuri Air Base in Ibaraki Prefecture, where it will be operated by the upgraded F-2 fighter.

The Ministry of Defense will begin mass production of hypersonic guided missiles, which can fly at more than five times the speed of sound, from the next fiscal year. For the first time, the ministry has secured a budget of 30.1 billion yen for the acquisition of these missiles and ground equipment.

As for the fourth pillar of enhancing “cross-domain operational capabilities,” the ministry secured about 174 billion yen to strengthen the security infrastructure for outer space. It plans to reorganize the Air Self-Defense Force into the Air and Space Self-Defense Force during the next fiscal year.

The ministry’s Acquisition, Technology, and Logistics Agency (ATLA) earmarked 160.2 billion yen to keep developing its next-generation fighter program in partnership with the United Kingdom and Italy. It plans to continue developing a basic design for the future fighter’s fuselage and the detailed engineering of its engines. A Defense Ministry official said the first flight of the next-generation fighter jet is scheduled for around 2030.

In addition, it secured 4.8 billion yen for research and development of unmanned aircraft to be used in conjunction with this next-generation fighter jet. Specifically, it will carry out the conceptual design of a collaborative unmanned aircraft that utilizes artificial intelligence to enable autonomous situational and flight decisions and other behavioral decisions.

The MSDF also earmarked 28.5 billion yen to continue modifying its two Izumo-class helicopter carriers – JS Izumo and JS Kaga – into aircraft carriers capable of enabling Lockheed Martin F-35B fighter operations. 

As for the Izumo, the defense official said 900 million yen was allocated to install deck status lights on the ship, which allow deck workers to share the status of the deck, and to cover the test cost of the landing guidance system on the Izumo.

As for the Kaga, 27.6 million yen was allocated for hull　modifications, including upgrades to hangar facilities.

The Ministry of Defense said JS Izumo‘s modification is scheduled to be completed in fiscal 2027, and JS Kaga‘s in fiscal 2028.

This is a news article from The Diplomat (a publication covering the Asia-Pacific region) titled "Japan Accelerates Defense Buildup With Record Budget and Expanded Unmanned Capabilities," written by Takahashi Kosuke and published December 26, 2025, in the Asia Defense/Security/East Asia sections.

KEY DETAILS:
- On December 26, 2025, the cabinet of Japanese Prime Minister Takaichi Sanae approved a draft defense budget for fiscal year 2026 totaling 9.04 trillion yen ($58 billion), including expenditures related to the realignment of U.S. forces in Japan.
- The budget is a 3.8% increase from the previous year, exceeding 9 trillion yen for the first time and marking a record-high for the 12th consecutive year.
- It was increased by about 190 billion yen from the initial August request of 8.85 trillion yen.
- The budget is the fourth year of the Defense Buildup Program (FY2023-2027), a five-year framework totaling 43 trillion yen ($275 billion), with a goal of raising defense-related spending to 2% of GDP by FY2027.
- Due to a ~1.1 trillion yen supplementary budget for FY2025, Japan is on track to reach the 2%-of-GDP target two years ahead of schedule, responding to Trump administration pressure on allies to boost defense spending.

SEVEN KEY PILLARS OF THE BUDGET: (1) stand-off defense capabilities (longer-range missiles), (2) comprehensive air and missile defense, (3) unmanned asset defense capabilities, (4) cross-domain operational capabilities (space, cyberspace, electromagnetic), (5) command and control/intelligence, (6) maneuvering and deployment capability, (7) sustainability and resiliency.

MAJOR ALLOCATIONS:
- 100.1 billion yen for "SHIELD" (Synchronized, Hybrid, Integrated and Enhanced Littoral Defense) coastal defense system by FY2027 using unmanned air, sea, and underwater vehicles.
- 76.5 billion yen for four more MQ-9B SkyGuardian UAVs for the MSDF.
- 2.2 billion yen for demonstration tests of simultaneous control of large numbers of unmanned assets.
- 104.3 billion yen for the sixth upgraded Mogami-class multirole frigate ("New FFM" / 06FFM); lead ship laid down FY2025, commissioned FY2028; all 12 vessels expected in service by FY2032.
- 177 billion yen for a new upgraded ground-based Type 12 surface-to-ship missile (SSM) with ~1,000 km range, deployed to GSDF 5th Surface-to-Ship Missile Regiment at Camp Kengun (Kumamoto Prefecture, Kyushu) in FY2025-2026 and Camp Fuji (Shizuoka Prefecture) in FY2027.
- 35.7 billion yen for long-range ship-launched improved Type 12 SSM; JS Teruzuki (DD-116) to begin operating it in FY2027.
- Upgraded air-launched Type 12 SSM to enter service FY2027 at ASDF Hyakuri Air Base (Ibaraki Prefecture) on the upgraded F-2 fighter.
- 30.1 billion yen (first-time budget) for mass production of hypersonic guided missiles (flying at more than 5 times the speed of sound) starting next fiscal year.
- ~174 billion yen to strengthen outer space security infrastructure; ASDF to be reorganized into the Air and Space Self-Defense Force next fiscal year.
- 160.2 billion yen for the next-generation fighter program with the UK and Italy (GCAP); first flight scheduled around 2030.
- 4.8 billion yen for R&D of AI-enabled collaborative unmanned aircraft for the next-generation fighter.
- 28.5 billion yen to continue converting the two Izumo-class helicopter carriers (JS Izumo and JS Kaga) into aircraft carriers for F-35B operations; JS Izumo modification to be completed FY2027, JS Kaga FY2028. Also 900 million yen for deck status lights and landing guidance system testing on Izumo, and 27.6 million yen for Kaga hull modifications.

The article frames Japan's buildup as driven by military pressure from China, North Korea, and Russia (three nuclear-armed neighbors) and U.S. demands for higher spending. It includes related article links on Japan's prior defense budget increases and related defense topics.

<webpage_content>
Headings

# Japan govt approves record budget, including for defence

Tokyo (AFP) –  The Japanese government approved a record budget for the upcoming fiscal year on Friday, to pay for everything from bigger defence spending to ballooning social security costs as inflation persists.

Issued on: 26/12/2025 - 03:07Modified: 26/12/2025 - 10:05

The 122.3-trillion-yen ($782 billion) budget for the fiscal year from April 2026 will include a record nine trillion yen for defence spending, as Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi aims to accelerate Tokyo's sweeping upgrade of its military in the face of worsening relations with China.

"This budget is the least we need to fulfil our defence responsibilities as Japan faces its most severe and complex security environment since the end of the war," Defence Minister Shinjiro Koizumi told a news conference.

Japan has been shedding its strict pacifist stance in recent years, moving to obtain "counterstrike" capabilities and doubling military spending to two percent of GDP.

At the core of its request is 100 billion yen for the so-called SHIELD coastal defence system, which would marshal drones to block any invasion by foreign troops.

Japan is hoping that SHIELD -- Synchronised, Hybrid, Integrated and Enhanced Littoral Defence -- will be completed by March 2028, with no details yet about to which part of Japan's coastline it will be linked.

The budget plan comes as China and Japan are enmeshed in a spat over Takaichi's suggestion in November that Tokyo could intervene militarily in any attack on Taiwan.

Beijing claims self-ruled, democratic Taiwan as part of its territory and has threatened to use force to bring it under its control.

## Market worries

The expanding budget also arrives as the market worries about Takaichi's big spending policies adding to Japan's public debts.

The 122-trillion-yen figure compares with the 115 trillion yen sought for the current fiscal year to March, which was also a record.

Japan already has the biggest ratio of debt to gross domestic product (GDP) among major economies, projected to reach 232.7 percent this year, according to the International Monetary Fund.

Parliament approved a massive extra budget this month to pay for a 21.3-trillion-yen stimulus announced in November.

The market has reacted by driving down the value of the yen, while the benchmark yield rose for Japanese government bonds.

Some observers have drawn comparisons to the United Kingdom's 2022 bond market turmoil under then-premier Liz Truss.

Takaichi has advocated big government spending to spur economic growth.

The budget "is designed to make people live safely, receive necessary medicine, welfare and high-quality education and have jobs, no matter where they are in Japan," she told a news conference on Friday.

Takaichi stressed her commitment to Tokyo's fiscal health in an interview with the influential Nikkei business daily on Tuesday, rejecting any "irresponsible bond issuance or tax cuts".

The current size of the budget is unlikely to shock the bond market, Takahide Kiuchi, executive economist at Nomura Research Institute, wrote in a note before Friday.

But an increase to around 125 trillion yen or more, he said, would cause the "turmoil in the bond market, already in crisis mode, to deepen further".

Kiuchi noted that, under Takaichi, the extra budget quickly ballooned, reaching $18 trillion yen.

"Financial markets are likely on high alert for a similar occurrence," he said.

"Should the fall of the yen and bond prices further accelerate due to the size of the budget, it would increase worries about adverse effects on the economy and people's lives."

A weaker yen raises prices of imports for resource-poor Japan, which relies heavily on foreign food, energy and raw materials to power its economy.

Takaichi came to power in October with a pledge to fight inflation after anger over rising prices.

Another challenge is Japan's ageing population, caused by chronically low birth rates and a cautious approach to immigration.

The draft budget needs to be approved by parliament.
