URL: https://www.pimco.com/us/en/documents/826a7d563bf1fc56a22919c490956c676b58ce18d0a806ae70ddf6097bfbf6012e11db442f923446e7b97ae590a177dd?app=dot

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is a PIMCO Secular Forum 2026 presentation (as of 8 May 2026) by Peder Beck-Friis on global fiscal policy and debt sustainability. The document assesses the fiscal outlook across developed markets, debt sustainability risks, and five scenarios for US debt over the next five years.

KEY FINDINGS:
• The structural fiscal picture is largely unchanged from last year: debt is near record highs, fiscal space is limited, and this likely constrains active fiscal easing in the next recession, shifting more burden to central banks.
• Fiscal policy is likely to stay broadly neutral ahead, with cross-country divergence: Japan and Germany plan to ease, most of Europe looks to tighten, and the US plans to keep its structural deficit neutral at 6-7% of GDP.
• Future recessions will likely push US deficits to historically high levels, close to ~10% of GDP (the current US federal structural deficit is around 6-7%).
• Debt remains sustainable in most developed countries despite the sell-off in global yields. The US (and Belgium) stand out with unsustainable debt paths. France looks better than last year but only conditionally on uncertain tightening. The UK, Italy, and Japan remain vulnerable to new shocks but are sustainable under current fiscal plans.
• Markets have repriced yield curves to reflect debt differences: higher-debt countries now have steeper curves (unlike before the pandemic). Based on simple debt dynamics, curves look broadly fair across most countries. Japan stands out as relatively steep.
• US interest rates (R) may soon exceed GDP growth (G) for the first time since the 1990s, making the cost of running deficits much higher and debt dynamics unstable.

FIVE SCENARIOS FOR US DEBT (unchanged from prior two years):
1. "Status Quo" – Debt trends higher with no/modest orderly rise in term premium; fiscal credibility intact (e.g., US post-GFC). Very likely.
2. "Crisis" – Debt trends higher with sharp disorderly rise in term premium; no fiscal credibility (e.g., UK under Truss). Unlikely, but slightly higher under Trump.
3. "Fiscal Consolidation" – Debt stabilizes via fiscal tightening (e.g., US mid-90s). Unlikely near term, likely further out.
4. "Financial Repression" – Debt stabilizes via high inflation + low interest rates (e.g., post-WW2). Unlikely.
5. "Growth Revival" – Debt stabilizes via rising real GDP growth (e.g., Australia 1930s). Unlikely, but AI raises odds slightly.

SUPPORTING DATA AND CONTEXT:
• G7 deficits remain high (outside wars and crises) and will likely stay higher than pre-pandemic due to higher interest costs and other spending.
• US debt now exceeds the combined debt of all other advanced countries.
• The US interest burden is rising sharply and is now close to a record high.
• The dollar's reserve status remains strong (45-89% share across various global market segments), supporting US fiscal credibility.
• Unlike Europe, the US tax burden is far from facing "upper bound" Laffer curve constraints, which supports fiscal credibility.
• Some form of fiscal consolidation is likely beyond the secular horizon as the rising interest burden may eventually change political attitudes.
• Historic evidence shows that even successful debt reductions involving financial repression (1950s-80s) also involved budget cuts.
• Even under optimistic AI-driven growth assumptions, higher real trend growth alone is unlikely to make US debt sustainable.
• Political polarization is linked to higher deficits across countries and time.
</summary>

## CIC Released Annual Report 2018

**20-09-2019**

On September 20, 2019, China Investment Corporation (CIC) released the Annual Report 2018 (Annual Report) approved by the Board of Directors, the 11th annual report that CIC has released since its establishment.

The Annual Report disclosed CIC’s overseas portfolio, financial situations, performance and domestic equity management. It also elaborated on CIC’s progress made on corporate governance, investment strategies and management, risk management, human resources and global outreach.

Mr. Peng Chun, Chairman and CEO of CIC, said in the message that 2018 was a rough year for international institutional investors such as CIC. Given the wild swings of the global capital market and increased volatility of risk assets, major stock markets suffered their worst year in ten years. The entire CIC staff acted in concert to surmount difficulties, build institutional capacity, and hone operations and management processes for a good start in the new strategic period.

The Annual Report shows that Although major stock markets took a toll on CIC’s overseas investments, its 10-year cumulative annualized net return was 6.07% and exceeded the company’s ten-year performance target by 45 bps. In 2018, CIC’s net return exceeded the annual performance benchmark by 371 bps and outperformed the market. The performance of the 17 companies in which Central Huijin holds shares steadily improved, and their net profits harvested a 3.1% year-on-year increase. At the close of 2018, CIC’s assets had steadily grown, with USD 940.6 billion in gross assets and USD 858.8 billion in net assets. The annualized growth rate of state-owned capital had reached 13.46% since its inception. The gross assets and net assets of Central Huijin’s 17 holding companies in total had reached CNY 123 trillion and CNY 10.2 trillion, with a year-on-year increase of 6.0% and 9.0% respectively.

Public equity, fixed income, alternative investments and cash and others respectively take up 38.3%, 15.2%, 44.1%, and 2.4% of CIC’s global portfolio

**On investment strategies,** CIC adopts the Reference Portfolio framework, which consists of public market equities and fixed-income products. The framework also included the Three-year Policy Portfolio, the Annual Policy Portfolio/Target Portfolio, and the Actual Portfolio. The Three-year Policy Portfolio makes allocations to other asset classes and active strategies and is expected to outperform the Reference Portfolio with a higher risk-return profile. The Annual Policy Portfolio/Target Portfolio takes into account the progress of alternative investment and short-term market views. In 2018, the company effectively responded to market changes and progressively reduced portfolio risk and leverage. The actual portfolio return exceeded Policy Portfolio return, which in turn exceeded Reference Portfolio return. It also further optimized allocation efficiency for long-term assets. The weight of alternative investments (including direct investments) in the company’s overseas investment portfolio reached 44.1%, up 4.8 percentage points from the previous year.

**On investment management,** we continued to implement refined management of public market investments, adjust and optimise our investment strategy and the makeup of managers, and carry out new strategic investments such as risk factor investing. Progressively, we increased our investment in alternative assets, consolidated our private equity investments, increased investment in assets with stable returns and stepped up co-investments in various ways. We also continued to develop our professional platform for direct investment, and enhanced compliant interaction between private equity investment and direct investment. We continued seeking new approaches for overseas investment and actively participated in the Belt and Road Initiative by setting up new bilateral funds with the United States and Japan and seeking to establish bilateral funds with the United Kingdom and France as a step to further promote two-way cross-border investment cooperation.

**On investment support,** we fine-tuned our risk management tools, methods and systems, and employed effective risk management to convoy the company’s development. For lawful and compliant operation, strict firewalls exist between CIC International and CIC Capital in their overseas investments, and between the overseas investments conducted by CIC International and CIC Capital and the domestic investments undertaken by Central Huijin. We continued to improve the post-investment management system by strengthening monitoring and analysis and deepening management and value creation. We fostered synergy at various levels, ameliorating the research system, and deepening development of operational systems. We also implemented an assessment framework for net investment income, furthered benchmarking of cost effectiveness against peer organisations, and continuously enhanced investment payment capabilities.

**On investment cooperation,** CIC participated in multilateral meetings, mechanisms, and forums such as those of the G20, B20, Institute of International Finance and International Chamber of Commerce. It also engaged in bilateral dialogues and cooperation mechanisms such as those with France, Japan, Russia, the United Kingdom, and the United States. We strived to build a multi-dimensional cross-border investment ecosystem, having successfully organised events such as the CIC Forum, China-US Business Summit, and China-Japan Business Forum, thereby providing a platform for two-way cross-border investment exchange and cooperation.

**On domestic equity management,** Central Huijin celebrated its 15th anniversary in 2018. For 15 years, Central Huijin leveraged its market-oriented and professional platform to inject capital into 19 financial institutions, and assisted in the public listing of 11 financial institutions. Central Huijin indeed played a unique role in deepening the reform of the financial system, achieving preservation and appreciation of asset value, and maintaining financial stability. It has explored and established the unique "Huijin Model” for managing state-owned financial capital, a model that emphasizes capital management, features dispatching of equity directors, and adopts a market-oriented approach to exercising rights and performing obligations. In 2018, Central Huijin focused on intensifying the development of its investment and operation platform for state-owned financial capital, played the strategic leading role of driving its holding companies to serve the real economy, prevent and control financial risks, and deepen financial reform. At the end of 2018, Central Huijin managed state-owned financial capital worth CNY 4.3 trillion, approximately 40% of central state-owned financial capital.

2019 marks the 70th anniversary of the establishment of the People’s Republic of China and a key year for building a moderately prosperous society in an all-round way. With greater scientific rigour in decision-making, better efficiency in implementation and increased stringency in management, we will increase the rate of return of our investment portfolio, and remain as the ever faithful and responsible guardian and manager of state-owned assets.

As a Chinese poem goes, **“*without the continuous bitter cold, there can be no fragrant plum blossom*”**. The tougher the road, the sweeter the taste of success—pain precedes gain. Mr. Peng Chun, Chairman and CEO of CIC, said in the message that through years of exploration and relentless efforts, CIC put in place market-oriented systems and highly professional investment management teams as key assets and resources of the company. As we stand at the historical crossroads, CIC’s new leadership will bear in mind our mission and original aspiration, and strive to strengthen the company’s development. We will unite and work pragmatically, inheriting legacies and seeking to reform as we push on. And they will build on past achievements and thrive for a magnificent future.

args.summary:
This webpage is the official site of China Investment Corporation (CIC), a sovereign wealth fund established to diversify China's foreign exchange holdings and seek maximum returns for its shareholder within acceptable risk tolerance. The page provides an overview of CIC's structure (About, Governance, Investments, Media, Careers) and contains a featured press release announcing the release of the Annual Report 2018 on September 20, 2019.

Key details from the Annual Report 2018:
- This was the 11th annual report CIC released since its establishment.
- CIC's 10-year cumulative annualized net return was 6.07%, exceeding its ten-year performance target by 45 basis points.
- In 2018, CIC's net return exceeded the annual performance benchmark by 371 bps.
- At the close of 2018, CIC had USD 940.6 billion in gross assets and USD 858.8 billion in net assets.
- The annualized growth rate of state-owned capital reached 13.46% since inception.
- CIC's global portfolio composition: public equity 38.3%, fixed income 15.2%, alternative investments 44.1%, cash and others 2.4%.
- Alternative investments rose to 44.1% of the overseas portfolio, up 4.8 percentage points from the previous year.
- Central Huijin's 17 holding companies had gross assets of CNY 123 trillion and net assets of CNY 10.2 trillion (up 6.0% and 9.0% year-on-year respectively), with net profits growing 3.1% year-on-year.
- Central Huijin celebrated its 15th anniversary in 2018, having injected capital into 19 financial institutions and assisted in the public listing of 11 financial institutions. It managed CNY 4.3 trillion of state-owned financial capital (about 40% of central state-owned financial capital).

Investment strategy details: CIC uses a Reference Portfolio framework (public equities and fixed income), a Three-year Policy Portfolio, Annual Policy Portfolio/Target Portfolio, and Actual Portfolio. In 2018, the company reduced portfolio risk and leverage, with actual returns exceeding policy returns which exceeded reference returns. CIC participated in the Belt and Road Initiative, established bilateral funds with the US and Japan, and sought funds with the UK and France. CIC participated in G20, B20, IIF, and ICC forums, and engaged in bilateral cooperation with France, Japan, Russia, the UK, and the US.

Governance: CIC operates with a Board of Directors, Board of Supervisors, and Executive Committee in accordance with China's Company Law, and has implemented the Santiago Principles for transparency. Chairman and CEO at the time was Mr. Peng Chun.

The **Qatar Investment Authority** (**QIA**; [Arabic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arabic_language "Arabic language"): جهاز قطر للإستثمار) is [Qatar](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Qatar "Qatar")'s [sovereign wealth fund](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sovereign_wealth_fund "Sovereign wealth fund"),[[2]](#cite_note-2) founded by the State of Qatar in 2005 to strengthen the country's economy by diversifying into new asset classes. As of May 2026, the fund had an estimated $600 billion of [assets under management](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Assets_under_management "Assets under management").[[3]](#cite_note-3)

[![](//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/a/a3/The_Chancery_Rosewood%2C_Grosvenor_Square%2C_Mayfair%2C_August_2025.jpg/250px-The_Chancery_Rosewood%2C_Grosvenor_Square%2C_Mayfair%2C_August_2025.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:The_Chancery_Rosewood,_Grosvenor_Square,_Mayfair,_August_2025.jpg)

The Chancery [Rosewood](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rosewood_Hotels_&_Resorts "Rosewood Hotels & Resorts"), London

The QIA's structure and decision-making procedures have been characterized as non-transparent.[[4]](#cite_note-4)[[5]](#cite_note-5) Spending decisions regarding the fund have been linked to the emir and the prime minister (regardless of whether they sit on the board of the fund).[[6]](#cite_note-6)

## History and profile

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Qatar_Investment_Authority&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: History and profile")]

The QIA was founded in 2005 by the then-[emir of Qatar](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Emir_of_Qatar "Emir of Qatar"), [Hamad bin Khalifa Al Thani](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hamad_bin_Khalifa_Al_Thani "Hamad bin Khalifa Al Thani"), to manage the [oil](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Petroleum "Petroleum") and [natural gas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Natural_gas "Natural gas") surpluses of the [government of Qatar](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Politics_of_Qatar "Politics of Qatar").[[7]](#cite_note-7) As a result of its stated strategy to minimize risk from Qatar's reliance on energy prices, the fund predominantly invests in international markets (United States, Europe and Asia-Pacific) and within Qatar outside the energy sector. Prior to establishment of the QIA in 2005, Qatar's Ministry of Finance had a small in-house team to invest revenue from budget surpluses.[[8]](#cite_note-8) The [Qatar National Vision 2030](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Qatar_National_Vision_2030 "Qatar National Vision 2030") foresees the shift from natural gas based revenue to QIA-type investments between now and then.[[9]](#cite_note-:9-9) QIA does not publish its holdings to the market.

In June 2013, after the new emir's arrival to power, and a general reshuffle of Qatar's main organizations, Ahmad Al Sayed was appointed as QIA's chairman and [chief executive officer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chief_executive_officer "Chief executive officer"), replacing [Hamad bin Jassim Al Thani](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hamad_bin_Jassim_bin_Jaber_Al_Thani "Hamad bin Jassim bin Jaber Al Thani") in the post[[10]](#cite_note-10) while also remaining managing director and CEO of QIA's main subsidiary, Qatar Holding.[[11]](#cite_note-11) Sayed held the post for 16 months. In January 2015, Sheikh [Abdullah bin Mohammed bin Saud Al Thani](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abdullah_bin_Mohammed_bin_Saud_Al_Thani "Abdullah bin Mohammed bin Saud Al Thani"), chairman of Qatari telecommunications company [Ooredoo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ooredoo "Ooredoo"), was appointed as CEO and served until 2018.[[12]](#cite_note-12) From July 2022 to November 2024, [Mansoor Ebrahim Al-Mahmoud](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mansoor_bin_Ebrahim_bin_Saad_Al_Mahmoud "Mansoor bin Ebrahim bin Saad Al Mahmoud") has held the position of [CEO](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/CEO "CEO") of the company.[[1]](#cite_note-CEO-1) He was succeeded by Mohammed Saif Al-Sowaidi.[[13]](#cite_note-13) In March 2023, Sheikh Bandar bin Mohammed bin Saoud Al-Thani was appointed chairman and replaced his predecessor, Sheikh [Mohammed bin Abdulrahman bin Jassim Al Thani](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mohammed_bin_Abdulrahman_bin_Jassim_Al_Thani "Mohammed bin Abdulrahman bin Jassim Al Thani"), who was named as the country's [prime minister](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prime_Minister_of_Qatar "Prime Minister of Qatar") in addition to his long-standing role as Minister of Foreign Affairs.[[14]](#cite_note-14)

The fund is a founding member of the [International Forum of Sovereign Wealth Funds](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/International_Forum_of_Sovereign_Wealth_Funds "International Forum of Sovereign Wealth Funds").[[15]](#cite_note-IFSWF001-15)[[16]](#cite_note-:5-16)

As of 2021, the Qatar Investment Authority had more than half of its assets invested in private equity and listed shares.[[17]](#cite_note-17) According to *[Bloomberg](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bloomberg_News "Bloomberg News")*, QIA has increasingly targeted start-ups in growth markets, such as Asia and the US. It has invested in indoor farming and firms that make plant-based meat alternatives.[[18]](#cite_note-18)

## Structure

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Qatar_Investment_Authority&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Structure")]

### Executive management

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Qatar_Investment_Authority&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: Executive management")]

* Mohammed Saif Al-Sowaidi – CEO[[19]](#cite_note-:4-19)

### Board of directors

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Qatar_Investment_Authority&action=edit&section=4 "Edit section: Board of directors")]

* Bandar bin Mohammed bin Saoud Al-Thani – Chairman[[19]](#cite_note-:4-19)
* [Mohammed bin Hamad Bin Khalifa Al Thani](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mohammed_bin_Hamad_Al_Thani_(born_1988) "Mohammed bin Hamad Al Thani (born 1988)") – Vice chairman
* [Ali bin Ahmed Al-Kuwari](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ali_bin_Ahmed_Al_Kuwari "Ali bin Ahmed Al Kuwari")
* [Saad Sherida Al-Kaabi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saad_Sherida_al-Kaabi "Saad Sherida al-Kaabi")
* [Mohammed bin Hamad bin Qassim Al Abdullah Al Thani](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mohammed_bin_Hamad_bin_Qassim_Al_Abdullah_Al_Thani "Mohammed bin Hamad bin Qassim Al Abdullah Al Thani")
* [Hassan Al-Thawadi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hassan_Al-Thawadi "Hassan Al-Thawadi")
* [Faisal bin Thani bin Faisal Al Thani](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Faisal_bin_Thani_bin_Faisal_Al_Thani "Faisal bin Thani bin Faisal Al Thani")
* [Nasser Al-Khelaifi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nasser_Al-Khelaifi "Nasser Al-Khelaifi")

### Subsidiaries

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Qatar_Investment_Authority&action=edit&section=5 "Edit section: Subsidiaries")]

QIA's subsidiaries include [Es'hailSat](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Es'hailSat "Es'hailSat"),[[20]](#cite_note-20) [Hassad Food](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hassad_Food "Hassad Food"),[[21]](#cite_note-:14-21) [Katara Hospitality](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Katara_Hospitality "Katara Hospitality"),[[22]](#cite_note-:15-22) [Ooredoo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ooredoo "Ooredoo"),[[23]](#cite_note-23)[[24]](#cite_note-24) [Qatar Airways](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Qatar_Airways "Qatar Airways"),[[25]](#cite_note-25) Qatari Diar,[[26]](#cite_note-:7-26) Qatar Holding,[[27]](#cite_note-27) [Qatar Stock Exchange](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Qatar_Stock_Exchange "Qatar Stock Exchange"),[[28]](#cite_note-28) [QNB Group](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/QNB_Group "QNB Group")[[29]](#cite_note-29) and [QNBN](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Qatar_National_Broadband_Network_(Qnbn) "Qatar National Broadband Network (Qnbn)").[[30]](#cite_note-30)[[31]](#cite_note-31)

## Investments

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Qatar_Investment_Authority&action=edit&section=6 "Edit section: Investments")]

In January 2013, one writer pegged the QIA investment in Britain at €30 billion, France at €10 billion and Germany at €5 billion,[[9]](#cite_note-:9-9) while another reported that the total assets under management in June 2013 was on the order of $100 billion.[[32]](#cite_note-alj-32) Qatar Holding's stake in [Barclays](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Barclays "Barclays") rose to 12.7% following Barclays' capital raising in October 2008.[[33]](#cite_note-33) Qatar Investment Authority holds a small stake in [Fisker Automotive](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fisker_Automotive "Fisker Automotive"). It also holds about 17% stake in the [Volkswagen Group](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Volkswagen_Group "Volkswagen Group"), [Porsche](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Porsche "Porsche"), [Hochtief](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hochtief "Hochtief"),[[34]](#cite_note-nobs-34) as well as investments in [Sainsbury's](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sainsbury's "Sainsbury's").[[35]](#cite_note-35) The French government has made of Qatar a strategic partner, and the list of partnerships between the two states includes [Total](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Total_S.A. "Total S.A.") (4%), [EADS](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/EADS "EADS") (6%), [Technip](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Technip "Technip"), [Air Liquide](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Air_Liquide "Air Liquide"), [Vinci SA](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vinci_SA "Vinci SA") (5%), [GDF Suez](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/GDF_Suez "GDF Suez"), [Veolia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Veolia "Veolia") (5%), [Vivendi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vivendi "Vivendi"), Royal Monceau, [France Telecom](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/France_Telecom "France Telecom") and [Areva](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Areva "Areva").[[9]](#cite_note-:9-9)[[34]](#cite_note-nobs-34)[[36]](#cite_note-lem-36) In February 2009, France accorded special beyond-[OECD](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Organisation_for_Economic_Co-operation_and_Development "Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development") investment privileges to Qatar and its [state-owned enterprises](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Agence_des_participations_de_l'État "Agence des participations de l'État"); one example is [capital gains](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Capital_gain "Capital gain") exemptions in France.[[36]](#cite_note-lem-36) The QIA is also reported to hold 8.2% of [Glencore](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Glencore "Glencore").[[32]](#cite_note-alj-32)

QIA holds a 6% stake in Credit Suisse. The French government has offered tax exemptions for Qatari real estate investments in the country and have acquired almost $4 billion of property.[[37]](#cite_note-Sayare-37) In May 2012, it acquired a stake below 3% in [Royal Dutch Shell](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Royal_Dutch_Shell "Royal Dutch Shell"). It has announced a plan to raise its stake to 7%.[[38]](#cite_note-upstream070912-38)

In November 2012, QIA and [Cassa Depositi e Prestiti](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cassa_Depositi_e_Prestiti "Cassa Depositi e Prestiti") signed the starting agreement of IQ Made in Italy Venture, a four-year cooperation to promote [Made in Italy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Made_in_Italy "Made in Italy") in Qatar's Arabic partners and to push them to invest in Italian economic sectors like fashion, luxury, design, food, tourism, lifestyle & leisure.[[39]](#cite_note-39)[[40]](#cite_note-40)[[41]](#cite_note-41)

In January 2013, Qatar Holding, an indirect subsidiary of QIA, said it would invest $5 billion into petrochemical projects in [Malaysia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Malaysia "Malaysia") in three to four years. The investment was said to help Malaysia compete with neighbouring [Singapore](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Singapore "Singapore") to become the region's top petrochemical hub.[[42]](#cite_note-42) The QIA was planning to invest $200 million in residential property in [India](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/India "India") through Kotak Realty Fund in late December 2013.[[43]](#cite_note-43) In August 2018, Qatar Investment Authority signed Memorandum of Understanding (MoU) to invest up to $500mn in tourism in [Indonesia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Indonesia "Indonesia").[[44]](#cite_note-44)

In October 2014 Qatar Investment Authority signed an agreement with [CITIC Group](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/CITIC_Group "CITIC Group") Corp to launch a $10 billion fund to invest in [China](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/China "China").[[45]](#cite_note-45) The QIA announced its intention to invest $35b in the [US](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States "United States") during the next five years, starting in September 2015.[[46]](#cite_note-46)[[47]](#cite_note-47)[[48]](#cite_note-48)

Via Mannai Corporation, it is currently in a process of acquiring the French computer science group GFI.[[49]](#cite_note-49) In 2021, QIA with its subsidiary unit - Locus Engineering Management and Services Co. W.L.L. is investing in a sub-Saharan African renewable energy platform being led by Enel Green Power.[[50]](#cite_note-50)

During the 2021 St Petersburg Economic Forum, Sheikh [Tamim bin Hamad Al Thani](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tamim_bin_Hamad_Al_Thani "Tamim bin Hamad Al Thani") highlighted [Qatar](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Qatar "Qatar")'s solid historic relations with [Russia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Russia "Russia") and announced that his country will increase investments in the Russian Federation. He also called on [Russia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Russia "Russia")'s private sector and the world to explore [Qatar](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Qatar "Qatar")'s promising business environment in many projects and several spheres.[[51]](#cite_note-51)

On 23 January 2023, Qatar Investment Authority has doubled its stake in [Credit Suisse Group](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Credit_Suisse "Credit Suisse"), becoming the second-biggest shareholder and underlining the growing importance of Middle Eastern investors to the ailing Swiss bank.[[52]](#cite_note-52)[[53]](#cite_note-53)

In June 2024, *[Reuters](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Reuters "Reuters")* wrote that QIA had agreed to buy a 10% stake in [ChinaAMC](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/China_Asset_Management "China Asset Management") and was awaiting approval by Chinese regulators.[[54]](#cite_note-54)

### Real estate

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Qatar_Investment_Authority&action=edit&section=7 "Edit section: Real estate")]

The QIA real estate portfolio includes direct ownership, joint ventures,[[55]](#cite_note-55) trusts and funds.[[56]](#cite_note-56) It wholly controls Qatari Diar, a property investment company,[[57]](#cite_note-57) and also owns Katara Hospitality, a global hotel owner, developer and operator.[[58]](#cite_note-58)

In 2013, QIA acquired a 40% stake in the [Porta Nuova business district in Milan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Porta_Nuova_(Milan) "Porta Nuova (Milan)"),[[59]](#cite_note-59) later purchasing the remaining interest in 2015.[[60]](#cite_note-60)

QIA has purchased $3.78 billion in Manhattan properties since 2014, including 111 West 33rd Street, 501 Seventh Avenue and 250 West 57th Street.[[61]](#cite_note-61) In 2015, in a joint venture with [Brookfield Property Partners](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brookfield_Property_Partners "Brookfield Property Partners"), QIA acquired a 44% stake in the [Manhattan West](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Manhattan_West "Manhattan West") development.[[62]](#cite_note-62)[[63]](#cite_note-63)[[64]](#cite_note-64) In 2022, QIA and Brookfield sold a 49% shareholding in the project to Blackstone Real Estate.[[65]](#cite_note-65)

QIA and Brookfield jointly acquired [Canary Wharf Group](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Canary_Wharf_Group "Canary Wharf Group") for £2.6 billion.[[66]](#cite_note-66)[[67]](#cite_note-:10-67) The Canary Wharf Group is London's largest property owner, with almost 21.5m sq ft of space on its books, according to data from the research firm Datscha.[[68]](#cite_note-qia-68)

QIA has also made investments in [Asia Square](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Asia_Square "Asia Square") in Singapore[[69]](#cite_note-69)[[70]](#cite_note-70) and the [HSBC Tower](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/8_Canada_Square "8 Canada Square") in London.[[67]](#cite_note-:10-67) In 2016, QIA purchased a 9.9% stake in [Empire State Realty Trust](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Empire_State_Building "Empire State Building").[[71]](#cite_note-71)

Qatar Investment Authority is a major shareholder in [Heathrow Airport](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Heathrow_Airport "Heathrow Airport"), holding 20 percent of the airport. In 2017, the company invested a further £650 million (US$807 million).[[72]](#cite_note-72)

QIA has held a 20% stake in [Inmobiliaria Colonial](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Inmobiliaria_Colonial "Inmobiliaria Colonial") since 2018.[[73]](#cite_note-73) In August 2018, Brookfield signed a 99-year lease on [Jared Kushner](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jared_Kushner "Jared Kushner")'s financially troubled [666 Fifth Avenue](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/666_Fifth_Avenue "666 Fifth Avenue") skyscraper. The deal raised suspicions that the Qatar Investment Authority, a major investor in Brookfield, was attempting to influence the [Trump administration](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/First_presidency_of_Donald_Trump "First presidency of Donald Trump").[[74]](#cite_note-74)[[75]](#cite_note-75)

In 2019, QIA partnered with Crown Acquisitions to acquire a significant stake in [Vornado Realty Trust](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vornado_Realty_Trust "Vornado Realty Trust"), a portfolio of premium New York retail properties.[[76]](#cite_note-76)

QIA also owns luxury hotels including the St. Regis San Francisco,[[77]](#cite_note-77) the [St. Regis New York](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/St._Regis_New_York "St. Regis New York"),[[78]](#cite_note-78) and the [W Barcelona](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/W_Barcelona "W Barcelona").[[79]](#cite_note-79) In 2023, it acquired the [Park Lane Hotel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Park_Lane_Hotel_(Manhattan) "Park Lane Hotel (Manhattan)") in New York.[[80]](#cite_note-80)

#### Qatari Diar

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Qatar_Investment_Authority&action=edit&section=8 "Edit section: Qatari Diar")]

[![](//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/en/3/32/Qatari_Diar.gif?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail_unscaled)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Qatari_Diar.gif)

Logo of Qatari Diar

Qatari Diar is a [real estate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Real_estate "Real estate") company established by the Qatar Investment Authority in 2005 with headquarters in Lusail.[[26]](#cite_note-:7-26)

In 2008, Qatari Diar acquired French engineering company [Cegelec](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cegelec "Cegelec"),[[81]](#cite_note-81) which was later sold, in 2010, to [Vinci SA](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vinci_SA "Vinci SA") in exchange for 31.5 million Vinci shares.[[82]](#cite_note-82)

By 2011 the company had stakes in the utility [Suez Environnement](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Suez_Environnement "Suez Environnement") and in [Veolia Environnement](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Veolia_Environnement "Veolia Environnement") (4.6%, sold in 2018).[[83]](#cite_note-83) In 2011, Qatari Diar bought the Port Tarraco Marina in Tarragona, Spain.[[84]](#cite_note-84)[[85]](#cite_note-85) The company invested into [The Shard](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Shard "The Shard"), a skyscraper in London designed by [Renzo Piano](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Renzo_Piano "Renzo Piano"),[[86]](#cite_note-86)[[87]](#cite_note-87) and the former Royal Dutch Shell plc headquarters.[[88]](#cite_note-88) Other London investments include the [Chelsea Barracks](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chelsea_Barracks "Chelsea Barracks"),[[89]](#cite_note-89) the [US Embassy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Embassy_of_the_United_States,_London "Embassy of the United States, London"), [Elephant and Castle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elephant_and_Castle "Elephant and Castle") and Grosvenor Waterside.[[90]](#cite_note-90)

In 2012, it completed the acquisition of [Credit Suisse](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Credit_Suisse "Credit Suisse")'s headquarters in London.[[91]](#cite_note-91) Qatari Diar along with Canary Wharf, won a £300mn deal to redevelop the Shell Centre in London, the former London headquarters of [Royal Dutch Shell](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Royal_Dutch_Shell "Royal Dutch Shell").[[92]](#cite_note-92)

As of 2013, Qatari Diar was one of the major financiers of a recent development known as [CityCenterDC](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/CityCenterDC "CityCenterDC"), as it invested $650 million into the project.[[93]](#cite_note-93)[[94]](#cite_note-94) Qatari Diar also invested into [The Peninsula Paris](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Peninsula_Paris "The Peninsula Paris") hotel.[[95]](#cite_note-95) In 2018, Qatari Diar started to develop the Chancery [Rosewood](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rosewood_Hotels_&_Resorts "Rosewood Hotels & Resorts") hotel in the building of the former US Embassy at 30 [Grosvenor Square](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grosvenor_Square "Grosvenor Square") in [Mayfair](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mayfair "Mayfair"), London. The hotel was opened in September 2025.[[96]](#cite_note-96)[[97]](#cite_note-97)[[98]](#cite_note-98)[[99]](#cite_note-99)

In April 2023, the company sold its 22 per cent stake in the build-to-rent developer Get Living, which owns the publicly funded Olympic village also known as [East Village, London](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/East_Village,_London "East Village, London").[[100]](#cite_note-:6-100) Qatari Diar sold its shares to [Aware Super](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aware_Super "Aware Super"), an Australian pension fund.[[100]](#cite_note-:6-100)

In May 2010, Qatar Holding, an indirect subsidiary of QIA, purchased the [Harrods Group](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harrods_Group "Harrods Group") from [Mohamed Al-Fayed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mohamed_Al-Fayed "Mohamed Al-Fayed"), including the [Knightsbridge](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Knightsbridge "Knightsbridge") department store.[[127]](#cite_note-127)[[128]](#cite_note-control-128)[[129]](#cite_note-129) The sale was concluded in the early hours of 8 May, when [Qatari Prime Minister](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prime_Minister_of_Qatar "Prime Minister of Qatar") [Hamad bin Jassim bin Jaber Al Thani](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hamad_bin_Jassim_bin_Jaber_Al_Thani "Hamad bin Jassim bin Jaber Al Thani") came to London to finalise the deal, saying that the acquisition of Harrods would add "much value" to the investment portfolio of Qatar Holdings while his deputy, Hussain Ali Al-Abdulla, called it a "landmark transaction".[[130]](#cite_note-BBC-130) A spokesman for Mohamed Al-Fayed said "in reaching the decision to retire, [Fayed] wished to ensure that the legacy and traditions that he has built up in Harrods would be continued."[[130]](#cite_note-BBC-130) QIA is also the largest shareholder in [Sainsbury's](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sainsbury's "Sainsbury's").[[131]](#cite_note-131)

In 2021, QIA participated in an $1.5 billion funding round for the Turkish online retailer [Trendyol](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trendyol "Trendyol").[[138]](#cite_note-138)[[139]](#cite_note-139) In 2023, QIA bought a 1% stake in India's [Reliance Retail Ventures](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Reliance_Retail "Reliance Retail") for $1 billion.[[140]](#cite_note-140)[[141]](#cite_note-141)

### *Sunday Telegraph*'s campaign

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Qatar_Investment_Authority&action=edit&section=13 "Edit section: Sunday Telegraph's campaign")]

In October 2014 the British newspaper *[Sunday Telegraph](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Sunday_Telegraph "The Sunday Telegraph")* launched a campaign, called "Stop the Funding of Terror", to "press for action to end the flow of funds to extremist groups from individuals in states such as Qatar, Kuwait and Saudi Arabia". The campaign put special stress on the Qatari government and emir Hamad Al Thani, and on Qatari investments in the UK.[[195]](#cite_note-195)

### Barclays

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Qatar_Investment_Authority&action=edit&section=14 "Edit section: Barclays")]

In 2008 during the [2008 financial crisis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2008_financial_crisis "2008 financial crisis") Barclays raised about £11.8 billion, one of the investors among others was QIA. Barclays reportedly received €7.5 billion ($8.2 billion) cash injection from QIA's subsidiary but did not inform its shareholders.[[196]](#cite_note-:1-196) Barclays was charged with failing to act with integrity and breaching disclosure rules for UK listed companies.[[197]](#cite_note-:2-197) Barclays then made secret advisory deals with companies linked to QIA, agreeing to pay about £322 million in fees. These undisclosed deals were part of the incentive for Qatar to invest.[[198]](#cite_note-198)[[199]](#cite_note-199)[[200]](#cite_note-:11-200) In 2011 both the Serious Fraud Office and the Financial Conduct Authority (FCA) investigated Barclays' €2.4 billion ($2.7 billion) secret transaction with a Politically Exposed Person (PEP) from Qatar whose identity remains protected by the financial giant and FCA.[[196]](#cite_note-:1-196) A[[197]](#cite_note-:2-197) In that case, Barclays failed to conduct "due skill, care, and diligence" at the base of Britain's anti-money laundering rules.[[201]](#cite_note-:3-201) As a result, the UK financial watchdog meted out a record €92 million ($104 million) penalty against the financial giant.[[201]](#cite_note-:3-201) In August 2012, the UK's [Serious Fraud Office](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Serious_Fraud_Office_(United_Kingdom) "Serious Fraud Office (United Kingdom)") (SFO) started a criminal investigation regarding if Barclays had properly informed investors about these payments.[[200]](#cite_note-:11-200)[[202]](#cite_note-202) This criminal investigation led to charges against the bank and some top executives, including former CEO [John Varley](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Varley_(banker) "John Varley (banker)"), for conspiracy and giving unlawful financial help. By 2020, all the people involved were cleared, and the charges against the bank were dropped.[[203]](#cite_note-203)[[204]](#cite_note-:12-204) But at the same time, there were also civil lawsuits against the bank, most notable was the on from [Amanda Staveley](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amanda_Staveley "Amanda Staveley")’s PCP Capital, claiming Barclays lied about differences in the deal’s terms. In early 2021, a court said Barclays had committed “serious deceit,” but the claimant still lost the case.[[205]](#cite_note-:13-205)[[206]](#cite_note-206)

In October 2022, the [Financial Conduct Authority](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Financial_Conduct_Authority "Financial Conduct Authority") (FCA) announced that it will fine Barclays £50 million for breaking listing rules by not disclosing key information. Barclays appealed, and the fine was later reduced to £40 million. The bank didn't admit to the accusations but dropped its appeal to end the 16 year dispute and move forward.[[205]](#cite_note-:13-205)[[207]](#cite_note-207)

The Qatar Investment Authority (QIA) is Qatar's sovereign wealth fund, founded in 2005 by then-Emir Hamad bin Khalifa Al Thani to manage oil and natural gas surpluses and diversify Qatar's economy away from energy dependence. As of May 2026, the fund holds approximately US$600 billion in assets under management, making it one of the world's largest sovereign wealth funds. Headquartered in Doha's Ooredoo Tower, the QIA is wholly owned by the State of Qatar and is a founding member of the International Forum of Sovereign Wealth Funds.

Key leadership includes CEO Mohammed Saif Al-Sowaidi and Chairman Sheikh Bandar bin Mohammed bin Saoud Al-Thani. The fund's structure has been characterized as non-transparent, with spending decisions linked to the emir and prime minister. Its subsidiaries include QNB Group, Qatari Diar, Qatar Holding, Hassad Food, Katara Hospitality, Harrods Group, Es'hailSat, Ooredoo, Qatar Airways, Qatar Stock Exchange, and QNBN.

The fund's investment portfolio spans real estate, technology, media, telecom, consumer, and retail sectors globally. Major real estate holdings include Heathrow Airport (20%), Canary Wharf Group (with Brookfield, £2.6 billion), Manhattan properties ($3.78 billion since 2014), Empire State Realty Trust (9.9%), and the Porta Nuova district in Milan. Notable equity stakes include Volkswagen (17%), Sainsbury's (~9.5%), and Credit Suisse (doubled to become second-biggest shareholder in 2023). The fund made its highest-profile consumer acquisition in May 2010, purchasing the Harrods Group from Mohamed Al-Fayed.

In technology, QIA has invested in Miramax, Gigamon ($1.6 billion with Elliott), BYJU'S ($400 million total), Universal Music Group, Snyk, Builder.ai ($250 million), Anthropic, PsiQuantum ($1 billion), Databricks, Instabase, and xAI, among others. It has made strategic investments in China (a $10 billion fund with CITIC Group), the US ($35 billion commitment starting 2015), India, Indonesia, Russia, and Malaysia. The fund also holds stakes in Reliance Retail (1%, $1 billion), Flipkart ($150 million), Eat Just ($200 million), and CureVac ($126 million).

Controversies documented include a 2014 Sunday Telegraph campaign ("Stop the Funding of Terror"), and a long-running Barclays scandal stemming from 2008 financial crisis investments. Barclays received a €7.5 billion cash injection from QIA subsidiary without informing shareholders, leading to investigations by the SFO and FCA, a record €92 million FCA penalty, and criminal charges (later dropped by 2020). The FCA fined Barclays £50 million in October 2022 (reduced to £40 million on appeal) for breaking listing rules. The QIA also reportedly lost $5.9 billion on its Volkswagen stake in September 2015.
args.key_excerpts: "As of May 2026, the fund had an estimated $600 billion of assets under management."; "The QIA's structure and decision-making procedures have been characterized as non-transparent. Spending decisions regarding the fund have been linked to the emir and the prime minister (regardless of whether they sit on the board of the fund)."; "In May 2010, Qatar Holding, an indirect subsidiary of QIA, purchased the Harrods Group from Mohamed Al-Fayed... saying that the acquisition of Harrods would add 'much value' to the investment portfolio of Qatar Holdings while his deputy, Hussain Ali Al-Abdulla, called it a 'landmark transaction'."; "On 23 January 2023, Qatar Investment Authority has doubled its stake in Credit Suisse Group, becoming the second-biggest shareholder and underlining the growing importance of Middle Eastern investors to the ailing Swiss bank."; "In October 2022, the Financial Conduct Authority (FCA) announced that it will fine Barclays £50 million for breaking listing rules by not disclosing key information."

# Saudi Arabia’s PIF surpasses $765 billion in AUM, delivering 8.7 percent average annual shareholder return

**Published:** Tue 20 Aug 2024, 12:17 PM

**Last updated:** Tue 20 Aug 2024, 12:18 PM

Saudi Arabia’s Public Investment Fund (PIF) has released its 2023 annual report, showcasing its remarkable progress across various strategic sectors in Saudi Arabia and globally. The report highlights PIF’s commitment to driving economic transformation in line with Saudi Vision 2030, solidifying its position as a leading global investor.

The report, adhering to [GIPS international standards](https://www.gipsstandards.org/), demonstrates PIF’s strong performance in 2023. Assets under management (AUM) surged by 29 percent to SAR2.871 trillion ($765.16 billion) by year-end 2023, reaching $925 billion as of July 2024, SPA reported. Since its inception, PIF has achieved an average total shareholder return of 8.7 percent per year, demonstrating its commitment to delivering long-term, sustainable returns and economic transformation in Saudi Arabia.

## **Key initiatives and partnerships**

PIF’s commitment to transparency and good governance is evident in the report. Total net cash returns for both Saudi Sector Development (SSD) and Saudi Equity Holdings (SEH) pools reached SAR42 billion ($11.2 billion) for the year, surpassing the SAR20 billion ($5.3 billion) target. The Saudi Real Estate and Infrastructure Development (SREID) pool experienced a 15 percent year-on-year increase, reaching SAR233 billion ($62 billion) in AUM.

## **Driving growth in key sectors**

The inaugural Private Sector Forum, a significant milestone, provided local businesses with opportunities to align with and support PIF’s mandate. Key initiatives unveiled at the forum include MUSAHAMA, the local content growth program, and the Suppliers Development Program. These programs aim to enhance visibility for private sector companies seeking supplier and investment opportunities within PIF and its subsidiaries.

## **Expanding global investments**

PIF continues to invest significantly in Saudi Arabia, supporting growth in key economic sectors. This includes the launch of Riyadh Air, Saudi Arabia’s new national carrier, and the Electric Vehicle Infrastructure Company (EVIQ) to accelerate the adoption of electric vehicles. PIF further supports the car manufacturing ecosystem through Tasaru Mobility Investment and has launched Lifera, a new pharmaceutical investment company, along with Al Balad Development Company and Ardara in the real estate sector.

## **Job creation and economic impact**

Moreover, by year-end 2023, PIF had created over 730,000 direct and indirect jobs, reaching over 763,000 by Q1 2024.

PIF’s global investments have also expanded significantly. In 2023 alone, SAR586 billion ($156 billion) was invested internationally, representing a 14 percent year-over-year increase of SAR74 billion ($19.98 billion). PIF’s international investment portfolio further plays a crucial role in enhancing its global reach and developing capital over the long term. The focus is on impactful investments that generate significant returns over time by investing in future-oriented industries shaping the global economy, contributing to the localization of expertise, skills, and technologies in Saudi Arabia.

[**Read more: Saudi PIF affiliate invests $1.5 billion in EV maker Lucid Group**](https://economymiddleeast.com/news/saudi-pif-affiliate-invests-1-5-billion-in-ev-maker-lucid-group/)

## **Securing foreign direct investment**

Additionally, PIF has actively secured foreign direct investment, including a joint venture with Hyundai to establish a new factory in Saudi Arabia, a partnership with Pirelli to manufacture tires for domestic and export markets, and a joint venture with Baosteel to establish an integrated steel plate manufacturing complex.

Moreover, PIF has received a rating of A1 from Moody’s with a positive outlook and A+ from Fitch with a stable outlook.

As of [2026](gdp-indicators-2026.php), the United States and China rank as the world's two largest economies under both nominal GDP and purchasing power parity (PPP) GDP measures. In nominal terms, the gap between the two economies continues to narrow, as China's GDP is projected to grow by 4.41% in 2026, compared with 2.32% for the United States. Nevertheless, the United States is expected to remain the [largest economy](largest-economies-in-the-world.php) by nominal GDP, leading China by approximately US$11.5 trillion.

On a PPP basis, China remains the world's largest economy, with an estimated GDP that exceeds that of the United States by Int. $11.9 trillion in 2026. The gap is projected to widen further in the coming years, reflecting China's stronger economic growth. China is expected to retain its position as the largest economy by PPP GDP over the coming decades, while the United States continues to rank second. Although India is projected to remain the fastest-growing among the three largest economies, it is still substantially smaller than both China and the United States in PPP terms.

Germany overtook Japan in 2023 to become the world's third-largest economy by nominal GDP. The rankings of Japan, the United Kingdom, and India are expected to change over the coming years, as the three economies are projected to remain close in size, currently ranking fourth, fifth, and sixth, respectively.

In the PPP rankings, the top three positions are expected to remain unchanged, as each of the top three economies maintains a substantial lead over the next-ranked economy.

In the nominal GDP rankings, two changes are expected within the top 10. Italy is projected to overtake Russia, while Brazil is expected to replace Canada. Within the top 20, Australia and Mexico are both projected to move ahead of Spain and South Korea in the rankings. Among the top 50 economies, Colombia is expected to record the largest improvement, climbing five positions in the rankings, followed by Nigeria, which is projected to move up three places.

In the PPP rankings, no changes are expected within the top 20. Among the top 50 economies, Vietnam, Malaysia, and Ukraine are each projected to climb two places. In contrast, Iraq is expected to record the largest decline, falling four positions, followed by Iran, which is projected to drop three places.

Among the top 50 economies, Vietnam is projected to be the fastest-growing in 2026, with a GDP growth rate of 7.10%, followed by India (6.48%) and Taiwan (5.18%). Italy is projected to record the lowest GDP growth rate among the top 50 economies in 2026.

In nominal terms, the United States (1, 8) is the only economy that ranks among the top 10 in both GDP and GDP per capita. Germany (3, 18), Australia (12, 12), the Netherlands (18, 10), and Switzerland (20, 4) also rank among the top 20 in both GDP and GDP per capita. On a PPP basis, the United States (2, 12), Saudi Arabia (17, 20), and Taiwan (20, 9) are the only economies that rank among the top 20 in both GDP and GDP per capita.

This webpage from StatisticsTimes.com presents projected GDP rankings for 2026, based on the International Monetary Fund World Economic Outlook (April 2026 edition), dated 31 July 2026. It covers both nominal GDP and purchasing power parity (PPP) GDP rankings for countries worldwide.

KEY HEADLINE FINDINGS:
- The United States and China rank as the world's two largest economies under both nominal GDP and PPP measures as of 2026. The US leads China by approximately US$11.5 trillion in nominal terms, while China leads the US by Int. $11.9 trillion on a PPP basis.
- China's GDP is projected to grow 4.41% in 2026 vs. 2.32% for the US.
- Germany overtook Japan in 2023 as the world's third-largest economy by nominal GDP. Japan (4th), UK (5th), and India (6th) are projected to remain close in size.
- World nominal GDP is projected at US$126.295 trillion in 2026 (3.06% growth); world PPP GDP at Int. $222.760 trillion.

TOP 10 NOMINAL GDP (2026, billions of $): US (32,383.92), China (20,851.59), Germany (5,452.86), Japan (4,379.25), UK (4,264.79), India (4,153.19), France (3,596.09), Italy (2,738.16), Russia (2,656.45), Brazil (2,635.91).

TOP 10 PPP GDP (2026, billions of Int. $): China (44,295.45), US (32,383.92), India (18,902.32), Russia (7,525.16), Japan (7,262.16), Germany (6,408.42), Indonesia (5,449.15), Brazil (5,229.59), France (4,734.24), UK (4,720.86).

RANKING CHANGES EXPECTED (Nominal): Italy to overtake Russia; Brazil to replace Canada within top 10. Australia and Mexico to move ahead of Spain and South Korea within top 20. Colombia to climb five positions (largest improvement in top 50), followed by Nigeria moving up three.

RANKING CHANGES (PPP): No changes within top 20. Vietnam, Malaysia, and Ukraine each climb two places in top 50. Iraq to fall four positions (largest decline), Iran to drop three.

FASTEST-GROWING (top 50): Vietnam (7.10%), India (6.48%), Taiwan (5.18%). Italy projected to record the lowest growth among top 50. Iran and Iraq are projected to contract (-6.07% and -6.77% respectively).

GDP PER CAPITA HIGHLIGHTS: In nominal terms, the US (rank 8) is the only economy in the top 10 for both GDP and GDP per capita. Highest nominal GDP per capita: Switzerland ($126,177, rank 4), Ireland ($140,186, rank 3), Singapore ($107,758, rank 6). In PPP terms, highest per capita: Singapore (Int. $173,708, rank 2), Ireland (Int. $159,129, rank 3).

### Key Takeaways

The 2026 world economy has a cautious outlook, according to the [October report](https://www.imf.org/en/Publications/WEO/Issues/2025/10/14/world-economic-outlook-october-2025) put out by the International Monetary Fund (IMF).

The organization says that global growth is slowing amid fragmentation and rising protectionism. Significant downside risks are present, ranging from a potential tech stock repricing to eroding institutional independence which could weaken policy decisions.

Nevertheless, we take our annual look at every country’s GDP breakdown, using 2026 projections from the [IMF’s](https://www.imf.org/external/datamapper/NGDPD@WEO/WEOWORLD) datamapper, as of October 2025.

It tracks the size of each economy in current-dollar terms.

The **American economy** is expected to reach **$31.8 trillion** in GDP by 2026. This is roughly the size of China (2nd), Germany (3rd), and India (4th) combined.

However its growth projections have been revised downward since this time last year after trade wars rattled global markets and contributed to rising prices for the world’s largest consumer economy.

Meanwhile, **China’s** GDP is projected at **$20.7 trillion**, 35% below the U.S. total but still threefold that of the third-ranked Germany.

Structural headwinds—from an aging population to a tepid property market—are cooling GDP growth to the 4% range, the slowest multi-year pace in four decades.

Added disruption from tariffs on Chinese goods will also affect the world’s largest export sector.

**India** ($4.5 trillion) is on track to hold on to fourth place after leapfrogging Japan in 2025, helped by its domestic demand. Elsewhere, Indonesia and Türkiye edge up the list, illustrating the demographic advantage and policy reforms of many mid-income nations.

## Mapped: Where Homelessness Rates Are Highest in the U.S.

### Key Takeaways:

Homelessness rates vary widely across the United States, shaped in part by differences in housing costs, incomes, shelter availability, and local conditions.

This visualization maps homelessness rates using [2025 point-in-time estimates](https://www.huduser.gov/portal/datasets/ahar/2025-ahar-part-1-pit-estimates-of-homelessness-in-the-us.html) from the U.S. Department of Housing and Urban Development (HUD) and Census Bureau population [estimates](https://www2.census.gov/programs-surveys/popest/datasets/2020-2025/state/totals/NST-EST2025-ALLDATA.csv).

The gap between the highest and lowest rates is substantial. Washington, D.C. records 74 people experiencing homelessness per 10,000 residents, compared with just four in Mississippi. Among states, New York ranks highest at 73, followed by Oregon at 64.

High poverty rates do not necessarily correspond with high homelessness rates. Mississippi, Louisiana, and Alabama are among the poorer U.S. states, yet each records eight or fewer people experiencing homelessness per 10,000 residents. Housing affordability is an important part of the equation, especially as the [cost of securing a home](https://www.visualcapitalist.com/how-long-it-takes-to-save-for-a-home-in-every-u-s-state/) varies significantly across the country.

## What Counts as Homelessness?

HUD’s point-in-time count measures people experiencing both sheltered and unsheltered homelessness on a single night in January. Sheltered homelessness includes people in emergency or transitional shelters, while unsheltered homelessness includes people sleeping in cars, encampments, abandoned buildings, or other places not intended for habitation.

However, the count does not capture everyone experiencing housing instability. People temporarily staying with friends or relatives, for example, can be missed, as can people in locations unknown to survey teams.

## Homelessness Fell in 2025, But Remains Elevated

The 745,652 people counted in January 2025 represented a 3.3% decline from 2024. However, this followed sharp increases of 12.1% in 2023 and 18.1% in 2024, leaving homelessness well above levels seen during much of the previous decade.

Housing affordability remains a central factor. The National Alliance to End Homelessness [highlights](https://endhomelessness.org/state-of-homelessness/) shortages of affordable housing, low incomes, limited rental assistance, and weakened safety nets as major drivers. These pressures can be particularly acute for households already living near the [poverty line](https://www.visualcapitalist.com/mapped-the-number-of-people-in-poverty-in-u-s-cities/).

Veteran homelessness provides one example of long-term progress. The number of veterans experiencing homelessness fell from 73,367 in 2009 to 32,495 in 2025, a decline of roughly 56%. Researchers and service organizations also point to affordable housing, rental assistance, and healthcare as important tools for reducing homelessness.

Washington, D.C. leads the ranking at $277,689 per person, ahead of Liechtenstein at $217,928. Massachusetts ($114,635) sits just below Switzerland, while California ($108,012) ranks ahead of Singapore and Iceland.

GDP measures the value of goods and services produced within an economy. On a per capita basis, differences can reflect productivity, workforce and industry composition, and resource endowments, rather than household wealth or living standards.

These factors help explain why GDP per person [varies](https://2012books.lardbucket.org/books/theory-and-applications-of-economics/s25-02-four-reasons-why-gdp-varies-ac.html) so widely internationally and why some of the [richest countries](https://www.visualcapitalist.com/ranked-richest-countries-by-gdp-per-capita/) often have highly productive, specialized economies.

## How American States Compare

The scale and diversity of the U.S. [economy](https://www.voanews.com/a/how-us-states-are-richer-than-some-foreign-nations/4844942.html) allow individual states to develop highly productive industry clusters. Finance and professional services are important in New York, technology plays a major role on the West Coast, and energy production supports output in several resource-rich states.

Altogether, 13 U.S. states plus Washington, D.C. rank above the national figure of $89,991. Even Maine, ranked 50th in the graphic at $72,688, sits relatively close to the Netherlands at $73,833.

Still, GDP per capita should not be interpreted as average income. It measures production rather than how that output is distributed among residents. Fiscal structures also differ significantly between economies, as illustrated by our look at [tax revenue as a share of GDP](https://www.visualcapitalist.com/ranked-tax-revenue-as-a-share-of-gdp-by-country/).

## What Is SAFE Investment Company (China)?

The [SAFE](https://www.investopedia.com/terms/s/state-administration-of-foreign-exchange.asp) Investment Company is the Hong Kong branch of the Chinese [sovereign wealth fund](https://www.investopedia.com/terms/s/sovereign_wealth_fund.asp). SAFE is an acronym for State Administration of Foreign Exchange. SAFE’s Hong Kong subsidiary opened in 1997 with $20 billion in capital. Today, the SAFE Investment Company is a private company, however, officials from the Chinese State Administration of Foreign Exchange (SAFE) department serve on its Board of Directors. The fund is set aside primarily as a foreign currency reserve.

### Key Takeaways

Get personalized, AI-powered answers built on 27+ years of trusted expertise.

## Understanding SAFE Investment Company (China)

As of May 2026, China holds approximately $3.4 trillion in [foreign currency reserves](https://www.investopedia.com/ask/answers/06/reserverequirements.asp). The SAFE Investment Company is able to invest in a wide variety of instruments including foreign and domestic equities and [fixed income](https://www.investopedia.com/terms/f/fixedincome.asp) securities. The chief objectives of the SAFE Investment Company are to gain investment returns, increase diversification of holdings and to reduce China's exposure to fluctuations in the value of the U.S. dollar. Since 1997, all SAFE operations are undertaken by the [Peoples Bank of China](https://www.investopedia.com/terms/p/peoples-bank-china-pboc.asp) (PBoC).

## SAFE Investment Company (China) and Sovereign Wealth Funds

The majority of developed nations have [sovereign wealth funds](https://www.investopedia.com/terms/s/sovereign_wealth_fund.asp) (SWF) that they deploy in various ways to benefit the country's economy and citizens. As with SAFE in Hong Kong, the funding for a sovereign wealth fund comes from accumulated central [bank reserves](https://www.investopedia.com/terms/b/bank-reserve.asp) from budget and trade surpluses.

Some countries have created SWFs to diversify their revenue streams. For example, the United Arab Emirates (UAE) uses a portion of its SWF to invest in assets separate from oil, the main driver of their economy. This helps protect the country against any oil-related risk, such as the development of alternative energy technologies. In the United States, the [Alaska Permanent Fund](https://www.investopedia.com/get-paid-for-living-in-alaska-11745087) ticks in at $86 billion, and the Texas Permanent School Fund has $60.6 billion. Both have strong origins in oil and natural resources and were established in 1976 and 1854, respectively.

This Investopedia article provides an overview of the SAFE Investment Company (China), the Hong Kong branch of China's sovereign wealth fund. SAFE is an acronym for the State Administration of Foreign Exchange. The Hong Kong subsidiary was opened in 1997 with $20 billion in capital and functions as a private company, though officials from China's SAFE department serve on its Board of Directors. The fund is primarily set aside as a foreign currency reserve.

As of May 2026, China holds approximately $3.4 trillion in foreign currency reserves. The SAFE Investment Company can invest in a wide range of instruments, including foreign and domestic equities and fixed income securities. Its chief objectives are to gain investment returns, increase diversification of holdings, and reduce China's exposure to fluctuations in the value of the U.S. dollar. Since 1997, all SAFE operations have been undertaken by the People's Bank of China (PBoC).

The article also discusses sovereign wealth funds more broadly, noting that most developed nations have SWFs funded by accumulated central bank reserves from budget and trade surpluses. It provides context with examples like the UAE, which uses its SWF to diversify away from oil dependence, and mentions the Alaska Permanent Fund ($86 billion) and Texas Permanent School Fund ($60.6 billion) in the United States. The article cites the Sovereign Wealth Fund Institute's May 2025 rankings of top SWFs by assets under management. Sources referenced include Rhys Jenkins' book "How China is Reshaping the Global Economy" (Oxford University Press, 2018), Trading Economics, and the Sovereign Wealth Fund Institute.

[Cao Li](/author/cao-li)and[Aileen Chuang](/author/aileen-chuang)

Halfway up a 37-storey tower overlooking Hong Kong’s Victoria Harbour, within walking distance from the People’s Liberation Army barracks and the classy Hong Kong Club, sits an unassuming office of a fund manager with an outsize role in the global financial markets.

The spartan office, with two tiny flags of China and Hong Kong providing the only splashes of warmth in a grey, cold ambience, belongs to SAFE Investment Company, the custodian of a third of China’s [US$3.227 trillion](https://www.scmp.com/economy/china-economy/article/3285834/china-searches-safe-havens-amid-us-debt-woes-dollar-weaponisation?module=inline&pgtype=article?module=inline&pgtype=article) foreign exchange reserves, according to official records.

Established a month before Hong Kong’s formal return to China’s sovereignty in 1997, the unit was the first of [four so-called “golden flowers”](https://www.scmp.com/business/banking-finance/article/3302433/chinas-4-golden-flowers-how-beijing-invests-its-us32-trillion-reserves?module=inline&pgtype=article) – Hua’an, Huaxin, Hua’ou and Huamei – set up by the State Administration of Foreign Exchanges (SAFE) to diversify its reserves and maximise returns. Hua’an, the Chinese name of its Hong Kong unit, signifies the wish for the nation’s security.

Its existence was alluded to in mid-January, a week before Donald Trump’s formal return to the White House, when Pan Gongsheng, governor of the [People’s Bank of China](https://www.scmp.com/topics/peoples-bank-china?module=inline&pgtype=article) (PBOC), said the central bank would [“significantly increase”](https://www.scmp.com/business/banking-finance/article/3294495/china-unveils-us13-billion-trade-finance-facility-boost-yuan-hub-hong-kong?module=inline&pgtype=article) the allocation of the nation’s reserves [to Hong Kong](https://www.scmp.com/opinion/comment/article/3294607/shot-arm-hong-kong-key-financial-facilitator?module=inline&pgtype=article).

![SAFE investment Company at the AIA Central tower in Hong Kong on March 6, 2025. Photo: Jonathan Wong](https://img.i-scmp.com/cdn-cgi/image/fit=contain,width=1024,format=auto/sites/default/files/d8/images/canvas/2025/03/14/6ea117c4-c83d-4475-aed4-3d83566e3151_a56d9be1.jpg "SAFE investment Company at the AIA Central tower in Hong Kong on March 6, 2025. Photo: Jonathan Wong")

SAFE investment Company at the AIA Central tower in Hong Kong on March 6, 2025. Photo: Jonathan Wong

That statement provoked more questions than answers, with analysts, academics and lawmakers quizzing officials on the amount, rationale, strategy and timing behind that financial support.

Xia Chun, the chief economist at SSC Research Institute in Hong Kong, estimates that about 16 per cent of China’s foreign exchange reserves are kept in Hong Kong. A “substantial increase”, as hinted by PBOC, could mean almost tripling that allocation over the long run, he said.

The SAFE Investment Company is the investment arm of China’s State Administration of Foreign Exchange, managing an estimated $1 trillion or more in international assets. As a vehicle for investing a portion of China’s massive foreign exchange reserves (over $3 trillion in total), SAFE Investment Company is one of the largest sovereign investment entities in the world.

Registered in Hong Kong, the SAFE Investment Company operates alongside China Investment Corporation (CIC) as one of China’s two primary sovereign investment vehicles. While CIC is the more publicly visible entity with a formal [sovereign wealth fund](/glossary/sovereign-wealth-fund) structure, SAFE Investment Company manages assets that may equal or exceed CIC’s portfolio.

## Investment Strategy

SAFE Investment Company maintains a globally diversified portfolio spanning public equities, sovereign and corporate bonds, real estate, and alternative investments. The entity’s investment mandate is rooted in the preservation and growth of China’s foreign exchange reserves, with a focus on international purchasing power and long-term real returns.

In public equities, SAFE Investment Company has been identified through regulatory filings as a significant shareholder in companies listed across Europe, the United Kingdom, Australia, and other markets. Holdings have spanned financial services, energy, utilities, consumer goods, technology, and other sectors. The portfolio appears to be broadly diversified rather than concentrated in specific sectors or themes.

Fixed income investments likely represent a substantial allocation, consistent with the reserve management origins of the entity. These holdings include sovereign bonds from developed markets (particularly U.S. Treasuries), agency securities, and corporate bonds. The fixed income portfolio serves both as a source of income and as a liquidity buffer.

Given the limited public disclosure, the precise [asset allocation](/glossary/asset-allocation) and investment process remain partially opaque. However, the scale of assets and the observable equity holdings suggest a sophisticated, globally diversified investment approach.

## Private Markets Approach

SAFE Investment Company has participated in private markets through multiple channels. Real estate investments have been documented in major global markets, including commercial properties in London, New York, and other gateway cities. These investments have been made both directly and through investment platforms and joint ventures.

[Private equity](/glossary/private-equity) exposure has been built through fund commitments to global GPs and through co-investments and direct transactions. Given the scale of assets under management, even a modest percentage allocation to private equity would represent billions of dollars in commitments.

Infrastructure investments have also been reported, consistent with China’s broader interest in international infrastructure assets and the entity’s long-term investment horizon. Energy, transportation, and utilities assets in developed markets align with the fund’s likely return and diversification objectives.

The limited transparency around SAFE Investment Company’s operations makes it difficult to assess the full scope of its private markets program. However, the entity’s enormous asset base, long time horizon, and sophisticated investment capabilities position it as a significant participant in global private markets, even if its activities are less visible than those of peer sovereign wealth funds.

 What is the SAFE Investment Company?

SAFE Investment Company manages an estimated $1 trillion or more in diversified international investments, making it one of the largest sovereign investment vehicles in the world.  How does SAFE Investment Company invest?

SAFE Investment Company invests across public equities, fixed income, real estate, private equity, and other asset classes in international markets. The entity has been identified as a significant shareholder in publicly listed companies across Europe, the UK, and other markets. Its investment approach appears to prioritize diversification, long-term returns, and preserving the purchasing power of China's foreign exchange reserves.

 How transparent is SAFE Investment Company?

SAFE Investment Company operates with significantly less transparency than most sovereign wealth funds. It does not publish annual reports, portfolio details, or investment returns. Its holdings are identified primarily through regulatory filings in countries that require disclosure of significant shareholdings. --- SOURCE 1: World Investment Report 2026 ---
URL: https://unctad.org/system/files/official-document/wir2026_en.pdf

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This webpage presents the United Nations Conference on Trade and Development (UNCTAD) World Investment Report 2026, titled "International Investment in a Turbulent Era," published in Geneva in 2026 (UNCTAD/WIR/2026, ISBN: 978-92-1-154998-0).

KEY HEADLINE FINDINGS:
- Global foreign direct investment (FDI) rose by 6% to $1.6 trillion in 2025, following two consecutive years of decline, but growth remains fragile and uneven. Excluding conduit flows through major European financial centres, global FDI increased 4%.
- Inflows rose 11% in developed economies (to $723 billion) but only 2% in developing economies (to just over $901 billion).
- Investment activity is increasingly concentrated in a few capital- and technology-intensive sectors—data centres, semiconductors, oil and gas, clean energy, and critical minerals. These strategic sectors now represent almost half of all announced greenfield projects in 2025. Most other sectors, including renewable energy and manufacturing, registered significant declines.
- FDI in least developed countries (LDCs) rose 21% but remained highly concentrated in a small number of resource-rich economies. LDCs and lower-middle-income countries attract barely 10% of strategic sector projects, versus more than 20% in other industries.
- The top 20 recipients accounted for more than 80% of global FDI inflows. The United States remained the largest recipient ($277 billion), followed by Singapore, Hong Kong (China), and China. Developing economies represent half of the top 20.
- Global FDI outflows: the US remained largest source ($263 billion), followed by Japan ($186 billion) and China ($174 billion). Developing Asia accounts for one third of global outflows. Gulf Cooperation Council economies are increasingly prominent outward investors, including through sovereign wealth funds.
- The global investor landscape has become more diverse: more than a quarter of the top 100 MNEs are State-owned, and private equity international acquisitions account for about 20% of global M&As.
- Cross-border M&A values declined 7%. Greenfield project values remained near 2024 levels but were driven mainly by megaprojects. International project finance rose only 3%, remaining about 25% below its 2021 peak.
- FDI remains the largest source of external finance for developing economies (about 50% of total), ahead of remittances, ODA, and portfolio flows.

POLICY AND GOVERNANCE CONTEXT:
- Governments are becoming increasingly active in shaping investment flows, with new investment policy measures reaching a record high in 2025—strongly supporting strategic sectors, industrial upgrading, digital transformation, and green transition.
- The report emphasizes that investment is shifting from following cost and efficiency (where developing countries competed) to following strategic calculation, industrial policy, subsidies, economic security, and technological advantage—a logic that rewards deep pockets and established ecosystems.
- New opportunities exist for developing economies in supply-chain reconfiguration: alternative manufacturing locations, processing hubs for critical minerals, and gateways to regional markets.
- At UNCTAD 16 in October 2025, 170 countries adopted the Geneva Consensus, renewing commitment to an open, equitable, and development-oriented investment environment.
- The report references the Sevilla Commitment's global call to address limited access to finance for developing countries.

OUTLOOK (2026):
- Global FDI prospects remain uncertain with significant downside risks from trade policy uncertainty, geopolitical tensions (including the 2026 Middle East conflict), and conflicts. The geopolitical risk index rose sharply to 230.8 in the 2026 forecast from 145.1, while energy prices are forecast to rise significantly. However, moderating interest rates and foreign exchange volatility provide some positive signals.

The report was prepared by an UNCTAD team led by Nan Li Collins, Director of the Division on Investment and Enterprise, with a preface by UN Secretary-General António Guterres and foreword by UNCTAD Acting Secretary-General Pedro Manuel Moreno. The report contains three main chapters covering international investment trends, investment policy trends, and the theme chapter on "International investment in a turbulent era: Trends and policy response."
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"In 2025, global foreign direct investment rose by 6 per cent to reach $1.6 trillion. But this growth masks underlying fragility and disparities across countries, regions and sectors." - António Guterres, UN Secretary-General
</key_excerpts>
