--- SOURCE 16: Expenditure on research and development (R&D) in Germany has grown considerably since 2005 | KfW ---
URL: https://www.kfw.de/About-KfW/Newsroom/Latest-News/Pressemitteilungen-Details_729344.html

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This KfW press release (2022-10-05) reports on a ZEW Mannheim study analyzing Germany's research and development (R&D) growth. Real R&D expenditure grew at an average of 3.4% per annum from 2005 to 2019, up from 1.4% per annum between 1991 and 2005. Germany's R&D-to-GDP ratio rose from 2.1% in 1994 to 3.17% in 2019, placing Germany sixth among comparison countries, on par with the US and ahead of China and similar-sized European countries. German R&D growth surpassed Japan (0.7%), France (1.6%), and the UK (2.2%), but lagged China (13.0%), South Korea (8.0%), and Israel (6.0%). The positive trend is attributed to a broad realignment of research policy from 2006 and economic upswing; Germany targets 3.5% of GDP by 2025 (EU target: 3.0%).

Key findings: (1) The private sector funded 64% of German R&D in 2019 (up from 62% in 1991), while public share dropped from 36% to 28%; comparison countries saw a steeper shift (private 59%→69%, public 35%→21%). (2) Private R&D is concentrated in automotive (37.3%), electronics/measuring/optics (18.5%), mechanical engineering (10.3%), pharmaceuticals (6.7%), and chemicals (5.9%), totaling ~79%; ICT services are not a German R&D priority, and sectoral concentration has increased since 2009 unlike in comparison countries. (3) Large enterprises (500+ employees) account for 88% of R&D expenditure (2018), second only to Japan (90%). (4) Germany's overall private sector R&D intensity is below what its economic structure suggests; raising below-average sectors to comparison-country averages could increase private R&D expenditure by nearly 30%.

KfW Chief Economist Dr Fritzi Köhler-Geib stressed the importance of continuing the Federal Government's high-tech strategy, providing R&D incentives for SMEs, integrating R&D and digitalization into support schemes, and addressing the skilled worker shortage through expanded education, training, and skilled migration policy.
</summary>

--- SOURCE 2: Trends in World Military Expenditure, 2025 ---
URL: https://www.sipri.org/sites/default/files/2026-04/2604_milex_2025.pdf

SUMMARY:
<summary>
The SIPRI Fact Sheet (April 2026) reports that world military expenditure rose by 2.9 per cent in real terms to $2,887 billion in 2025, marking the 11th consecutive year of growth and the highest level ever recorded by SIPRI. Total military expenditure accounted for 2.5 per cent of global GDP. The five biggest spenders—the United States ($954 billion), China ($336 billion), Russia ($190 billion), Germany ($114 billion), and India ($92.1 billion)—accounted for 58 per cent of world military spending.

Key trends: The USA's military spending fell by 7.5 per cent to $954 billion, mainly due to the end of supplemental appropriations for financial military assistance to Ukraine and Israel. China's spending rose by 7.4 per cent (its 31st consecutive year of growth), Russia increased spending by 5.9 per cent (7.5 per cent of GDP), and Ukraine's spending rose by 20 per cent to $84.1 billion (40 per cent of GDP). Military expenditure grew in all world regions except the Americas. European spending rose by 14 per cent to $864 billion, and Asian/Oceanian spending rose by 8.1 per cent to $681 billion.

Regional highlights: NATO members (32) spent $1,581 billion (55 per cent of global spending), with European NATO members spending $559 billion; 23 of the 32 NATO members met the 2.0 per cent GDP target. In June 2025, NATO agreed to raise its spending target to 5.0 per cent of GDP by 2035, prompting concerns about "creative accounting" and blurred definitions of military-related spending. Germany's spending exceeded 2.0 per cent of GDP for the first time since 1990. Spain recorded the largest increase among top spenders (up by 50 per cent). Algeria's military burden (8.8 per cent of GDP) was the second largest globally after Ukraine.

Notable country developments: Taiwan's military spending rose by 14 per cent (largest increase since 1988) amid rising tensions in the Taiwan Strait, with a pledge to reach 5.0 per cent of GDP by 2030. Japan reached its highest military burden (1.4 per cent of GDP) since 1958. Ukraine received $52.2 billion in partner support in 2025. The Middle East's spending was roughly flat (+0.1 per cent) at $218 billion, with Israel's spending falling 4.9 per cent following the Gaza ceasefire. The global military burden rose to its highest level since 2009 at 2.5 per cent of GDP, with the Middle East having the highest regional burden (3.8 per cent of GDP).
</summary>

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is the UK Ministry of Defence's Finance and Economics Annual Statistical Bulletin: International Defence 2025, published 4 December 2025. It provides comparative data on UK and international defence spending, covering NATO member nations, global top military spenders, and detailed trends focusing on the UK, USA, France and Germany.

Key findings include: Total NATO military expenditure reached $1,451 billion in 2024, an increase of $127 billion from 2023 (inflation-adjusted)—the largest annual increase since the time series began in 2014. Eighteen NATO countries met the 2% of GDP spending guideline in 2024, with eight new countries meeting it (Czechia, France, Germany, Netherlands, Norway, Romania, Sweden, Turkey). The UK spent 2.33% of GDP on defence (up from 2.25%), meeting the 2% target every year since 2006. The USA remained the largest NATO spender at $935 billion (3.21% of GDP), accounting for 64% of NATO total. Germany's expenditure rose 24% ($18.2 billion increase) to $93.7 billion, overtaking the UK (at $84.2 billion) to become NATO's second-largest spender—the first time since 2014 the UK has not been second. Poland led NATO rankings at 3.79% of GDP and was the only country meeting the new 2035 commitment of 3.5% of GDP agreed at the 2025 NATO Summit in The Hague.

On equipment spending, the UK spent 33.36% of its defence budget on equipment, one of 28 countries meeting NATO's 20% equipment guideline (only Belgium, Canada and Portugal failed). --- SOURCE 12: Federal R&D funding ---
URL: https://emergingtechpolicy.org/policy-levers/federal-rd-funding

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This webpage is a comprehensive policy guide on US Federal R&D funding, explaining how and why the government invests in scientific and technological research. Federal R&D is described as one of the strongest policy tools for shaping national innovation, with the US government spending roughly $200 billion annually (approximately $210 billion in FY2024) across more than 30 federal agencies and hundreds of thousands of researchers.

**Reasons for government R&D investment include:**
1. Addressing market failures (private sector underinvests in basic/high-risk research)
2. De-risking emerging technologies (bridging the "valley of death" between discovery and commercialization)
3. Advancing national priorities (defense, pandemic preparedness, energy security)
4. Steering technology toward public values (safety, privacy, openness)
5. Responding to crises (e.g., Operation Warp Speed, which invested $18 billion to deliver 300 million vaccine doses in under a year)
6. Workforce development

**Funding categories span:** Basic research, applied research, development, and commercialization/technology transition. The Department of War (DOW) organizes its R&D through Budget Activity 6 (RDT&E), which is divided into eight activity codes (6.1–6.8) commonly referenced in defense circles.

**Key agencies:** DOW and HHS (primarily NIH) account for ~75% of total federal R&D spending, with the remaining 25% going to DOE, NASA, and NSF. Federal R&D has risen from about $90 billion in 1976 to ~$190 billion in 2023 (constant 2022 dollars), though it has declined from nearly 12% of the federal budget in the 1960s to under 3% today.

**Funding models:** Traditional programs (peer-reviewed grants, dominant at NIH/NSF), ARPA-style programs ("high-risk, high-reward" with hands-on program managers, e.g., DARPA, IARPA, ARPA-E, ARPA-H), translation/commercialization programs (e.g., BARDA, Defense Innovation Unit, In-Q-Tel), and moonshot programs (e.g., Cancer Moonshot, moon landing).

**Funding mechanisms include:** Grants, contracts, cooperative agreements, prize competitions, advance market commitments, resource provision, loans/loan guarantees, Other Transaction Authorities (OTAs), and milestone-based funding.

**Emerging technology impact:** Many defining technologies began as federal R&D initiatives, including the Internet (ARPANET), GPS, smartphone components (multi-touch screens, microprocessors, lithium-ion batteries, voice assistants), AI/neural networks, Google's search algorithm (PageRank), self-driving cars (DARPA Grand Challenges), semiconductors, and the Human Genome Project. Over 70% of US Nobel Laureates were funded by NSF during their careers.

**Recent policy timeline highlights:**
- Nov 2025: White House OSTP issues RFI on "Accelerating the American Scientific Enterprise"
- Sep 2025: NSF solicits proposals for a $35M NAIRR operations center
- Jun 2025: Senate adds $150M for DOE AI R&D; Trump FY2026 budget proposes significant R&D cuts (65% cut to NSF CISE, 43% to TIP)
- Oct 2023: Biden Executive Order launches National AI Research Resource (NAIRR) pilot
- Aug 2022: CHIPS and Science Act provides $36B new NSF funding including $20B for TIP directorate
- Mar 2022: ARPA-H established with $1B
- Jan 2021: National AI Initiative Act formalizes coordinated national AI R&D strategy
- Sep 2018: DARPA launches AI Next campaign with $2B+ commitment
- May 2020: Operation Warp Speed launched

**Career considerations:** Working in R&D funding offers upstream influence on emerging technologies, incentives-based policy, long-term bet support, and leveraged impact. Program managers can oversee hundreds of millions in funding; ARPA PMs typically lead 2-5 programs with budgets of $20-80M each. Tradeoffs include high risk of failure, slow feedback loops (~20-year average lag from funding to application), limited downstream control, bureaucratic complexity, low political salience, and institutional bottlenecks.

**Funding process stages:** (1) Budget and policy direction setting (White House via OMB/OSTP, plus Congress's authorization and appropriations processes), (2) Grant-making and program execution, (3) Conducting the actual R&D, (4) Coordination (OSTP, NSTC, interagency working groups), (5) Oversight (Congress, OMB, GAO). In FY2025, seven agencies received ~97% of total federal R&D funding, led by DOW at 46%.

**Role and Value of Federal S&T R&D:**
- In FY 2019, the U.S. spent more than $656 billion on R&D (3.06% of GDP)
- More than two-thirds of U.S. R&D is funded by private corporations; approximately 20% is federally funded
- Industry accounts for 85% of U.S. development total, while federal spending favors basic and applied research
- Since the mid-1990s, government spending on basic research has declined or stagnated as a share of GDP
- The COVID-19 pandemic reinforced the need for robust R&D infrastructure

**U.S. Federal Budget Process for S&T R&D:**
- Total annual federal budget exceeds $4.8 trillion; discretionary spending (31% of budget in FY 2021) contains the entire federal R&D budget
- The process has four phases spanning three years: internal agency planning, White House OMB review, congressional appropriation, and budget implementation
- Federal R&D has accounted for approximately 12% of the total discretionary budget since the late 1970s
- Since the early 2000s, almost half of nondefense R&D spending has focused on health/biomedical research
- OSTP has advisory-only authority; there is no central mechanism to coordinate annual R&D budgets
- The FY 2019 budget cycle saw a 35-day government shutdown (Dec 22, 2018 – Jan 25, 2019) due to appropriation failures

**R&D Funding During the Trump Administration:**
- Trump's four annual budget requests called for R&D cuts (e.g., FY 2020 requested 8% reduction from ~$164B to $151B)
- Congress largely ignored these proposals and raised discretionary budget caps
- Final 2021 proposal called for 8.4% ($13.2 billion) cuts, but Congress appropriated modest increases: 3% for NIH, 2.5% for NSF, 0.4% for DOE Office of Science
- Five of six COVID-19 emergency relief bills provided R&D funding; BARDA and CDC received $25B+ each in stimulus funding; NIH received $5B; NSF received $676M

**Future of Federal R&D Funding:**
- Biden's FY 2022 budget request recommended a 9% overall increase to federal R&D, including 10% for basic research and 14% for applied research
- Proposal favored 21% increase to NIH and 20% boost to NSF, while cutting DOD basic/applied research by 11% and 16%
- Two competing bills: the Endless Frontier Act (passed by Senate June 8, 2021 as part of USICA, with $52B for semiconductor manufacturing, $29B for NSF technology directorate) and the NSF for the Future Act (House, would roughly double NSF budget to $18.3B by FY 2026)
- Challenges include record federal deficit spending and uncertain discretionary budget caps

**Conclusion:**
The report emphasizes that scientists must engage in public outreach and "civic science" to build public trust and support for federal R&D funding, particularly as Congress deliberates on research, innovation, and STEM education policy.

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is a CSIS ("CSIS Charts") analysis article by Chris Borges, published July 23, 2025, arguing that proposed cuts to federal R&D funding undermine U.S. national security and long-term economic growth.

Key points:
- The President's FY 2026 budget proposal (released May 2025) requests a 22% cut to federal R&D funding, including a 36% decrease to non-defense R&D funding.
- The National Science Foundation (NSF) faces the steepest cuts at 56%, followed by the National Institutes of Health (NIH) at 43% and the Department of Energy (DOE) at 31%. The Department of Defense's R&D budget faces a 6% cut, which would be offset by provisions in the recently passed budget reconciliation bill.
- The article argues that increasing overall defense spending while cutting non-defense R&D overlooks the fundamental connection between R&D and national security. Federally funded R&D provides considerable economic benefits and lays the groundwork for transformative future industries (from wireless communications and supercomputers to biothreat countermeasures and nuclear security).
- Ultimately, Congress holds responsibility for these funding decisions. Some congressional committees are proposing less severe cuts, while others are pushing back on cuts altogether, recognizing the U.S. R&D enterprise as a strategic advantage. As other nations increase their R&D funding amid global competition for critical technologies, the article concludes now is not the time for the U.S. to end its strategic commitment to advancing science.

The author, Chris Borges, is a Fellow and Senior Program Manager in the Economic Security and Technology Department. A related item, "Innovation Lightbulb: Visualizing Proposed Cuts to Federal R&D Funding" (newsletter, July 17, 2025), is linked. The page also lists upcoming CSIS events (August 24 – September 1, 2026) and extensive program/region/topic navigation menus.

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This Eurostat article presents preliminary data (extracted November 2025) on research and development (R&D) expenditure within the European Union for 2024.

**Headline figures:**
- In 2024, EU R&D expenditure reached €403 billion, with R&D intensity (GERD as % of GDP) at 2.24%, slightly down from 2.26% in 2023 but up from 2.09% in 2014.
- R&D expenditure per inhabitant was €897 in 2024 (up 3.2% from €869 in 2023 and up 59.6% from €562 in 2014).
- EU R&D intensity remained well below Japan (3.44%, 2023), the United States (3.45%, 2023), and South Korea (4.96%, 2023); China stood at 2.58% in 2023.

**Country rankings (2024):**
- Highest R&D intensity: Sweden (3.57%), Belgium (3.36%), Austria (3.26%), Finland (3.22%), Germany (3.13%), Denmark (3.01%).
- Lowest R&D intensities: Romania (0.46%), Malta (0.51%), Cyprus (0.65%), Bulgaria (0.77%), Latvia (0.92%), Slovakia (0.98%), Luxembourg (0.99%).
- Biggest intensity increases 2014-2024: Belgium (+1.00 pp), Greece (+0.69 pp), Estonia and Croatia (both +0.58 pp); biggest decreases in Slovenia and Luxembourg (both -0.23 pp).

**Sector of performance (EU, 2014-2024):**
- Business enterprise sector rose from 1.34% of GDP to 1.49% (+11.19%), remaining the dominant performer.
- Higher education sector stable at 0.48%; Government sector fell slightly from 0.26% to 0.24%; Private non-profit rose from 0.01% to 0.03%.
- Business enterprise R&D reached 3.93% of GDP in South Korea (2023), 2.72% in Japan, 2.70% in the US, and 2.23% in Switzerland.

**Source of funds (2023):**
- Business enterprises funded 56.7% of total EU R&D; government 30.1%; Rest of the world 10.9%; Higher education 1.3%.
- Business funding shares were much higher in China (79.3%), Japan (78.0%), South Korea (76.1%), and the US (69.6%).
- Government funding was highest in Luxembourg (50.0%), Greece (41.6%), and Spain (38.3%); Rest of the world funding was high in Ireland (42.4%) and Bulgaria (41.9%).

**Context:** The article notes the EU's target of 3% R&D investment (set by the EU Council) and that the EU's R&D funding structure differs from key competitors. Data follow the OECD Frascati Manual 2015 and Commission Implementing Regulation (EU) No 1197/2020. --- SOURCE 19: Global Innovation Index 2025 - Global Innovation Tracker ---
URL: https://www.wipo.int/web-publications/global-innovation-index-2025/en/global-innovation-tracker.html

SUMMARY:
<summary>
The Global Innovation Index (GII) 2025 Tracker, published by WIPO, analyzes global innovation performance across four stages of the innovation cycle: science and innovation investment, technological progress, technology adoption, and socioeconomic impact. The overall picture for 2024 shows uneven but across-the-board growth, with only three indicators in decline (VC deal counts, drug launches, and global warming) — an improvement over the GII 2024 (five declining indicators) and GII 2023 (seven).

**Key Findings by Stage:**

**1. Science and Innovation Investment**
- Science and innovation investment showed only partial, uneven recovery in 2024 after a sharp 2023 downturn. Only scientific publications were above trend; R&D, VC, and patents fell below.
- Global R&D growth slowed to 2.9% in 2024, projected to fall to 2.3% in 2025 — the weakest expansion in over a decade. Top firms' R&D spending rose only 3% nominally (below decade average of 8%). Software and ICT services more than doubled 2018 R&D by 2024, while automotive, construction, and consumer goods saw declining R&D.
- Scientific publications rose 5.6% in 2024 to nearly 2 million (a new record), driven by China (14% increase, 26% global share) and India (7.7% growth).
- Corporate R&D reached nearly USD 1.3 trillion (historic high) but with slowest nominal growth since 2010; R&D intensity rose to 5.5%.
- VC deal values rose 7.7% to USD 384 billion (still well below 2021's USD 750 billion peak), but deal counts fell 4.4% to ~43,000 — third consecutive year of decline. VC is reconcentrating in the US (72% share by 2025) and AI/software sectors (software hit 50% of VC funding in 2025). AI megadeals (OpenAI, Anthropic, xAI, Databricks, Waymo) totaled ~USD 40 billion in 2024.
- International patent filings rose a modest 0.5% to 273,900 (PCT), recovering from 2023's 1.9% decline, but below the 2.5% decade average. China remained top filer; Korea grew 7.1% (27-year streak); US, Japan, and Germany declined.

**2. Technological Progress**
- Supercomputer efficiency of top 50 "greenest" supercomputers rose 65% (well above 35% decade rate), but overall supercomputer performance growth slowed (from 85%/year in 2003–2013 to 37%/year in 2013–2024).
- Microchip transistor count grew 37% (slightly below Moore's Law's 42%, but 10-year average aligns at 42%).
- Solar PV costs fell 90% since 2010 (now 56% cheaper than fossil fuels); onshore wind down 67% cheaper; offshore wind 25% lower.
- Lithium-ion battery prices fell 20% to a record low of USD 115/kWh in 2024 (85% drop since 2013, while lithium production rose 550%).
- Genome sequencing costs declined 11.1% annually (slower than the 21.5% long-term rate); cost dropped from ~USD 100 million in 2001 to just over USD 500 in 2023. Chinese firms may bring costs to USD 10/genome within 3 years.
- Drug launches fell ~19% to 65 new drugs in 2024 (vs. 80 in 2023, peak of 93 in 2021); median development timeline was 14 years.

**3. Technology Adoption**
- Global EV stock grew 45% in 2024 (18 million units), but this was below the 55% decade rate. Western markets slowed sharply (France: 49%→11%; US: 59%→35%; Germany: 34%→24%), while China held at 55% and emerging economies (Russia, Vietnam, India, Türkiye, Brazil) exceeded 100% growth. As of 2025, 4.5 per 100 cars are electric.
- Industrial robots grew just under 10% (down 5+ percentage points from earlier years); China holds 41% of global stock.
- 5G reached half the global population by 2024, but 84% of high-income populations had access vs. just 4% in low-income economies.
- High-speed rail (new indicator) expanded 5% in 2023 (below 9% decade rate); China accounts for ~70% of global high-speed rail (adding ~45,400 km since 2008).
- Safe sanitation reached 58% of global population (up from 47% in 2014); cancer radiotherapy equipment (LINACs) grew 1.3% per capita, with persistent divides in lower-income countries.

**4. Socioeconomic Impact**
- Labor productivity rose 2.5% (near the 2.2% decade average), reaching ~USD 55,000 PPP per worker. Fastest growth in China (5.9%), Vietnam (5.4%), and Ethiopia (5%).
- Extreme poverty fell 0.6% to 817 million people (under half of 20 years ago). South Asia cut poverty by 84% and East Asia/Pacific by 93%, but Eastern/Southern Africa saw poverty rise 50%.
- Life expectancy rose 0.7% in 2023 to 73 years (up from 63 in 1988), a record high, though healthy life expectancy growth (0.1%/year) lags life expectancy growth (0.3%/year).
- Global temperatures hit a record 1.29°C above the 1951–1980 baseline in 2024, near the 1.5–2°C Paris Agreement limits, following a 15-month streak of record monthly temperatures. CO2 emissions rose 0.8% (below the 1.7% average since 1994), with most major emitters declining except India (+4.6%).

**Conclusion:** Innovation demonstrated overall resilience in 2024 with all four stages recording progress, though gains were uneven and sector-specific, with persistent slowdowns in R&D growth, VC contraction, and climate concerns.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
Only three indicators were in decline in GII 2025: venture capital (VC) deal counts, drug launches and global warming. Global R&D growth continued to slow – down to 2.9 percent in 2024 and projected to fall further to 2.3 percent in 2025 – marking the weakest expansion in over a decade. In 2024, VC deal values rose by 7.7 percent... the number of VC deals continued to decline in 2024, falling by 4.4 percent to around 43,000 deals. Global temperatures in 2024 reached 1.29°C above the 20th-century baseline (1951–1980)... surpassing the record set in 2023.
</key_excerpts>

--- SOURCE 20: Tracking R&D expenditure across G20 nations ---
URL: https://www.b20globalinstitute.org/tracking_r&D_expenditure_across_G20_nations

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This issue brief, part of the "Digital Transformation, Advanced Technologies, and Cyber Security" thematic area, tracks research and development (R&D) expenditure across G20 nations. Globally, countries spend an average of 2.62% of national GDP on R&D, while G20 nations average 3.03%. Within the G20, South Korea has the highest R&D expenditure as a percentage of GDP at 4.93%, followed by the United States (3.46%), Japan (3.30%), Germany (3.14%), and the United Kingdom (2.91%). Mexico and Indonesia spend the least at 0.27% and 0.28% respectively. Higher per capita GDP nations generally have larger R&D expenditure ratios.

Key details by nation include:
- Republic of Korea: KRW 24.8 trillion R&D budget for 2025 (up from KRW 21.9 trillion in 2024), focused on AI, semiconductors, advanced biotechnology, and quantum technology, plus digital bio infrastructure, OLED/iLED, quantum computing, KRW 1 trillion for KASA (moon landing by 2032, Mars by 2045), and defence R&D (K-9 artillery, KM-SAM).
- United States: Approximately USD 885.6 billion in R&D as of 2022, with the commercial sector contributing USD 693 billion (78%), followed by higher education (USD 91.4 billion) and federal government (USD 73.3 billion). Five industries (information/software, chemicals, computer/electronics, professional/technical services, transportation equipment) contribute ~79% of R&D funding.
- Japan: Approximately JPY 20.7 trillion in R&D in 2022 (up 4.9% year-over-year), with funding directed at AI (JPY 272.5 billion), biotechnology (JPY 385 billion), and quantum technology (JPY 132.2 billion). Japan employs ~910,400 R&D workers; businesses contribute 73.1% (JPY 15.13 trillion), universities 18.6% (JPY 3.84 trillion).
- Germany: Record EUR 132 billion R&D expenditure in 2023, employing ~785,000 individuals; commercial sector contributes 67%, higher education 18%, government ~15%. Germany is Europe's largest R&D spender at ~36% of European R&D spending.
- United Kingdom: Approximately GBP 70.2 billion R&D expenditure in 2022 (up GBP 4.4 billion); commercial sector contributes 71% (GBP 49.9 billion), higher education 23% (GBP 16.3 billion), government 5% (GBP 3.6 billion), non-profit 1% (GBP 0.9 billion).

The brief also covers B20 initiatives to promote R&D. The B20 India Task Force on Tech, Innovation, and R&D recommended: promoting a Virtual Digital Lab & Library for cross-collaboration; institutionalizing a Collaboration Forum for Deep and Emerging Tech Advancement; creating a Collaboration Body for technology-driven cancer research; and developing a program providing opportunities for women in STEM and funding for women-led startups. The B20 Brazil Task Force on Digital Transformation called for educational programs and digital learning resources to close digital skill gaps. The brief concludes that G20 and B20 should improve access to funding and develop multilateral initiatives to improve global R&D investment.
</summary>

--- SOURCE 1: Sizing up Welfare States: How do OECD countries compare? ---
URL: https://oecdstatistics.blog/2023/02/02/sizing-up-welfare-states-how-do-oecd-countries-compare

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This blog post from the OECD Statistics (oecdstatistics.blog), published February 2, 2023, analyzes the size and composition of welfare states across OECD countries, based on the latest update of the OECD Social Expenditure Database (SOCX) released on January 26, 2023.

Key findings include:

**Overall trends:** Public social expenditure was less than 10% of GDP in 1960 but has more than doubled to just over 20% of GDP on average across the OECD. Two-thirds of public social spending goes toward pensions and health services.

**Country comparisons (2022):** France and Italy have the highest public social expenditure at over 30% of GDP, while Costa Rica, Ireland, Korea, Mexico, and Türkiye spend less than 15% of GDP. Private social spending averages 3.1% of GDP across the OECD but exceeds 10% of GDP in the Netherlands, Switzerland, and the United States.

**COVID-19 impact:** Public social spending-to-GDP ratios rose from about 20% in 2019 to 23% in 2020 on average (over 80% of the increase driven by higher spending, the rest by GDP decline). Ratios fell nearly as rapidly afterward, declining to an estimated 21% in 2022. Canada (6.9 ppts), Spain (6.5 ppts), and the United States (6 ppts) saw the largest increases between 2019 and 2020. Spending declined in all countries except Korea and Latvia by 2022, with Estonia, Denmark, Finland, Greece, Hungary, Norway, and Sweden falling below their 2019 levels.

**Main spending areas:** Old-age and survivor pensions (7.7% of GDP) and health (5.8% of GDP) are the largest areas of public spending. Greece and Italy spend over 15% of GDP on pensions, while Chile, Iceland, Korea, and Mexico spend around 3%. France, Germany, Japan, and the United States spend over 8% of GDP on health. "Other social spending" (6.5% of GDP) includes disability payments (1.6%), family cash benefits (1.1%), unemployment benefits (0.6%), and non-health social services (2.3%, including Early Childhood Education and Care).

**Tax system influence:** Governments recoup part of social spending through taxes on transfers, an effect largest in Denmark (7.2% of GDP) and smallest in non-European OECD countries. Tax Breaks with a Social Purpose (TBSPs) are largest in the United States at just under 2% of GDP, over half directed to employer contributions to medical insurance. Accounting for both private spending and TBSPs moves the United States from 23rd place in gross public social spending to 2nd place in net total social spending. France ranks first on both measures. However, higher net social spending does not necessarily lead to more equal outcomes, as tax advantages often benefit high-income workers more.

The post was authored by Willem Adema, Pauline Fron, and Maxime Ladaique of the OECD Directorate for Employment, Labour and Social Affairs.
</summary>

URL: https://www.piie.com/publications/working-papers/local-government-spending-solving-mystery-japanese-fiscal-packages

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is a Peterson Institute for International Economics (PIIE) working paper (98-5) by Hiroko Ishii and Erika Wada examining why Japanese fiscal stimulus packages failed to boost economic growth following the 1990 asset-price bubble burst. The Japanese government announced over 65 trillion yen in discretionary fiscal spending from fiscal years 1992-1996, with half going to public works and 20% to tax cuts. Despite these measures, Japanese economic growth remained stagnant (0.9% average annual growth from 1992-1995).

Main findings: Real discretionary fiscal spending on public works was only about 21 trillion yen (two-thirds of the announced 31 trillion), while tax revenues declined by about 33 trillion yen. The key finding is that local governments (not the central government) failed to spend announced discretionary fiscal spending—spending about 10 trillion yen less than planned. The central government spent as announced (about 25 trillion yen), but local governments underspent, including spending 3.7 trillion yen less than their initial budgets.

Methodology: The authors compared initial budgets with actual spending for 1965-1996, using the gap between initial budgets and actual spending to measure real discretionary spending, applied cumulatively for 1992-1996.

The paper identifies the rigid fiscal relationship between central and local governments as the root cause. The central government collects 55% of total government revenue but directs local governments (over 3,000 local bodies including 47 prefectures) to conduct most spending. Local governments must receive Ministry of Home Affairs approval to change tax rates or issue bonds, and the central government can only "request"—not force—local public works spending. In 1996, only 143 of 3,000+ local governments (4.3%) could balance budgets without central aid. Local government debt reached 103 trillion yen by end of FY1996, nearly twice their ordinary tax revenue.

The paper also finds public investment quality is low: regression analysis (1970-1996) shows public capital stock is not relevant in determining private capital productivity (coefficient 0.113, t-value 0.859), implying negligible spillover from public investment. The Economic Planning Agency found the public spending multiplier was only about one in the 1990s.

Recommendations: (1) Create markets for local bonds, (2) create a system to evaluate potential returns and effectiveness of public investment projects, and (3) promote financial independence and accountability of local governments.
</summary>

--- SOURCE 1: Trends in World Military Expenditure, 2025 ---
URL: https://www.sipri.org/sites/default/files/2026-04/2604_milex_2025.pdf

SUMMARY:
<summary>
The SIPRI Fact Sheet (April 2026) reports that world military expenditure rose by 2.9 per cent in real terms to $2,887 billion in 2025, marking the 11th consecutive year of growth and the highest level ever recorded by SIPRI. Total military expenditure accounted for 2.5 per cent of global GDP. The five biggest spenders—the United States ($954 billion), China ($336 billion), Russia ($190 billion), Germany ($114 billion), and India ($92.1 billion)—accounted for 58 per cent of world military spending.

Key trends: The USA's military spending fell by 7.5 per cent to $954 billion, mainly due to the end of supplemental appropriations for financial military assistance to Ukraine and Israel. China's spending rose by 7.4 per cent (its 31st consecutive year of growth), Russia increased spending by 5.9 per cent (7.5 per cent of GDP), and Ukraine's spending rose by 20 per cent to $84.1 billion (40 per cent of GDP). Military expenditure grew in all world regions except the Americas. European spending rose by 14 per cent to $864 billion, and Asian/Oceanian spending rose by 8.1 per cent to $681 billion.

Regional highlights: NATO members (32) spent $1,581 billion (55 per cent of global spending), with European NATO members spending $559 billion; 23 of the 32 NATO members met the 2.0 per cent GDP target. In June 2025, NATO agreed to raise its spending target to 5.0 per cent of GDP by 2035, prompting concerns about "creative accounting" and blurred definitions of military-related spending. Germany's spending exceeded 2.0 per cent of GDP for the first time since 1990. Spain recorded the largest increase among top spenders (up by 50 per cent). Algeria's military burden (8.8 per cent of GDP) was the second largest globally after Ukraine.

Notable country developments: Taiwan's military spending rose by 14 per cent (largest increase since 1988) amid rising tensions in the Taiwan Strait, with a pledge to reach 5.0 per cent of GDP by 2030. Japan reached its highest military burden (1.4 per cent of GDP) since 1958. Ukraine received $52.2 billion in partner support in 2025. The Middle East's spending was roughly flat (+0.1 per cent) at $218 billion, with Israel's spending falling 4.9 per cent following the Gaza ceasefire. The global military burden rose to its highest level since 2009 at 2.5 per cent of GDP, with the Middle East having the highest regional burden (3.8 per cent of GDP).
</summary>

"World military expenditure rose by 2.9 per cent in real terms to reach $2887 billion in 2025, which was the 11th consecutive year of growth... Global spending has gone up by 41 per cent over the past decade (2016–25)."

URL: https://www.gov.uk/government/publications/international-defence-expenditure-2025/finance-and-economics-annual-statistical-bulletin-international-defence-2025

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is the UK Ministry of Defence's Finance and Economics Annual Statistical Bulletin: International Defence 2025, published 4 December 2025. It provides comparative data on UK and international defence spending, covering NATO member nations, global top military spenders, and detailed trends focusing on the UK, USA, France and Germany.

Key findings include: Total NATO military expenditure reached $1,451 billion in 2024, an increase of $127 billion from 2023 (inflation-adjusted)—the largest annual increase since the time series began in 2014. Eighteen NATO countries met the 2% of GDP spending guideline in 2024, with eight new countries meeting it (Czechia, France, Germany, Netherlands, Norway, Romania, Sweden, Turkey). The UK spent 2.33% of GDP on defence (up from 2.25%), meeting the 2% target every year since 2006. The USA remained the largest NATO spender at $935 billion (3.21% of GDP), accounting for 64% of NATO total. Germany's expenditure rose 24% ($18.2 billion increase) to $93.7 billion, overtaking the UK (at $84.2 billion) to become NATO's second-largest spender—the first time since 2014 the UK has not been second. Poland led NATO rankings at 3.79% of GDP and was the only country meeting the new 2035 commitment of 3.5% of GDP agreed at the 2025 NATO Summit in The Hague.

On equipment spending, the UK spent 33.36% of its defence budget on equipment, one of 28 countries meeting NATO's 20% equipment guideline (only Belgium, Canada and Portugal failed). Luxembourg topped with 51%. Czechia rose from 23rd to 5th following its national security strategy, and Denmark moved from bottom to 12th (31%).

Global comparisons using SIPRI and IISS sources: Global military expenditure in 2024 was estimated at $2,718 billion by SIPRI, with NATO members comprising 55%. The USA made up 37% of global spending. Rankings differed between sources—for example, the UK was 5th globally per IISS but 6th per SIPRI (with India between). Germany was 4th in both.

Long-term trends (1980-2024) for the UK, USA, France and Germany show: all four nations now meet NATO's 2% target for the first time; UK spending per capita reached $1,216 in 2024 (highest since 1987); the UK has the lowest military personnel per thousand population since 1980; and spending per service person has increased for all four countries since 2022, with the UK increasing by $105,000 per service person between 2020 and 2024.

The bulletin notes this is not an Official Statistics publication as the data originates from NATO, SIPRI and IISS sources. It also contains a detailed methodology section on data limitations, including definitional differences, currency conversion issues (MER vs PPP), and a glossary of key terms.
</summary>

Total military expenditure of NATO members in 2024 was $1,451 billion, an increase of $127 billion since 2023 when adjusted for inflation, the biggest annual increase since the time series began in 2014. 18 NATO countries met the guideline to spend 2% of GDP on defence in 2024, with an additional eight countries meeting the guideline compared to the previous year (Czechia, France, Germany, Netherlands, Norway, Romania, Sweden and Turkey). The UK spent 2.33% of national GDP on defence in 2024, meeting NATO's 2% target every year since its introduction in 2006. Germany's defence expenditure rose by 24% in 2024, an additional $18.2 billion, overtaking the UK to become the second highest spender in NATO behind the USA. The UK was the 5th largest global defence spender in 2024 according to IISS, and 6th according to SIPRI.

--- SOURCE 3: Military spending as a share of GDP | Our World in Data ---
URL: https://ourworldindata.org/grapher/military-spending-as-a-share-of-gdp-sipri

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This webpage from Our World in Data presents data on "Military spending as a share of GDP," sourced from the Stockholm International Peace Research Institute (SIPRI) Military Expenditure Database. The indicator measures total military expenditure divided by gross domestic product, expressed as a percentage.

**Key indicator details:**
- Date range: 1949–2025
- Unit: % of GDP
- Last updated: April 27, 2026; next expected update: April 2027
- Source: SIPRI (2026), with minor processing by Our World in Data

**What the data includes (per SIPRI definition):**
- Military and civil personnel, operations and maintenance, procurement, military research and development (R&D), infrastructure (including military bases), and military aid
- Armed forces (including peacekeeping forces), defence ministries, paramilitary forces (when trained and equipped for military operations), and military space activities
- Personnel expenditure covers salaries, retirement pensions of military personnel, and social services

**What is excluded:** Civil defense and current expenditures on previous military activities (veterans' benefits, demobilization, conversion, and weapon destruction).

**Data methodology notes:**
- SIPRI data is based on open sources only
- Data availability varies by country, but most independent countries have data from at least the late 1950s
- No estimates for total world military expenditure exist before 1988 due to lack of data for the Soviet Union
- Figures are available in constant (2024) US dollars, current US dollars, as share of GDP, per capita, and as share of government expenditure
- SIPRI prioritizes uniform definitions over time for each country rather than adjusting single years to a common definition, so data is best suited for comparisons over time rather than close comparison between individual countries
- Database DOI: https://doi.org/10.55163/CQGC9685

**Related research:** The page links to "Long-run trends in military spending and personnel: four key facts from new data" by Esteban Ortiz-Ospina.

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is the landing page for the SIPRI (Stockholm International Peace Research Institute) Military Expenditure Database. The database provides consistent time series on military spending for countries covering the period 1949–2025 and is updated annually. Data is sourced exclusively from open sources.

Key details about the data:

--- SOURCE 6: Japan’s Cabinet OKs record defense budget that aims to deter China ---
URL: https://www.defensenews.com/global/asia-pacific/2025/12/26/japans-cabinet-oks-record-defense-budget-that-aims-to-deter-china

SUMMARY:
<summary>
Japan's Cabinet approved a record defense budget exceeding 9 trillion yen ($58 billion) for fiscal year 2026 (beginning April), a 9.4% increase from 2025. This marks the fourth year of Japan's five-year program to double annual arms spending to 2% of GDP. Defense Minister Shinjiro Koizumi described it as "the minimum needed" as Japan faces its "severest and most complex security environment in the postwar era."

The budget focuses on strengthening Japan's strike-back capability and coastal defense amid rising tensions with China. Key allocations include: over 970 billion yen ($6.2 billion) for "standoff" missile capability, including a 177 billion-yen ($1.13 billion) purchase of domestically developed Type-12 surface-to-ship missiles (range ~1,000 km/620 miles); 100 billion yen ($640 million) for a "SHIELD" unmanned drone system for coastal surveillance and defense (planned for March 2028, initially relying on imports possibly from Turkey or Israel); and over 160 billion yen ($1 billion) for joint development of a next-generation fighter jet with Britain and Italy (deployment in 2035), plus R&D for AI-operated drones.

Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi's government pledged to achieve the 2% GDP defense target by March, two years earlier than planned, under U.S. pressure. Tensions with China escalated following Takaichi's November remarks about potential Japanese military involvement if China acted against Taiwan. China's Foreign Ministry spokesperson Lin Jian accused Japan of "deviating from the path of peaceful development" and moving "in a dangerous direction." The Defense Ministry will open a new office to study China's Pacific operations after two Chinese aircraft carriers were spotted near Iwo Jima in June.

Japan is also strengthening its defense industry through joint development and foreign sales, with Australia selecting Mitsubishi Heavy Industries to upgrade the Mogami-class frigate. The budget requires parliamentary approval by March as part of a 122.3 trillion yen ($784 billion) national budget bill. The five-year buildup would make Japan the world's third-largest defense spender after the U.S. and China. Funding will come from corporate, tobacco, and (from 2027) income tax increases, though future growth prospects at higher GDP percentages remain unclear.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"It is the minimum needed as Japan faces the severest and most complex security environment in the postwar era," Defense Minister Shinjiro Koizumi said, stressing his country's determination to pursue military buildup and protect its people. "It does not change our path as a peace-loving nation," he said.

--- SOURCE 12: Sizing up Welfare States: How do OECD countries compare? ---
URL: https://oecdstatistics.blog/2023/02/02/sizing-up-welfare-states-how-do-oecd-countries-compare

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This blog post from the OECD Statistics (oecdstatistics.blog), published February 2, 2023, analyzes the size and composition of welfare states across OECD countries, based on the latest update of the OECD Social Expenditure Database (SOCX) released on January 26, 2023.

Key findings include:

**Overall trends:** Public social expenditure was less than 10% of GDP in 1960 but has more than doubled to just over 20% of GDP on average across the OECD. Two-thirds of public social spending goes toward pensions and health services.

**Country comparisons (2022):** France and Italy have the highest public social expenditure at over 30% of GDP, while Costa Rica, Ireland, Korea, Mexico, and Türkiye spend less than 15% of GDP. Private social spending averages 3.1% of GDP across the OECD but exceeds 10% of GDP in the Netherlands, Switzerland, and the United States.

**COVID-19 impact:** Public social spending-to-GDP ratios rose from about 20% in 2019 to 23% in 2020 on average (over 80% of the increase driven by higher spending, the rest by GDP decline). Ratios fell nearly as rapidly afterward, declining to an estimated 21% in 2022. Canada (6.9 ppts), Spain (6.5 ppts), and the United States (6 ppts) saw the largest increases between 2019 and 2020. Spending declined in all countries except Korea and Latvia by 2022, with Estonia, Denmark, Finland, Greece, Hungary, Norway, and Sweden falling below their 2019 levels.

**Main spending areas:** Old-age and survivor pensions (7.7% of GDP) and health (5.8% of GDP) are the largest areas of public spending. Greece and Italy spend over 15% of GDP on pensions, while Chile, Iceland, Korea, and Mexico spend around 3%. France, Germany, Japan, and the United States spend over 8% of GDP on health. "Other social spending" (6.5% of GDP) includes disability payments (1.6%), family cash benefits (1.1%), unemployment benefits (0.6%), and non-health social services (2.3%, including Early Childhood Education and Care).

**Tax system influence:** Governments recoup part of social spending through taxes on transfers, an effect largest in Denmark (7.2% of GDP) and smallest in non-European OECD countries. Tax Breaks with a Social Purpose (TBSPs) are largest in the United States at just under 2% of GDP, over half directed to employer contributions to medical insurance. Accounting for both private spending and TBSPs moves the United States from 23rd place in gross public social spending to 2nd place in net total social spending. France ranks first on both measures. However, higher net social spending does not necessarily lead to more equal outcomes, as tax advantages often benefit high-income workers more.

The post was authored by Willem Adema, Pauline Fron, and Maxime Ladaique of the OECD Directorate for Employment, Labour and Social Affairs.
</summary>

--- SOURCE 1: PIF $8 Billion Writedown: Giga-Project Losses, Budget Shift, ---
URL: https://vision2030.ai/analysis/pif-8-billion-writedown

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is an analytical editorial from Vision2030.AI (published August 2025, dated page August 1, 2026) examining Saudi Arabia's Public Investment Fund (PIF) $8 billion writedown on its giga-project portfolio, disclosed in August 2025.

**The Writedown:**
- PIF disclosed an $8 billion writedown on its domestic giga-project portfolio in its 2024 annual results (end-of-2024 valuations), representing a 12.4% decline — from approximately $64.2 billion to $56.2 billion (211 billion Saudi riyals).
- Giga-projects fell from 8% (2023) to 6% (2024) of PIF's total assets.
- Portfolio includes NEOM, Red Sea Global, Diriyah Gate, Qiddiya, ROSHN, and Jeddah Central Development Company.
- PIF's total AUM grew from ~$880 billion (2023) to ~$925 billion (2024), a net $45 billion increase.

**Contributing Factors:**
- NEOM's contraction: The Line's suspension, Trojena cancellations, Mukaab's pause; $50 billion spent against 2.4 km of foundation work. An internal audit found completion would cost $8.8 trillion.
- Red Sea Global complications: environmental restrictions slowed development and raised costs; only nine resorts open.
- Budget overruns from geological challenges in the Tabuk desert.
- Lower oil prices: IMF fiscal breakeven for 2024 was $96.20/barrel (19% YoY increase) while Brent traded at $60-65. Aramco cut its 2025 dividend ~one-third to $84.5 billion, reducing PIF income by at least $6 billion. PIF cash reserves fell to ~$15 billion by late 2024 (lowest since 2020). In December 2024, PIF board approved a minimum 20% spending cut across 100+ portfolio companies, with some budgets cut up to 60%.

**What the Writedown Does NOT Cover:**

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is an analysis article by Andrew Leber, published March 10, 2025 on Carnegie Endowment for International Peace, examining Saudi Arabia's Vision 2030 program as it enters its final five years. The article argues that while Vision 2030 has achieved notable successes—including non-oil revenue expansion, social liberalization, and private sector job growth—it faces significant challenges including a lack of accountability, prioritization of elite interests over citizen needs, and risky top-down investments.

**Background and Political Context:** Vision 2030, launched as a white paper in April 2016, encompasses personalization of power around Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman (MBS), administrative state restructuring, social liberalization, economic diversification, and repression of dissent. A turning point came in June 2017 when MBS sidelined rival Muhammad bin Nayef, followed by the November 2017 "Night at the Ritz" detention of hundreds of royal family members, business leaders, and officials. The Khashoggi assassination in October 2018 demonstrated MBS's unchallenged control despite international backlash.

**Key Achievements:** Non-oil revenues now cover approximately 66% of public-sector payroll and account for over 40% of overall revenue (2024 Ministry of Finance estimates). Unemployment is down with jobs growth primarily in the private sector, including 70,000+ new Saudi jobs in food and beverage since 2016. Women can now drive, gender segregation in restaurants has ended, and cinemas and concerts have returned.

**The "High Modernist" Phase:** The article applies James Scott's concept of "high modernism" to critique Vision 2030's third phase, identifying three major problems: (1) ignoring practical barriers (e.g., the $5 billion Trojena ski resort in the desert, The Line city scaled back to 1.5 miles, Neom delays and cost overruns), (2) prioritizing aesthetics over material gains (nation-branding, LIV Golf investment driven by PIF Chairman Rumayyan's personal interest), and (3) lack of bottom-up accountability (repression of critics, detention of economist Essam al-Zamel since 2017, narrow public discourse limited to controlled podcasts and interviews).

**Tourism Case Study:** The Public Investment Fund (PIF), now one of the world's largest sovereign wealth funds with 70-80% invested domestically, has heavily invested in tourism. While domestic tourism has grown (82 million overnight stays in 2023, an 80% increase over 2015-2016), most international tourism growth reflects religious pilgrimage to Mecca rather than new non-religious travel. Mecca accounts for 60% of increased international overnight stays and over 80% of increased spending. Meanwhile, marquee luxury projects like AlUla ($10 billion invested vs. $265 million in 2023 receipts) and Red Sea resorts show questionable returns. Saudi citizens privately criticize these projects for targeting ultra-luxury/wealthy constituencies rather than ordinary Saudis.

**Conclusion:** The article warns that without introducing bottom-up accountability, Vision 2030 risks becoming "Trojan horses for hollowing out the welfare state and enriching elite individuals and institutions," potentially failing to provide meaningful jobs for citizens and triggering future social unrest. It suggests institutionalizing regional governor authority and incorporating local representation into policymaking.
</summary>

URL: https://www.oecd.org/content/dam/oecd/en/publications/reports/2026/05/oecd-economic-surveys-japan-2026_9457bba4/54cc833d-en.pdf

SUMMARY:
<summary>
The OECD Economic Surveys: Japan 2026 report (May 2026, Volume 2026/12) provides a comprehensive assessment of Japan's economy, which has remained resilient despite multiple shocks and is transitioning from three decades of near-zero inflation to a new equilibrium of higher prices and wages. The survey was prepared by Müge Adalet McGowan, Patrizio Sicari, Tetsuya Yoshioka and Natia Mosiashvili under the supervision of Douglas Sutherland, and was approved by the Economic and Development Review Committee on 25 March 2026.

KEY MACROECONOMIC OUTLOOK: Real GDP grew 1.2% in 2025 and is projected to moderate to 0.7% in 2026 and 0.9% in 2027, driven mainly by domestic demand. Headline consumer price inflation has been above the 2% target between April 2022 and December 2025, with inflation projected at 2.0% in 2026 and 1.9% in 2027. Nominal wages recorded their strongest growth since the 1990s, with the 2025 Shunto wage negotiations agreeing to a historically high 5.25% total wage increase and 3.7% base pay increase. Minimum wage rose to JPY 1,121 in FY2025. The unemployment rate is near historic lows at 2.5-2.7%. Downside risks include elevated energy prices, geopolitical tensions, and trade fragmentation.

MONETARY POLICY: The survey recommends continuing gradual monetary policy normalisation, with further increases in the policy rate in a data-driven and flexible manner, given higher inflation expectations, solid nominal wage growth, and a closed output gap. The financial system appears sound, but the rising interconnectedness of non-bank financial intermediaries (NBFIs) poses spillover risks requiring continued monitoring.

FISCAL POLICY: Japan faces significant medium-term fiscal sustainability challenges with gross public debt at around 206% of GDP in 2024 (highest in the OECD), projected to decline to 197.4% in 2025, 194.2% in 2026, and 189.7% in 2027. The elderly-to-working-age population ratio is projected to reach 79% by 2060. Recommendations include: limiting use of supplementary budgets to large shocks with ex-post evaluation; elaborating a credible medium-term fiscal plan to achieve and maintain primary surpluses; linking pension eligibility age to life expectancy; boosting elderly co-payment rates through means-testing; and gradually raising tax revenues, including increasing the consumption tax rate (currently 10%, among the lowest in OECD) in small increments. Various personal income tax deductions that erode the tax base should be addressed, with targeted support for low-income households.

LABOUR MARKET: Japan has boosted female and older worker employment, but these groups remain concentrated in non-regular employment with lower wages and job quality. Recommendations include breaking down labour-market dualism, relaxing employment protection for regular workers, improving childcare access, continuing efforts to attract and integrate foreign workers (whose numbers are at record highs but remain low internationally), and improving adult learning programmes. Participation gaps in adult learning are significant for female, older, and non-regular workers; targeted training linked to in-demand digital skills is recommended.

CLIMATE/ENERGY: Accelerated action is needed to meet the net-zero target by 2050. The GX2040 Vision includes JPY 20 trillion in upfront investment support with carbon pricing planned later in the decade. Recommendations include: ensuring additionality of GX financial support through competitive and transparent selection; establishing swiftly the details of the GX-surcharge and emissions trading scheme (ETS); streamlining permitting procedures for renewables; boosting grid capacity; and establishing an independent climate advisory body. Renewables currently provide 8.2% of total primary energy supply, and emissions have declined since peaking in 2013 but remain heavily fossil-fuel dependent.

PRODUCTIVITY (Chapter 2): Hourly labour productivity lags the OECD average, driven by weak capital deepening since 2000 and historically low multi-factor productivity growth. Business dynamism is weak, with complex business registration procedures. Inward FDI is the lowest in the OECD at around 5% of GDP. The STEM graduate share is below the OECD average, and lowest for women at 3.6%. Public loan guarantees remain high, potentially keeping non-viable firms afloat (zombie firms prevalence is relatively high, especially among smaller firms). The venture capital market is small, pushing innovative AI and deep tech start-ups to go public prematurely. Recommendations include digital integration of government services with 'once-only' and 'silence is consent' principles, empowering inward FDI one-stop shops, promoting STEM participation especially for women, lowering public loan guarantee coverage rates, and strengthening public venture capital initiatives with mezzanine finance options.

BASIC STATISTICS (2025): Population 124.0 million; life expectancy 84.1 years; GDP of USD 4,437.9 billion; per capita GDP of USD 54.2 thousand PPP; employment rate 62.2%; unemployment rate 2.5%; R&D spending 3.6% of GDP; Gini coefficient 0.338; relative poverty rate 15.4%; PISA scores: reading 516, mathematics 536, science 547.
</summary>

--- SOURCE 13: Boosting efficiency in public investment in times of fiscal constraint ---
URL: https://www.ecb.europa.eu/press/economic-bulletin/articles/2026/html/ecb.ebart202602_01~7989f7715e.en.html

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This ECB Economic Bulletin article (Issue 2/2026) examines how boosting efficiency in public investment can address Europe's massive strategic investment needs (digitalisation, infrastructure, climate, defence) amid limited fiscal space. The EU faces annual public funding needs of approximately €510 billion for defence, green and digital transitions (Bouabdallah et al., 2025), while aggregate public debt-to-GDP stood at 80.7% in 2024 and nearly half of Member States exceed the 3% deficit threshold.

Key findings on public investment: Public investment accounts for ~17% of total EU investment (2024), ranging from ~30% in Luxembourg to ~13% in Belgium, and is expected to average 3.8% of GDP in 2025 (rising from 3.1% in 2019) and ~4% by 2027. Transport infrastructure is the largest component, averaging 27% of public investment (0.9% of GDP in 2023).

Using Data Envelopment Analysis (DEA) and Stochastic Frontier Analysis (SFA) methodologies on EU transport infrastructure investment, the analysis finds significant efficiency gaps. The median DEA efficiency score is ~50% when measured against transport network density (slightly lower for non-euro area and high fiscal-risk countries) and ~65% when measured against public transport quality. SFA results show lower median scores: 38% for railway investment and 43% for motorway investment — considerably lower than efficiency scores above 90% reported for health and education spending.

Closing the efficiency gap could yield potential savings of approximately €46-50 billion annually, though results carry high uncertainty. The article recommends improved public investment management frameworks, reducing red tape, streamlining regulatory requirements, strengthening administrative capacity, and conducting spending reviews (as done in Denmark, Spain and the Netherlands). The Germany case study (Box 1) demonstrates that shifting spending composition toward productive investment has significant positive macroeconomic effects, with scenario modeling showing a ten-year cumulative multiplier of ~1 when all public investment is productive.
</summary>

--- SOURCE 14: IMF Fiscal Monitor, October 2025. Spending Smarter: How Efficient and Well-Allocated Public Spending Can Boost Economic Growth ---
URL: https://www.imf.org/-/media/files/publications/fiscal-monitor/2025/october/english/text.pdf

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is the October 2025 International Monetary Fund (IMF) Fiscal Monitor report, titled "Spending Smarter: How Efficient and Well-Allocated Public Spending Can Boost Economic Growth." The report analyzes how governments can enhance spending efficiency and strategically reallocate resources—particularly toward infrastructure, human capital, and research and development (R&D)—to improve growth prospects without increasing overall spending.

KEY PROJECTIONS AND CONTEXT:
- Global public debt is projected to rise above 100 percent of GDP by 2029, the highest level since 1948. With a 5 percent risk scenario, debt could reach 124 percent in 2029.
- Countries with debt above 100 percent of GDP among the G20 include Canada, China, France, Italy, Japan, the United Kingdom, and the United States.
- Fifty-five countries are experiencing debt distress or are at high risk of distress, despite debt ratios often below 60 percent of GDP.
- More than 70 developing countries have tax-to-GDP ratios below 15 percent—the level needed for a growth takeoff.
- Labor productivity growth has slowed in about 70 percent of economies since the pandemic.

KEY FINDINGS ON PUBLIC SPENDING:
- Government spending reached 42 percent of GDP in advanced economies and 32 percent in emerging markets in 2023 (doubling since the 1960s), while low-income developing countries reached 18 percent.
- Public investment has declined globally to 18 percent of total expenditure; public education spending remains modest at about 11 percent; public wage bills account for about one-quarter of total expenditure.
- Public sector wage premiums average about 13 percent in emerging markets and 10 percent in low-income developing countries.
- Spending rigidity (institutional/legal constraints limiting budget flexibility) is highest in advanced economies at 0.33, versus 0.26 in emerging markets and 0.29 in low-income developing countries.

EFFICIENCY GAPS:
- Efficiency gaps (difference between actual and best-possible spending outcomes) stand at about 31 percent in advanced economies, 34 percent in emerging markets, and 39 percent in low-income developing countries.
- Gaps are most pronounced in public spending on investment and R&D. Investment efficiency gaps average 38 percent (advanced), 42 percent (emerging markets), and 53 percent (low-income developing countries).
- Countries could get 30–40 percent more value for money by adopting best performers' practices.

PROJECTED OUTPUT GAINS:
- Increasing infrastructure investment by 1 percent of GDP (offset by cutting government consumption) is associated with long-term output increases of ~1.5 percent in advanced economies and ~3.5 percent in emerging market and developing economies.
- Reallocating 1 percent of GDP from government consumption to human capital investment could lift output by ~3 percent in advanced economies and ~6 percent in emerging market and developing economies.
- Closing efficiency gaps could add another 1.5 percent output in advanced economies and 2.5–7.5 percent in emerging market and developing economies; accelerating closure could add 2 percent more.

POLICY RECOMMENDATIONS:
- Prioritize institution-building reforms: combat corruption, enhance transparency and accountability, competitive procurement.
- Strengthen public investment management systems, including project appraisal and maintenance funding.
- Implement multiyear budgeting frameworks and leverage digitalization.
- Align public sector wages with private sector benchmarks.
- Reform pension and health care systems for sustainability.
- Better target social assistance programs.
- Use spending reviews systematically and integrate them into budget processes.
- Expand private sector involvement (outsourcing noncore functions) while managing fiscal risks.
- Pro-growth spending on investment and education can also reduce income inequality (no trade-off with equity).

The report introduces novel global datasets on public spending efficiency (174 countries, 1980–2023) and rigidity (151 countries, 2000–2022), combining stochastic frontier analysis, empirical and theoretical models, and country case studies. The report was discussed by IMF Executive Directors on September 29, 2025, and authored by IMF Fiscal Affairs Department staff under the guidance of Vitor Gaspar.
</summary>

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is a PIMCO Secular Forum 2026 presentation (as of 8 May 2026) by Peder Beck-Friis on global fiscal policy and debt sustainability. The document assesses the fiscal outlook across developed markets, debt sustainability risks, and five scenarios for US debt over the next five years.

KEY FINDINGS:
• The structural fiscal picture is largely unchanged from last year: debt is near record highs, fiscal space is limited, and this likely constrains active fiscal easing in the next recession, shifting more burden to central banks.
• Fiscal policy is likely to stay broadly neutral ahead, with cross-country divergence: Japan and Germany plan to ease, most of Europe looks to tighten, and the US plans to keep its structural deficit neutral at 6-7% of GDP.
• Future recessions will likely push US deficits to historically high levels, close to ~10% of GDP (the current US federal structural deficit is around 6-7%).
• Debt remains sustainable in most developed countries despite the sell-off in global yields. The US (and Belgium) stand out with unsustainable debt paths. France looks better than last year but only conditionally on uncertain tightening. The UK, Italy, and Japan remain vulnerable to new shocks but are sustainable under current fiscal plans.
• Markets have repriced yield curves to reflect debt differences: higher-debt countries now have steeper curves (unlike before the pandemic). Based on simple debt dynamics, curves look broadly fair across most countries. Japan stands out as relatively steep.
• US interest rates (R) may soon exceed GDP growth (G) for the first time since the 1990s, making the cost of running deficits much higher and debt dynamics unstable.

FIVE SCENARIOS FOR US DEBT (unchanged from prior two years):
1. "Status Quo" – Debt trends higher with no/modest orderly rise in term premium; fiscal credibility intact (e.g., US post-GFC). Very likely.
2. "Crisis" – Debt trends higher with sharp disorderly rise in term premium; no fiscal credibility (e.g., UK under Truss). Unlikely, but slightly higher under Trump.
3. "Fiscal Consolidation" – Debt stabilizes via fiscal tightening (e.g., US mid-90s). Unlikely near term, likely further out.
4. "Financial Repression" – Debt stabilizes via high inflation + low interest rates (e.g., post-WW2). Unlikely.
5. "Growth Revival" – Debt stabilizes via rising real GDP growth (e.g., Australia 1930s). Unlikely, but AI raises odds slightly.

SUPPORTING DATA AND CONTEXT:
• G7 deficits remain high (outside wars and crises) and will likely stay higher than pre-pandemic due to higher interest costs and other spending.
• US debt now exceeds the combined debt of all other advanced countries.
• The US interest burden is rising sharply and is now close to a record high.
• The dollar's reserve status remains strong (45-89% share across various global market segments), supporting US fiscal credibility.
• Unlike Europe, the US tax burden is far from facing "upper bound" Laffer curve constraints, which supports fiscal credibility.
• Some form of fiscal consolidation is likely beyond the secular horizon as the rising interest burden may eventually change political attitudes.
• Historic evidence shows that even successful debt reductions involving financial repression (1950s-80s) also involved budget cuts.
• Even under optimistic AI-driven growth assumptions, higher real trend growth alone is unlikely to make US debt sustainable.
• Political polarization is linked to higher deficits across countries and time.
</summary>

SUMMARY:
<summary>
The SIPRI Fact Sheet (April 2026) reports that world military expenditure rose by 2.9 per cent in real terms to $2,887 billion in 2025, marking the 11th consecutive year of growth and the highest level ever recorded by SIPRI. Total military expenditure accounted for 2.5 per cent of global GDP. The five biggest spenders—the United States ($954 billion), China ($336 billion), Russia ($190 billion), Germany ($114 billion), and India ($92.1 billion)—accounted for 58 per cent of world military spending.

Key trends: The USA's military spending fell by 7.5 per cent to $954 billion, mainly due to the end of supplemental appropriations for financial military assistance to Ukraine and Israel. China's spending rose by 7.4 per cent (its 31st consecutive year of growth), Russia increased spending by 5.9 per cent (7.5 per cent of GDP), and Ukraine's spending rose by 20 per cent to $84.1 billion (40 per cent of GDP). Military expenditure grew in all world regions except the Americas. European spending rose by 14 per cent to $864 billion, and Asian/Oceanian spending rose by 8.1 per cent to $681 billion.

Regional highlights: NATO members (32) spent $1,581 billion (55 per cent of global spending), with European NATO members spending $559 billion; 23 of the 32 NATO members met the 2.0 per cent GDP target. In June 2025, NATO agreed to raise its spending target to 5.0 per cent of GDP by 2035, prompting concerns about "creative accounting" and blurred definitions of military-related spending. Germany's spending exceeded 2.0 per cent of GDP for the first time since 1990. Spain recorded the largest increase among top spenders (up by 50 per cent). Algeria's military burden (8.8 per cent of GDP) was the second largest globally after Ukraine.

Notable country developments: Taiwan's military spending rose by 14 per cent (largest increase since 1988) amid rising tensions in the Taiwan Strait, with a pledge to reach 5.0 per cent of GDP by 2030. Japan reached its highest military burden (1.4 per cent of GDP) since 1958. Ukraine received $52.2 billion in partner support in 2025. The Middle East's spending was roughly flat (+0.1 per cent) at $218 billion, with Israel's spending falling 4.9 per cent following the Gaza ceasefire. The global military burden rose to its highest level since 2009 at 2.5 per cent of GDP, with the Middle East having the highest regional burden (3.8 per cent of GDP).
</summary>

SUMMARY:

This is an opinion/analysis article from the Institute for Social Vision Design (ISVD) by Naoya Yokota, examining Japan's chronic underinvestment in education relative to OECD peers and the inequality this perpetuates.

**Key statistics:**
- Japan's public funding share for tertiary education is 37.5%, versus the OECD average of 67.4% (approximately 56% of the benchmark)
- About half of tertiary education funding in Japan is borne by households, against an OECD average of 19% — roughly 2.7 times the international norm
- Total spending on educational institutions (primary through tertiary) is 3.9% of GDP vs. OECD average of 4.7%
- Education's share of government expenditure is 7.1%, ranking 37th out of 42 OECD members (sixth from bottom)
- In FY2025 budget, defense spending (8.7 trillion yen) is approximately 2.05 times the education allocation (4.23 trillion yen); defense budget expanded ~1.6-fold since FY2022 (from 5.4 trillion yen)
- Japan's tertiary attainment rate among young adults (25-34) is 66%, far surpassing the OECD average of 48% (top five countries) — a "paradox of high attainment, low public investment"
- Japan's public spending on pre-primary education is just 0.1% of GDP (lowest in OECD) vs. OECD average of ~0.8%
- Primary teacher statutory salaries: USD 34,863–66,530 vs. OECD averages of USD 44,153–74,896; real wages declined 6% over 8 years while OECD average rose 4%
- Class sizes: 27 students in primary (vs. 21 OECD), 32 in lower secondary (vs. 23 OECD); at upper secondary, ~30% of teachers' time is spent teaching vs. 43% OECD average
- Between 2005-2010, OECD countries increased education spending ~40% while Japan rose only 5%

**Key arguments:**
- Japan treats education as "personal (household) investment" rather than "infrastructure borne by society as a whole" — a "social investment deficit"
- Heckman's research (Carolina Abecedarian Project) shows 13% annual ROI on early childhood education (ages 0-5), exceeding long-term stock market returns; Japan invests least in this high-return period
- Esping-Andersen's social investment state theory (Why We Need a New Welfare State, 2002) argues early public investment in education/childcare is key to breaking intergenerational reproduction of inequality; Japan is classified closest to the conservative welfare type but carries strong liberal-type characteristics due to high household burden
- Matsuoka's "Educational Inequality" (2019) empirically shows Japanese educational attainment is strongly determined by parental education, income, and region
- Sano's "The Economics of Education Investment" (2024) argues insufficient public investment is a bottleneck in human capital formation
- Panel data analysis of 107 countries (1970-2019) confirms public education investment has statistically significant positive impact on real GDP per capita

**Recent policy developments:**
- From April 2025, income limits on high school tuition support abolished (annual cap of 118,800 yen extended to all households)
- FY2026: support ceiling for private high schools to rise from 396,000 to 457,200 yen (estimated +0.1% of GDP impact)
- OECD Economic Survey of Japan (January 2024) recommended raising teacher salaries, expanding public investment in early childhood education, and increasing public funding for tertiary education

**Context:** Social security spending consumes roughly 33% of the general account budget and continues rising with population aging; Japan's Fiscal System Council (November 2024) emphasized efficiency gains and leveraging private funds rather than expanding public investment.

--- SOURCE 17: Sizing up Welfare States: How do OECD countries compare? ---
URL: https://oecdstatistics.blog/2023/02/02/sizing-up-welfare-states-how-do-oecd-countries-compare

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This blog post from the OECD Statistics (oecdstatistics.blog), published February 2, 2023, analyzes the size and composition of welfare states across OECD countries, based on the latest update of the OECD Social Expenditure Database (SOCX) released on January 26, 2023.

Key findings include:

**Overall trends:** Public social expenditure was less than 10% of GDP in 1960 but has more than doubled to just over 20% of GDP on average across the OECD. Two-thirds of public social spending goes toward pensions and health services.

**Country comparisons (2022):** France and Italy have the highest public social expenditure at over 30% of GDP, while Costa Rica, Ireland, Korea, Mexico, and Türkiye spend less than 15% of GDP. Private social spending averages 3.1% of GDP across the OECD but exceeds 10% of GDP in the Netherlands, Switzerland, and the United States.

**COVID-19 impact:** Public social spending-to-GDP ratios rose from about 20% in 2019 to 23% in 2020 on average (over 80% of the increase driven by higher spending, the rest by GDP decline). Ratios fell nearly as rapidly afterward, declining to an estimated 21% in 2022. Canada (6.9 ppts), Spain (6.5 ppts), and the United States (6 ppts) saw the largest increases between 2019 and 2020. Spending declined in all countries except Korea and Latvia by 2022, with Estonia, Denmark, Finland, Greece, Hungary, Norway, and Sweden falling below their 2019 levels.

**Main spending areas:** Old-age and survivor pensions (7.7% of GDP) and health (5.8% of GDP) are the largest areas of public spending. Greece and Italy spend over 15% of GDP on pensions, while Chile, Iceland, Korea, and Mexico spend around 3%. France, Germany, Japan, and the United States spend over 8% of GDP on health. "Other social spending" (6.5% of GDP) includes disability payments (1.6%), family cash benefits (1.1%), unemployment benefits (0.6%), and non-health social services (2.3%, including Early Childhood Education and Care).

**Tax system influence:** Governments recoup part of social spending through taxes on transfers, an effect largest in Denmark (7.2% of GDP) and smallest in non-European OECD countries. Tax Breaks with a Social Purpose (TBSPs) are largest in the United States at just under 2% of GDP, over half directed to employer contributions to medical insurance. Accounting for both private spending and TBSPs moves the United States from 23rd place in gross public social spending to 2nd place in net total social spending. France ranks first on both measures. However, higher net social spending does not necessarily lead to more equal outcomes, as tax advantages often benefit high-income workers more.

The post was authored by Willem Adema, Pauline Fron, and Maxime Ladaique of the OECD Directorate for Employment, Labour and Social Affairs.
</summary>
