### Foreign Trade Zones/Free Ports/Trade Facilitation

Norway has no foreign trade zones and does not currently have plans to establish any.

### Performance and Data Localization Requirements

Norway generally does not impose performance requirements on foreign investors, nor offer significant general tax incentives for either domestic or foreign investors. There is an exception, however, for investments in sparsely settled northern Norway where reduced payroll taxes and other incentives apply. There are no free-trade zones, although taxes are lower on Svalbard, a remote Arctic archipelago, which is subject to the Svalbard Treaty of 1920 but administered by Norway. A state industry and regional development fund provides support (e.g., investment grants and financial assistance) for industrial development in areas with special employment difficulties or with low levels of economic activity.

Norway does not require “forced localization” or impose requirements on data storage, but data is nonetheless subject to data protection laws. Any transfer of personal data out of the EEA requires a special basis to be lawful. On February 26, the Norwegian Data Protection Authority (Datatilsynet) issued a guide to the existing rules that apply to the transfer of personal data to the United States in response to numerous inquiries about the rules. In 2023, the European Commission approved, as an exception to the general rule, a so-called adequacy decision for the United States that states which companies can transfer personal information to the United States under the Data Privacy Framework Program (the companies are listed in the  [Data Privacy Framework List](https://www.dataprivacyframework.gov/)). It also explains what the rules say about the transfer of personal data to U.S. companies that are not on the list. It is the European Commission that decides whether a country should receive an adequacy decision, which is binding on the data protection authorities. The Norwegian Data Protection Authority cannot revoke an adequacy decision or prohibit transfers that take place in accordance with it.

Section 5.

## Protection of Property Rights

### Real Property

Norway recognizes secured interests in property, both movable and real. The system for recording interests in property is recognized and reliable. Norway maintains an open and effective legal and judicial system that protects and facilitates acquisition and disposition of rights in property, including land, buildings, and mortgages.

Norway is one of the 86 contracting parties to the 2001 Cape Town Convention on Mobile Equipment (CTC) and the Protocol on Matters Specific to Aircraft Equipment (Aircraft Protocol).

### Intellectual Property

Norway has strong enforcement and legal structure for protecting intellectual property (IP) and adheres to key international agreements (e.g., the Paris Union Convention for the Protection of Industrial Property, the Berne Copyright Convention, the Universal Copyright Convention of 1952, and the Rome Convention). It has notified the World Trade Organization (WTO) of its main IP laws, as included in the WTO’s Agreement on Trade-Related Aspects of Intellectual Property Rights (TRIPS).

The chief domestic statutes governing IP include: the Patents Act of December 15, 1967, as amended; the Designs Act of March 14, 2003; the Copyrights Act of May 12, 1961, as amended; the Layout-design Act of June 15, 1990, as amended; the Marketing Act of January 9, 2009; and the Trademarks Act of March 26, 2010. As an EEA member, Norway adopted legislation intended to implement the 2001 EU Copyright Directive. Amendments to the Norwegian Trademarks Act implementing the Trademarks Directive (EU) 2015/2436 into Norwegian law entered into force in 2023. This set of legislation also protects trade secrets and industrial designs, including semiconductor chip layout design.

In June 2005 Norway enacted legislation based on the EU’s 2001 Copyright Directive to combat internet piracy, but subsequent court cases showed that the law did not provide sufficient grounds for enforcement. Norway passed a modernized Copyright Act in 2018. The Act clarifies the process for gaining access to infringers’ identifying information and introducing a site-blocking mechanism. Positive developments on the enforcement side are complemented by the popularity of legal streaming alternatives.

Acts of counterfeiting can be sanctioned pursuant to the general provisions of the Trademarks Act and Copyright Act. In addition, counterfeiting can, under certain conditions, constitute fraud under Section 371 of the Penal Code. Counterfeit products may be subject to seizure or destruction by the customs authorities. If the rightsholder does not pursue the case or respond to the notice issued by the Norwegian Customs, the goods are released to the importer (unless considered harmful). In 2015, the Norwegian government launched a new website and an awareness campaign titled  [velgekte.no, *Choose the Real Deal*](https://www.velgekte.no/).

Norway has implemented several of the EU directives relating to trademarks and copyright into its national law. Accordingly, case law from the Court of Justice of the European Union (the CJEU) carries significant weight when interpreting the Norwegian Trademarks and Copyright Acts. Rightsholders report that law enforcement authorities have begun to investigate major copyright infringement cases, resulting in the closing of several internet sites facilitating infringement.

In Norway, questions surrounding Artificial Intelligence (AI), especially concerning who owns generative AI outputs and what constitutes infringement within copyright law, have sparked considerable debate. Norway has signed the Council of Europe Framework Convention on Artificial Intelligence, Human Rights, Democracy and the Rule of Law (2024), which is the first global AI binding regulation instrument. Given that Norwegian copyright is regulated by the Copyright Act, which implements EU directives, EU legal acts like the convention and the upcoming implementation of the EU AI Act into Norwegian law is likely to influence how Norway addresses issues of ownership and infringement of IP related to AI-generated works.

Norway was placed on the U.S. Trade Representative’s (USTR’s) Special 301 Watch List in 2008 due to concerns about pharmaceutical patent protection but has not been listed since 2013. Norway is not on the Notorious Markets List.

For additional information about national laws and points of contact at local IP office, please see  [WIPO’s country profiles](https://www.wipo.int/directory/en/). See also the  [Norwegian Industrial Property Office](https://www.patentstyret.no/en/).

Section 6.

## Financial Sector

### Capital Markets and Portfolio Investment

Norway has a highly developed online banking system that provides a full range of banking services, including internet banking. There are no significant impediments to the free market-determined flow of financial resources. Foreign and domestic investors have access to a wide variety of credit instruments. The financial regulatory system is transparent and consistent with international norms. The Oslo Stock Exchange, which was acquired by Europe’s largest stock exchange Euronext in 2019, facilitates portfolio investment and securities transactions in general.

### Money and Banking System

Norwegian banks satisfy capital and liquidity requirements by a solid margin and are highly profitable. As of early 2025, the banking sector held approximately NOK 7.5 trillion (approx. $700 billion) in assets. Conservative asset/liquidity requirements limited the exposure of banks to the global financial crisis in 2008-2009. The countercyclical capital buffer is intended to strengthen banks’ solvency and mitigate the risk that banks are amplifying an economic downturn. Banks’ corporate credit losses increased somewhat in the first three quarters of 2024 but are still low. The most recent solvency stress test in the Central Bank Financial Stability Report 2024 shows that banks can absorb large credit losses, while still maintaining lending. The Central Bank’s Monetary Policy and Financial Stability Committee decided on January 22, 2025, to maintain the countercyclical capital buffer rate at 2.5 percent.

Foreign banks have been permitted to establish branches in Norway since 1996.

### Foreign Exchange and Remittances

#### Foreign Exchange

Norway’s currency is the Norwegian Krone. Dividends, profits, interest on loans, debentures, mortgages, and repatriation of invested capital are freely and fully remittable, subject to Central Bank reporting requirements. Ordinary payments from Norway to foreign entities can normally be made without formalities through commercial banks. Norway is a member of the Financial Action Task Force and has a floating exchange rate.

#### Remittance Policies

There are no restrictions on remittances.

### Sovereign Wealth Funds

Norway’s sovereign wealth fund, the Government Pension Fund Global (GPFG), was established in 1990 and had a value of NOK 19.7 trillion (approx. $1.6 trillion) at the end of 2024. The management mandate requires the fund to be invested widely, outside Norway. Petroleum revenues are invested in global stocks and bonds, and the current portfolio includes approximately 8,659 companies. GPFG owns on average 1.5 percent of those stocks. The fund is invested across four asset classes. The fund aims to invest in most markets, countries, and currencies to achieve broad exposure to global economic growth. Fifty-three percent of the fund’s investments in 2024 were in the United States. The fund plays an active role in its investments and aims to vote in almost all general shareholder meetings.

In 2004, Norway adopted ethical guidelines for GPFG investments that prohibit investment in companies engaged in various forms of weapons production, environmental degradation, tobacco production, human rights violations, and what it terms “other particularly serious violations of fundamental ethical norms.” The Central Bank’s Executive Board makes the final decision on exclusion, observation, or active ownership. In 2024, Norges Bank announced the exclusion of 14 companies, while reversing the exclusion of seven companies and removing six from observation.

Risk-based divestments are financial decisions that are not considered by the Executive Board. In 2024 the fund made 49 risk-based divestments following ESG risks assessments. Of these, 27 decisions involved companies that entered the Fund’s benchmark index during 2024. Altogether, the fund’s management has made 575 divestment decisions since 2012.

Though originally part of the International Forum of Sovereign Wealth Funds, Norway’s SWF subsequently left the organization. The Norwegian government still fully supports the Santiago Principles.

Section 7.

## State-owned Enterprises

The government continues to play a strong role in the Norwegian economy through its ownership or control of many of the country’s leading commercial firms. The State manages significant values on behalf of the society through direct ownership in 69 companies, which employ more than 336,000 people. The State’s direct ownership is managed by 13 ministries. The State’s goal as owner of companies that primarily operate in competition with others is the highest possible return over time in a sustainable manner (Category 1). Category 1 totals 22 companies that operate within different sectors such as energy, transport, telecoms, finance, technology, and industry. The State’s ownership in these companies is mainly managed by the Ministry of Trade, Industry, and Fisheries. Forty-four of the companies in the State’s portfolio are public policy companies (Category 2), which primarily do not operate in competition with others. These companies operate in areas such as healthcare, performing arts, and infrastructure. The State’s ownership in these companies is mainly managed by the relevant sector ministry. The Norwegian state owns assets worth approximately NOK 1.375 trillion (approx. $131 billion). Private ownership is the main rule in Norwegian business and industry, but state ownership, together with other public ownership, makes a significant contribution to national ownership in Norway. Successive Norwegian governments have sustained stable levels of strong, transparent, and predictable government ownership. All stock exchange listed companies, and a significant number of the non-listed, compete in the international market, including in the United States.

The Norwegian State’s ownership is exercised in accordance with the OECD Guidelines on Corporate Governance of State-Owned Enterprises. The provisions in the EEA Agreement are neutral with regard to public and private ownership. Norway is party to the Government Procurement Agreement (GPA) within the framework of the World Trade Organization (WTO) and a signatory to all relevant annexes. SOEs are covered under the WTO Government Procurement Agreement (GPA) through Norway’s EFTA membership. The Norwegian government publishes  [the annual state ownership report](https://www.regjeringen.no/en/dokumenter/state-ownership-report-2023/id3044645/).

In October 2022, the government introduced a  [white paper on the State’s direct ownership of companies](https://www.regjeringen.no/en/dokumenter/meld.-st.-6-20222023/id2937164/).

### Privatization Program

Norway has no current plans to privatize any SOEs.

Section 8.

## Corruption

Business is generally conducted “above the table” in Norway, and Norway has a zero-tolerance policy on corruption. Corrupt activity by Norwegian or foreign officials is a criminal offense under Norway’s Penal Code. Norway’s anti-corruption laws cover illicit activities overseas, subjecting Norwegian nationals/companies who bribe officials in foreign countries to criminal penalties in Norwegian courts.

Norway does not have a central government body dedicated to mitigating public integrity risks in the public sector. Various institutions are responsible for mitigating public integrity risks within their respective fields:

Norway is a member of the Council of Europe’s anti-corruption watchdog Group of States against Corruption (GRECO) and ratified the Criminal Law Convention on Corruption in 2004, without any reservations. Norway has ratified the UN Anticorruption Convention (2006) and is a signatory of the OECD Convention on Combating Bribery. Norway ranked fifth out of 180 countries on Transparency International’s Corruption Perceptions Index in 2024.

## Political and Security Environment

Norway is a vibrant, stable democracy. Violent political protests or incidents are extremely rare, as are politically motivated attacks on foreign commercial projects or property. On February 12, 2025, the Norwegian Intelligence Service (Focus 2025), Police Security Service (National Threat Assessment 2025), and National Security Authority (Risk Assessment 2025) published their respective annual reports. The documents address the security situation and note the complex threats confronting Norway over the past year, such as intelligence activity, strategic acquisitions, cyber-attacks, and possible acts of sabotage. Security services expect that China and Russia will continue representing the main security threats, attempting to procure Norwegian goods, services, and technology in 2025. Technological development areas with potential for military use, such as sensor and detection technology, autonomous maritime technology, semiconductors, biotechnology, satellite, drone, and communications technology, and emerging artificial intelligence and quantum computing, will be targets.

Section 10.

## Labor Policies and Practices

Obtaining work permits for foreign labor coming from outside the EEA, particularly for semi-skilled workers, can be cumbersome. Norway has a common Nordic labor market with Sweden, Denmark, Finland, and Iceland. All Nordic citizens can travel freely within the Nordic countries to work. Through the EEA Agreement, Norway is part of the common European labor market; therefore, EEA citizens can reside and work in Norway without having to apply for a residence permit.

Skilled and semi-skilled labor is usually available in Norway, although there are shortages in some sectors. The high level of economic activity and the weakening of the Norwegian currency have made it somewhat less attractive for other European workers to look for jobs in Norway. The labor force as of year-end 2024 totaled approximately three million, representing a labor force participation rate of 72.9 percent of the working-age population. 2.9 million people were employed or had an economic activity, with unemployment at 3.3 percent.

Norway has union membership of nearly 2.1 million people, or 67.2 percent of the labor force. The unions are independent of the government but some, such as the largest labor organization, Landsorganisasjonen (LO), have close and historic ties with the Labor Party. Norway has a highly centralized and constructive system of collective bargaining. The government may impose mandatory wage arbitration should strikes threaten key sectors of the economy, particularly the oil and gas and transportation sectors. Mandatory wage arbitration has been used 170 times since 1953, most recently in 2024, when the government imposed wage arbitration to resolve the dispute between the Ministry of Digitalization and Public Administration and the Akademikerne union in connection with the yearly basic settlement.

Employee benefits are relatively generous, including one year paid parental leave (shared between parents, and financed chiefly by the social insurance system), and unemployment benefits for up to 104 weeks. There are special provisions for layoffs linked to lower activity for the employer.

The average number of hours worked per week in one’s primary job was 34.8 at the end of 2023, which is the third lowest in the OECD, after the Netherlands and Denmark. Productivity, however, is high – significantly higher than the EU average. According to the Working Environment Act, the norm for working hours is 40 hours per week. However, the standard laid down in all collective agreements is 37.5 hours per week.

Norwegian blue-collar hourly earnings are comparatively high. High wages encourage the use of relatively capital-intensive technologies in Norwegian industry. Top-level executives and highly skilled engineers, on the other hand, are generally paid considerably less than their U.S. counterparts, which, when combined with relatively high wages at the bottom of the wage scale, contributes to Norway’s very high level of income equality relative to other OECD countries.

This is the U.S. State Department's 2025 Investment Climate Statement for Norway, providing a comprehensive overview of Norway's business and investment environment. Norway is a highly developed economy with one of the highest per capita GDPs in the world, driven largely by its oil and gas sector, alongside shipping, shipbuilding, and aquaculture. The government welcomes foreign direct investment and generally grants national treatment to foreign investors, though ownership restrictions exist on some natural resources and activities (fishing/maritime/road transport). FDI in Norway stood at NOK 1.87 trillion (approx. $178 billion) at end of 2023, with approximately 9,882 foreign-owned companies, including about 882 registered U.S. companies employing over 53,000 people.

Key economic context: 2024 was characterized by high inflation and monetary tightening. The Norwegian Krone depreciated, and the Central Bank maintained the interest policy rate at 4.5 percent since 2023. New taxes introduced in 2024 include resource rent taxes on onshore wind power and aquaculture. Norway is an EEA member (not EU), benefiting from the "four freedoms" (capital, personnel, services, goods).

Investment regulations: Foreign investment is screened under the 2019 Security Act (Chapter 10 "Ownership Control") for national security concerns. In March 2021, the government blocked sale of a marine engine manufacturer to a Russian investor. In June 2024, it stopped negotiations to sell Søre Fagerfjord property in Svalbard on national security grounds. Foreign ownership caps include 25 percent in banks and insurance companies and 49 percent in telecommunications providers. Government monopolies exist in postal services, railways, and retail alcohol sales (partially relaxed in 2004).

Treaties: Norway has bilateral investment treaties with eight countries, is part of EFTA with 33 joint free trade agreements, signed an FTA with Mercosur in 2023 (pending ratification), and has a bilateral taxation treaty with the U.S. in force since 1972.

Legal regime: Norway has a transparent regulatory system on par with the EU, adopts EU directives via the EEA, has a civil law system, and follows the UNCITRAL Model Law for arbitration. Norway ranks among the top countries for rule of law. It has ratified the New York Convention and ICSID Convention.

Industrial policies: SkatteFUNN is the R&D tax incentive scheme. Norway has no foreign trade zones or free ports. It generally does not impose performance requirements or forced localization, though data transfer out of the EEA requires special legal basis (U.S. adequacy decision under Data Privacy Framework applies).

Property rights: Norway has strong IP protection, adhering to key international agreements (Paris, Berne, Rome conventions, TRIPS). It passed a modernized Copyright Act in 2018 and signed the Council of Europe Framework Convention on AI (2024). Norway was on the USTR Special 301 Watch List in 2008 but not since 2013.

Financial sector: Banks hold approximately NOK 7.5 trillion (approx. $700 billion) in assets as of early 2025. The Government Pension Fund Global (GPFG) was valued at NOK 19.7 trillion (approx. $1.6 trillion) at end of 2024, owning about 1.5 percent of the world's listed shares, with 53 percent invested in the U.S. The Oslo Stock Exchange was acquired by Euronext in 2019. Currency (NOK) is freely remittable with no restrictions.

State-owned enterprises: The state directly owns 69 companies employing over 336,000 people, with assets worth approximately NOK 1.375 trillion (approx. $131 billion). No privatization plans exist.

Corruption: Norway has zero-tolerance anti-corruption policy, ranked fifth out of 180 on Transparency International's 2024 Corruption Perceptions Index. It is a member of GRECO and ratified the UN Anticorruption Convention.

Security: Norway is a stable democracy. Security services expect China and Russia to remain the main security threats in 2025, targeting technologies with potential military use (sensors, autonomous maritime tech, semiconductors, biotechnology, satellite, drone, AI, and quantum computing).

Labor: Labor force totals about three million (72.9 percent participation rate), with unemployment at 3.3 percent as of year-end 2024. Union membership is 67.2 percent of the labor force. Working hours average 34.8 per week (third lowest in OECD). Norway has generous benefits including one year paid parental leave and unemployment benefits up to 104 weeks. EEA citizens can work in Norway without a residence permit; non-EEA work permits can be cumbersome.

This is a Reuters company page for the Abu Dhabi Investment Authority (ADIA), one of the world's largest sovereign wealth funds based in the UAE. The page aggregates 29 news articles related to ADIA and affiliated Abu Dhabi investment entities (including IHC, Mubadala, and subsidiaries). Key developments and investments include:

- March 2026: Abu Dhabi's Judan Financial (subsidiary of International Holding Company) acquired a 50.1% stake in U.S.-based Alpha Wave to build a global asset-management platform.
- February 2026: IHC announced plans to launch Judan Financial, a new international financial services holding company expected to oversee more than 870 billion dirhams ($236.88 billion) in assets under management.
- November 2025: ADIA to sell 5% stake (160.5 million shares, about half its shareholding) in Qatari telecom Ooredoo via secondary share offering.
- October 2025: IHC to acquire 43.5% stake in India's Sammaan Capital for 88.50 billion rupees ($997.7 million), betting on India's housing finance market.
- September 2025: ADIA stated technology would remain a focus after expanding private credit investments in 2024, with risk assets posting a second consecutive year of "significant gains."
- September 2025: Vantage Data Centers secured $1.6 billion investment led by GIC affiliate and ADIA unit for Asia-Pacific expansion, including data centre campus in Malaysia.
- August 2025: Logistics firm GLP secured up to $1.5 billion investment from ADIA subsidiary.
- May 2025: Mubadala's assets under management jumped 9.1% to 1.2 trillion dirhams ($326.74 billion), with increased investments in technology, manufacturing, and private credit.
- April 2025: Warburg Pincus and ADIA units to invest $877 million in India's IDFC FIRST Bank.
- January 2025: ADIA invested $500 million in Alpha Generation, a U.S. power infrastructure company.
- October 2024: ADIA invested $750 million in debt of India's GMR Group (aviation sector).
- October 2024: ADIA began operations in India's new tax-neutral finance hub (GIFT City in Gujarat).
- July 2024: ADIA and Qatar Investment Authority invested in Adani Energy Solutions' up to $1 billion share sale.
- April 2024: Prestige Estates signed $240 million deal with ADIA and Kotak AIF for residential projects in India.
- March 2024: Cheyne Capital secured investment from ADIA subsidiary for its European real estate debt fund.
- February 2024 (EXCLUSIVE): ADIA planned a $4-5 billion fund to invest in India through the Gujarat finance hub.
- October 2023: ADIA optimistic on public equities and private credit after turbulent 2022.
- October 2023: Reliance Retail raised $598 million from ADIA.

The page shows ADIA's heavy investment focus on India (multiple deals), private credit, technology, power infrastructure, real estate, and logistics, reflecting a broad global asset allocation strategy.

The **Abu Dhabi Investment Authority** (**ADIA**) is a [sovereign wealth fund](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sovereign_wealth_fund "Sovereign wealth fund") owned by the [Emirate of Abu Dhabi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Emirate_of_Abu_Dhabi "Emirate of Abu Dhabi") in the [United Arab Emirates](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_Arab_Emirates "United Arab Emirates"), founded to invest funds on behalf of the [Government of Abu Dhabi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Government_of_Abu_Dhabi "Government of Abu Dhabi"). It manages the emirate's excess [oil reserves](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oil_and_gas_reserves_and_resource_quantification "Oil and gas reserves and resource quantification") and is estimated to manage $1.128 trillion.[[2]](#cite_note-2) ADIA is one of the largest sovereign wealth funds in the world.[[3]](#cite_note-3)

ADIA's operations have been characterized as secretive and opaque.[[4]](#cite_note-:0-4)[[5]](#cite_note-5)[[6]](#cite_note-:1-6)

## History

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Abu_Dhabi_Investment_Authority&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: History")]

In 1967, Abu Dhabi emirate created the Financial Investments Board which operated within its Department of Finance and was responsible for managing the Emirate's excess oil revenues. However, in 1976, Sheikh [Zayed bin Sultan Al Nahyan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Zayed_bin_Sultan_Al_Nahyan "Zayed bin Sultan Al Nahyan"), the founding president of the [United Arab Emirates](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_Arab_Emirates "United Arab Emirates"), converted it into the Abu Dhabi Investment Authority.[[7]](#cite_note-7) The goal was to invest the Abu Dhabi government's surpluses across various asset classes, with low risk.[[8]](#cite_note-euromoney-8) At the time it was novel for a government to invest its reserves in anything other than [gold](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Official_gold_reserves "Official gold reserves") or short-term credit. Even today, investment in short-term paper remains the strategy for the vast majority of countries.[[8]](#cite_note-euromoney-8)[*[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")*]

In the [Bank of Credit and Commerce International](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bank_of_Credit_and_Commerce_International "Bank of Credit and Commerce International") scandal of the 1990s, ADIA reportedly lost hundreds of millions of dollars.[[6]](#cite_note-:1-6)

The operations of ADIA have historically and to the present been secretive and opaque.[[6]](#cite_note-:1-6)[[4]](#cite_note-:0-4)

The fund is a member of the [International Forum of Sovereign Wealth Funds](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/International_Forum_of_Sovereign_Wealth_Funds "International Forum of Sovereign Wealth Funds").[[9]](#cite_note-IFSWF001-9)

## Investments and strategy

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Abu_Dhabi_Investment_Authority&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Investments and strategy")]

ADIA manages a substantial amount of capital and is one of the world's largest investment funds.[[10]](#cite_note-10) Due to its size, the fund has been influential in international finance. In 2008, ADIA co-chaired the International Working Group of 26 sovereign wealth funds that produced the "Generally Accepted Principles and Practices of sovereign wealth funds" (known as the [Santiago Principles](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Santiago_Principles "Santiago Principles")). These principles were created to demonstrate to home and recipient countries and the international financial markets that sovereign wealth funds had robust internal frameworks and governance practices and that their investments were made only on an economic and financial basis.[[11]](#cite_note-11)

Today ADIA invests in all the international markets — equities, fixed income and treasury, infrastructure, real estate, [private equity](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Private_equity "Private equity"), and alternatives (hedge funds and commodity trading advisers — CTAs).[[8]](#cite_note-euromoney-8) ADIA's global portfolio is broken down into sub-funds covering a specific asset class. Each asset class has its own fund managers and in-house analysts covering it. Almost every asset class is managed both internally and externally. Overall between 70% and 80% of the organization's assets are managed outside, and over the last few years, the fund has become more indexed which given its unique asset liability structure is somewhat perplexing. The Abu Dhabi Investment Authority (ADIA) is a major purchaser of U.S. institutional real estate through various sub-entities. It often buys partial interest ownerships with leading real estate managers.[[12]](#cite_note-12) ADIA also invests in development projects including malls.[[13]](#cite_note-13)

Many of ADIA's investments have decreased substantially since investments were made at market peaks in 2007 and 2008. The $7 billion investment in [Citigroup](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Citigroup "Citigroup") has lost approximately 90% of its value as of 26 November 2009, 2 years after it acquired a sizable stake in the bank. Its investments in global real-estate at the market top in 2008 have also decreased substantially in value. Though it talks of its long-term success in generating returns, the fact that it has moved closer to the index and manages most of its funds through external third-party fund managers shows that its tolerance for risk-taking has greatly diminished over the years. However, ADIA's ratio of third-party fund managers is being actively managed. In 2006, between 70% and 80% of the organization's assets were managed outside with an aim to bring that down to between 60% and 70%. In the year 2005, Abu Dhabi Investment Company purchased 51 percent of shares of Massar (Company) from Abu Dhabi Power Corporation, a subsidiary of Abu Dhabi Water & Electricity Authority.[[14]](#cite_note-14)[[15]](#cite_note-15)

On 27 May 2013, ADIA published its 2012 Review, with an overview of its activities during the past year as well as an explanation of its approach to investing – strategy, governance, and risk management.[[16]](#cite_note-16)

In June 2018, ADIA acquired 21.4% of Pension Insurance Corporation Group from [J.C. Flowers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/J.C._Flowers_&_Co. "J.C. Flowers & Co.").[[17]](#cite_note-17)[[18]](#cite_note-18) In the same year, the fund increased its stake in [Axis Bank](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Axis_Bank "Axis Bank") to 1.19%.[[19]](#cite_note-19)

In February 2019, ADIA and Triton acquired 100% of IFCO, each receiving an equal 50% co-controlling stake. In 2025, ADIA agreed to sell their stake to [Stonepeak](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stonepeak "Stonepeak").[[20]](#cite_note-20)[*[dead link](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Link_rot "Wikipedia:Link rot")*][[21]](#cite_note-21) In 2019, ADIA announced that it would be investing over $1 billion into [Saudi Aramco](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saudi_Aramco "Saudi Aramco")'s [initial public offering](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Initial_public_offering "Initial public offering").[[22]](#cite_note-22) In 2020 the AIDA disclosed a share of $615 million in [Cheniere Energry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cheniere_Energy "Cheniere Energy").[[23]](#cite_note-23) In June 2020, ADIA acquired a minority stake in India’s [Jio Platforms](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jio_Platforms "Jio Platforms"), a provider of digital services and mobile networks, for $752.1 million.[[24]](#cite_note-24)[[25]](#cite_note-25) In October of the same year, ADIA acquired a 1.2% stake in [Reliance Retail](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Reliance_Retail "Reliance Retail"), an subsidiary of [Reliance Industries](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Reliance_Industries "Reliance Industries"), for $751.13 million,[[26]](#cite_note-26) followed by buying another $598 million stake in October 2023.[[27]](#cite_note-27)[[28]](#cite_note-28) In July 2021 made a $500 million contribution to EdgePoint Infrastructure, a telecom tower platform in Southeast Asia.[[29]](#cite_note-29) In October of the same year, ADIA took part in a $400 million pre-IPO funding round for the [GoTo Group](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/GoTo_(Indonesian_company) "GoTo (Indonesian company)"), an Indonesian firm operating across e-commerce, mobility, and digital payments.[[30]](#cite_note-30)

In April 2022, ADIA purchased a 10% interest in HDFC Capital Advisors in India from [HDFC Ltd](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Housing_Development_Finance_Corporation "Housing Development Finance Corporation") for $24.06 million.[[31]](#cite_note-31)[[32]](#cite_note-32) In 2022, ADIA contributed $2 billion to a data-centre development programme in Asia-Pacific, in a partnership with SC Capital.[[33]](#cite_note-33)[[34]](#cite_note-34) In March 2023, the fund put $500 million into Indian eyewear e-commerce firm [Lenskart](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lenskart "Lenskart").[[35]](#cite_note-35)[[36]](#cite_note-36)

In June 2024, together with [Advent International](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Advent_International "Advent International"), ADIA announced the purchase of a minority stake in United States-based [Fisher Investments](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fisher_Investments "Fisher Investments") for $3 billion, which they finished in January 2025.[[37]](#cite_note-37)[[38]](#cite_note-38)

In 2024, AIDA invested $1.7 billion into [Fisher Investments](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fisher_Investments "Fisher Investments") together with Lunate, $2.8 billion into Trans-Java Toll Roads with [INA](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Indonesia_Investment_Authority "Indonesia Investment Authority") and [APG](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/APG_(pension_fund) "APG (pension fund)"), as well as $5.6 billion into NetCo SRL together with [CDP Eq](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/CDP_Equity "CDP Equity") and [CPP](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/CPP_Investments "CPP Investments").[[39]](#cite_note-39)

In 2024, ADIA acquired a 40% stake in [DigitalBridge](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/DigitalBridge "DigitalBridge"), a U.S.-based data-centre platform and subsidiary of Landmark Dividend.[[40]](#cite_note-40) Later in the year, ADIA bought a minority stake in Qlik Technologies, a U.S. data integration and analytics company,[[41]](#cite_note-41)[[42]](#cite_note-42) and participated in the recapitalisation of [IFS](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/IFS_AB "IFS AB"), a Swedish software firm.[[43]](#cite_note-43)[[44]](#cite_note-44)

ADIA began using a division of data scientists made up of 125 people to assist with in-house investing in November 2024 providing a strategic shift towards private equity and private credits.[[45]](#cite_note-45)

In 2025, ADIA was selling mature assets and reallocating funds into growth sectors in an active portfolio re-balancing strategy.[[46]](#cite_note-46)

In January 2025, ADIA became a shareholder in Innocap Investment Management, with an agreement permitting it to increase its stake to 10%.[[47]](#cite_note-47)[[48]](#cite_note-48) In April 2025, ADIA invested ₹‎26.24 billion in [IDFC FIRST Bank](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/IDFC_First_Bank "IDFC First Bank") in India for a 5.1% stake.[[49]](#cite_note-49)

Tawreed Investments is a subsidiary of ADIA that has investments in several Australian infrastructure projects including [Queensland Motorways](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Queensland_Motorways "Queensland Motorways"),[[50]](#cite_note-50) [TransGrid](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/TransGrid "TransGrid"),[[51]](#cite_note-51) and [WestConnex](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/WestConnex "WestConnex").[[52]](#cite_note-52)

ADIA invested $200 million in to Meril, a medical devices firm, in July 2025 acquiring a 3% stake in the company.[[53]](#cite_note-53)

In February 2026, ADIA sold its 50% stake in a [Sydney](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sydney "Sydney") office precinct to [Charter Hall](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charter_Hall "Charter Hall"), an Australian fund manager, for $351 million.[[54]](#cite_note-54)

## Board of directors

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Abu_Dhabi_Investment_Authority&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: Board of directors")]

The board members currently serve for a period of three years and can be renewed. They are appointed by Emiri decree. As of 2023, the board consisted of:[[55]](#cite_note-55)

* [Tahnoun bin Zayed Al Nahyan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tahnoun_bin_Zayed_Al_Nahyan_(national_security_advisor) "Tahnoun bin Zayed Al Nahyan (national security advisor)"), Chairman
* [Hamed bin Zayed Al Nahyan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hamed_bin_Zayed_Al_Nahyan "Hamed bin Zayed Al Nahyan"), Managing Director
* [Khaled bin Mohamed bin Zayed Al Nahyan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Khaled_bin_Mohamed_Al_Nahyan "Khaled bin Mohamed Al Nahyan")
* [Mansour bin Zayed Al Nahyan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mansour_bin_Zayed_Al_Nahyan "Mansour bin Zayed Al Nahyan")
* Khalil Mohammed Sharif Foulathi
* Jassem Mohamed Bu Ataba Al Zaabi
* Hamad Mohammed Al Hurr Al Suwaidi

Former important board members include:

* [Ahmed bin Zayed Al Nahyan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ahmed_bin_Zayed_Al_Nahyan "Ahmed bin Zayed Al Nahyan") (1969–2010), appointed as Managing Director in 1997, while still in his twenties. He died in 2010 and was replaced by his half-brother Sheikh [Hamed bin Zayed Al Nahyan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hamed_bin_Zayed_Al_Nahyan "Hamed bin Zayed Al Nahyan").[[56]](#cite_note-56)
* [Jouan Salem Al Dhaheri](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jouan_Salem_Al_Dhaheri "Jouan Salem Al Dhaheri") (1948–2013), appointed in 1977.[[57]](#cite_note-wam.ae-57) He served as Deputy Managing Director, Deputy Head of the Investment Committee, and Head of the Audit Committee.[[57]](#cite_note-wam.ae-57)[[58]](#cite_note-58)[[59]](#cite_note-59)
* [Khalifa Muhammad Khalifa Al Kindi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Khalifa_Muhammad_Khalifa_Al_Kindi?action=edit&redlink=1 "Khalifa Muhammad Khalifa Al Kindi (page does not exist)") (born 1959), appointed as Deputy Managing Director in 1997. He served until 2007 when he was dispatched to manage the newly established [Abu Dhabi Investment Council](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abu_Dhabi_Investment_Council "Abu Dhabi Investment Council") (ADIC).[[60]](#cite_note-60)
* Ghanim Faris Ghanim Ateish Al Mazrui, former financial advisor to Sheikh [Zayed bin Sultan Al Nahyan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Zayed_bin_Sultan_Al_Nahyan "Zayed bin Sultan Al Nahyan"), and former chairman of ADIA and former director of the UAE Central Bank.[[61]](#cite_note-61)[[62]](#cite_note-62)

## Abu Dhabi Investment Authority (ADIA) - Wikipedia Overview

The Abu Dhabi Investment Authority (ADIA) is a sovereign wealth fund owned by the Emirate of Abu Dhabi in the United Arab Emirates, founded on March 21, 1976, to invest the emirate's excess oil reserves on behalf of the Government of Abu Dhabi. It manages an estimated US$1.128 trillion in assets, making it one of the largest sovereign wealth funds in the world. ADIA's operations have been characterized as secretive and opaque.

### History
- 1967: Abu Dhabi created the Financial Investments Board within its Department of Finance to manage excess oil revenues.
- 1976: Sheikh Zayed bin Sultan Al Nahyan, founding president of the UAE, converted the Board into ADIA, with a goal of low-risk investment across various asset classes—novel at a time when governments typically invested reserves only in gold or short-term credit.
- 1990s: ADIA reportedly lost hundreds of millions of dollars in the Bank of Credit and Commerce International scandal.
- ADIA is a member of the International Forum of Sovereign Wealth Funds.

### Investments and Strategy
- In 2008, ADIA co-chaired the International Working Group of 26 sovereign wealth funds that produced the "Santiago Principles" (Generally Accepted Principles and Practices).
- ADIA invests across all international markets: equities, fixed income, treasury, infrastructure, real estate, private equity, and alternatives (hedge funds and CTAs).
- 70-80% of assets are managed externally; the fund has increasingly become more indexed over time.
- ADIA is a major purchaser of U.S. institutional real estate and invests in development projects including malls.

### Key Transactions (Chronological)
- **2007-2008**: $7 billion investment in Citigroup lost ~90% of its value by November 2009; global real-estate investments made at market peak also declined substantially.
- **2013**: Published its 2012 Review on May 27.
- **June 2018**: Acquired 21.4% of Pension Insurance Corporation Group from J.C. Flowers; increased stake in Axis Bank to 1.19%.
- **February 2019**: ADIA and Triton acquired 100% of IFCO (50/50 co-controlling stake); in 2025, ADIA agreed to sell to Stonepeak.
- **2019**: Announced over $1 billion investment in Saudi Aramco's IPO.
- **2020**: Disclosed $615 million share in Cheniere Energy; acquired minority stake in India's Jio Platforms for $752.1 million (June); acquired 1.2% stake in Reliance Retail for $751.13 million (October), with an additional $598 million stake in October 2023.
- **July 2021**: $500 million contribution to EdgePoint Infrastructure (Southeast Asia telecom towers).
- **October 2021**: Participated in $400 million pre-IPO funding round for GoTo Group (Indonesia).
- **April 2022**: Purchased 10% interest in HDFC Capital Advisors (India) for $24.06 million.
- **2022**: Contributed $2 billion to an Asia-Pacific data-centre development programme with SC Capital.
- **March 2023**: $500 million into Indian eyewear e-commerce firm Lenskart.
- **June 2024**: With Advent International, announced purchase of minority stake in Fisher Investments (US) for $3 billion, completed January 2025.
- **2024**: Invested $1.7 billion into Fisher Investments with Lunate; $2.8 billion into Trans-Java Toll Roads with INA and APG; $5.6 billion into NetCo SRL with CDP Eq and CPP. Acquired 40% stake in DigitalBridge (US data-centre platform); bought minority stake in Qlik Technologies; participated in recapitalisation of IFS (Swedish software firm).
- **November 2024**: Began using a division of 125 data scientists for in-house investing, marking a strategic shift toward private equity and private credits.
- **2025**: Active portfolio re-balancing—selling mature assets and reallocating funds into growth sectors.
- **January 2025**: Became shareholder in Innocap Investment Management (with option to increase stake to 10%); invested ₹26.24 billion in IDFC FIRST Bank (India) for a 5.1% stake (April 2025).
- **July 2025**: Invested $200 million in Meril (medical devices firm), acquiring 3% stake.
- **February 2026**: Sold 50% stake in a Sydney office precinct to Charter Hall for $351 million.

Tawreed Investments, an ADIA subsidiary, holds investments in Australian infrastructure projects including Queensland Motorways, TransGrid, and WestConnex.

### Board of Directors (as of 2023)
Board members serve three-year terms appointed by Emiri decree:
- **Tahnoun bin Zayed Al Nahyan** – Chairman
- **Hamed bin Zayed Al Nahyan** – Managing Director
- **Khaled bin Mohamed bin Zayed Al Nahyan**
- **Mansour bin Zayed Al Nahyan**
- **Khalil Mohammed Sharif Foulathi**
- **Jassem Mohamed Bu Ataba Al Zaabi**
- **Hamad Mohammed Al Hurr Al Suwaidi**

Former notable board members include Ahmed bin Zayed Al Nahyan (Managing Director 1997-2010), Jouan Salem Al Dhaheri (appointed 1977), Khalifa Muhammad Khalifa Al Kindi (Deputy Managing Director 1997-2007), and Ghanim Faris Ghanim Ateish Al Mazrui (former chairman and former director of UAE Central Bank).

### Key Facts
- Headquarters: Abu Dhabi, United Arab Emirates (at the Abu Dhabi Investment Authority Tower)
- Type: Sovereign wealth fund; Industry: Institutional investor
- Owner: Government of Abu Dhabi
- Website: www.adia.ae

It manages the emirate's excess oil reserves and is estimated to manage $1.128 trillion. ADIA is one of the largest sovereign wealth funds in the world.", "ADIA's operations have been characterized as secretive and opaque.", "These principles were created to demonstrate to home and recipient countries and the international financial markets that sovereign wealth funds had robust internal frameworks and governance practices and that their investments were made only on an economic and financial basis.", "Overall between 70% and 80% of the organization's assets are managed outside, and over the last few years, the fund has become more indexed which given its unique asset liability structure is somewhat perplexing.", "The $7 billion investment in Citigroup has lost approximately 90% of its value as of 26 November 2009, 2 years after it acquired a sizable stake in the bank."

**China Investment Corporation** (**CIC**) is a [sovereign wealth fund](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sovereign_wealth_fund "Sovereign wealth fund") that manages part of [China's foreign exchange reserves](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Foreign-exchange_reserves_of_China "Foreign-exchange reserves of China"). China's largest [sovereign fund](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sovereign_funds_of_China "Sovereign funds of China"), CIC was established in 2007 with about US$200 billion of [assets under management](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Assets_under_management "Assets under management"). In May 2026 the fund had US$1.567 trillion in assets under management.[[2]](#cite_note-Sovereign_Wealth_Fund-2)

## History

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=China_Investment_Corporation&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: History")]

As of 2007, the People's Republic of China had US$1.4 trillion in [currency reserves](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Currency_reserves "Currency reserves").[[4]](#cite_note-ATimes-2007-10-02-4) That year, the China Investment Corporation was established with the intent of using these reserves for the benefit of the state by investing abroad in investments that are higher risk and higher reward than government bonds.[[5]](#cite_note-:32-5): 14

CIC's funding resulted from the state use of [leverage](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Leverage_(finance) "Leverage (finance)") and is therefore unlike most non-Chinese [sovereign funds](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sovereign_wealth_fund "Sovereign wealth fund"), which tend to be funded through state revenue from national resources like oil.[[5]](#cite_note-:32-5): 95 CIC was capitalized as follows: (1) the Ministry of Finance issued bonds, (2) the [Ministry of Finance](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ministry_of_Finance_of_the_People's_Republic_of_China "Ministry of Finance of the People's Republic of China") used the proceeds of the bond issuance to buy foreign exchange reserves from the [People's Bank of China](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/People's_Bank_of_China "People's Bank of China"), and (3) these reserves were used to fund CIC.[[5]](#cite_note-:32-5): 29

The state-owned [Central Huijin Investment Corporation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Central_Huijin_Investment "Central Huijin Investment") was merged into CIC as a wholly owned subsidiary,[[4]](#cite_note-ATimes-2007-10-02-4) a process that was completed in 2008.[[5]](#cite_note-:32-5): 36 To acquire Central Huijin from the [State Administration of Foreign Exchange](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/State_Administration_of_Foreign_Exchange "State Administration of Foreign Exchange"), CIC paid $67 billion of its initial $200 billion capital.[[5]](#cite_note-:32-5): 136 Central Huijin manages more than two-thirds of CIC's assets.[[5]](#cite_note-:32-5): 87

In 2008, CIC joined the [International Forum of Sovereign Wealth Funds](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/International_Forum_of_Sovereign_Wealth_Funds "International Forum of Sovereign Wealth Funds")[[6]](#cite_note-IFSWF001-6) and signed up to the [Santiago Principles](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Santiago_Principles "Santiago Principles") on best practice in managing sovereign wealth funds.[[7]](#cite_note-IFSWF004-7) CIC also sought to improve its credibility by assembling an international advisory council of important individuals from the West.[[5]](#cite_note-:32-5): 199

CIC's early foreign investment activities resulted in losses, as it significantly invested in the United States financial sector just before the [2008 financial crisis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2008_financial_crisis "2008 financial crisis").[[5]](#cite_note-:32-5): 109–111 As a result, it shifted its focus in 2009 to prioritize investments in natural resources.[[5]](#cite_note-:32-5): 110 It also replaced its previous asset-class based divisions with new divisions organized based on strategic priorities: Public Market Investments, Tactical Investments, Private Market Investments, and Special Investments.[[5]](#cite_note-:32-5): 110

In 2009, the [Ministry of Finance](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ministry_of_Finance_of_the_People's_Republic_of_China "Ministry of Finance of the People's Republic of China") converted its ownership of $200 billion of CIC's debt into [equity](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Equity_(finance) "Equity (finance)"), a result which relieved CIC of interest payments on the special treasury bonds that had initially capitalized it and instead resulted in CIC paying an annual dividend to the Ministry of Finance.[[5]](#cite_note-:32-5): 110–111 CIC has owned the Fullbloom Investment Corporation as a subsidiary since at least 2009.[[8]](#cite_note-8)[[9]](#cite_note-9)

In 2010, CIC established a new subsidiary, CIC International (Hong Kong) Co in Hong Kong and appointed [Lawrence Lau](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lawrence_Lau "Lawrence Lau") as its chairman.[[10]](#cite_note-10)

In 2011, CIC established its first foreign office in [Toronto](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Toronto "Toronto"), Canada.[[11]](#cite_note-11)

### Chairman Ding Xuedong's tenure

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=China_Investment_Corporation&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Chairman Ding Xuedong's tenure")]

In July 2013, the [Chinese Communist Party](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chinese_Communist_Party "Chinese Communist Party") appointed [Ding Xuedong](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ding_Xuedong "Ding Xuedong") as CIC's chairman.[[5]](#cite_note-:32-5): 112 Ding oversaw a restructuring of CIC and an increased focus on internal discipline.[[5]](#cite_note-:32-5): 112–113 He required senior executives and over 400 CIC employees to submit [self-criticisms](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Self-criticism_(Marxism–Leninism) "Self-criticism (Marxism–Leninism)") in which they detailed their errors, apologized, and pledged not to repeat those errors.[[5]](#cite_note-:32-5): 112

Under Ding's tenure, an audit begun under predecessor [Lou Jiwei](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lou_Jiwei "Lou Jiwei") was concluded.[[5]](#cite_note-:32-5): 113 The audit found that CIC's early losses were primarily due to dereliction of duty by key personnel, inadequate due diligence, inadequate post-investment management, and a general lack of professionalism.[[5]](#cite_note-:32-5): 113 Amid the [nationwide anti-corruption campaign](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anti-corruption_campaign_under_Xi_Jinping "Anti-corruption campaign under Xi Jinping") in 2015, CIC launched an internal investigation in which 495 personnel from CIC and its subsidiaries were disciplined.[[5]](#cite_note-:32-5): 113

CIC's investment strategy changed during Ding's tenure, with an increased focus on the agricultural sector, including industries such as irrigation and animal feed, which other institutional investors have tended to overlook.[[5]](#cite_note-:32-5): 113 Other points of emphasis during Ding's time as CIC Chair included technology, real estate, and infrastructure investments.[[5]](#cite_note-:32-5): 113

In 2014, CIC contributed some of the initial capital for the [Silk Road Fund](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Silk_Road_Fund "Silk Road Fund").[[12]](#cite_note-:0-12): 221

In January 2015, CIC made its Special Investments Division into a separate, wholly owned subsidiary called CIC Capital.[[5]](#cite_note-:32-5): 114 This move was intended to support the [Belt and Road Initiative](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Belt_and_Road_Initiative "Belt and Road Initiative") including by conducting [foreign direct investment](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Foreign_direct_investment "Foreign direct investment") and by supporting [state-owned enterprises of China](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/State-owned_enterprises_of_China "State-owned enterprises of China") engaged in mergers and acquisitions in economic sectors prioritized by the state.[[5]](#cite_note-:32-5): 114

During Ding's tenure, CIC closed its Toronto office, moving its foreign office presence to New York.[[5]](#cite_note-:32-5): 114

The Communist Party viewed Ding's tenure at CIC as a success and in February 2017 promoted Ding to secretary general of the [State Council](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/State_Council_of_the_People's_Republic_of_China "State Council of the People's Republic of China").[[5]](#cite_note-:32-5): 116

### Vice Chairman Tu Guangshao's tenure

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=China_Investment_Corporation&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: Vice Chairman Tu Guangshao's tenure")]

CIC Vice Chairman and general manager Tu Guangshao led CIC for a two-year period following Ding's promotion to the State Council.[[5]](#cite_note-:32-5): 116–117 CIC did not have a chairman during this period.[[5]](#cite_note-:32-5): 117

Tu supervised CIC's continued process of aligning its investments with the priorities of the Belt and Road Initiative.[[5]](#cite_note-:32-5): 116 Responding to Western countries' hostility to Chinese state-led investment, Tu established a strategy of CIC partnering with well-established Western institutions including [Goldman Sachs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Goldman_Sachs "Goldman Sachs") to form cooperation funds that could better satisfy the requirements of foreign direct investment screening processes.[[5]](#cite_note-:32-5): 116

### Chairman Peng Chun's tenure

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=China_Investment_Corporation&action=edit&section=4 "Edit section: Chairman Peng Chun's tenure")]

In April 2019, [Peng Chun](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peng_Chun "Peng Chun") was appointed CIC's Chairman.[[5]](#cite_note-:32-5): 117

Peng has continued former Vice Chairman Tu Guangshao's cooperation fund strategy.[[5]](#cite_note-:32-5): 118 In 2020, CIC formed the France-China Cooperation Fund, the China-Italy Industrial Cooperation Fund, the UK-China Cooperation Fund, and the Japan-China Industrial Cooperation Fund.[[5]](#cite_note-:32-5): 118

Under Peng's leadership, CIC unwound its 2015 spinoff of CIC Capital as a separate subsidiary.[[5]](#cite_note-:32-5): 118

In early 2024 Liu Haoling became Vice Chairman, President and [CIO](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chief_investment_officer "Chief investment officer") of CIC.[[13]](#cite_note-13)

In December 2024, Peng Chun was replaced by Zhang Qingsong as chairman and CEO.[[14]](#cite_note-14)[[15]](#cite_note-15)

### Notable individual investments

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=China_Investment_Corporation&action=edit&section=5 "Edit section: Notable individual investments")]

In September 2013, the fund acquired a 12.5% stake in [Russian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Russia "Russia") [potash](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Potash "Potash") fertiliser company [Uralkali](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Uralkali "Uralkali") for a rumoured $2 billion through its subsidiary Chengdong Investment Corporation.[[16]](#cite_note-16)[[17]](#cite_note-17)

In March 2014, CIC acquired a $40 million stake in iKang Health Group.[[18]](#cite_note-18) In October 2015, the CIC provided capital in a deal between Carnival Corporation and China State Shipbuilding Corporation[[19]](#cite_note-19)

In October 2015, [CSSC Carnival Cruise Shipping](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/CSSC_Carnival_Cruise_Shipping "CSSC Carnival Cruise Shipping"), a joint venture between the CIC, the [China State Shipbuilding Corporation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/China_State_Shipbuilding_Corporation "China State Shipbuilding Corporation"), and [Carnival Corporation & plc](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carnival_Corporation_&_plc "Carnival Corporation & plc"), was founded, with operations expected to commence in 2019.[[20]](#cite_note-20)[[21]](#cite_note-21)

CIC invested $3 billion together with Goldman Sachs into US-based Boyd in 2018.[[22]](#cite_note-22)[[23]](#cite_note-23)

### Real estate investments

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=China_Investment_Corporation&action=edit&section=6 "Edit section: Real estate investments")]

In August 2009, CIC and Qatar Holding became the two largest shareholders of Songbird Estates,[[24]](#cite_note-24) the parent company of London's [Canary Warf Group](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Canary_Wharf_Group "Canary Wharf Group"). [Canary Wharf](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Canary_Wharf "Canary Wharf") is home to several major financial institutions, including [Barclays](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Barclays "Barclays") and [HSBC](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/HSBC "HSBC"). Earlier that year, CIC had already purchased a 19% stake in Songbird Estates.[[25]](#cite_note-25) In November 2012, CIC entered into a joint venture with Invesco Real Estate to acquire the Winchester House in London from German fund manager KanAm for $389 million. The building was used as the London headquarters of [Deutsche Bank](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Deutsche_Bank "Deutsche Bank") at the time.[[26]](#cite_note-26)[[27]](#cite_note-27) In May 2023, it was sold for $316 million, resulting in a financial loss.[[28]](#cite_note-28)[[29]](#cite_note-29) Also in November 2012, CIC purchased a 10% stake in [Heathrow Airport Holdings](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Heathrow_Airport_Holdings "Heathrow Airport Holdings") for $726 million, consisting of a 5.7% stake from [Ferrovial](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ferrovial "Ferrovial") and a 4.3% stake from FGP Topco.[[30]](#cite_note-30)

In early 2014 CIC completed its purchase of the [Chiswick Business Park](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chiswick_Business_Park "Chiswick Business Park") in [London](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/London "London") from the [Blackstone Group](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Blackstone_Group "The Blackstone Group") for about £800 million.[[31]](#cite_note-31)[[32]](#cite_note-32)

In December 2016, CIC acquired a 45% stake in the office skyscraper [1221 Avenue of the Americas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1221_Avenue_of_the_Americas "1221 Avenue of the Americas"), [New York City](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_York_City "New York City"), for $1 billion, which valued the building at $2.3 billion.[[33]](#cite_note-33)[[34]](#cite_note-34) In November 2017, CIC purchased [Logicor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Logicor "Logicor"), a European warehouse company, from [The Blackstone Group](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Blackstone_Group "The Blackstone Group") L.P. for $13.49 billion.[[35]](#cite_note-35) Other companies were also bidding for Logicor.[[36]](#cite_note-The_Wall_Street_Journal-pgrant-36)

As of January 2023, CIC owns over 250 properties in Britain though various companies. These properties include key logistics and distribution centres for food and consumer goods in different regions of the UK.[[37]](#cite_note-37)

### Financial institutions

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=China_Investment_Corporation&action=edit&section=7 "Edit section: Financial institutions")]

In 2007, CIC invested $5.5 billion in US investment bank [Morgan Stanley](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Morgan_Stanley "Morgan Stanley") through its subsidiary *Best Investment Corporation*.[[38]](#cite_note-38)[[39]](#cite_note-39) At the time of the investment, Morgan Stanley had suffered massive trading losses.[[40]](#cite_note-40) In 2009, CIC purchased $1.2 billion of common stock in Morgan Stanley.[[41]](#cite_note-41)[[42]](#cite_note-42) In July of the following year, CIC sold shares valued at $264 to $396.5 million, reducing its stake to under 10 per cent.[[43]](#cite_note-43)[[44]](#cite_note-44)

In May 2007, CIC bought a $3 billion stake (constituting 9.9% of nonvoting shares) in the [Blackstone Group](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Blackstone_Group "The Blackstone Group"), shortly before Blackstone's public listing.[[5]](#cite_note-:32-5): 108 In 2012, CIC sold most of its 3 per cent stake in the company.[[45]](#cite_note-45) CIC left the relationship in February 2018 via Beijing Wonderful Investments.[[5]](#cite_note-:32-5): 108

In July 2009, CIC acquired a 40 per cent stake in the [CITIC Group](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/CITIC_Group "CITIC Group").[[46]](#cite_note-46)[[47]](#cite_note-47) In December the following year, the fund joined a consortium investing $1.8 billion in [BTG Pactual](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/BTG_Pactual "BTG Pactual").[[48]](#cite_note-48)[[49]](#cite_note-49) In 2011, CIC invested $100 million in [VTB Bank](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/VTB_Bank "VTB Bank").[[50]](#cite_note-50)[[51]](#cite_note-51) In 2012, the fund bought a minority stake in [EIG Global Energy Partners](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/EIG_Global_Energy_Partners "EIG Global Energy Partners").[[52]](#cite_note-52)

## Impact

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=China_Investment_Corporation&action=edit&section=8 "Edit section: Impact")]

In addition to its pursuit of financial returns, CIC's investments are also intended to promote China's national interests.[[5]](#cite_note-:32-5): 29 For example, its investments in natural resources both support China's development and support the Communist Party's strategic priorities.[[5]](#cite_note-:32-5): 146–147

Having entered the global market in 2007 shortly before the [2008 financial crisis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2008_financial_crisis "2008 financial crisis"), CIC's initial performance was lackluster.[[5]](#cite_note-:32-5): 14 This created a political opportunity for the [State Administration of Foreign Exchange](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/State_Administration_of_Foreign_Exchange "State Administration of Foreign Exchange") in 2013 to expand the sovereign funds under its jurisdiction.[[5]](#cite_note-:32-5): 14

CIC is among the worldwide sovereign funds whose investments tend to prompt other institutional investors to perceive investing alongside the fund as comparatively more safe.[[5]](#cite_note-:32-5): 9

CIC has been described as a [unicorn](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Unicorn_(finance) "Unicorn (finance)")-maker for its role in fueling the growth of Chinese tech sector through its early support of [Alibaba](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alibaba_Group "Alibaba Group") and [DiDi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/DiDi "DiDi").[[5]](#cite_note-:32-5): 129 It has also provided important funding to companies in [China's semiconductor industry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Semiconductor_industry_in_China "Semiconductor industry in China").[[5]](#cite_note-:32-5): 147

## Governance

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=China_Investment_Corporation&action=edit&section=9 "Edit section: Governance")]

The management and board of the China Investment Corporation ultimately reports to the [State Council of the People's Republic of China](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/State_Council_of_the_People's_Republic_of_China "State Council of the People's Republic of China"). The China Investment Corporation is seen as being "firmly entrenched" in the political establishment as the composition of its board of directors implies "considerable influence on the part of China's Ministry of Finance."[[53]](#cite_note-53)

The China Investment Corporation (CIC) is a sovereign wealth fund that manages part of China's foreign exchange reserves. It is China's largest sovereign fund, established in 2007 with approximately US$200 billion in assets under management. As of May 2026, the fund had US$1.567 trillion in assets under management, with total assets of US$1.330 trillion (2025). Headquartered in Beijing at New Beijing Poly Plaza, CIC's current leadership includes Zhang Qingsong (Chairman and CEO) and Liu Haoling (Vice Chairman, President and CIO).

**History:** CIC was established in 2007 to invest China's US$1.4 trillion currency reserves abroad in higher-risk, higher-reward investments than government bonds. It was capitalized through a complex structure where the Ministry of Finance issued bonds, used proceeds to buy foreign exchange reserves from the People's Bank of China, and funded CIC with those reserves. The state-owned Central Huijin Investment was merged into CIC as a wholly owned subsidiary (completed 2008), with CIC paying $67 billion of its initial capital to acquire it. CIC manages more than two-thirds of its assets through Central Huijin.

CIC joined the International Forum of Sovereign Wealth Funds in 2008 and signed the Santiago Principles. Early foreign investments resulted in losses due to significant investment in the US financial sector before the 2008 financial crisis, prompting a 2009 shift toward natural resources investments.

**Leadership tenures:**
- Chairman Ding Xuedong (July 2013-February 2017): Oversaw restructuring, required self-criticisms from 400+ employees, concluded an audit finding early losses were due to dereliction of duty and inadequate due diligence, launched internal investigation disciplining 495 personnel amid the anti-corruption campaign, shifted focus to agriculture/technology/real estate/infrastructure, contributed initial capital to the Silk Road Fund (2014), spun off Special Investments into CIC Capital (2015) to support the Belt and Road Initiative, closed Toronto office and moved foreign presence to New York.
- Vice Chairman Tu Guangshao (2017-2019): Led CIC without a chairman for two years, aligned investments with Belt and Road priorities, established cooperation fund strategy with Western institutions like Goldman Sachs.
- Chairman Peng Chun (April 2019-December 2024): Continued cooperation fund strategy (formed France-China, China-Italy, UK-China, Japan-China cooperation funds in 2020), unwound CIC Capital spinoff, replaced by Zhang Qingsong in December 2024.

**Notable investments:** 12.5% stake in Uralkali (Russia, 2013); $40 million in iKang Health Group (2014); CSSC Carnival Cruise Shipping joint venture (2015); $3 billion with Goldman Sachs in US-based Boyd (2018). Real estate: stakes in Songbird Estates/Canary Wharf, Winchester House (London), 10% of Heathrow Airport Holdings, Chiswick Business Park, 45% of 1221 Avenue of the Americas (NYC), Logicor (European warehouse company, $13.49 billion), and over 250 UK properties as of January 2023. Financial institutions: Morgan Stanley ($5.5 billion in 2007), Blackstone Group ($3 billion in 2007), 40% stake in CITIC Group (2009), BTG Pactual consortium ($1.8 billion, 2010), VTB Bank ($100 million, 2011), EIG Global Energy Partners (2012).

**Impact:** CIC's investments promote China's national interests in addition to financial returns. Its initial performance was lackluster due to the 2008 financial crisis. It has been described as a "unicorn-maker" for fueling Chinese tech growth through early support of Alibaba and DiDi, and provides funding to China's semiconductor industry. Its investments tend to make other institutional investors perceive co-investing as comparatively safer.

**Governance:** CIC's management and board report to China's State Council. The board includes Zhang Qingsong (Chairman & CEO), Liu Haoling (Vice Chairman, President & CIO), and various executive, non-executive, independent, and employee directors. The International Advisory Council includes notable figures like Zhou Xiaochuan, Justin Yifu Lin, Frederick Ma, John L. Thornton, and Gerhard Schröder. CIC's subsidiary includes Central Huijin Investment, CIC International, CIC Capital, Best Investment Corporation, Fullbloom Investment Corporation, and Chengdong Investment Corporation. It holds a 30% interest in GDF Suez Exploration & Production International (joint venture with Engie).

Headquartered in Beijing, China Investment Corporation (CIC) was founded on 29 September 2007 as China's sovereign wealth fund incorporated in accordance with China's Company Law, with a registered capital of $200 billion.

 

CIC was established as a vehicle to diversify China’s foreign exchange holdings and seek maximum returns for its shareholder within acceptable risk tolerance. CIC is mandated to make overseas investments and equity investments in financial institutions in China through its three subsidiaries, CIC International Co., Ltd. (CIC International), CIC Capital Corporation (CIC Capital), and Central Huijin Investment Ltd. (Central Huijin).

 

CIC’s overseas investment activities, undertaken by CIC International and CIC Capital, include public equity and bond investments; hedge fund and multi-asset investments; industry-wide private equity and private credit investments; direct investments and fund investments in sectors such as real estate, infrastructure, resources and commodities, and agriculture; and managing bilateral and multilateral funds.

 

Central Huijin undertakes equity investments in state-owned financial institutions in China. Without interfering in the day-to-day operations of its portfolio companies, Central Huijin exercises its rights and performs its obligations as a shareholder to the extent of its capital contribution.

 

Strict firewalls separate the overseas investment activities of CIC International and CIC Capital and the domestic equity management operations of Central Huijin.

 

CIC has three overseas branches, CIC International (Hong Kong) Co., Ltd., the New York Representative office and the London Representative Office.

# China Launches Government Venture Capital Fund for Technology Development

31 March 2026

4 min read

The government of the People’s Republic of China (PRC) is taking steps to “greatly boost [China’s] scientific and technological self-reliance” and “cultivate and enhance the development of emerging and futuristic industries,” as outlined in China’s 15th Five-Year Plan (FYP), which runs from 2026 to 2030.

This is clearly illustrated by their launch of the National Venture Capital Guidance Fund (国家创投引导基金; NVCGF) on 26 December 2025.[[1]](#_ftn1) The central government has allocated CNY 100 billion (approximately USD 14 billion) as seed capital for the fund.[[2]](#_ftn2) Ultimately, by integrating funds from local governments, central state-owned enterprises, financial institutions, and private capital, the NVCGF will form a CNY 1 trillion (approximately USD 144 billion) fund.[[3]](#_ftn3)

As a state-backed venture capital (VC) fund, the NVCGF and therefore, its investment priorities, will reflect and support the Chinese Communist Party leadership’s strategic objectives. As a result, international companies can expect increased opportunities and risks related to key technologies and industries, notably semiconductors, biomedicine, aerospace, and low-altitude economy (drones and eVTOL). The fund will focus on supporting small start-ups—which are expected to receive no less than 70 percent of the fund—involved in developing “hard core technologies.”[[4]](#_ftn4) According to the Chinese government, “hard core technologies” are “important indicators of a country’s core competitiveness”[[5]](#_ftn5) and require long-term R&D inputs and sustained efforts, characterized by high technological thresholds, and which are difficult to “duplicate and copy.” The following are technologies of particular interest to the Chinese government[[6]](#_ftn6):

* Integrated circuit (i.e., semiconductors)
* Artificial intelligence
* Quantum technology
* Brain-machine interface
* Biomedicine
* Aviation and aerospace
* Low-altitude economy (drones and eVTOL)
* Green energies

Additionally, 6G communications, robotics, new materials, new energy storage, hydrogen energy, and nuclear fusion are related technologies and industries likely to benefit from the NVCGF. PRC officials have reiterated the government’s insistence that the NVCGF will be primarily used to support early-stage developmental technologies and long-term investments (up to 20 years).[[7]](#_ftn7)

## Regional Funds

Like other state-backed VC funds in China,  the NVCGF has a fund structure that includes regional funds, and currently has three operational regional funds centered on the Beijing-Tianjin-Hebei region, the Yangtze River Delta (Shanghai-Jiangsu-Zhejiang) region, and the Guangdong-Hong Kong-Macau region.[[8]](#_ftn8) Each regional fund has signed letters of intent (LOI) to invest and established direct-investment projects directed at integrated circuits, quantum technology, biomedicine, brain-machine interface, and aviation and aerospace.[[9]](#_ftn9) Each is expected to raise CNY 50 billion (approximately USD 7.2 billion).[[10]](#_ftn10)

All three regional funds have reportedly signed investment LOIs with 49 portfolio funds and 27 direct investment projects, and are expected to establish over 600 portfolio funds in their respective regions to target emerging and future industries.[[11]](#_ftn11)

## Regulations Governing State VC Activities

Laws and regulations form the legal basis for PRC policies in areas of interest to the PRC leadership, and the VC sector is no different.

In January 2025, the General Office of the State Council issued its “Guiding Opinions Regarding the Promotion of the High-Quality Development of Government Investment Funds” (国务院办公厅关于促进政府投资基金高质量发展的指导意见).[[12]](#_ftn12) The document refers to government investment funds at the central, provincial, and sub-provincial levels, stipulating that government investment funds are aimed at “major strategies, key areas, and weak links in which the market is unable to fully exercise its function.”

The “Guiding Opinions” also distinguish between two types of government investment funds:

* “Industry investment funds” “lead and drive” activities to support the building of “globally competitive industrial clusters.”
* “Venture capital funds” “support technological innovations” with the goal of “accelerating the achievement of a high level of technological self-reliance.”

China’s government investment funds, whether they support industrial modernization or the development of cutting-edge technologies, must “play an active role” to “serve national strategies, promote industrial upgrades, and facilitate innovations and entrepreneurship,” according to the January 2025 State Council “Guiding Opinions.”

*In short, China’s state VC funds, like other government investment funds, are designed to support the CCP leadership’s political objectives through the mobilization of resources toward the development of strategic technologies and key industries*.

## Opportunities and Risks

International companies involved in technologies and industries targeted by the NVCGF may benefit, particularly if they partner with Chinese entities. However, they should identify and mitigate potential risks before establishing those partnerships, by conducting research into the backgrounds and connections of prospective PRC partners to understand complex ownership structures, setting up internal guardrails to protect company crown jewels, understanding the terms of limited partnerships, and being cautious about requests for sensitive data during due diligence.

International companies can also expect to experience intensified competition from Chinese companies in the global export market. China’s weak domestic consumption, particularly with respect to hi-tech products, will continue to compel Chinese producers to rely on overseas markets. Critical to their strategic planning, International companies are advised to conduct competitive intelligence research to understand their Chinese counterparts’ global footprint.

China is a potentially lucrative destination for Western products based on market size as well as the availability of Chinese talent, knowledge, and a strong supply ecosystem that can deliver on high global standards. In this respect, China continues to present opportunities for international companies,

However, China’s economic structure continues to present risks, such as excessive competition and incentives to disregard rules. Moreover, international companies face Chinese competitors who have an expanding global presence.

In short, PRC government measures, such as the NVCGF, are likely to further complicate the existing China business environment for international companies.
